Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat (anchored or free). Hands behind your head or across your chest. Sit up until your torso is about three-quarters of the way to vertical. Stop before reaching full upright — this keeps tension on the abs. Lower under control back to the floor. The key is stopping before the hip flexors take over at the top. Maintain constant ab tension. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Maintains constant ab tension throughout; Avoids hip flexor dominance at the top; Builds ab strength through optimal range; No equipment needed; Simple modification of standard sit-ups; Better ab isolation than full sit-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary); Hip flexors (reduced vs full sit-up)

Description: Position yourself sideways on a 45-degree back extension bench. Your hip is on the pad, feet locked. Your torso hangs freely to the side. Cross your arms over your chest or place hands behind your head. Lower your torso sideways toward the floor (lateral flexion). Contract your obliques to lift your torso back to horizontal or slightly above. Complete reps, then switch sides. Hold a plate for added resistance when bodyweight becomes easy. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Greater oblique range and load than standing side bends; Gravity provides constant resistance; Easy to add weight with a plate; Builds oblique strength through full range; Develops lateral core power; Simple setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Erector spinae

Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent at ninety degrees and feet flat. Set the arms at the sides palms down. Brace your core and lift the head and shoulders slightly. Crunch sideways to one side. Reach the hand down to touch the heel on that side. Return to the center. Crunch sideways to the other side and touch the other heel. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Targets the obliques; Strong core finisher; No equipment needed; Useful ab builder; Builds the side abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Core

Description: Place an ab mat (or a folded towel) on the floor. Sit on the floor with the mat positioned just below your lower back. Lie back so the mat supports your lumbar spine. Your shoulders should rest just behind the mat on the floor. Bend your knees and bring the soles of your feet together in a butterfly position. This stabilizes you without engaging the hip flexors heavily. Place your hands behind your head with fingers lightly touching, or extend them overhead. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Sit up by curling your torso forward. Drive through your abs to bring your hands to or past your feet. At the top, your torso should be roughly upright. Squeeze your abs hard. Lower your torso under control back to the start position. Touch your shoulders to the floor behind the mat before the next rep.
Benefits: Longer range of motion than flat-floor sit-ups; Supports the lumbar spine and reduces lower-back strain; Butterfly leg position reduces hip flexor dominance; Builds the rectus abdominis through full range; Easy to scale by adding weight (chest hold or overhead); Standard CrossFit movement with established progression standards
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary); Hip flexors (less than standard sit-up due to butterfly position); Transverse abdominis

Description: Kneel on the floor. Grip an ab wheel with both hands below your shoulders. Brace your core hard. Tuck your pelvis. Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your body. Continue until your body is extended as far as your core can hold without arching. Pull the wheel back to start by contracting your abs and lats. Do not let your lower back arch at any point. Start with partial range and increase distance over time. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: One of the most effective core exercises; Builds anti-extension core strength; Develops lat and shoulder involvement; Scalable by range of motion; Inexpensive equipment; Builds total core stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (heavy); Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi; Anterior deltoid

Description: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet off the ground. Lean back slightly with your torso at about 45 degrees. Place your hands on the floor behind you for support. Brace your abs to balance. Tuck your knees in toward your chest. Squeeze your abs at the tucked position. Extend your legs straight out without touching the floor. Continue tucking and extending in a smooth motion.
Benefits: Strong lower ab activation; Builds core strength with bodyweight; Develops balance and stability; No equipment required; Easy to scale by tucking only; Useful for ab specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower fibers); Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Get into a four-point kneeling position with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Set your back flat with a neutral spine. Brace your core and keep your head neutral. Lift one hand a few inches off the floor. At the same time lift the opposite foot off the floor. Hold the position with the body steady. Lower the hand and foot back down. Switch to the other side and repeat.
Benefits: Builds deep core stability; Trains anti-rotation; No equipment needed; Useful prehab drill; Easy to learn; Strong bird-dog progression
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Spinal erectors

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Place your hands behind your head, fingers lightly touching. Lift your right knee up while simultaneously rotating your torso to bring your left elbow toward your right knee. Return to standing and immediately drive your left knee up while rotating to bring your right elbow toward it. Continue alternating in a rhythmic, cycling motion. Stay on the ball of the grounded foot. Move with control, not just speed. Keep your chest tall — do not hunch forward. Perform for time (20 to 45 seconds) or reps. Increase speed for more cardiovascular demand or slow down for more core focus.
Benefits: Trains the core and cardiovascular system simultaneously; Builds hip flexor endurance; Improves coordination and balance; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Easy to scale by adjusting tempo; Excellent warm-up or HIIT exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Quadriceps; Calves

Description: Set up on a 45 degree back extension bench. Position the pads at the hip crease. Cross the arms over the chest or hold a light weight. Round the upper back slightly to shift the focus to the glutes. Brace the core and lower the torso by hinging at the hips. Stop when you feel a stretch in the glutes and hamstrings. Squeeze the glutes hard to lift the torso back up. Stop just short of full extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds glute and hamstring strength.; Rounded back position biases the glutes over the lower back.; Carryover to deadlifts and hip thrusts.; Easy to load with a plate or dumbbell.; Improves hip extension force.; Develops posterior chain endurance.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Adductors

Description: Set up on a 45 degree decline bench. Hook the feet under the foot pads. Place the hands behind the head. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Crunch up by curling the torso forward. Twist the torso to bring an elbow toward the opposite knee. Extend the other leg straight at the same time. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Loads the obliques; Strong ab builder; Trains rotation; Builds the core; Useful core move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip Flexors

Description: Set up on a 45 degree hyperextension bench. Hook the heels under the foot pads and the hips against the pad. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace your core and start with the torso angled down. Extend the hips lifting the torso to a straight line. At the top twist the torso to one side. Twist back through center to the other side. Lower the torso back down to the start. Continue alternating twists.
Benefits: Strong posterior chain and oblique combo; Trains rotational core; Builds the lower back; Useful back move; Builds the obliques; Strong combo move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Spinal erectors; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Hamstrings

Description: Set up on a 45-degree back extension bench. Hips on the pad, feet locked. Cross arms over your chest or place hands behind your head. Lower your torso forward by hinging at the hips. Continue until your torso is roughly perpendicular to your legs. Extend back up by contracting your erector spinae and glutes. Rise until your body is in line with the bench angle. Do not hyperextend past the bench angle. Aim for 12 to 15 reps. Hold a plate for added resistance.
Benefits: Builds erector spinae and glute strength; Consistent 45-degree resistance profile; Easy to add weight with a plate; Available in most gyms; Develops lower back endurance; Useful for back health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Set up sideways in a 45 degree hyperextension bench. Hook the bottom foot under the foot pad. Place the top foot on the platform. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Lower the torso sideways toward the floor. Pause briefly at the bottom. Drive the obliques to lift the torso back up.
Benefits: Targets the obliques; Strong side bend variation; Builds the core; Useful for core size; Trains the side abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Erector spinae

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Look straight ahead. Sit your hips back as if reaching for a chair behind you. Bend your knees and lower your hips down. Knees track over your toes. Descend until your hip crease drops below the top of your knees (at least parallel). Drive through your full foot — especially the heels — to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 15 to 50 reps as a warm-up or conditioning exercise.
Benefits: Foundational bodyweight squat for all fitness levels; Excellent warm-up before loaded squats; Builds quad and glute endurance; Teaches the squat movement pattern; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Used in CrossFit, military training, and rehabilitation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hands behind your head. Lift your right knee while rotating to bring your left elbow toward it. Crunch and twist to make contact or come as close as possible. Return to standing. Lift your left knee and twist your right elbow toward it. Continue alternating. Move with control and deliberate rotation. Aim for 12 to 20 total reps.
Benefits: Standing core exercise — no floor needed; Targets obliques and abs together; No equipment needed; Builds coordination; Useful for warm-ups or circuits; Accessible anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Sit at a lat pulldown station. Attach a single D-handle to the cable. Grip the handle with your right hand. Left hand at your side or on the thigh pad. Pull the handle down to your right shoulder by driving your right elbow down and back. Squeeze your right lat at the bottom. Let the handle return overhead under control. Complete the desired reps, then switch to your left hand. Use lighter weight than bilateral pulldowns. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Exposes left-right lat imbalances; Greater range of motion per arm; Builds the lats unilaterally; Develops core anti-rotation; Easy to load progressively; Useful for lat symmetry
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Core (anti-rotation)

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Arms at your sides. Crunch up slightly — lift your shoulders off the floor. Reach your right hand toward your right heel by bending laterally. Return to center. Reach your left hand toward your left heel. Continue alternating side to side. Keep shoulders off the floor throughout for constant tension. Aim for 15 to 25 touches per side.
Benefits: Targets the obliques through lateral reaching; Constant ab tension from sustained crunch; No equipment needed; Beginner-friendly oblique exercise; Simple and effective; Burns out the obliques efficiently
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Lift your right leg straight forward as high as comfortable, keeping it straight. Lower it back to the floor. Lift your left leg straight forward. Continue alternating. Keep your torso upright — avoid leaning back. Move with control — not momentum. Aim for 10 to 15 lifts per leg.
Benefits: Builds hip flexor strength; Improves balance and stability; Useful dynamic warm-up; No equipment needed; Develops standing core stability; Beginner-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Quadriceps (leg hold); Core (stabilizer); Gluteus medius (standing leg)

Exercise Name: Alternate Leg Raise with Head Up
Description: Lie on your back with the legs extended. Place the hands at the temples or behind the head. Brace the core and lift the head and shoulders off the floor. Hold the crunch position throughout the set. Lift one leg up toward the ceiling keeping it straight. Lower the leg back to just above the floor. Lift the other leg up. Continue alternating for the desired number of repetitions per leg.
Benefits: Trains the upper and lower abs together.; Builds core endurance under continuous tension.; No equipment needed.; Hammers the hip flexors.; Carryover to V ups and hanging leg raises.; Develops total core stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Quadriceps

Description: Lie flat on your back. Arms at your sides, palms down. Press your lower back into the floor. Raise your right leg straight up toward the ceiling to about 90 degrees. As you lower your right leg, begin raising your left leg. Continue alternating in a smooth scissor pattern. Keep each leg straight throughout. Maintain lower back contact with the floor. Move with control — no swinging. Aim for 10 to 15 raises per leg.
Benefits: Constant lower ab tension through alternating pattern; Easier than double-leg raises; Builds hip flexor and lower ab strength; No equipment needed; Beginner-friendly progression; Teaches pelvic stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors; Obliques (slight); Quadriceps (keeping legs straight)

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Hands behind your head. Crunch up and to the right — bring your left shoulder toward your right knee. Lower back to center. Crunch up and to the left — bring your right shoulder toward your left knee. Continue alternating. Focus on the oblique contraction with each side crunch. Control the movement — no swinging. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Targets each oblique in alternation; Builds oblique strength and definition; No equipment needed; Simple and accessible; Beginner-friendly; Classic oblique exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis

Description: Lie flat on your back with both legs straight up toward the ceiling. Place your hands at your sides or under your hips for support. Brace the core and press the lower back into the floor. Slowly lower one leg toward the floor while keeping it straight. Lightly tap the heel to the floor without losing core engagement. Lift the leg back to vertical with control. Repeat with the opposite leg. Continue alternating taps for the full set.
Benefits: Builds lower abdominal strength and control.; Trains the hip flexors with strict eccentrics.; Improves lumbo pelvic stability.; Joint friendly and beginner accessible.; No equipment needed.; Excellent core warm up before lifting.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Quadriceps; Obliques

Description: Stand tall with feet hip width apart. Bring the fists up to the chin in a boxing guard. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Curl one heel up toward the glute by bending the knee. At the same time throw a punch with the opposite arm. Reset the foot to the floor. Curl the other heel up while throwing a punch with the other arm. Continue alternating heel curls and punches.
Benefits: Combo cardio and hamstring builder; Trains coordination; Builds cardio capacity; No equipment needed; Useful conditioning move; Builds shoulder endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Anterior deltoid; Rectus abdominis

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with a very wide overhand grip — as wide as the bar allows. Pull your body up while shifting toward your right hand, pulling primarily with your right arm. As you rise, your left arm straightens out along the bar. At the top, your right arm is fully bent and your left arm is nearly straight. Your chest should approach your right hand at the top. Squeeze your right lat hard. Lower under control back to a full hang. On the next rep, pull toward your left hand. Alternate sides or complete all reps on one side. If this is too difficult, start with assisted archer pull-ups using a resistance band. Aim for low reps (2 to 5 per side). Quality matters more than volume.
Benefits: Primary progression toward a one-arm pull-up; Heavily loads one side of the back; Builds unilateral lat and bicep strength; Develops body control and coordination; Builds grip strength asymmetrically; Impressive advanced calisthenics skill
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (working side — heavy); Biceps brachii (working side — heavy); Trapezius and rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Forearms and grip; Core (anti-rotation)

Description: Stand tall with feet together and arms at your sides. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Step one foot out wide to the side. Bend the knee on the stepping leg into a lateral lunge. Keep the trail leg straight with the foot flat on the floor. Push back through the working leg heel to return to the start. Bring the foot back to the standing position. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Builds lateral hip strength; Trains the adductors; No equipment needed; Easy to scale; Useful warm-up move; Strong glute medius work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Quadriceps; Gluteus medius

Description: Lie face down with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Lift your right arm and left leg a few inches off the floor simultaneously. Hold briefly. Lower them. Lift your left arm and right leg. Continue alternating. Keep neck neutral — look at the floor. Move with control. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds posterior chain with less intensity than full Superman; Develops opposite-limb coordination; No equipment needed; Beginner-friendly; Useful warm-up or rehab exercise; Strengthens lower back and glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Posterior deltoid (arm lift); Hamstrings

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands very wide apart. Shift your body toward your right hand. Your right arm bends while your left arm stays extended. Lower your chest toward the floor over your right hand. Press back up using primarily your right arm. Shift to the left side — left arm bends, right stays extended. Continue alternating. The extended arm provides minimal assistance. Aim for 5 to 8 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds unilateral pressing strength; Progression toward one-arm push-ups; Shifts load to one arm at a time; No equipment needed; Develops chest and tricep strength; Advanced push-up variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (pressing arm); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (anti-rotation); Serratus anterior

Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Reach the arms straight overhead on the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Sit up by curling the torso forward. Reach the arms forward and up as you sit up. Bring the chest toward the knees at the top. Lower with control back to the start. Reach the arms back overhead.
Benefits: Full range sit up; Loads the abs hard; Strong ab builder; Useful for core size; No equipment needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip Flexors; Obliques

Description: Lie face down on the floor. Extend the arms straight overhead and the legs straight back. Brace your core and lift the chest and legs off the floor. Hold the superman position. Sweep the arms out to the sides while keeping them off the floor. Continue the sweep until the hands touch at the lower back. Reverse the path back overhead. Continue circling the arms.
Benefits: Builds the upper back; Trains the posterior chain; Strong superman variation; Useful for back health; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Posterior deltoid; Gluteus maximus; Trapezius

Description: Lie face down on the floor with legs straight and arms overhead. Lift the chest, arms, and legs off the floor into a superman position. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes to support the back. Sweep the arms wide out to the sides at shoulder height. Continue sweeping the arms back along the body to the hips. Reverse the path back to the wide position. Sweep the arms forward overhead to the start. Maintain the lifted superman position throughout the full sweep.
Benefits: Hammers the upper back through the full sweep.; Strengthens the rear deltoids and rhomboids.; Trains the spinal erectors with the superman hold.; Improves shoulder mobility through full range.; No equipment needed.; Excellent posture and back health drill.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus

Description: Place your rear foot on a bench behind you. Stand on your front foot. Hold a rack upright, pole, or TRX strap with one or both hands for balance. Lower your back knee toward the floor by bending your front knee. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor. Drive through your front foot to rise. Use the support for balance only — not to pull yourself up. Complete reps, then switch legs. Progress to unassisted Bulgarian split squats over time.
Benefits: Removes balance challenge from Bulgarian split squats; Allows focus on building single-leg strength; Beginner-friendly regression; Progresses toward unassisted version; No weights needed; Develops single-leg squat mechanics
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (developing)

Exercise Name: Assisted Close Grip Underhand Chin Up
Description: Set the assistance weight on an assisted pull up machine. Grip the close handles with palms facing you. Step or kneel onto the assistance pad. Hang from the handles with arms fully extended. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Pull the chest up toward the hands. Squeeze the biceps and lats at the top. Lower with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Builds the biceps; Trains the lats; Strong chin up progression; Useful for beginners; Builds upper back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Rhomboids

Description: Loop a resistance band over a pull up bar. Hang from the bar with hands gripping the bar at right angles to each other. Place a knee or foot in the band loop for assistance. Brace your core. Pull yourself up so your head clears the bar to the right side. Lower yourself back to the hang position. Pull yourself up so your head clears the bar to the left side. Continue alternating sides for desired reps.
Benefits: Stepping stone to commando pull ups; Builds back and arm strength; Trains alternating pulling strength; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Develops grip strength; Useful for pull up progression
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Brachialis

Description: Set up a pull up assist machine with a knee pad. Set the assistance weight to scale the load. Step onto the knee pad with both knees. Grip the upper handles with both hands. Hang from the bar with the knee pad supporting some bodyweight. Brace your core hard. Raise the knees up toward the chest by curling the pelvis. Lower back down with control.
Benefits: Beginner friendly abs move; Trains the rectus abdominis; Useful pull up progression; Builds the abs; Strong machine move; Easy to scale loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Exercise Name: Assisted Hanging Knee Raise with Throw Down
Description: Hang from a pull up bar with hands shoulder width apart. Engage the lats and brace the core. Raise the knees toward the chest with control. At the top, have your partner gently push your knees back down. Resist the throw down by keeping the abs braced. Lower the legs slowly and avoid swinging. Reset under the bar with control between reps. Repeat the knee raise and partner throw down for all reps.
Benefits: Overloads the abs eccentrically through the throw down.; Strengthens the entire abdominal wall and hip flexors.; Builds grip strength through long bar hangs.; Trains anti extension as the legs are pushed down.; Adds variety to standard hanging leg raise work.; Develops control needed for harder calisthenic moves.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Anchor your feet under a stable hold such as a loaded barbell or partner. Kneel with your feet anchored and torso upright. Place your hands at chest level for protection on the way down. Have a partner provide light support if available. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Slowly lean forward, lengthening your hamstrings under load. Lower yourself toward the floor with control as long as possible. Use your hands or partner assistance to return to the upright kneeling position.
Benefits: Builds eccentric hamstring strength; Stepping stone to bodyweight Nordic curls; Useful rehab exercise; Strong glute and hamstring engagement; Develops control under hamstring stretch; No machine required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Gastrocnemius

Exercise Name: Assisted Lying Leg Raise with Lateral Throw Down
Description: Lie flat on your back with the partner standing at your head. Reach up and grasp the partner ankles for stability. Brace the core and lift both legs straight up to vertical. When the legs reach the top the partner pushes them to one side. Resist the push and lower the legs slowly with control. Stop just before the heels touch the floor on the side. Lift the legs back up to the top with control. Continue the leg raise and alternating side throws for all reps.
Benefits: Hammers the obliques through eccentric throw downs.; Builds rotational core strength.; Trains the abs and hip flexors together.; Adds challenge beyond standard leg raises.; Develops anti rotation control.; Excellent finisher for serious ab work.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Quadriceps

Exercise Name: Assisted Lying Leg Raise with Throw Down
Description: Lie flat on your back with the partner standing at your head. Reach up and grasp the partner ankles for stability. Brace the core and lift both legs straight up to vertical. When the legs reach the top the partner pushes them back down. Resist the push and lower the legs slowly with control. Stop just before the heels touch the floor. Lift the legs back up to the top under control. Continue the leg raise and throw down for all reps.
Benefits: Builds powerful lower abs through eccentric overload.; Trains the core to resist sudden force.; Strengthens hip flexors with full leg raises.; Adds intensity beyond standard leg raises.; Excellent finisher for ab workouts.; Improves anti extension control of the lumbar spine.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Quadriceps

Description: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and feet flat. Hold a cable handle with both hands at the chest. Lean back to a comfortable angle. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Twist the torso to one side against the cable. Pause briefly at the rotated position. Twist back to the other side. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Loads the obliques; Constant cable tension; Strong twist variation; Builds the core; Useful oblique builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Core

Exercise Name: Assisted Parallel Close Grip Pull Up
Description: Set the counterweight on the assisted pull-up machine. Higher weight means more assistance. Grip the parallel handles or pull-up bar with a close grip (hands shoulder-width or narrower). Kneel or stand on the assistance pad. Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and back until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats and biceps at the top. Lower under control over two to three seconds. Reduce the counterweight over weeks as you get stronger. Progress toward unassisted pull-ups.
Benefits: Develops pull-up strength progressively; Close grip emphasizes biceps and lower lats; Adjustable assistance for all levels; Builds pulling strength toward unassisted reps; Safe and controlled; Excellent for beginners
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii (increased with close grip); Brachialis; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Forearms

Exercise Name: Assisted Pistol Squat with Bed Sheet
Description: Anchor a sturdy bed sheet in a closed door. Stand facing the door with the sheet ends in both hands. Lift one leg straight off the floor in front of you. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lower into a single leg squat using the sheet for assistance. Reach the back hand toward the floor as the hips lower. Drive through the planted foot to stand back up. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Single leg progression; Builds the quads; Strong pistol variation; Useful for travel; No equipment needed; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Set the counterweight on the machine. Higher weight means more assistance — start heavier and reduce over time. Grip the wide pull-up handles with an overhand grip. Kneel or stand on the assistance pad. Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and back until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats at the top. Lower under control over two to three seconds. Reduce the counterweight by 5 to 10 lbs as you get stronger. Goal: work toward zero assistance and unassisted pull-ups.
Benefits: Develops pull-up strength progressively; Adjustable assistance for all fitness levels; Safe and controlled; Available in most commercial gyms; Builds pulling strength toward unassisted pull-ups; Excellent for beginners
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Forearms and grip

Description: Sit on a leg press machine with both feet on the platform. Position your feet hip-width apart in the middle of the platform. Release the safety stops. Press the platform up to full extension with both legs. Place one foot off the platform. Lower the platform slowly with just the working leg. When you reach the bottom, place both feet back on to press up. Complete reps on one side before switching legs.
Benefits: Eccentric overload on one leg; Builds single-leg strength; Useful for fixing imbalances; Allows heavier loading than true single-leg; Builds quad and glute size; Reduces injury risk
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent at roughly 45 to 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor. For assistance, anchor your feet under a couch, sturdy bar, or have a partner hold them. Place your hands lightly behind your head with elbows pointing wide. Brace your core. Curl your torso up toward your knees, lifting your shoulders, then your full back off the floor. Continue until you sit fully upright. Slowly lower back to the floor under control over two to three seconds. For more help: place hands on the back of your thighs and gently pull as you sit up.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly sit-up variation; Builds core strength progressively; Works at home without equipment; Easy to scale by anchor position; Useful for rehab and beginners; Builds toward unassisted sit-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques (slight); Quadriceps (anchored feet)

Description: Set up a low bench or sturdy chair behind you. Place the hands on the edge of the bench shoulder width apart. Step the feet forward keeping the legs bent for support. Lower the body by bending the elbows. Keep the elbows tracking back behind the body. Lower until the upper arms are parallel to the floor. Press the body up by extending the elbows assisted by the legs. Squeeze the triceps hard at the top.
Benefits: Beginner friendly tricep move; Builds the triceps; No machines needed; Easy to scale by leg assist; Useful tricep starter; Strong tricep finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Set up on an assisted dip machine. Select the appropriate counterweight — more weight means more assistance. Kneel or stand on the assistance platform. Grip the parallel bars with arms locked out, supporting your weight. Keep your torso upright for tricep emphasis (or lean forward for more chest involvement). Tuck your elbows close to your sides. Brace your core. Lower your body by bending at the elbows. Descend until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor. Press back up by extending at the elbows. Drive your hands into the bars. Lock out at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Reduce the assistance weight over time as you get stronger, progressing toward bodyweight dips.
Benefits: Effective progression toward bodyweight dips; Adjustable difficulty via counterweight selection; Trains the triceps, chest, and shoulders with reduced load; Allows higher rep volume than bodyweight dips for beginners; Builds the pressing strength needed for advanced calisthenics; Easy to track progress by reducing assistance over time
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major (sternal head); Anterior deltoid; Rhomboids and trapezius (stabilizers); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Wear a weighted vest or have a partner place a plate on your upper back. Attach a resistance band overhead and across your torso for assistance. Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Use the band assistance to help with the upward press. Press through your hands to full lockout. Lower with control on the next rep.
Benefits: Bridges to full weighted push-ups; Builds chest strength under load; Useful for progression; Adjustable assistance via band tension; Reduces injury risk; Develops pressing power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Description: Lie face down on a stability ball with your hips on the ball and your feet planted on the floor against a wall for stability. Place your hands behind your head with elbows wide. Brace your core. Position your body so the ball supports your hips and you can hinge over it. Lower your torso forward over the ball, hinging at the hips. Extend your torso up and back by contracting your lower back and glutes. Stop at a straight body line — do not hyperextend. Lower under control back to the start. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps. Keep your neck neutral throughout.
Benefits: Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings; Mimics hyperextension bench at home; Ball adds stabilizer demand; No bench needed; Joint-friendly; Useful for posterior chain endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level. Use a pronated grip with palms facing forward. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Kick one leg straight back behind you. As the leg kicks back, press both dumbbells overhead. Lock out the arms and squeeze the glute on the working leg. Lower the leg back down and the dumbbells back to shoulder level. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Combines glute and shoulder work; Trains balance and stability; Builds full-body coordination; Time-efficient combo move; Useful for athletic conditioning; Improves single-leg strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Triceps brachii; Hamstrings

Description: Hang from a bar or rings. Pull yourself up and over into a skin-the-cat position (inverted hang). Slowly lower your body from the inverted position toward horizontal. Extend your body until it is parallel to the ground, face up, below the bar. Hold the horizontal position. Arms are straight above you gripping the bar. Start with a tucked back lever (knees to chest) and progress to full. Progressions: tuck → advanced tuck → straddle → full. Hold for 5 to 15 seconds at each progression level. This is an advanced skill requiring months of progression.
Benefits: Builds elite straight-arm strength; Foundational gymnastics skill; Develops shoulder, lat, and core strength; Impressive calisthenics achievement; Builds body control and awareness; Progressive skill with clear progressions
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (heavy); Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (straight-arm hold); Core (heavy anti-extension); Erector spinae; Forearms and grip

Description: Place a balance board, rocker board, or Bosu ball (flat side up) on a non-slip surface. Carefully step onto the board with both feet. Position feet hip-width apart. Find your balance. Engage your core and ankle stabilizers. Try to keep the board level — do not let the edges touch the floor. Hold the balanced position for 30 to 60 seconds. For progression: close your eyes, stand on one leg, add small squats, or catch and throw a ball. Use a wall or chair nearby for safety when first learning. Practice 3 to 5 sets per session.
Benefits: Develops proprioception and body awareness; Builds ankle stability and control; Useful for rehabilitation after ankle injuries; Improves neuromuscular control; Engages deep stabilizer muscles; Widely used in physical therapy and sport training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Ankle stabilizers (tibialis anterior, peroneals); Calves; Core (stabilizer); Gluteus medius (hip stabilizer); Foot intrinsic muscles

Description: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Rotate your wrists so the backs of your hands face forward. Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout. Brace your core and stand tall. Raise the dumbbells out to the sides with the back of the hand leading the lift. Continue until the dumbbells reach shoulder height. Squeeze the medial and rear delts at the top. Lower the dumbbells back down with control.
Benefits: Different angle than standard lateral raise; Hits medial and rear delts; Useful for breaking through shoulder plateaus; Builds shoulder width and definition; Strong rotator cuff engagement; Easy to scale by changing dumbbell weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (upper)

Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing forward. Bring your arms out to about 45 degrees from your body. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Curl the handles up toward your shoulders. Maintain the 45-degree arm angle throughout. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower the handles slowly back to the start.
Benefits: Targets the biceps long head; Emphasizes the outer arm; Increasing tension at the top; Builds biceps peak; Joint-friendly variation; Useful for arm shape and detail
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long head); Brachialis; Forearms

Exercise Name: Band Alternate Incline Chest Press with Twist
Description: Anchor a resistance band at floor level behind you. Grip a band handle in each hand. Step forward into a staggered stance. Bring the handles to the chest. Press one handle up at an incline angle. Twist the torso into the press. Lower with control and press the other side. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Trains the upper chest; Adds rotation; Strong band variation; Useful for travel; Builds the obliques
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Obliques

Exercise Name: Band Alternate Lat Pulldown with Twist
Description: Anchor a resistance band overhead to a sturdy point. Stand or kneel below the anchor. Grip the band with both hands overhead. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Pull one elbow down to the side rotating the torso toward that side. Squeeze the lat and obliques at the bottom. Return with control to the start. Pull the other arm down with the opposite twist. Alternate sides.
Benefits: Combo lat and rotation move; Trains rotational core; No machine needed; Builds the lats; Strong band combo; Useful at-home back move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Obliques; Rhomboids

Exercise Name: Band Alternate Low Row with Twist
Description: Anchor a resistance band at low height and grasp a handle in each hand. Step back to create tension and stand with knees slightly bent. Hinge slightly forward at the hips with a tall back. Pull one handle back toward the hip while rotating the torso. Squeeze the back of the shoulder and keep the elbow tucked. Return the arm forward and untwist back to center. Repeat the row and twist with the opposite arm. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Builds the lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoids unilaterally.; Trains the obliques through controlled rotation.; Improves anti rotation control as the opposite side stabilizes.; Joint friendly resistance from the band.; Carryover to athletic rotational pulling movements.; Adds rotational variety to standard rowing patterns.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Obliques; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point. Grip a handle in each hand and step forward to take tension. Stand with feet staggered for stability. Brace your core and set the chest tall. Start with arms down at the sides slightly bent. Sweep one arm up across the body to chest height. Squeeze the chest hard at the top. Lower with control as you sweep the other arm up. Alternate sides.
Benefits: Strong upper chest builder; Trains unilateral chest control; Easy to do anywhere; Strong band move; Useful chest finisher; Builds chest size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (clavicular head); Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the band ends in each hand with palms facing forward. Allow the bands to be taut at thigh level. Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides. Curl the right band end up by bending only at the elbow. Squeeze the bicep at the top of the curl. Lower the band back down with control to thigh level. Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Constant band tension through the range; Resistance increases as the band stretches; Single-arm pattern corrects imbalances; Strong forearm engagement; Useful for home training; Easy to scale by changing band tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Anchor a band to a low point and lie on the floor with feet toward the anchor. Hold both ends of the band with hands stacked overhead. Lie flat with legs straight and core braced. Lift one leg straight up while pulling the band-loaded hands forward. Bring the hands and the lifted foot together over your hips. Reach a tall v-up position briefly. Lower the leg and the arms back to the floor. Repeat with the other leg. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Loaded core builder; Hits abs and obliques; Trains hip flexor strength; Single-leg pattern; Constant band tension; Strong ab finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Band Around Feet Lying Hip Internal Rotation
Description: Loop a resistance band around both feet. Lie on one side with the knees bent at ninety degrees. Stack the hips and shoulders. Brace your core and keep the knees together. Rotate the top foot inward toward the floor. Hold the rotation against the band tension. Return with control to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains hip internal rotation; Builds hip stability; Strong rotator move; Useful warm-up; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Hip Flexors

Description: Loop a thick resistance band over a pull-up bar. Pull one end through the other to create a hanging loop. Grip the bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Place one or both knees (or feet) in the hanging band loop. Hang from the bar with arms extended. The band should be pulling you upward. Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and back. Chin should clear the bar. Squeeze your lats and biceps at the top. Lower under control over two to three seconds. Use progressively thinner bands as you get stronger until you no longer need assistance.
Benefits: Most popular chin-up regression; Allows progressive overload by changing band thickness; Develops pulling strength toward unassisted chin-ups; Builds lats, biceps, and grip; Inexpensive equipment; Better than machine-assisted — allows natural bar path
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Forearms and grip

Exercise Name: Band Assisted Floor Glute Ham Raise
Description: Anchor a resistance band overhead in front of you. Place the band across the chest or under the arms. Kneel on a soft mat with feet hooked under a sturdy support. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lower the body forward toward the floor. Use the band assistance to control the descent. Engage the hamstrings to pull the body back up. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the hamstrings; Strong Nordic curl; Useful for beginners; Builds the glutes; Trains the posterior chain
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves

Description: Loop a thick resistance band over one dip bar handle. Pull the other end to the opposite bar to create a loop between them. Grip the bars and place one or both knees in the band loop below you. Start with arms locked out, body supported above the bars. Lower your body by bending at the elbows until your upper arms are at least parallel to the floor. The band assists you by pushing upward. Press back up to lockout by extending your elbows. Use progressively thinner bands as you get stronger. Goal: work toward unassisted dips.
Benefits: Best dip regression for strength development; Adjustable assistance with band thickness; Allows proper dip form while building strength; Builds chest, tricep, and shoulder strength; Natural movement path unlike machine-assisted; Inexpensive equipment
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (lower fibers); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Loop a resistance band over a pull up bar so it hangs down. Step or kneel into the band loop with one foot or knee. Reach up and grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart. Brace your core and pull yourself up explosively. Drive the chest up to the bar and continue pulling over. Use the band assistance to transition through to the dip position. Press up to lockout above the bar. Lower with control back to the hang.
Benefits: Trains the muscle up motion; Useful pull up progression; Builds the transition phase; Adjustable assistance; Strong upper body builder; Excellent calisthenics drill
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Biceps brachii; Standard Muscle Up; Assisted Pull Up; Bar Dip; Explosive Pull Up; Muscle Up; Weighted Muscle-up; Kipping Muscle Up

Description: Loop a long resistance band around a sturdy pull-up bar. Pull one end through the other to secure it. Reach up and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Place one foot or both knees in the bottom loop of the band. Lift your body off the floor and let the band stretch under your weight. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Brace your core. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down toward your hips. The band assists most at the bottom and least at the top. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats at the top. Lower yourself under control to a full hang. Do not let the band snap you down. Use thinner bands as you get stronger. Heavier bands provide more assistance.
Benefits: Effective progression toward unassisted pull-ups; Builds full-range pull-up strength while reducing the load; Allows higher rep volume than negatives or partials; Can be scaled in small steps by changing band thickness; Easy to set up at home with a doorframe pull-up bar; Trains the same muscles as a regular pull-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii and brachialis; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizers)

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a high point above your start position. Attach the other end around your hips or torso with a belt. Kneel on the floor holding an ab wheel. Brace your core hard and tuck your hips slightly. Roll the wheel forward by extending your arms and hips. Stop just before your stomach touches the floor. Use the band assistance to help pull yourself back to the start. Keep the core engaged through the entire motion.
Benefits: Useful ab wheel progression; Builds toward unassisted rollouts; Trains anti-extension strength; Adjustable band tension; Strong core builder; Excellent ab challenge
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi; Hip flexors

Description: Loop a resistance band around the base of a hyperextension bench. Loop the other end around the back of your neck (use a pad or towel). Set up on the bench with the pad below your hips and feet locked. Start hinged forward. The band should be under tension at the bottom. Extend your torso up by contracting your glutes and lower back. The band tension increases as you rise. Stop at a straight body line — do not hyperextend. Lower under control back to the starting position. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a lighter band to start — the increasing tension is deceptively challenging.
Benefits: Adds progressive loading to hyperextensions; Band tension increases at the top for stronger glute contraction; Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings; Easy to set up with a band and bench; Useful when weight plates are not available; Scalable by changing band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point. Loop the other end around one ankle. Step back to take tension on the band. Bend forward at the hips with hands on a bench or wall for support. Keep the working leg straight or slightly bent. Kick the working leg straight back behind the body. Squeeze the glute hard at the top. Lower the leg back down with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong glute builder; Targets the gluteus maximus; Easy to do anywhere; Builds the posterior chain; Useful glute finisher; Strong unilateral move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Sit on the floor and loop a resistance band across your upper back, holding both ends. Lie back on the floor. The band should be flat across your upper back beneath you. Hold the ends of the band at chest height with palms facing forward. Brace your core. Press both ends of the band straight up toward the ceiling. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. The band tension is highest here. Lower under control back to your chest over two seconds. Use a thicker band for more resistance, or step on more of the band for difficulty. Perform 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Effective at-home chest exercise; Increasing band tension loads the lockout; Highly portable; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Joint-friendly with controlled loading; Useful when no bench or weights are available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Band Bent Over Rear Lateral Raise
Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip width. Grip a handle in each hand with palms facing each other. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Let the arms hang straight down with the band taut. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Raise both arms out to the sides until parallel to the floor. Squeeze the rear delts and shoulder blades hard at the top. Lower the arms back down with control.
Benefits: Strong rear delt isolation; Builds upper back thickness; Easy to do anywhere; Useful posture builder; Strong band move; Trains the rhomboids
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Trapezius

Description: Anchor a resistance band overhead, such as in a doorway. Stand facing the anchor and grab a handle in each hand. Step back to add tension to the band. Hinge forward at the hips with a slight bend in the knees. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Start with arms extended overhead toward the anchor. Pull the handles down toward your hips by driving the elbows down. Squeeze the lats hard, then return slowly to the start.
Benefits: Targets the lats; Easy to set up at home; No machine required; Builds back width; Joint-friendly variation; Strong lat builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Rear deltoid

Exercise Name: Band Bent Over Wide Grip Row
Description: Stand on a resistance band with feet at shoulder width. Grip the band with both hands wider than shoulder width. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Brace your core and let the band hang at arms length. Pinch the shoulder blades together. Row the hands up wide with elbows flared out. Drive the elbows back at shoulder height. Squeeze the upper back. Lower with control.
Benefits: Strong upper back builder; Trains the rear delts; No machine needed; Useful at-home back move; Strong band move; Builds back thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends of the band (or the band itself). Hinge forward at the hips to roughly 45 degrees. Let the band hang at arm’s length. Set your back flat and brace your core. Row both hands up toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Hold one second. Lower under control. Maintain the hip-hinge position throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a thicker band or choke up on the band for more resistance.
Benefits: Builds the back with increasing tension at peak contraction; Highly portable — needs only one band; Effective at-home back exercise; Trains the lats, mid-traps, and rear delts; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Joint-friendly with lower absolute loads
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends of the band with palms facing forward (supinated grip). Stand tall. Pin your elbows at your sides. Curl both ends up toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows. Squeeze your biceps at the top. Lower under control over two seconds. Keep your upper arms still throughout — only your forearms move. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Most basic at-home bicep exercise; Increasing tension at the peak contraction; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Joint-friendly; Simple execution
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low point behind your head. Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees, feet off the floor. Grip the band with both hands at your forehead, elbows wide. Brace your core and lift your shoulders off the floor. Twist your torso to bring your right elbow toward your left knee. At the same time, extend your right leg straight out. Reverse to bring your left elbow toward your right knee while extending the left leg. Continue alternating in a cycling motion against band tension.
Benefits: Adds resistance to standard bicycle crunches; Strong oblique engagement; Builds core rotational strength; Constant band tension through the range; Trains the core under fatigue; Easy to scale by changing band tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (internal and external); Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with the balls of your feet. Hold both ends at your shoulders or at your sides. Stand tall with knees mostly straight. Keep the band under tension. Rise up onto your toes as high as possible by contracting your calves. Squeeze your calves at the top for one second. The band tension is highest here. Lower under control over two seconds. Return to the starting position. Use a step or platform under the balls of your feet for greater range of motion. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps per set. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Adds resistance to calf raises with portable equipment; Increasing tension at the top for strong peak contraction; Works at home with one band; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Builds calf size and endurance; Useful when no weights or machines are available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus (secondary); Tibialis posterior

Description: Anchor a resistance band behind you at roughly chest height — around a sturdy pole, door anchor, or squat rack. Grip one end of the band in each hand. Step forward until the band is under tension with your arms out to your sides. Stagger your stance for stability. Set a slight bend in your elbows and lock it in. Bring both hands together in a wide arc in front of your chest. Squeeze your chest hard when your hands meet. Slowly let your hands travel back out to your sides under control. Feel the stretch in your chest. Maintain the slight elbow bend throughout — this is a fly, not a press. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use higher reps (12 to 20) for best results. Step further forward for more tension, or use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Chest isolation with increasing tension at peak contraction; Highly portable — works anywhere with a band and anchor; No heavy equipment required; Easy to scale by changing band thickness or stepping distance; Excellent finisher for home chest workouts; Joint-friendly with lower absolute loads
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid (secondary); Biceps brachii (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Hold a handle in each hand with hands closer than shoulder-width. Use an underhand grip with palms forward. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Curl the handles up toward your shoulders. Keep your elbows pinned at your sides. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower the handles slowly back to the start.
Benefits: Targets the biceps long head; Builds the inner upper arm; Increasing tension at the top; Strong peak contraction; Easy to set up at home; Useful for arm shape and detail
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long head); Brachialis; Forearms

Description: Anchor a resistance band at a high point overhead. Kneel or stand facing the anchor. Grip the band with both hands close together (6 to 12 inches apart). Start with arms extended overhead. Pull the band down toward your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back. Squeeze your lats and biceps at the bottom. Slowly extend back overhead under control. Keep your torso upright throughout. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Close grip emphasizes biceps and lower lats; Mimics close-grip lat pulldown at home; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Builds pulling strength; Useful when no cable machine is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (lower fibers); Biceps brachii (increased); Brachialis; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids

Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height in front of you, or sit on the floor with band looped around your feet. Grip both ends of the band with hands close together (6 to 12 inches apart), palms facing each other. Start with arms extended forward. Row the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back along your sides. Squeeze your lats and biceps at the end of the row. Slowly extend forward under control. Keep your torso upright. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Close grip increases bicep involvement; Emphasizes the lower lats; Mimics close-grip cable row; Highly portable; Easy to scale; Builds back thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (lower fibers); Biceps brachii (increased); Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids

Description: Wrap a resistance band across your upper back, holding the ends in your hands. Get into a push-up position with hands closer than shoulder-width. Position your hands directly under your shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Keep your elbows tucked close to your ribs. Press through your hands to drive back up. Lock out the elbows at the top against the band tension.
Benefits: Builds triceps strength; Accommodating resistance overloads the lockout; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Develops chest and triceps together; Strong tricep finisher; No bench needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Front deltoid

Description: Sit on a chair or bench. Loop a resistance band under your right foot. Hold the other end of the band with your right hand. Place the back of your right upper arm (just above the elbow) against your right inner thigh. Start with your arm extended and the band taut. Curl your right hand toward your right shoulder by bending at the elbow. Squeeze your bicep hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control over two seconds. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Strict bicep isolation — no body english; Builds the bicep peak; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no dumbbells are available; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially short head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Loop a resistance band around your ankles. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, hands on your hips. Cross your right leg in front of your left to start. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Abduct the right leg out to the side against the band tension. Lift the leg as high as the band allows without leaning. Hold the squeeze for one count. Lower the leg back to the crossed starting position with control. Switch sides.
Benefits: Strong glute medius activation; Improves hip stability; Helps with knee tracking issues; Useful for warmups and activation; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Builds lateral hip strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Tensor fasciae latae

Exercise Name: Band Cross Body One Arm Chest Press
Description: Anchor a resistance band behind you at chest height. Grip the band handle with one hand. Step forward into a staggered stance. Bring the handle to the side of the chest. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Press the band across the body to the opposite side. Squeeze the chest hard at full extension. Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains the chest; Strong band variation; Cross body adduction; Useful for travel; Builds the chest; Trains each side
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing your body (neutral grip). Brace your core and keep your chest up. Curl one handle up and across your body toward the opposite shoulder. Pin your elbow against your ribs throughout. Squeeze the biceps and brachialis at the top. Lower the handle slowly back to the start. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Targets the brachialis; Builds outer arm thickness; Strong neutral-grip variation; Useful for arm width; Reduces wrist strain; Easy to set up at home
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Forearms

Exercise Name: Band Deadlift With Single Arm Row
Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip the band ends in each hand at your sides. Bend at the hips and knees to lower the bands toward the floor. Drive through your heels to stand back up. At the top, hinge slightly forward and row the right band end up to your hip. Squeeze your right shoulder blade at the top of the row. Lower the right band end back down to your side. Repeat the deadlift and row with the left arm. Alternate sides.
Benefits: Trains posterior chain and back together; Time-efficient compound combo; Builds full body strength; Strong functional movement pattern; Useful for home training; Easy to scale by changing band tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Erector spinae

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Reach down and grip both ends of the band (or the band itself if using a loop band) with both hands. Hinge at the hips with a slight knee bend. Set your back flat, chest tall, and shoulders pulled back. Brace your core. Take a deep breath. Drive through your feet and extend your hips to stand up tall. The band tension increases as you rise. Lock out by squeezing your glutes hard at the top. The band should be at its tightest at full standing. Slowly hinge back down under control. Maintain a flat back throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a thicker band or double-loop the band for more resistance.
