Exercise Name: Band One Arm Twisting Seated Row
Description: Anchor a resistance band low at chest height in front of you. Sit on the floor with legs extended. Grip the band with one hand at arms length. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Pull the band back rowing the elbow past the body. At the same time twist the torso toward the working side. Squeeze the lat and obliques at the top. Untwist and return with control. Switch sides.
Benefits: Combo back and rotation move; Trains rotational core; Strong unilateral back move; Builds the lats; Strong band combo; Useful core builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Obliques; Rhomboids

Description: Stand on one end of a resistance band with one foot. Hold the other end of the band in the same-side hand. Press the band-holding arm straight up overhead. Brace your core and stand tall. Side bend the torso away from the band side. Allow the band to stretch as you lean over. Pull the torso back upright using the obliques. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Loaded oblique builder; Constant band tension; Hits side core hard; Travel-friendly equipment; Single-arm focus; Strong oblique move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Hold both ends of the band behind your head with both hands, elbows pointing up. Your upper arms should be vertical, pointing toward the ceiling. Extend your elbows, pressing the band up overhead. Lock out at the top. Squeeze your triceps. Lower the band back behind your head under control over two seconds. Keep your elbows pointing up throughout — do not let them flare forward. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Targets the long head of the tricep; Overhead position stretches the long head for max activation; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no cable or dumbbells are available; Builds tricep size and strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (especially long head); Anconeus

Description: Hold a resistance band at arm’s length in front of you at shoulder height. Grip one end in each hand. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Arms extended forward, palms facing down. The band should have slight tension. Pull both hands apart and out to your sides, stretching the band across your chest. Continue until your arms are out to the sides at shoulder height. Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard at the end position. Slowly let the band return to the starting position over two seconds. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps. Use a thinner band for higher reps.
Benefits: Builds the rear delts and mid-traps; Improves shoulder health and posture; Highly portable; Excellent warm-up before pressing; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Counteracts forward-rounded shoulders
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Infraspinatus (rotator cuff)

Exercise Name: Band Overhead Single Arm Triceps Extension
Description: Anchor a resistance band under one foot. Grip the band handle with one hand. Bring the hand up so the elbow is by the ear. Brace your core and keep the back straight. Extend the arm fully overhead. Squeeze the tricep hard at the top. Lower the hand behind the head with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains the triceps; Strong band variation; Builds the long head; Useful for travel; Trains each side; Builds the upper arms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Posterior deltoid

Description: Anchor a resistance band to the floor behind your head. Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Grip the band ends with both hands at chest level. Brace your abs hard. Sit up by curling your torso up. As you sit up, press both band ends forward. Continue until your torso is upright with arms extended. Lower yourself back down with control as the bands return.
Benefits: Combines ab and chest work; Builds total core strength; Strong tricep involvement; Constant band tension; Time-efficient combo movement; Useful for full body training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Band One Arm Twisting Chest Press
Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height behind you. Grip the handle with one hand and step forward. Set the staggered stance for stability. Bring the handle to the chest with elbow back. Brace your core and set the hips facing forward. Press the handle forward while rotating the torso. Squeeze the chest and obliques at full extension. Pull back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Combo chest and rotation move; Trains rotational power; Strong unilateral chest move; Builds the obliques; Strong band move; Useful functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Obliques; Triceps brachii

Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height in front of you. Grip both ends of the band. Step back until the band is taut. Stand tall. Arms extended forward at chest height. Row the band toward your face by pulling with wide elbows — elbows go out to the sides at shoulder height. Squeeze your rear delts and shoulder blades together at the end. Slowly extend your arms back forward. The wide elbows are the key cue — they shift the emphasis to rear delts. Use moderate band thickness. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Targets the rear delts with constant tension; Wide elbows shift emphasis from lats to rear delts; Highly portable; Builds shoulder balance; Easy to scale; Useful warm-up or isolation exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Infraspinatus

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low point in front of you (base of a squat rack or sturdy object). Lie on your back with your head near the anchor. Loop the band around both feet. Move away from the anchor until the band is taut with your legs extended. Bend your knees and bring your feet up (knees at 90 degrees). Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Curl your hips up and toward your ribs by contracting your lower abs. Fight the band tension. Lower your hips back down under control. Repeat for the desired reps. Use a thinner band for more reps or thicker for strength.
Benefits: Adds progressive resistance to reverse crunches; Targets the lower abs effectively; Easy to scale by band thickness; Portable and inexpensive; Useful progression when bodyweight is too easy; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially lower); Hip flexors; Obliques; Transverse abdominis

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends of the band with palms facing down (overhand/pronated grip). Stand tall. Pin your elbows at your sides. Curl both ends of the band upward by bending at the elbows. Continue until your forearms are parallel to the floor or higher. Squeeze the top of your forearms at the peak. Lower under control over two seconds. Maintain the overhand grip throughout. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Targets the brachioradialis and forearm extensors; Builds forearm size and grip; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no dumbbells are available; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachioradialis (primary); Brachialis; Wrist extensors; Biceps brachii (reduced involvement)

Description: Loop a resistance band around your waist or hold the ends down with your feet. Anchor the other end of the band to the floor or a low point. Hang from a pull-up bar with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down. Pull your body up by bending at the elbows against the added band tension. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your back and biceps at the top. Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Adds resistance to bodyweight chin ups; Builds advanced pulling strength; Useful for breaking through chin up plateaus; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Functional strength carryover; Strong lat and bicep development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Rhomboids

Description: Sit on a bench or chair with feet flat. Loop one end of a resistance band under your right foot. Grip the other end with your right hand using an overhand grip (palm down). Rest your right forearm on your right thigh with your wrist extended just past the knee. Let the band tension pull your wrist down toward the floor. Curl your wrist upward (extension) by lifting the back of your hand toward your forearm. Squeeze your forearm extensors hard at the top. Slowly lower under control over two seconds. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Strengthens the wrist extensors; Helps prevent and rehabilitate tennis elbow; Builds forearm size and definition; Highly portable — works at home with one band; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Critical for racquet sport athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist extensors (extensor carpi radialis, extensor carpi ulnaris); Forearm extensors; Brachioradialis (secondary)

Description: Sit on a bench or chair with the feet flat on the floor. Loop a resistance band around the knees. Sit tall with the chest up and back straight. Brace your core and keep the feet planted. Press the knees outward against the band. Squeeze the glutes hard at the wide position. Hold for a beat at the top. Return with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the glute medius; Trains the hip rotators; Strong activation drill; Useful warm-up; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Hip Flexors

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low point behind you. Stand facing away from the anchor. Pass the band between your legs. Grip the band with both hands in front of your hips. Step forward until the band is taut. Feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back. Let the band pull your hands back between your legs. Maintain a flat back throughout. Keep your knees slightly bent. Drive your hips forward explosively by squeezing your glutes. Stand tall at the top. Squeeze your glutes hard. Slowly hinge back and repeat. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds glute and hamstring strength with hip-hinge pattern; Teaches proper hinge mechanics; Constant band tension throughout; Highly portable; Easy to scale; Useful when no cable machine is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low point such as a sturdy chair leg. Sit on a bench or chair facing away from the anchor. Loop the other end of the band around your right ankle. Sit tall with chest up and grip the bench for stability. Brace your core and start with your right knee bent. Extend your right knee fully to straighten the leg. Squeeze your quad at the top of the extension. Lower the leg back down with control. Switch legs.
Benefits: Trains quadriceps without a machine; Constant band tension through the range; Single-leg work corrects imbalances; Useful for home training; Builds quad size and strength; Easy to scale by changing band tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus femoris; Vastus lateralis; Vastus medialis

Description: Sit on the floor with legs extended in front. Loop a resistance band around the soles of your feet. Grip both ends of the band with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Sit up tall with chest lifted and feet flexed. Brace your core. Row both hands back toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back along your sides. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the row. Slowly extend your arms forward back to the start. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps per set. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Effective at-home back exercise; Builds the lats, mid-traps, and rhomboids; Mimics cable seated row with minimal equipment; Highly portable; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Erector spinae (postural)

Description: Anchor a resistance band at a high point (top of doorframe, pull-up bar, or high hook). Grip both ends of the band with both hands. Stand facing the anchor. Pin your elbows against your sides. Forearms start parallel to the floor. Push the band down by extending at the elbows. Keep upper arms still. Continue until arms are fully extended. Squeeze your triceps at the bottom. Slowly let the band pull your forearms back up over two seconds. Maintain control — the band pulls harder as it stretches less at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Effective at-home tricep exercise; Increasing band tension at the bottom loads the lockout; Highly portable; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Useful when no cable machine is available; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (especially lateral head); Anconeus

Description: Sit on the floor with legs extended in front of you. Loop a resistance band around both feet. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing up (supinated grip). Sit upright with a tall, straight back. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Pull the handles back toward your lower ribs. Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides. Squeeze your back hard, then return slowly.
Benefits: Bicep-biased row; Builds the lower lats; Easy to set up at home; Joint-friendly variation; Strong back builder; No machine required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Rear deltoid

Description: Sit on the floor with legs extended in front of you. Loop a resistance band around both feet. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing down. Sit upright with a tall, straight back. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Pull the handles back toward your upper chest with elbows flared wide. Lead with the elbows out to the sides at shoulder height. Squeeze the upper back hard, then return slowly.
Benefits: Builds upper back detail; Targets rhomboids and rear delts; Improves posture; Easy to set up at home; Joint-friendly variation; Strong upper back builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rhomboids; Rear deltoid; Traps; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends of the band with palms facing forward, hands at shoulder height. Stand tall. Brace your core. Engage your glutes. Press both ends straight up overhead by extending your elbows. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. The band tension is highest here. Lower under control back to shoulder height over two seconds. Use a thicker band or step on more of the band for greater resistance. Keep your wrists strong and stable throughout.
Benefits: Effective at-home shoulder press; Increasing tension at the top loads the lockout; Highly portable; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Joint-friendly with controlled loading; Useful when no weights are available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band at about chest height to your left side. Sit on the floor facing forward, knees bent, feet flat. Grip the band with both hands at your chest. Brace your core. Sit up tall. Rotate your torso to the right against the band tension. Squeeze your obliques at the fully rotated position. Slowly return to center under control. Complete reps rotating to the right, then switch the anchor to the other side. Use moderate band thickness. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Loaded rotational core exercise at home; Constant band tension throughout; Builds oblique strength; Highly portable; Easy to scale; Mimics cable rotation exercises
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Erector spinae

Description: Anchor a resistance band to the floor or a low post. Stand tall with the anchor on your right side, feet hip-width apart. Grip the band with your right hand at your side. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Bend laterally to the left, pulling the band away from the anchor. Lower as far as your mobility allows. Squeeze the left obliques at the bottom. Return to the upright position with control. Switch sides after the set.
Benefits: Direct oblique loading; Constant band tension through the bend; Builds oblique strength; Improves lateral core stability; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Useful for waist and obliques training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Quadratus lumborum; Erector spinae

Description: Sit on a bench with one foot flat on the floor. Anchor a resistance band to the inside of the working foot. Loop the band around the foot. Sit tall with the chest up and back straight. Brace your core and keep the knee in line. Rotate the foot inward against the band tension. Hold briefly at the rotated position. Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains hip internal rotation; Builds hip stability; Strong rotator drill; Useful warm-up; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Hip Flexors

Exercise Name: Band Side Step with Horizontal Pallof Hold
Description: Loop a small band around the lower legs above the knees. Anchor a second band at chest height to one side. Hold the second band with both hands and press it out from the chest. Stand sideways to the chest height anchor. Brace the core and step sideways away from the anchor. Bring the trail leg in to follow. Continue stepping while resisting rotation toward the anchor. Step in the opposite direction to return then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains the glute medius and anti rotation core.; Combines two excellent band drills.; Carryover to athletic stability.; Improves hip control under load.; Develops total body coordination.; Easy to scale by adjusting band tension.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Obliques; Gluteus maximus; Rectus abdominis

Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height. Stand sideways to the anchor with the right side closer. Grip the band end with your right hand. Bring your right elbow up to shoulder level out to the side. Bend your right elbow to 90 degrees with hand near your face. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Extend the elbow to straighten the arm out to the side. Squeeze the tricep at the lockout, then bend the elbow back. Switch sides.
Benefits: Direct lateral tricep head emphasis; Different angle than standard extensions; Builds tricep size and detail; Constant band tension; No weights required; Useful for tricep variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (lateral head); Triceps brachii (medial head); Anconeus

Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with one foot. Hold a handle in each hand at shoulder level. Lift the other foot off the floor and balance on the working leg. Hold a wall or rack for balance if needed. Brace your core and keep your standing leg slightly bent. Press up onto your toes by lifting your heel high. Squeeze the calf hard at the top. Lower slowly back to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Builds the calves; Single-leg loading; Easy to set up at home; No machine required; Trains balance; Increasing band tension at top
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Soleus; Gastrocnemius

Exercise Name: Band Single Leg Reverse Calf Raise
Description: Anchor a resistance band low in front of you. Loop the other end around the toes of one foot. Sit on a bench or stand against a wall. Set the heel on the floor with the band taking tension. Brace your core and keep the leg fixed. Pull the toes up toward the shin against the band. Squeeze the front of the shin hard at the top. Lower with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Strong shin builder; Useful for runners; Builds tibialis size; Trains ankle dorsiflexion; Strong band move; Useful for shin splints
Muscles Worked (Raw): Tibialis anterior; Peroneals; Calves

Description: Loop a resistance band under your right foot. Hold the other end of the band in both hands at your sides. Stand tall on your right leg with the left foot slightly behind. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Hinge at the hips and lower your torso forward. Lift the left leg back behind you for balance. Continue until your torso is parallel to the floor. Squeeze your glute to return to standing. Switch sides.
Benefits: Builds posterior chain strength; Develops balance and stability; Constant band tension; No heavy weights required; Useful for home or travel training; Strong glute and hamstring engagement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Band Single Stiff Leg Deadlift with Single Arm Row
Description: Stand on one leg with a resistance band anchored in front. Grip the band handle with the opposite hand. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Hinge at the hip and lift the back leg behind you. Lower the torso toward parallel with the floor. Row the band handle to the lower ribs at the bottom. Lower the band and stand back up to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the posterior chain; Trains balance; Combines hinge and row; Strong combo move; Useful functional move; Builds the back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Latissimus dorsi; Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Band Single Stiff Leg DL w Row
Description: Anchor a resistance band at floor level in front of you. Stand on one leg with the opposite hand on the band handle. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Hinge at the hip and lift the back leg behind you. Lower the torso toward parallel with the floor. Row the handle up to the lower ribs at the bottom. Lower the band and stand back up to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the posterior chain; Trains balance; Combines hinge and row; Strong portable combo; Useful functional move; Builds the back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Latissimus dorsi; Erector spinae

Description: Anchor a resistance band at a low point behind your head. Lie on your back. Grip both ends of the band overhead with palms facing forward. Start with elbows bent, band behind your head (like the bottom of a skull crusher). Extend your elbows to press the band straight up to lockout. Squeeze your triceps at the top. Slowly bend your elbows to lower the band back behind your head. Keep your upper arms vertical throughout. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Mimics skull crushers at home; Increasing band tension at lockout; Builds tricep size and strength; Highly portable; Easy to scale; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (all heads); Anconeus

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a high point overhead. Kneel facing perpendicular to the anchor with the band in your right hand. Bring the band end to the side of your head. Brace your core and sit tall with hips over heels. Crunch your torso laterally to your right by contracting your right obliques. Bring your right elbow toward your right hip. Squeeze your obliques at the bottom of the crunch. Slowly return to the upright position with control. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Targets obliques directly with resistance; Constant band tension through the range; Builds oblique size and strength; Useful for waist definition; Easy to scale by changing band tension; No machine required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Quadratus lumborum; Rectus abdominis

Exercise Name: Band Split Squat with Horizontal Pallof Hold
Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to the side. Stand in a split stance perpendicular to the anchor. Hold the band handle with both hands at the chest. Press the band out horizontally to full arm extension. Brace your core and resist the rotation. Lower into a split squat by bending both knees. Stand back up while holding the band extended. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains anti-rotation core; Builds split squat strength; Combo leg and core move; Strong functional drill; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Core

Description: Stand on a resistance band with your right foot. Hold both ends at shoulder height. Step your left foot back into a split stance. Lower your left knee toward the floor by bending both knees. Descend until your left knee is just above the floor. Drive through your right foot to stand against the band tension. The band provides increasing resistance as you rise. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Adds progressive resistance to split squats; Increasing tension at the top loads the lockout; Builds single-leg strength at home; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no weights are available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Band Squat with Horizontal Pallof Hold
Description: Anchor a band at chest height to one side. Stand sideways to the anchor and grip the handle with both hands. Press the handle straight out from your chest with arms long. Resist the rotation pull from the band. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Squat down keeping the handle pressed out and stable. Drive through the heels to stand back up. Maintain the pallof hold throughout. Switch sides each set.
Benefits: Trains legs and core together; Brutal anti-rotation challenge; Combo move saves time; Builds full-body strength; Useful for athletes; Strong functional move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Core

Description: Loop a resistance band under your right foot. Bring the band ends over your shoulders, holding with both hands. Step your left leg back into a split stance. Stand tall with chest up and core braced. Lower into a split squat by bending both knees. Continue until your back knee almost touches the floor. Drive up through the front foot to standing, fighting band tension. Complete reps on the right side, then switch legs.
Benefits: Adds resistance to bodyweight split squats; Accommodating band resistance; Builds unilateral leg strength; No heavy weights required; Useful for home or travel training; Strong glute and quad engagement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to a sturdy post. Stand with the anchor on your right side, feet shoulder-width apart. Hold the band with both hands extended to your right at chest height. Step away from the anchor to create tension in the band. Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back. As you stand back up, rotate your torso to the left and pull the band across your body. Finish with the band pulled to your left hip and feet flat. Reverse the motion back to the starting position. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains rotational core strength under load; Builds leg drive linked to core rotation; Constant band tension through the range; Strong carryover to athletic movement; Time-efficient compound combo; Easy to scale by changing band tension or step distance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Rectus abdominis

Description: Anchor a resistance band at roughly waist height in front of you. Grip both ends of the band. Step back until the band is taut with arms extended. Squat down by sitting your hips back with arms still extended forward. Stand up from the squat. As you reach standing, row the band toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the row. Extend your arms back forward as you descend into the next squat. Continue fluidly. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Full-body compound exercise at home; Builds legs and back simultaneously; Constant band tension throughout; Highly portable; Time-efficient; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Trapezius (middle); Biceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height behind you (around a sturdy pole or in a door anchor). Face away from the anchor. Hold both ends of the band at your chest. Step forward into a split stance for stability. Press both handles forward simultaneously until arms are fully extended. Squeeze your chest hard at lockout. Slowly return to your chest under control. Maintain upright posture. Brace your core throughout. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Effective at-home chest press; Constant band tension throughout; Standing position adds core demand; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no bench is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band at a high point behind you. Hold the band behind your head with both hands near your ears. Face away from the anchor. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Crunch forward by flexing your spine — bring your chest toward your hips. Squeeze your abs hard at the bottom of the crunch. Slowly return to upright under control. Keep constant band tension throughout. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Loaded standing core exercise at home; Mimics cable crunch standing; Constant band tension throughout; Highly portable; Easy to scale; Useful when no cable machine is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors (slight)

Exercise Name: Band Squat With Single Arm Row
Description: Anchor a resistance band low in front of you. Stand on the band or grip the ends in your hands. Set your feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core and squat down by bending your knees and hips. Stand back up to the starting position. At the top, row the right band end up to your hip with one arm. Squeeze your right shoulder blade at the top of the row. Lower the band back down. Alternate row arms each rep.
Benefits: Trains legs and back together; Time-efficient compound combo; Builds full body strength; Strong functional movement pattern; Useful for home training; Easy to scale by changing band tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Hold both ends of the band at your shoulders. Loop the band over each shoulder if it is long enough for stability. Stand tall. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Sit your hips back and down into a squat. Lower until your thighs are parallel or your hip crease drops below your knees. Drive through your full foot to stand. The band tension increases as you rise. Squeeze your glutes at the top against the peak band tension. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Adds progressive resistance to bodyweight squats; Increasing tension at the top loads the lockout; Highly portable; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Useful when no weights are available; Mimics accommodating resistance in powerlifting
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band low behind you. Stand facing away from the anchor with a handle in each hand. Hold the handles at the sides of your chest. Step forward to add tension to the band. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Press both handles up and forward at a 45-degree angle. Lock out the arms with hands meeting in front of your face. Lower the handles slowly back to the start.
Benefits: Targets the upper chest; Mimics incline bench press; No bench required; Easy to set up at home; Builds upper chest strength; Joint-friendly variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (upper); Front deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Anchor a resistance band at elbow height. Stand sideways to the anchor with the working arm closest to the band. Grip the band handle with the elbow tucked at the side. Bend the elbow at ninety degrees with the forearm out to the side. Brace your core and keep the elbow pinned. Rotate the forearm inward across the body. Hold briefly at the rotated position. Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains internal rotation; Builds the rotator cuff; Strong shoulder drill; Useful warm-up; Builds shoulder stability

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low post or fixed object in front of you. Loop the band around your right ankle. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Benefits: Bodyweight bicep exercise; Supinated grip maximizes bicep emphasis; Adjustable difficulty by body angle; No weights needed; Builds bicep pulling strength; Useful when no dumbbells are available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (primary focus); Brachialis; Latissimus dorsi; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set safety pins in the rack at the bottom of your squat depth. Place the barbell on the pins and load it. Step under the bar and set it on your upper back. Squat down to where the bar rests on the pins. Plant your feet and brace your core hard. Drive through your heels to stand up out of the bottom. Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended. Lower the bar back down to rest on the pins between reps.
Benefits: Builds raw concentric strength; Removes stretch reflex; Improves out-of-the-hole power; Strongman classic; Strong squat accessory; Useful for sticking points
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Spinal erectors; Hamstrings

Description: Stand with your back to a barbell on a low rack or held at hip level. Reach behind you and grip the bar with a wide overhand grip. Stand upright with the bar resting against the back of your thighs. Brace your core and stand tall. Pull the bar slightly away from your body for tension. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Hold the squeeze for one count at the top. Lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Targets lower traps and rhomboids; Behind-the-back position changes pull angle; Wide grip emphasizes middle traps; Builds full trap development; Useful for back posture work; Different stimulus than standard shrugs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower and middle fibers); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set up a power rack with a bench or box behind you at parallel-squat height. Anchor resistance bands to the bottom of the rack and loop them over the barbell. Position the barbell across your upper back and unrack it. Step back into your squat stance with feet shoulder-width apart. Sit back and down to the bench until your glutes touch. Pause briefly on the bench while keeping tension. Drive up explosively, fighting against the increasing band tension. Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance gets harder at lockout; Box squat enforces consistent depth; Builds explosive drive out of the bottom; Develops lockout strength; Common westside-style training method; Strong carryover to competition squat
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Erector spinae

Description: Set the safety pins in a power rack at your bottom squat depth — bar height matches your bar position when you’re fully squatted. Position the barbell on the pins and load it. Step under the bar and set it across your upper back. Stand into a quarter squat to unrack the bar from the pins, then squat down until the bar settles back onto the pins. Pause for a full second with the bar resting on the pins. Release tension briefly. Brace your core, drive through your heels, and stand up explosively from the dead stop. Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended. Lower under control until the bar settles on the pins again — pause, then repeat. Aim for 4 to 6 reps. The dead-stop nature makes higher reps very fatiguing.
Benefits: Builds raw concentric strength out of the bottom position; Eliminates the stretch reflex to expose weak points; Teaches explosive drive from a dead stop; Forces strict form by removing momentum; Direct carryover to bottom-end squat strength; Builds confidence under heavy loads in the danger zone; Excellent accessory for raw squatters and powerlifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Erector spinae; Core stabilizers

Description: Set up a power rack with bands looped over the top crossbar and attached to each side of the barbell. Adjust band length so the bands are stretched tight at the bottom of the lift. Step up to the bar in a conventional deadlift stance. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar just outside your legs. Engage your lats and brace your core hard. Pull the bar off the floor. The bands will assist heavily at the bottom. Continue pulling, with the bands deloading as you stand. You take more of the weight. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended. Lower the bar back to the floor under control.
Benefits: Allows supramaximal loading at lockout; Builds confidence under heavy bar weights; Strengthens the lockout phase of the deadlift; Reduces stress on the lower back at the start of the lift; Useful method in conjugate-style training; Helps overcome lockout sticking points
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius

Description: Set up a power rack or platform with bands anchored to the floor or rack base. Position a loaded barbell on the platform and loop bands over each end. Stand over the bar with a wide sumo stance, toes turned out at 30 to 45 degrees. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with hands inside your legs. Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and engage your lats. Drive your knees out and push the floor away to start the bar moving. Continue pulling against increasing band tension as you stand. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance builds lockout strength; Sumo stance emphasizes glutes and adductors; Forces explosive drive off the floor; Common method in conjugate-style training; Useful variation to break sumo deadlift plateaus; Reduces stress on the lower back compared to conventional
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hamstrings; Quadriceps; Erector spinae

Description: Loop resistance bands around the barbell and anchor them under your feet or to the base of a rack. Stand on the bands with feet hip-width apart. Hold the barbell with an overhand grip. The bands should be taut at the top and slack at the bottom. Hinge at the hips to perform a standard RDL. The bands provide minimal resistance at the bottom. As you stand, the band tension increases — loading the lockout more heavily. Squeeze your glutes hard against the combined barbell and band tension at the top. Lower under control and repeat. Use lighter barbell weight than standard RDL to account for band tension.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance loads the lockout; Builds glute drive at the top; Teaches aggressive hip extension; Develops lockout strength; Used in Westside/conjugate training; Combines barbell and band loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus (heavy at top); Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Set up a barbell in a power rack with bands anchored to the floor or to the bottom of the rack. Loop the bands over each end of the barbell. Step under the bar and place it across your upper back, gripping it firmly. Unrack the bar and step back into your squat stance. Brace your core, sit back, and squat down to depth. Drive up through your heels with explosive force, fighting against the band tension. Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended. The bands should reach maximum tension at the top of the lift.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance gets harder as leverage improves; Builds explosive drive out of the bottom; Develops lockout strength; Trains acceleration through the entire range; Common method in conjugate-style powerlifting; Forces fast, intentional concentric drive
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Erector spinae

Description: Anchor a resistance band at low height to a stable point. Stand sideways to the anchor with feet shoulder width apart. Grab the band overhead with the far side hand. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Stand tall with the band stretched. Bend laterally away from the anchor. Squeeze the working oblique on the bending side. Return to the start and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Hammers the obliques.; Band tension increases at end range.; Builds lateral core strength.; Useful for rotational athletes.; Improves spinal control.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Stand with the barbell on the floor directly behind your heels. Bend at the hips and knees and reach behind you to grip the bar with palms facing back. Use a shoulder-width grip just outside your hips. Pull your shoulders back and engage your lats. Brace your core and lift your chest. Drive through your heels to stand up, lifting the bar along the back of your legs. Lock out at the top with the bar against the back of your thighs. Lower the bar back to the floor by hinging at the hips and bending the knees.
Benefits: Targets quads and traps differently than conventional deadlift; Old-school strongman variation; Strong grip and forearm work from the unusual position; Reduces lower back stress compared to floor pulls; Builds upper trap mass; Useful variation for breaking through deadlift plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Trapezius; Forearm flexors; Erector spinae

Description: Set a barbell on a rack at hip height, or pick it up from the floor. Stand with the barbell behind you at arm’s length, gripping it with an overhand grip behind your hips. Stand tall. Pull your shoulders back and down. Brace your core. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Squeeze your traps hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower the bar under control. Keep your arms straight throughout — only your shoulders move. Use moderate weight. Maintain perfect upright posture.
Benefits: Targets the lower and middle traps; Different stimulus than front shrugs; Builds upper back thickness; Useful for trap development; Improves shoulder posture; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower and middle fibers); Levator scapulae; Rhomboids; Forearms (grip)

Exercise Name: Barbell Behind The Back Push Press
Description: Set up a barbell across the rear delts at the base of the neck. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, bar resting on traps. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Brace your core and stand tall with chest up. Dip slightly by bending your knees and hips. Drive up explosively through your heels to start the bar moving up. Press the bar overhead until your arms are fully extended. Lower the bar back to the starting position behind your neck with control.
Benefits: Allows heavier loads than strict behind-neck press; Builds shoulder power and strength; Different stimulus than front rack press; Trains hip drive coordinated with press; Develops overhead lockout strength; Useful for shoulder specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Quadriceps; Trapezius

Description: Have a training partner hold 2 boards on your chest, or strap them onto your shirt. Lie on a flat bench under the loaded barbell. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back. Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control until it touches the top board. Press the bar back up explosively, locking out at the top. Re-rack the bar carefully when finished.
Benefits: Partial range allows heavier loads than full bench; Builds lockout and triceps strength; Different board heights target different sticking points; Reduces stress on the shoulders; Common method in powerlifting accessory work; Helps overcome bench press plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid

Description: Have a training partner hold 1 board on your chest, or strap them onto your shirt. Lie on a flat bench under the loaded barbell. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back. Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control until it touches the top board. Press the bar back up explosively, locking out at the top. Re-rack the bar carefully when finished.
Benefits: Partial range allows heavier loads than full bench; Builds lockout and triceps strength; Different board heights target different sticking points; Reduces stress on the shoulders; Common method in powerlifting accessory work; Helps overcome bench press plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie back on a flat bench with your eyes directly under the bar. Plant both feet firmly on the floor and create a slight natural arch in your lower back. Pull your shoulder blades down and back, pinning them to the bench. Keep this tightness throughout every rep. Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar (do not use a thumbless grip) and stack your wrists over your elbows. Unrack the bar with straight arms and bring it over your chest. Take a deep breath into your belly and brace your core. Lower the bar under control to the lower portion of your chest, allowing your elbows to flare to roughly 45 to 75 degrees from your torso, not pinned to your sides and not at 90 degrees. Press the bar back up and slightly toward your face, finishing with your arms straight over your shoulders. Exhale at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps, then rack the bar safely with the help of a spotter when working near maximum loads.
Benefits: Builds size and strength in the chest, front deltoids, and triceps; One of the most reliable measures of upper-body pressing strength; Allows progressive overload across a long career of training; Improves performance in sports requiring pushing power; Easily programmed across rep ranges for hypertrophy or maximum strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoids; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior (stabilizer)

Description: Set up a flat bench with chains attached to each end of the barbell. Adjust chain length so most of the chain rests on the floor at the bottom of the press. Lie on the bench with eyes under the bar and feet planted on the floor. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width and pull your shoulder blades back. Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control to mid-chest. The chains should pile up on the floor. Press the bar back up explosively. The load increases as the chains lift off the floor. Lock out hard at the top, then lower for the next rep.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance builds lockout strength; Forces explosive drive through the press; Trains the triceps under increasing load; Common method in westside-style training; Reduces chain noise from bouncing; Develops bar control under variable load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Have a training partner hold 3 boards on your chest, or strap them onto your shirt. Lie on a flat bench under the loaded barbell. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back. Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control until it touches the top board. Press the bar back up explosively, locking out at the top. Re-rack the bar carefully when finished.
Benefits: Partial range allows heavier loads than full bench; Builds lockout and triceps strength; Different board heights target different sticking points; Reduces stress on the shoulders; Common method in powerlifting accessory work; Helps overcome bench press plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a barbell at your chest with elbows bent at 90 degrees. Keep your elbows bent at roughly 90 degrees throughout. Arc the bar behind your head by hinging at the shoulders. Elbows stay bent. Lower until you feel a stretch in your chest and lats. Pull the bar back over to your chest, maintaining the bent-arm position. Squeeze your chest at the top. Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps. The bent arms allow heavier loading than straight-arm pullovers.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis toward the chest; Allows heavier loading than straight-arm version; Builds chest and lat size; Different stimulus from standard pullover; Old-school bodybuilding exercise; Builds ribcage expansion (traditional belief)
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (increased); Latissimus dorsi; Serratus anterior; Triceps brachii; Teres major

Exercise Name: Barbell Bench Press With Band Suspended Kettlebell
Description: Set up a bench press with bands looped over each end of the barbell. Attach a kettlebell to each band so the kettlebells hang below the bar. Lie on the bench with feet flat and shoulder blades pulled back. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Unrack the bar carefully. The kettlebells will swing as you move. Lower the bar to your chest while controlling the swinging kettlebells. Press the bar back up to lockout, fighting the kettlebell swing. Re-rack carefully when finished.
Benefits: Trains shoulder stability under chaos; Builds rotator cuff and stabilizer strength; Reduces effective load through instability; Useful for training control under fatigue; Common method in westside-style training; Improves bar control significantly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Rotator cuff; Serratus anterior

Description: Place a flat bench behind you in a power rack. Set the barbell on the rack. Unrack the bar across your upper traps. Step back so the bench is just behind your heels. Set feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Sit your hips back and down. Squat down until your glutes lightly touch the bench. Do NOT collapse onto the bench — just touch and stand. Drive through your feet to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Benefits: Consistent depth from bench reference; Forces sitting back into hips; Builds posterior chain involvement; Easier to learn proper depth; Useful powerlifting accessory; Builds glute drive out of the hole
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus (heavy); Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Barbell Bent Over Wide Alternate Row Plus
Description: Set up a barbell on the floor or low rack. Grip the bar with a wide overhand grip outside shoulder width. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Brace your core and let the bar hang at arms length. Pull one side of the bar up toward the lower chest. Squeeze the upper back hard at the top. Lower that side back down as you pull the other side up. Continue alternating row pulls.
Benefits: Strong upper back builder; Trains the lats wide grip; Builds back thickness; Strong unilateral focus; Useful back move; Builds rotational core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Posterior deltoid

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart in front of a loaded barbell on the floor. Hinge at the hips and bend your knees slightly to grip the bar with hands just outside your knees, using a double-overhand grip. Stand up with the bar, then hinge forward at the hips again until your torso is roughly 45 degrees from horizontal — not parallel to the floor (that puts more strain on the lower back). Let the bar hang at arm’s length just below your knees. Brace your core, pull your shoulders down and back, and lock in your back angle. Pull the bar to your lower chest or upper abdomen by driving your elbows up and back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Pause briefly with the bar against your body, then lower it under control back to the start position. Maintain the same torso angle throughout the entire set — do not rock or use momentum. Repeat for the desired number of reps, then lower the bar to the floor between sets if needed.
Benefits: Builds the entire back: lats, rhomboids, traps, rear delts; Develops grip strength and biceps as secondary movers; Strengthens the lower back and core through the isometric hold; Carries over to deadlift lockout and posture; Allows heavy loading for serious back development; One of the best mass-building exercises for the upper body
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower fibers); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii and brachialis; Erector spinae (isometric); Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Barbell Bent Over Wide Grip Row
Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Grip a barbell with a wide overhand grip (1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width). Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor. Let the bar hang with arms extended. Row the bar toward your upper chest with elbows flared wide — elbows point to the sides. Squeeze your upper back and rear delts at the top. Lower under control. The wide grip and high touch point targets the upper back more than the lats. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to rear delts and upper back; Builds upper back thickness; Different stimulus from standard-grip rows; Develops rhomboids and mid-traps; Useful for posture and shoulder balance; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid (increased); Trapezius (middle and upper); Rhomboids; Latissimus dorsi (reduced); Biceps brachii; Erector spinae (isometric)

Exercise Name: Barbell Bent Over Wide Row Plus
Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell with a wide grip. Position your hands wider than shoulder-width with palms facing down. Hinge at the hips and lower your torso to about parallel. Allow the bar to hang at full arm extension. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Pull the bar up to your lower chest by leading with the elbows out wide. Squeeze the upper back hard at the top. Lower the bar back down with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Wide grip emphasizes upper back; Strong rear delt and rhomboid engagement; Builds back thickness; Different stimulus than standard bent over row; Useful for upper back specialization; Posture-focused training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Posterior deltoid

Description: Set up with a loaded barbell on the floor. Stand with feet hip-width apart, bar over mid-foot. Hinge down and grip the bar shoulder-width apart with hook or overhand grip. Set your back flat, chest tall. Brace your core. Pull the bar off the floor, keeping it close to your body through the first pull. As the bar passes the knees, explode through “triple extension” of the hips, knees, and ankles. Shrug the bar up. Pull yourself under the bar and catch it in the front-rack position (across the front shoulders, elbows up) in a deep front squat. Stand up from the front squat with the bar racked. This completes the clean. For the jerk: brace your core, dip with vertical torso (knees only, ~10-15 cm), then drive explosively up. As legs extend, press the bar overhead while jumping under it (split or power stance). Catch the bar locked overhead, recover to standing with feet aligned. Lower the bar carefully (or drop with bumper plates).
Benefits: Develops the highest absolute strength of any overhead lift; Builds total-body power, mobility, and coordination; Trains the entire posterior chain explosively; Improves shoulder, hip, and ankle mobility; Direct carryover to athletic performance; Olympic-tested benchmark of total-body strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Trapezius (heavy involvement); Anterior, lateral, and posterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip; Calves

Description: Set up a barbell in a power rack at upper chest height. Step under the bar with elbows up and palms facing the ceiling. Let the bar rest across your front shoulders with fingertips loosely under it. Stand up to unrack the bar and step back into your stance. Set your feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Brace your core hard and keep your elbows pointed forward. Squat down by sitting back and bending the knees, keeping your torso upright. Drive up through your heels while keeping your elbows high. Lock out at the top.
Benefits: Olympic lifting standard squat position; Forces upright torso and strong core engagement; Builds quad-dominant leg strength; Develops wrist and upper back mobility; Strong carryover to clean and jerk; Trains the rack position under heavy load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Erector spinae; Core; Upper back

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. The barbell should be just above your feet. Grip the bar with a clean grip — slightly wider than shoulder-width, hook grip if comfortable. Set up: hips slightly higher than knees, chest up, shoulders directly over the bar (or slightly in front), back flat. Brace your core. Lift the bar by extending your knees first, maintaining the chest-up position. Keep the bar close to your shins and thighs throughout the pull. Continue lifting until you stand fully upright with the bar at thigh level. Reverse the motion: hinge hips back, slide bar down legs, return to floor. Maintain control throughout. This is a strength and technique exercise — not explosive.
Benefits: Trains the first pull of the clean; Builds posterior chain strength; Develops proper bar path; Useful for Olympic lift technique work; Easier on the wrists than a clean; Great strength accessory
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Quadriceps; Trapezius; Forearms (heavy grip)

Exercise Name: Barbell Chest Press on Stability Ball
Description: Sit on a stability ball with a barbell across your lap. Walk your feet forward and roll down until your upper back rests on the ball. Bridge your hips up so your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Press the barbell up from your chest to lockout. Keep the ball stable. Lower the bar to your mid-chest under control. Press back up. Maintain the bridge throughout. Have a spotter available — the unstable surface adds risk. Use significantly lighter weight than flat bench press. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Adds core and hip stability demand to bench press; Builds glute and hamstring endurance (bridge hold); Challenges stabilizers more than a bench; Useful variation for balance and stability training; Engages the full body; No bench needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Gluteus maximus (bridge hold); Core (heavy stabilizer); Hamstrings (bridge hold)

Description: Stand over a barbell with feet hip-width apart. Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. Power clean the bar from the floor to the front rack position. Stand tall. Brace your core. Strictly press the bar overhead by extending your elbows. No leg drive. Lock out overhead with bar over your midfoot. Lower the bar back to the front rack, then to the floor. Reset and repeat. Use moderate weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps per set.
Benefits: Combines clean with strict press; Original third Olympic lift; Builds total-body strength and power; Time-efficient compound exercise; Develops pulling and pressing simultaneously; Excellent conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Quadriceps; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Trapezius; Core (heavy stabilizer)

Description: Place a sturdy box (or stack of plates) directly behind you at the appropriate squat depth — typically just below parallel. Set a barbell at upper-back height in a power rack. Step under and place it across your upper traps. Unrack and step back. Stand directly in front of the box with feet shoulder-width apart. Sit your hips back as if reaching for the box. Continue lowering until your butt touches the box. Pause completely on the box for one to two seconds. Do not collapse — maintain tension. Drive through your full feet to explode back up to standing. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Maintain perfect bar position and brace throughout.
Benefits: Teaches consistent squat depth; Trains sitting back into the squat; Builds explosive concentric strength; Reduces stress on the knees; Foundational powerlifting variation; Builds posterior chain
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus (heavy involvement); Hamstrings; Adductors; Erector spinae; Core (heavy bracing)

Exercise Name: Barbell Complex Stiff Leg Deadlift Clean Step
Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart, the bar on the floor in front of you. Begin with a stiff leg deadlift, lifting the bar to standing. Lower the bar to mid-thigh. From mid-thigh, perform a power clean to the front rack position. Catch the bar in the front rack with elbows high. Step forward into a lunge while maintaining the front rack. Drive back to standing. Lower the bar back to the floor. That sequence is one rep.
Benefits: Trains multiple lifts in one continuous flow; Strong conditioning and metabolic demand; Builds Olympic lifting skill; Develops explosive total body strength; Time-efficient compound training; Useful for off-season athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Erector spinae; Trapezius; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie on a flat bench with eyes under the bar. Lift your feet off the floor and place them flat on the bench or hold them in the air. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width or slightly closer. Pull your shoulder blades back and brace your core hard. Unrack the bar and hold it over your chest with arms extended. Lower the bar to your chest while keeping elbows tucked. Press the bar back up by extending the elbows and squeezing the chest. Maintain the elevated foot position throughout the set.
Benefits: Removes leg drive entirely; Forces strict upper body work; Heavy tricep loading; Builds bench press technique; Strong core engagement; Useful for breaking through bench plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Anconeus

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Grip the barbell with hands roughly shoulder-width apart (or slightly narrower — but not so narrow that wrists strain). Unrack the bar. Lower the bar to your lower chest, keeping your elbows close to your body. Press the bar up to lockout, focusing on extending at the elbows. Squeeze your triceps at the top. Keep your elbows tucked at about 30 degrees from your torso. Use moderate weight. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per set. Avoid extremely narrow grips that strain the wrists.
Benefits: Heavy tricep mass building; Builds inner chest; Develops bench press lockout strength; Useful bench press accessory; Allows heavy tricep loading; Easier on shoulders than wide grip
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (heavy); Pectoralis major (inner); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart, holding a barbell with an underhand grip about shoulder-width. Begin with the bar resting at your thighs, arms fully extended. Curl the bar up to shoulder height by bending at the elbows, keeping your upper arms still. From the top of the curl, press the bar straight overhead until your arms are fully extended. Lower the bar behind your head by bending only at the elbows, performing an overhead triceps extension. Press the bar back overhead by extending your elbows. Lower the bar to shoulder height, then reverse the curl to bring the bar back down to your thighs. That is one rep. Continue with smooth, controlled motion through the full complex.
Benefits: Hits biceps, shoulders, and triceps in one efficient sequence; Builds coordination across multiple movement patterns; Time-efficient arm training; Improves shoulder mobility through the overhead positions; Strong cardiovascular component when performed continuously; Excellent finisher for upper body sessions
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Brachialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a barbell with an underhand (supinated) grip just outside shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Let the bar hang at arm’s length in front of your thighs. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Pin your elbows against your sides. They should not move forward or backward during the lift. Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows, contracting your biceps hard. Keep your wrists straight (not bent back). Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps for one second at the top. Lower the bar under control back to the start position over a count of two seconds. Fully extend your arms at the bottom. Do not swing your torso, lean back, or use momentum. Strict form is what builds bicep size. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use an EZ bar instead if a straight barbell bothers your wrists.
Benefits: Builds the biceps brachii more effectively than most other bicep exercises; Allows heavier loading than dumbbell curls; Trains both arms together, which exposes any weak side; Builds grip and forearm strength as a byproduct; The benchmark exercise for measuring bicep strength progress; Easy to load and progress over time
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long and short heads); Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors; Anterior deltoid (minor stabilizer)

Description: Set up a barbell with chains attached to each end. Adjust chain length so most of the chain rests on the floor at the start. Approach the bar in a conventional deadlift stance. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar just outside your legs. Pull the slack out, engage your lats, and brace your core. Drive through your heels to start the bar moving. As you stand, more chain weight lifts off the floor and adds to the load. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended. Lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance builds lockout strength; Forces explosive drive off the floor; Common method in westside-style training; Trains acceleration through the pull; Useful for breaking through deadlift sticking points; Develops bar control under variable load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius

Description: Stack blocks or platforms on each side of the lifting area to raise the bar. Set the bar height so the plates rest just below or above your knees, depending on the variation. Approach the bar in a conventional deadlift stance with feet hip-width apart. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar just outside your legs. Pull the slack out of the bar, engage your lats, and brace your core. Drive through your heels to stand up with the bar. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended and shoulders pulled back. Lower the bar back to the blocks with control.
Benefits: Allows heavier loads than full deadlifts; Builds lockout strength; Overloads the upper back, traps, and grip; Reduces stress on the lower back compared to a floor pull; Excellent accessory for competition deadlift; Useful for working through deadlift sticking points
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius; Forearm flexors

Description: Stand on a small platform or 25 to 45 pound weight plates, around 1 to 4 inches tall. Set up over a loaded barbell with your feet hip-width apart. Bend at the hips and knees to reach the bar with your hands just outside your legs. Pull the slack out of the bar and engage your lats. Brace your core hard. The deeper start position requires more bracing. Drive through your feet to lift the bar off the floor. Stand up tall with the bar, locking out hips and knees. Lower the bar with control back to the platform.
Benefits: Extended range of motion builds bottom-end strength; Forces deeper hinge and stronger leg drive; Develops explosive drive off the floor; Builds quad and glute strength at the start of the pull; Improves competition deadlift starting position; Tougher than standard deadlifts at the same weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Quadriceps; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Set safety pins in a power rack at knee height or position the bar on the floor. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart over the bar. Bend forward at the hips with a flat back, knees slightly bent. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Row the bar up explosively to your lower chest. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower the bar back to the pins or floor for a dead stop. Reset before the next rep.
Benefits: Builds dead-stop rowing strength; Eliminates stretch reflex; Forces strict pulling form; Builds explosive back strength; Useful for breaking through row sticking points; Strong carryover to deadlifts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Biceps brachii; Erector spinae

Description: Set up on a fixed decline bench or set an adjustable bench to a decline of roughly 15 to 30 degrees. Lock your feet under the leg pads. Lie back with your eyes roughly under the bar. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with thumbs wrapped. Have a spotter help you unrack — the angle makes self-unracking trickier than flat bench. Pull your shoulder blades down and back into the bench, brace your core, and lift your chest. Lower the bar under control to your lower chest, allowing your elbows to flare to roughly 45 to 70 degrees. Press the bar back up and slightly toward your face, finishing with arms locked out over your lower chest. Exhale as you press. For each rep, control the descent — the decline angle makes the bar drop fast if you let it. Have a spotter help re-rack the bar at the end of the set.
Benefits: Targets the lower (sternal) head of the pectoralis major most directly; Allows heavier loading than flat or incline barbell pressing for most lifters; Reduces shoulder demand, often more comfortable for lifters with shoulder issues; Useful variation for breaking through bench press plateaus; Builds lower-chest thickness that flat pressing misses; Good chest exercise for athletes with overhead-throwing shoulder discomfort
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially the sternal/lower head); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid (reduced involvement vs flat press); Serratus anterior (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on a decline bench with feet hooked under the pads. Hold a barbell over your chest with elbows bent. Use a shoulder-width grip with palms facing forward. Brace your core and keep your back against the bench. Maintain the bent arm position throughout. Lower the bar back behind your head in an arc. Continue until you feel a deep lat and chest stretch. Pull the bar back over your chest using the lats.
Benefits: Deep lat stretch; Builds the lats and chest; Bent arms reduce shoulder strain; Decline angle increases stretch; Strong upper torso builder; Useful for chest and back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Triceps (long head)

Exercise Name: Barbell Decline Close Grip to Skull Press
Description: Set up a decline bench and load a barbell on the rack. Lie back on the decline bench and grip the bar shoulder width. Unrack the bar and hold it over the lower chest with arms locked. Lower the bar down toward the upper chest by bending the elbows. Tuck the elbows in tight as the bar comes down. Stop the bar just above the chest and pause briefly. Press the bar back up to lockout by extending the elbows hard. Squeeze the triceps at the top.
Benefits: Strong tricep builder; Trains the JM press groove; Useful for bench lockout; Strong powerlifting move; Builds tricep mass; Trains the close grip pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Load the barbell on the floor and stand with your mid-foot directly under the bar, feet roughly hip-width apart with toes slightly turned out. Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to grip the bar just outside your shins. Use a double-overhand grip or a mixed grip for heavier loads. Drop your hips so your shins touch the bar, lift your chest, and pull the slack out of the bar. Your shoulders should be slightly in front of the bar and your back flat. Take a deep breath, brace your core, and drive your feet through the floor. Keep the bar in contact with your legs as it rises. Lock out by standing tall with hips and knees fully extended. Do not lean back or hyperextend the lower back. Reverse the movement by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees once the bar passes them. Lower the bar under control to the floor and reset before the next rep.
Benefits: Builds total-body strength by training the posterior chain, core, and grip together; Improves posture and spinal stability through heavy hip-hinge loading; Develops grip strength and forearm size; Carries over to athletic movements like sprinting, jumping, and Olympic lifts; Stimulates significant muscle growth and is highly time-efficient
Muscles Worked (Raw): Glutes; Hamstrings; Erector spinae (lower back); Quadriceps; Trapezius and rhomboids; Forearms and grip; Core (rectus abdominis and obliques as stabilizers)

Description: Set a barbell across your upper traps. Unrack and step back. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step your right foot back and across behind your left leg (like a curtsey). Lower your right knee toward the floor by bending both knees. Drive through your front (left) foot to return to standing. Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side. The cross-behind position targets the upper glute. Use moderate weight — the position is unstable.
Benefits: Targets the gluteus medius for upper glute development; Loads the adductors through the crossover pattern; Barbell allows heavier loading than dumbbells; Builds the upper glute shelf; Different stimulus from standard lunges; Develops hip control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set up a decline bench with feet secured on the foot pads. Lie back with eyes under the bar. Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width. Pull your shoulder blades back into the bench. Unrack the bar and hold it over your lower chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control to your lower chest. Allow your elbows to flare more than a standard press. Press the bar back up by squeezing the chest.
Benefits: Targets outer lower chest fibers; Wide grip emphasizes outer pec; Decline angle hits lower chest; Builds chest width and depth; Useful for chest specialization; Strong pec stretch at the bottom
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (outer and lower fibers); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand tall holding a barbell with an underhand grip at your thighs. Pull your elbows back so the bar can drag along your body. Curl the bar up by bending at the elbows, keeping the bar in contact with your torso. The bar travels straight up along your body — not in an arc. Continue until the bar reaches your lower chest. Your elbows pull back further as you rise. Squeeze your biceps at the top. Lower the bar back down along your body. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Emphasizes the long head of the bicep; Unique bar path with elbow pull-back; Builds bicep peak; Different stimulus from standard curls; Easy to set up; Engaging variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long head emphasis); Brachialis; Posterior deltoid (slight)

Description: Place small plates, a wedge, or wear weightlifting shoes to elevate your heels around 1 to 2 inches. Set up under a barbell in a power rack with the bar across your upper back. Step back with your feet shoulder-width apart, heels on the elevation. Brace your core and pull the bar tight to your back. Squat down by sitting back and bending the knees, allowing them to track over the toes. Descend as deep as your mobility allows. Drive through your heels to stand back up to lockout. Maintain an upright torso throughout the lift.
Benefits: Maximally targets the quadriceps; Allows deeper squat depth; Forces a more upright torso position; Useful for lifters with poor ankle mobility; Builds quad size and detail; Trains the same pattern as Olympic weightlifting shoe squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Erector spinae

Description: Lie on a decline bench with feet hooked under the pads. Hold a barbell over your chest with a grip wider than shoulder-width. Use a pronated grip with palms facing forward. Brace your core and keep your back against the bench. Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout. Lower the bar back behind your head in an arc. Continue until you feel a deep lat and chest stretch. Pull the bar back over your chest using the lats.
Benefits: Deep lat stretch; Builds back width; Decline angle increases stretch; Strong upper torso builder; Builds the chest and lats; Wide grip biases the back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Triceps (long head)

Description: Set a decline bench to 15 to 30 degrees. Hook your feet under the pads. Hold a barbell with a shoulder-width grip above your chest, arms extended. Slowly arc the bar behind your head and toward the floor. Continue until you feel a deep stretch in your lats and chest. Pull the bar back over to above your chest using your lats and chest. Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps. The decline angle allows a deeper stretch than flat.
Benefits: Increased range of motion from decline angle; Deeper lat stretch than flat pullover; Targets lats, chest, and serratus; Builds overhead flexibility; Useful for chest and back development; Different angle from standard pullover
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Triceps brachii (long head); Teres major

Description: Set up a bench or box behind your standing position. Place a barbell across your upper back as in a back squat. Step forward with your front leg and place the top of your back foot on the bench behind you. Stand tall with most of your weight on the front leg. Brace your core and lower into a split squat by bending the front knee. Descend until your front thigh is parallel to the floor and the back knee is just above the floor. Drive through the front foot to stand back up to the starting position. Complete reps on one leg before switching sides.
Benefits: Heavily loads single-leg strength; Builds quads, glutes, and hamstrings unilaterally; Corrects left-right imbalances; Improves balance and hip stability; Less spinal load than a standard squat at heavy weights; Excellent accessory for athletes and lifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Core stabilizers
