Benefits: Wider grip emphasizes medial delts; Reduces internal shoulder rotation; Shoulder-friendlier than narrow grip upright rows; Builds shoulder width; Trains the upper traps; Useful upright row variation for sensitive shoulders
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Trapezius (upper); Brachialis

Description: Set up a barbell with chains attached to each end. Adjust chain length so most of the chain rests on the floor at the start. Stand over the bar with a wide sumo stance, toes turned out. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with hands inside your legs. Pull the slack out, engage your lats, and brace your core. Drive your knees out and push the floor away to start the lift. As you stand, more chain weight lifts off the floor and adds load. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended. Lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance builds lockout strength; Forces explosive drive off the floor; Common method in westside-style training; Sumo specific accessory; Useful for breaking through sumo deadlift sticking points; Develops bar control under variable load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Stand with your feet hip-width apart, with the barbell over the middle of your feet. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the bar with your hands just outside your legs. Pull your shoulders back, lift your chest, and engage your lats by pulling the slack out of the bar. Brace your core hard, as if preparing to take a punch. Drive through your heels and push the floor away to stand up with the bar. Keep the bar close to your body throughout the lift. Lock out at the top with your hips and knees fully extended, shoulders back. Lower the bar by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees once the bar passes them.
Benefits: Builds total body strength like no other lift; Develops the entire posterior chain; Massive grip and forearm work; Foundation for measurable strength progression; Heaviest possible loading in any single lift; Functional carryover to athletic and daily lifting
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius; Forearm flexors

Description: Lie flat on a bench with your eyes positioned directly under the barbell. Grip the bar with your hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, wrists stacked over your elbows. Plant your feet flat on the floor and pull your shoulder blades down and back into the bench. Unrack the bar and position it directly over your shoulders with arms extended. Lower the bar with control to your mid-chest, allowing your elbows to tuck slightly. Pause briefly when the bar touches the chest. Do not bounce. Drive the bar back up by pressing through your chest and triceps, locking out at the top. Re-rack the bar carefully when finished, using a spotter for heavy loads.
Benefits: Builds chest size and pressing strength; Develops triceps and anterior deltoids alongside the pecs; Foundation for measurable upper body strength progression; Allows the heaviest pressing loads in standard training; Carries over to any horizontal pressing movement; Highly skill-driven and progressive over time
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (sternal head); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Coracobrachialis

Description: Stand next to a loaded barbell on the floor. Grip the center of the bar with one hand. Deadlift the bar up. Stand tall — do not lean to the loaded side. Brace your core hard. Maintain perfectly upright posture. Walk forward with controlled strides. Keep the bar level — it will want to tilt. Grip and forearm demand is extreme. Walk for the desired distance, then switch hands. The bar’s length makes balancing harder than dumbbells. Use moderate weight. Start light.
Benefits: Extreme anti-lateral flexion core demand; Builds grip and forearm strength; Barbell balance challenge adds difficulty; Develops oblique strength; Unique loaded carry variation; Builds real-world carrying strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy anti-lateral flexion); Forearms and grip (extreme); Quadratus lumborum; Core (stabilizer); Trapezius

Description: Stand a barbell on end and hug it to your chest with both arms wrapped around it. Hold the bar vertically against your chest with elbows tucked tight. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core hard and lift your chest. Squat down by sitting back and bending your knees. Maintain an upright torso to keep the bar pressed to your chest. Descend until your thighs are parallel to the floor or deeper. Drive up through your heels to return to standing.
Benefits: Forces upright torso for safer squat mechanics; Builds strong core engagement; Emphasizes quad development; Alternative for lifters with wrist mobility issues; Strong arm and grip workout from holding the bar; Allows heavier loading than goblet squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Biceps brachii (isometric); Core

Exercise Name: Barbell Wide Reverse Grip Bench Press
Description: Lie on a flat bench with eyes under the bar. Grip the bar with palms facing you (underhand grip), wider than shoulder-width. Pull your shoulder blades back and engage your lats. Use a spotter to safely hand off the bar. Hold the bar over your upper chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control to your upper chest. Press the bar back up by driving through the chest and triceps. Lock out at the top, then lower carefully for the next rep.
Benefits: Targets the upper chest fibers heavily; Reduces shoulder strain compared to the standard pronated grip; Wide grip increases pec stretch; Builds chest definition and detail; Useful upper-chest specialization variation; Pairs well with incline pressing in the same workout
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (upper fibers); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand with a barbell at hip level, gripping it with a wide overhand grip. Use a grip width similar to a snatch (well outside the shoulders). Stand tall with chest up and shoulders pulled back. Brace your core and let the bar hang at arms length. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Hold the contraction at the top for one count. Lower the bar back down slowly with control. Avoid rolling your shoulders. Move them straight up and straight down.
Benefits: Builds upper trap mass; Wide grip increases middle trap and rhomboid engagement; Useful variation alongside standard shrugs; Strong grip and forearm work from the wide hold; Allows heavy progressive loading; Improves overall upper back development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (upper and middle fibers); Rhomboids; Levator scapulae; Forearm flexors

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, the bar on the floor in front of you. Begin with a deadlift, lifting the bar to standing. Lower the bar to mid-thigh, then perform a hang clean to the front rack position. From the front rack, drop into a front squat to depth. Drive up out of the front squat to standing. Perform a push press by dipping and driving the bar overhead. Lower the bar back to the front rack, then to mid-thigh, then to the floor. That sequence is one rep of the complex.
Benefits: Trains multiple lifts in one continuous flow; Strong conditioning and metabolic demand; Builds Olympic lifting skill; Develops explosive total body strength; Time-efficient compound training; Useful for off-season athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Anterior deltoid; Trapezius

Description: Set a barbell at upper-back height. Step under and position it across your upper traps. Unrack the bar. Set your feet 1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Sit your hips back and down. Push your knees out toward your toes. Descend to parallel or below. Drive through your full foot to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Keep your torso as upright as possible. Wider stance allows heavier loading for many lifters.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to adductors and glutes; Requires less ankle mobility than narrow squats; Popular in powerlifting; Often allows heavier loading; Builds hip strength in the frontal plane; Different stimulus for squat programming
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus (increased); Adductors (increased); Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie flat on a bench with your eyes directly under the barbell. Grip the bar wider than your normal bench press grip, around the rings on a standard barbell. Plant your feet flat on the floor and squeeze your shoulder blades back and down. Unrack the bar and hold it over your upper chest with arms extended. Lower the bar with control to the upper chest area. The wider grip will shorten the descent. Allow your elbows to flare more than in a standard press, but keep wrists stacked over elbows. Drive the bar back up by pushing through the chest and squeezing the pecs at the top. Re-rack the bar carefully. Avoid extreme grip widths that strain the shoulders.
Benefits: Emphasizes outer chest fibers; Shorter bar path with greater pec stretch; Reduces triceps contribution compared to standard grip; Builds chest width; Useful variation to break through pressing plateaus; Improves chest activation for chest-dominant lifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (outer fibers); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior

Description: Set a barbell at hip height in a rack. Step into the bar and cradle it in the crooks of your elbows. Clasp your hands together in front of you. The bar rests in your elbow creases. Stand up with the bar. Pull your shoulders back. Chest tall. Brace your core hard — the bar pulls you forward. Walk forward with controlled strides. Maintain upright posture throughout. Walk for the desired distance. Use padding on the bar for elbow comfort. Use moderate weight. Aim for 30 to 60 seconds per set.
Benefits: Builds anti-flexion core strength; Develops bicep and forearm endurance; Trains upper back posture under load; Unique loaded carry variation; Builds total-body conditioning; Named after strongman Ed Zercher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (heavy isometric); Core (anti-flexion); Upper trapezius; Erector spinae; Quadriceps; Forearms

Description: Set up a barbell on the floor or on low pins (just above your shins). Squat down so the bar sits behind the elbow joint of each arm. Hook your elbows under the bar with your palms facing up. Clasp your hands together to lock the bar in place. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back to lock in the upper-back position. Drive through your feet to stand up, keeping your torso as upright as possible. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended and chest tall. Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips and bending the knees. Aim for 4 to 8 reps. Use a folded towel or pad in the elbows to reduce discomfort.
Benefits: Brutal core and upper-back development; Forces upright torso position useful for squats; Builds biceps isometrically; Excellent carryover to atlas stones and strongman lifts; Less spinal shear than conventional deadlift; Develops the often-weak front squat rack position
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Trapezius and rhomboids; Biceps brachii (isometric); Core

Description: Set a barbell on the floor or in a low rack position. Squat down and place the bar in the crooks of your elbows. Cross your forearms in front of your chest to hold the bar. Brace your core hard and keep your chest up. Drive through your heels to stand up with the bar. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended. Lower the bar back down by hinging at the hips and bending the knees. Set the bar back on the floor with control.
Benefits: Builds quad and upper back strength; More upright torso position; Reduces lower back stress; Brutal core challenge; Improves grip and arm strength; Useful for strongman training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Upper back; Biceps brachii; Spinal erectors

Description: Sit on a bench. Place your forearms flat on the bench with wrists hanging off the edge, palms up. Hold a barbell with an underhand grip. Let your wrists extend down, lowering the bar. Curl your wrists upward, raising the bar. Squeeze your forearm flexors at the top. Lower under control. Full range every rep. Keep your forearms pinned to the bench — only your wrists move. Use moderate weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Builds forearm flexor strength and size; Easy to load progressively; Important for grip-intensive activities; Simple setup; Develops wrist flexion strength; Useful for climbers, lifters, and athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors (flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris); Flexor digitorum; Palmaris longus

Description: Set a barbell at chest height in a power rack while sitting on the floor with your legs extended straight in front of you. Sit with your back perpendicular to the floor, legs straight, feet flexed. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Brace your core hard. Sit tall. Press the bar straight up overhead by extending your elbows. Lock out at the top with the bar directly above your shoulders. Lower the bar slowly back to the starting position at chest height. Use lighter weight than standing presses. The position is unforgiving.
Benefits: Most honest measure of overhead pressing strength; Eliminates leg drive entirely; Builds elite core stability; Reveals weak links in pressing; Improves seated overhead position; Builds shoulder strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Core (heavy bracing); Hip flexors (seated position)

Description: Set the barbell in a power rack at roughly mid-torso height. Use a barbell pad or wrap a towel around the bar — the bar will dig into the crook of your elbows. Step up to the bar and hook your forearms underneath it so the bar sits in the crooks of your elbows. Bring your hands together in a closed-fist or palms-up position in front of your face. Take a deep breath, brace your core hard, and lift the bar out of the rack. Step back into your stance. Set your feet just outside shoulder-width with toes slightly turned out. Sit straight down with a tall torso, keeping your elbows tucked into your sides and the bar held tight against your chest. Squat to a depth where your elbows pass between your thighs — most lifters can go below parallel comfortably. Drive through your feet and stand up tall, maintaining that elbow position throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps, then carefully rack the bar.
Benefits: Builds the quadriceps, glutes, and core with an extreme front-loaded stimulus; Strengthens the upper back, biceps, and forearms isometrically; Forces a deep, upright squat that is often more knee-friendly than back squats; Hard to cheat — poor positions immediately drop the bar; Excellent strongman and odd-object training carryover; Builds mental toughness from the discomfort of the position
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Erector spinae and upper back (isometric); Biceps brachii (isometric hold); Core (rectus abdominis, obliques)

Description: Lie on a flat bench with your shoulders at the edge. Hold a barbell with both hands using a wide grip. Start with the bar held over your chest with arms extended. Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout. Lower the bar back behind your head in a wide arc. Continue lowering until you feel a strong stretch in your lats and chest. Pull the bar back up over your chest while maintaining the arc. Keep the wide grip and slight elbow bend throughout the rep.
Benefits: Wide grip emphasizes lats and outer chest; Stretches the lats and ribcage; Different stimulus than narrow pullovers; Builds upper body width; Useful for breaking through chest plateaus; Develops shoulder mobility
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Triceps brachii (long head); Teres major

Description: Sit on the floor. Place hands behind you, fingers pointing forward. Bend knees with feet flat on the floor. Lift your hips off the floor by pressing through your hands. Bend your elbows to lower your body. Press back up to lockout. Keep your back close to your hands. Extend legs for more difficulty. Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Easiest dip regression; No bench needed; Builds basic tricep strength; Accessible for beginners; Floor limits range for safety; Progresses to bench and bar dips
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (lower)

Description: Start on hands and knees in tabletop position. Hands directly under shoulders, knees under hips. Tuck your toes. Brace your core hard. Lift your knees just one to two inches off the floor — they should hover. Maintain a flat back. Keep your hips level. Hold this position for 20 to 60 seconds. Breathe steadily. Brace your core throughout. Lower your knees to rest. Repeat for 2 to 4 sets. Add shoulder taps or knee drives for variation.
Benefits: Builds elite core stability; Develops shoulder strength and stability; Foundational quadruped position; Progresses toward bear crawls; No equipment needed; Easy to scale by adjusting hold time
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core (entire trunk); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior; Hip flexors; Quadriceps

Exercise Name: Bench Dip with Legs on Bench
Description: Place two benches parallel about leg length apart. Sit on one bench and grip the edge with hands shoulder width apart. Place your heels on the second bench with legs straight. Lift the hips off the bench so your arms support your weight. Bend the elbows and lower your hips toward the floor. Keep the elbows tracking back and not flaring out. Stop when the upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor. Press through the palms back up to lockout and repeat.
Benefits: Hits the triceps hard with elevated bodyweight loading.; Engages the chest and front deltoids as supporting movers.; Builds upper body pushing strength without weights.; Easy to scale by adjusting bench heights.; Develops shoulder stability under bodyweight load.; Travel friendly with minimal equipment.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Anconeus

Description: Set up on hands and knees with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Brace the core and keep the back flat. Lift one leg with the knee bent and kick the foot straight back toward the ceiling. Squeeze the glute hard at the top of the back kick. Lower the knee back to start position. Lift the same leg and cross it over the standing knee toward the opposite side. Squeeze the side glute at the top of the cross. Continue alternating basic and cross kicks then switch sides.
Benefits: Hits the glute max with the straight back kick.; Targets the glute medius with the cross over.; Builds glute strength from two angles.; No equipment needed.; Improves hip mobility and stability.; Excellent finisher for glute training.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Sit on the edge of a bench with hands gripping the edge. Place the feet on top of a stability ball. Slide the hips off the bench. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lower the hips down by bending the elbows. Stop when the elbows reach about ninety degrees. Press through the palms to lock the elbows. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Trains the triceps; Builds core stability; Strong dip variation; Useful unstable surface; Builds the upper arms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anconeus

Description: Get into a quadruped position on hands and knees. Position your hands shoulder-width apart and knees under hips. Lift your knees to hover an inch off the floor (bear plank). Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Maintain a flat back parallel to the floor. Extend your right leg straight back, lifting it to hip height. Squeeze the right glute hard at the top of the kickback. Lower the leg back to the bear plank position. Alternate sides.
Benefits: Combines core stability with glute work; Builds glute strength; Strong anti-rotation core challenge; No equipment required; Builds hip and core control; Useful for athletic conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Rectus abdominis; Hamstrings; Obliques

Description: Lie face down on a flat bench with hips at the edge. Grip the bench for stability. Legs hang off the bench toward the floor. Lift both legs up by squeezing your glutes and extending your hips. Continue until your legs are in line with your body. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Hold briefly. Lower under control. Do not hyperextend your lower back. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Simple glute isolation on a bench; No specialized equipment needed; Builds hip extension strength; Useful warm-up or finisher; Beginner-friendly; Targets glutes directly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae (slight)

Description: Place a bench under a pull-up bar. Grip the bar. Place one or both feet on the bench. Use your legs for partial assistance while pulling up with your back and arms. Pull until your chin clears the bar. Lower under control. Use as little leg assistance as possible — focus on pulling with your back. Progress by using less leg drive over time. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Simple pull-up regression using a bench; Adjustable assistance — use less leg drive over time; Builds pulling strength toward full pull-ups; Minimal equipment needed; Natural movement pattern; Develops pull-up mechanics
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Forearms

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees, feet off the floor. Arms out to the sides. Keep your shoulders flat on the floor throughout. Drop both knees to the right side toward the floor. Go as far as comfortable while keeping shoulders down. Use your obliques to pull your knees back to center. Drop to the left side. Continue alternating. Aim for 10 to 15 drops per side.
Benefits: Mobilizes thoracic and lumbar spine; Builds oblique strength through rotation; Gentle and accessible; No equipment needed; Useful warm-up or cool-down; Promotes spinal health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Erector spinae; Hip rotators

Description: Lie on your back on a flat bench. Grip the bench overhead behind your head with both hands. Lift the legs straight up toward the ceiling. Brace your core hard. Begin circling the legs in big circles in the air. At the top of each circle reverse crunch the hips up off the bench. Lower the hips back down as the legs continue the circle. Continue circles in one direction. Reverse and repeat.
Benefits: Strong abs builder; Adds dynamic oblique work; Trains the hip flexors; Builds full core strength; Useful core finisher; Strong reverse crunch variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Lie on your right side. Bend both knees at 90 degrees. Place your right forearm on the floor, elbow under shoulder. Lift your hips off the floor. Support yourself on your forearm and knees. Body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Switch sides. The bent knees shorten the lever — much easier than full side plank. Progress to full side plank on feet when ready.
Benefits: Beginner regression for side planks; Shortened lever reduces difficulty; Builds oblique endurance for beginners; No equipment needed; Progressive toward full side plank; Safe and accessible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius; Core

Description: Stand on the center of a long towel with both feet. Grip both ends of the towel. Hinge forward at the hips. Pull up on both ends of the towel as if rowing — the towel resists your pull. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the row. Hold the peak contraction for 3 to 5 seconds. Release slightly, then pull again. Control your own resistance — pull harder for more difficulty. Perform 8 to 12 holds per set.
Benefits: Back training with zero equipment; Self-controlled resistance level; Isometric tension builds strength; Useful in hotel rooms or travel; Develops mind-muscle connection; Accessible anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip

Description: Get on your hands and knees in a tabletop position. Set the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips. Keep the working leg bent at 90 degrees. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Kick the bent leg up driving the heel toward the ceiling. Squeeze the glute hard at the top. Lower the knee back down with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Strong glute isolator; No equipment needed; Easy to scale; Builds glute size; Trains hip extension; Useful glute finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Lower back

Description: Lie on your back on the floor with hands behind your head, fingers lightly touching (do not pull on your neck). Lift both legs off the floor with knees bent at 90 degrees, shins parallel to the floor (tabletop position). Curl your upper body slightly off the floor. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Bring your right elbow toward your left knee while simultaneously extending your right leg straight out (parallel to the floor but not touching it). At the same time, pull your left knee toward your chest. Twist through the torso so your right elbow approaches the left knee. Reverse the motion by bringing your left elbow toward your right knee while extending your left leg and pulling your right knee toward your chest. Continue alternating in a smooth, controlled pedaling motion. Keep both shoulder blades off the floor throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps total (e.g., 20 = 10 per side).
Benefits: Trains both the rectus abdominis and obliques in one movement; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Builds core endurance and rotational strength; Easy to scale by changing tempo and rep count; Excellent core finisher; Improves hip mobility through the pedaling motion
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Internal and external obliques; Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis (stabilizer)

Description: Wrap a bed sheet around a sturdy door handle or fixed anchor at hip height. Grip both ends of the sheet with both hands. Step back to take tension on the sheet. Set the elbows tight against the sides. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Curl the hands up toward the shoulders pulling against the sheet. Apply self-resistance with the sheet to load the biceps. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Travel-friendly arm move; No equipment needed; Builds bicep size; Useful for hotel rooms; Strong creative arm move; Easy to scale by tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Lie on your back with hands behind your head, elbows out wide. Lift your shoulders off the floor and bring both knees up to 90 degrees. Brace your abs hard. Crunch up and twist to bring your right elbow toward your left knee. At the same time, extend your right leg straight out. Reverse the motion, twisting to bring the left elbow toward the right knee. Extend the left leg as the right knee comes up. Continue alternating in a smooth bicycle pedaling motion.
Benefits: Hits abs and obliques together; Builds rotational core strength; No equipment required; Strong rectus abdominis activation; Trains hip flexors; Classic ab exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (internal and external); Hip flexors

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Lower your chest to the floor in a controlled push-up. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Extend the right arm forward and the left leg back. Hold the bird dog position briefly. Return both limbs to the floor and complete another push-up. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Combines chest and core work; Builds anti-rotation core strength; Improves balance and stability; No equipment required; Useful for core conditioning; Time-efficient combo move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Core; Front deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Get on all fours. Hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Brace your core. Maintain a flat back. Simultaneously extend your right arm forward and left leg back. Hold for 5 to 10 seconds at full extension. Return to all fours. Extend left arm and right leg. Continue alternating. Aim for 8 to 10 holds per side. One of McGill’s “Big Three.”
Benefits: McGill’s “Big Three” core exercise; Builds anti-rotation core stability; Minimal spinal load — safe for back health; Develops glute and shoulder activation; No equipment needed; Evidence-based for back pain prevention
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core (anti-rotation); Gluteus maximus (extending leg); Anterior deltoid (extending arm); Erector spinae; Multifidus

Description: Get into a forearm plank position. Toes on the floor or on sliders. Brace your core hard. Rock your body forward by pushing through your toes — shoulders move past your elbows. Rock backward — shoulders move behind your elbows. Continue the rocking motion for the desired reps or time. The forward position is the hardest — shoulders far past elbows. Maintain a flat back throughout — no sagging or piking. Aim for 10 to 15 rocks or 30 to 45 seconds.
Benefits: Significantly harder than static planks; Dynamic anti-extension challenge; Continuously changing leverage makes it demanding; No equipment needed (sliders optional); Excellent plank progression; Builds advanced core stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Anterior deltoid (support); Serratus anterior

Description: Start in a forearm plank. Body straight, core braced. Press both hands into the floor simultaneously to push up to a high plank. Both arms extend at the same time — unlike alternating commando planks. Lower both forearms back to the floor simultaneously. Continue pressing up and lowering for reps. This requires significant tricep and shoulder strength. Maintain body alignment throughout. Aim for 5 to 10 reps.
Benefits: Simultaneous arm press builds tricep power; Harder than alternating commando planks; Develops explosive pressing from forearms; No equipment needed; Builds tricep and shoulder strength; Advanced plank variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (heavy); Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major; Core (anti-extension)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip width apart. Step one foot back so the toes line up with the front foot heel. Place hands behind the head with elbows wide. Brace the core and keep most of the weight on the front leg. Hinge at the hips by pushing the hips back. Keep the front leg slightly bent and the back foot light. Lower the torso until you feel a deep stretch in the front hamstring. Drive through the front heel to stand back up tall and complete all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds unilateral hamstring and glute strength.; B stance reveals and corrects imbalances.; Joint friendly bodyweight option.; Improves hip hinge mechanics.; No equipment needed.; Carryover to single leg deadlifts and lunges.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Adductors

Description: Place a sturdy bench (or chair) directly behind you. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Look forward. Sit your hips back as if reaching for the bench. Continue lowering until your butt touches the bench. Pause briefly when you touch the bench (do not collapse). Drive through your full feet to stand back up explosively. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for 10 to 20 reps. Adjust bench height for depth control.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly squat variation; Teaches consistent squat depth; Builds confidence in the squat pattern; Excellent for rehabilitation; Easy to set up at home; Builds toward unsupported squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Drop down quickly into a squat position by bending the knees and hips. Land softly with knees tracking over the toes. Continue down until thighs are parallel to the floor. As soon as you reach the bottom, drive up explosively. Jump up off the floor with full extension. Land softly and reset for the next rep.
Benefits: Builds reactive lower body power; Trains the stretch-shortening cycle; Strong plyometric stimulus; No equipment required; Develops athletic explosiveness; Useful for sports training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Gastrocnemius

Description: Place a small wedge, plate, or board behind you. Stand with the balls of your feet on the floor and heels on the elevation. Position your feet hip-width apart. Brace your core and stand tall. Squat down by sitting your hips back and bending the knees. Maintain an upright torso through the descent. Lower as deep as your mobility allows. Drive up through your heels to standing.
Benefits: Quad-focused squat pattern; Allows deeper squat depth; More upright torso position; Useful for quad specialization; Easier on lower back; No weights required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Sit on the floor with the soles of your feet pressed together. Let your knees fall out wide. Place your upper back against a sturdy bench. Brace your core and keep your chin tucked. Drive through the outer edges of your feet to lift your hips up. Reach a flat hip position with the body in a tabletop. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top. Lower the hips back down with control.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hamstrings; Gluteus medius

Description: Lie flat on the floor on your back. Press the soles of your feet together with knees out wide. Position your feet a foot or two from your hips. Place your hands at your sides for support. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Drive through the outer edges of your feet to lift your hips up. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top of each pump. Lower the hips back down and pump up again rapidly.
Benefits: High rep glute burnout; No equipment required; Hits outer glutes hard; Useful glute finisher; Easy to add to any session; Strong glute hypertrophy move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Gluteus medius

Exercise Name: Bodyweight Bent Over Rear Delt Fly
Description: Stand with the feet shoulder width apart. Hinge at the hips until the torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Allow the arms to hang straight down with palms facing each other. Brace the core and keep the back flat. Sweep the arms out to the sides by squeezing the shoulder blades. Stop at shoulder height with thumbs pointing up. Squeeze the rear delts and traps at the top. Lower the arms back down with control and repeat.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius; Rhomboids; Infraspinatus

Description: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench at about knee height. Place one foot flat on top of the box. Lean the torso forward at the hips with a flat back. Brace the core and shift your weight onto the front foot. Drive through the heel of the front foot to step up onto the box. Maintain the forward torso lean throughout the step up. Step back down with control, keeping the lean. Complete all reps on one side then switch legs.

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Place hands behind your head. Brace your core. Keep your back flat. Push your hips straight back and hinge forward at the waist. Continue until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Feel the stretch in your hamstrings. Drive your hips forward to stand. Squeeze your glutes. Maintain a flat back throughout. Aim for 12 to 15 reps as a warm-up.
Benefits: Teaches the hip hinge pattern with no load; Warms up the hamstrings and lower back; No equipment needed; Builds body awareness; Progression toward loaded good mornings; Excellent warm-up exercise

Exercise Name: Bodyweight Full Squat with Overhead Press
Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart and arms at your sides. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Squat down by sitting your hips back and bending the knees. Continue until your thighs are below parallel to the floor. Drive up through your heels to standing. As you stand tall, press your arms straight overhead. Lock out the arms with hands above your head. Lower the arms back to your sides as you start the next squat.

Description: Kneel on the floor with knees padded and feet planted behind you. Press your hips forward and squeeze your glutes. Brace your core and stand tall through the torso. Place your hands on your hips or extend them forward for balance. Slowly lean your torso backward by hinging only at the knees. Keep the hips and torso in a straight line. Continue until you feel a deep stretch in the quads. Drive back up to the upright position by squeezing the quads.

Description: Set up a sturdy bench or low surface. Place one hand on the edge of the bench. Walk the feet out to the side until the body is in a straight line. Stack the feet or place the top foot in front for stability. Brace your core and squeeze the bottom obliques. Hold the body in a straight diagonal line. Reach the top arm up to the ceiling for full effect. Hold the position for time. Switch sides and repeat.

Description: Get into a kneeling plank position with hands shoulder-width apart. Position your knees on the floor with body in a straight line from knees to head. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Lower your chest to the floor in a kneeling push up. Press back up to the starting position. Pull your right elbow back in a rowing motion, lifting the hand off the floor. Lower the right hand back to the floor. Repeat the push up and alternate the rowing arm.

Description: Begin in a tall kneeling position with both knees on the floor. Brace the core and keep the chest tall. Step one foot forward into a half kneeling position. Drive through the front heel to stand up to a tall stance. Stand fully tall with both feet under the hips. Step the same foot back and lower into the half kneeling position. Lower the back knee to return to the tall kneeling start. Repeat on the same side then switch.

Description: Lie on your side with the bottom arm under your head for support. Bend the top elbow to 90 degrees with the upper arm against your side. The forearm should rest across the abdomen. Brace the core and keep the upper arm pinned against the body. Rotate the forearm up by externally rotating the shoulder. Stop when the forearm is roughly vertical. Lower the forearm slowly back to the abdomen. Complete all reps on one side then switch.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Infraspinatus; Posterior deltoid; Trapezius

Description: Stand with feet narrower than shoulder-width, almost together. Hold your arms out in front for balance. Brace your core and stand tall. Squat down by bending your knees and hips. Keep your knees tracking over your toes. Allow your torso to lean slightly forward as you descend for balance. Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor or as deep as mobility allows. Drive up through your heels to stand back to the starting position.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors

Description: Kneel on a pad in front of a sturdy bench. Place the hands on the edge of the bench at shoulder width. Walk the knees back so the body forms a straight diagonal line. Set the upper arms parallel to the floor. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the body by bending the elbows toward the bench. Stop just before the forehead touches the bench. Press back up to extension by extending the elbows.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold your arms out in front for balance. Squat down until your thighs are parallel to the floor. From the parallel position, rise up only a few inches. Drop back down to the parallel squat position. Continue pulsing in the bottom range with short reps. Maintain an upright torso and bracing throughout. Continue for the duration of the set.
Benefits: Continuous tension on quads and glutes; Builds muscular endurance; Strong leg burn; No equipment required; Useful as a finisher; Easy to scale by changing depth
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Calves

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hands on hips or at your sides. Step your right foot back two to three feet. Lower your right knee toward the floor. Drive through your front (left) foot to return to standing. Alternate legs. Keep torso upright throughout. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per leg. Progress to weighted reverse lunges when ready.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Raise both arms straight overhead, biceps by your ears. Maintain the overhead arm position throughout. Squat down while keeping arms overhead. Descend as deep as your mobility allows. Keep arms directly above your midfoot — they should not drift forward. Drive through your feet to stand. If your arms fall forward, your thoracic or shoulder mobility needs work. Aim for 10 to 15 reps or use as a mobility assessment.
Benefits: Tests and develops total-body mobility; Assesses shoulder, thoracic, hip, and ankle mobility; Reveals movement weaknesses; No equipment needed; Useful coaching assessment tool; Progression toward loaded overhead squats

Description: Stand in front of a sturdy doorway and grip both sides of the frame. Walk your feet forward until your body leans back at an angle. Keep your arms straight and the body in a straight line. Brace your core and squeeze your shoulder blades down. Pull your chest toward the doorway by bending your elbows. Drive your elbows back and squeeze the upper back. Pause briefly at the top close to the frame. Lower with control back to arms straight.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Middle trapezius

Description: Set a sturdy bar or bench at chest height. Stand facing away from the bar. Reach overhead behind the head and grip the bar. Step the feet forward so the body leans back at an angle. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the body by bending the elbows behind the head. Stop when the elbows are fully bent. Press back up to extension by extending the elbows.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with hands shoulder-width apart and arms fully extended. Allow your shoulders to relax with shoulder blades pulled up toward your ears initially. Brace your core. Without bending your elbows, pull your shoulders down and back. Engage your lats and depress your scapulae fully. Hold the depressed position briefly. Allow your shoulders to passively elevate back to the starting position. Maintain straight arms throughout the entire movement.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Latissimus dorsi; Serratus anterior

Description: Stand tall in a split stance with right foot forward. Position your feet about a leg-length apart. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Lower into a deep split squat by bending both knees. Continue until your back knee almost touches the floor. Maintain an upright torso through the descent. Drive up through the front foot to standing. Complete reps on one side, then switch.

Description: Stand on your right leg. Arms at your sides or extended forward. Hinge at the right hip — push your left leg straight behind you as your torso lowers. Your body should form a straight line from your left heel to your head. Continue until you feel a hamstring stretch in your right leg. Drive through your right hip to stand back up. Complete reps, then switch legs. Move slowly and with control. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per leg.
Benefits: Teaches single-leg hinge pattern; Builds balance and proprioception; Develops hamstring flexibility; No equipment needed; Progression toward loaded single-leg deadlifts; Excellent warm-up exercise

Exercise Name: Bodyweight Single Leg KAS Glute Bridge

Brace the core and squeeze the glute on the working side. Lower the hips just slightly from the top position. Drive back up to lockout by squeezing the glute hard. Keep the range short and the tension on the glute. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.

Description: Stand on your right leg. Hinge at the right hip — push your left leg straight behind you. Lower your torso until you feel a hamstring stretch. Drive through your right hip to stand. Complete reps, then switch legs. Move slowly for balance. Arms can extend forward for counterbalance. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per leg.
Benefits: Teaches the single-leg hinge pattern; Builds balance and proprioception; Develops hamstring flexibility; No equipment needed; Progression toward loaded versions; Excellent warm-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer); Gluteus medius (balance)

Description: Stand facing a sturdy vertical pole, post, or door frame at arms length. Grip the pole firmly with both hands at chest height. Step your feet forward so you can lean back slightly with arms straight. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Squat down by bending the knees and hinging at the hips, leaning back as you descend. Allow your arms to extend fully at the bottom. Drive up through your heels while pulling yourself toward the pole with your arms. Return to the starting position with arms straight and chest tall.

Description: Stand with your back flat against a sturdy wall. Walk the feet out and slide down until the thighs are parallel to the floor. Set the feet hip width apart at first. Brace your core and keep the back flat on the wall. Lift one foot off the floor and extend the leg out straight. Keep the working leg in the wall sit position. Hold the single leg wall sit for time. Place the foot back down. Switch legs and repeat.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder width apart. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Begin lowering slowly into a squat over several seconds. Continue lowering until the thighs are parallel to the floor. Hold the bottom briefly. Drive through the heels and explode up powerfully. Either jump or rise quickly to a hard standing lockout. Land softly and reset for the next rep.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Calves

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Place your hands on a wall or chair for balance if needed. Brace your core. Stand evenly on both feet. Slowly rise up onto the balls of your feet by extending at the ankles. Continue rising until you are on your toes at full ankle extension. Squeeze your calves hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control over two to three seconds. For deeper range, perform on the edge of a step so heels can drop below the step level. Aim for 15 to 30 reps per set.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus (secondary); Tibialis posterior; Foot intrinsic muscles

Exercise Name: Bodyweight Standing Close Grip One Arm Row
Description: Stand facing a sturdy vertical anchor like a pole or door frame. Grip the anchor with one hand at chest height in a close neutral grip. Walk your feet forward so your bodyweight is leaning back on the arm. Brace the core and keep the body straight from heels to head. Pull your chest toward the hand by driving the elbow back. Keep the elbow tucked and squeeze the lat at the top. Lower yourself back to full arm extension under control. Complete all reps on one side then switch arms.
Benefits: Builds unilateral back strength using only bodyweight.; Trains anti rotation as the working side resists twisting.; Strengthens the biceps and forearms through the pull.; No equipment beyond a sturdy anchor needed.; Easy to adjust difficulty by changing foot position.; Develops grip and core stability simultaneously.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Core

Description: Place the hands on the floor near a wall. Kick up into a handstand with the heels touching the wall. Set the hands shoulder width apart. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Lower the body by bending the elbows. Stop just above the floor with the head near the hands. Press back up to lockout. Continue for the working set.

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Make a fist with one hand and place it inside the open palm of the other hand at chest level. Press the fist into the palm to create constant tension. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Press both hands together straight overhead. Maintain the isometric pressure between the hands throughout. Lock out at the top with arms straight. Lower the hands slowly back to chest level.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core

Description: Find a sturdy upright pole or support post. Grip the support with both hands close together. Lean back with the arms straight and feet planted. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the chest toward the support by bending the elbows. Squeeze the lats and upper back at the top. Lower with control to the start.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius

Description: Stand with the feet hip width apart. Set the toes pointing straight ahead. Brace your core and keep the legs straight. Press up onto the balls of the feet. Hold near the top of the calf raise. Lower a few inches and press back up in small pulses. Keep the pulses short and controlled. Continue until the calves fatigue.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Stand in front of a sturdy upright support. Grip the support with one hand at chest height. Lean back with the arm straight and feet planted. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Pinch the working shoulder blade back. Pull the chest toward the support by bending the elbow. Squeeze the lat and upper back at the top. Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids

Description: Stand facing a sturdy step box or low platform. Place one foot fully flat on top of the box. Drive through the front heel to step up onto the box. Stand tall with both feet on the box at the top. Step the same foot back down to the floor. Step the other foot down to return to the start. Repeat with the opposite leg leading the next step up. Continue alternating sides for the full set.

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Clasp hands together in front of you. Hinge at the hips. Swing your clasped hands between your legs. Drive your hips forward explosively. Your arms swing up to chest or eye height from the hip drive. Let your arms swing back between your legs as you hinge again. Continue the swing-hinge rhythm. The power comes from the hips — not the arms. Aim for 15 to 25 reps as a drill or warm-up.

Description: Stand tall with feet at hip-width and a clear path ahead. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Take a step forward with your right foot. As you plant the foot, rise onto the ball of the foot. Push off through the toes and bring the back foot through. Plant the left foot and rise onto the ball of that foot. Continue walking forward with a high toe raise on every step. Keep the rhythm smooth and the cadence steady.

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Rise up onto the balls of your feet. Press your hips forward and squeeze your glutes. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Hold a stable surface for balance if needed. Slowly lean your torso backward by hinging only at the knees. Keep your hips, torso, and shoulders in a straight line. Drive back up by squeezing the quads to the starting position.

Description: Position yourself under a pull-up bar with parallel handles or a v-grip attachment. Grip the parallel handles with palms facing each other, hands shoulder-width or closer. Hang from the bar with arms fully extended. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down. Pull your body up by bending at the elbows and driving them down toward your sides. Continue until your chin clears the handles or your chest reaches them. Squeeze your biceps and brachialis at the top. Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Close neutral grip targets brachialis; Builds arm thickness; Strong bicep engagement; Easier on the wrists than chin ups; Functional pulling pattern; Develops back and arm strength simultaneously
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachialis; Biceps brachii; Latissimus dorsi; Brachioradialis; Trapezius (middle)

Description: Grip parallel pull-up handles with a neutral grip (palms facing each other). Hang with arms fully extended. Pull yourself up until your chin clears the handles. Squeeze your back and arms at the top. Lower under control over 2 to 3 seconds. The neutral grip reduces bicep involvement and increases brachialis demand. Aim for 6 to 12 reps per set. Add weight when bodyweight becomes easy.
Benefits: Targets the brachialis for upper arm thickness; Neutral grip is often most comfortable for shoulders; Builds back pulling strength; Different stimulus than overhand or underhand grips; Easy on the wrists; Develops grip strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Brachialis (increased); Brachioradialis; Biceps brachii; Trapezius (lower); Forearms

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over Neutral Grip Kickback with Rope Attachment
Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting and attach a rope. Stand facing the cable holding one rope end in each hand. Hinge at the hips so the torso is angled forward. Tuck the elbows close to the sides at ninety degrees. Brace the core and keep the upper arms still. Extend the elbows back by squeezing the triceps. Stop at full extension with the rope ends pulled apart. Lower with control and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Isolates the triceps long head.; Cable provides constant tension throughout.; Rope allows the hands to separate at lockout.; Carryover to pressing strength.; Easy to scale by adjusting cable weight.; Develops triceps lockout strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set two cable pulleys to the lowest position. Place a flat bench between them. Lie on the bench. Grip a D-handle in each hand at chest level. Press both handles up and together above your chest. Squeeze your chest hard at the top — handles can converge for peak contraction. Lower under control back to your chest. Maintain constant cable tension. Never let the weight stack rest. Keep your elbows at roughly 45 degrees. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension including at lockout; Converging press path for peak chest squeeze; Easy to load progressively; Joint-friendly; Excellent for chest hypertrophy; Different resistance curve than barbell
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over Reverse Grip Row
Description: Set a cable to a low position with a straight bar attached. Stand facing the cable and grab the bar with an underhand grip. Step back and hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Keep a slight bend in your knees. Brace your core and let your arms hang straight down toward the cable. Pull the bar back toward your lower abdomen. Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides. Squeeze the lats and lower back, then return slowly.
Benefits: Targets the lower lats; Adds biceps involvement; Constant cable tension; Builds back thickness; Strong reverse grip variation; Useful for hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Rear deltoid

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over One Arm Lateral Raise
Description: Set a cable to the lowest setting with a single handle. Stand sideways to the cable stack. Grip the handle in the far hand reaching across the body. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Raise the working arm out to the side until parallel to the floor. Squeeze the rear delt hard at the top. Lower with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong rear delt isolation; Constant cable tension; Trains the rhomboids; Builds upper back thickness; Useful posture builder; Strong cable move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Trapezius

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over Row with Rope Attachment
Description: Attach a rope to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable with the feet hip width apart. Grip the rope ends with a neutral grip. Hinge at the hips until the torso is at a forty five degree angle. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Pull the rope toward the lower ribs. Flare the elbows out as the rope reaches the body. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Trains the upper back; Strong rope row; Constant cable tension; Builds the lats; Useful back builder; Trains the rear delts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over Row with Bar
Description: Attach a straight bar to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the machine with feet at shoulder-width. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and slight knee bend. Grip the bar with hands wider than shoulder-width. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Row the bar up to your lower chest by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row. Lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Constant cable tension; Builds upper back strength; Trains the lats and rhomboids; Strong bent over row variation; Excellent back day move; Adjustable resistance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Middle trapezius

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over Single Arm Kickback
Description: Set a cable to a low position with a single handle attached. Stand sideways to the cable in a hinged position. Grip the handle with the working arm. Pin the working elbow at the side at hip height. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Extend the arm straight back. Squeeze the tricep hard at full extension. Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Constant tension on triceps; Strong unilateral move; Builds the triceps; Useful tricep finisher; Trains each side; Builds the upper arms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Posterior deltoid

Description: Attach a straight bar or two D-handles to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine with feet hip-width apart. Grip the attachment. Step back, then hinge forward at the hips until your torso is at roughly 45 degrees from horizontal. Let your arms hang fully extended with the cable under tension. Brace your core and lock in your back angle. Row the attachment to your lower chest or upper abdomen by driving your elbows up and back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Pause briefly. Slowly extend your arms back to the start position. Maintain cable tension and your torso angle throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the entire range; Excellent for high-rep hypertrophy back work; Multiple attachment options for different stimuli; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Builds the lats, mid-traps, rhomboids, and rear delts; Easier to maintain strict form than free-weight rows
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip; Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or EZ bar. Grip the bar with hands about 6 inches apart (narrow grip), palms up. Stand tall. Pin your elbows at your sides. Curl the bar up toward your shoulders. Squeeze your biceps at the top. Focus on the outer head contraction. Lower under control over two seconds. Keep your upper arms still — only your forearms move. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Emphasizes the long (outer) head of the bicep; Builds bicep width from the front; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Different stimulus than wide-grip curls; Useful for complete bicep development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long head emphasis); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Exercise Name: Cable Close Grip Front Lat Pulldown
Description: Sit at a cable lat pulldown machine with thighs under the pads. Attach a close grip V-handle to the cable. Reach up and grab the handle with a neutral grip. Sit upright with a slight backward lean. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Pull the handle down to your upper chest. Keep your elbows tucked close to your sides. Squeeze the lats hard, then return slowly to the start.
Benefits: Targets the lower lats; Builds lat thickness; Adds biceps work; Strong neutral grip variation; Constant cable tension; Useful for back hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Rear deltoid

Exercise Name: Cable Bent Over Single Arm Neutral Grip Kickback with Rope
Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest setting and attach a rope. Stand facing the cable holding one end of the rope with one hand. Hinge at the hips so the torso is angled forward. Place the other hand on the thigh for support. Tuck the working elbow close to the side at ninety degrees. Brace the core and keep the upper arm still. Extend the elbow back by squeezing the triceps. Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Isolates one triceps at a time.; Cable provides constant tension throughout.; Neutral grip is shoulder friendly.; Carryover to pressing strength.; Improves arm symmetry.; Develops triceps lockout strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Posterior deltoid

Description: Stand between two high cable pulleys with single handles attached. Reach across with your right hand to grip the left cable handle. Reach across with your left hand to grip the right cable handle. Step back to create tension and stand tall. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down. Pull both handles down and out to your sides simultaneously. Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom of the pull. Slowly extend your arms back overhead to the starting position.
Benefits: Crossing tension hits each lat individually; Different angle than standard pulldown; Strong lat engagement; Builds back width; Constant cable tension through the pull; Useful for breaking through lat plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Teres major; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a low cable pulley with a D-handle. Place a bench near the cable. Sit on the bench facing the cable. Grip the handle with your right hand. Brace the back of your right upper arm against the inside of your right thigh. Curl the handle up by bending at the elbow. Keep your upper arm braced against your thigh. Continue until the handle reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your bicep hard for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Maintain cable tension throughout. Complete all reps on one side, then switch. Use moderate weight — contraction quality is the priority.
Benefits: Combines concentration curl strictness with constant cable tension; Maximum peak bicep contraction; Eliminates all body english; Excellent bicep finishing exercise; Easy to load progressively; Builds bicep peak and detail
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially the short head); Brachialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Set the cable pulleys at or slightly above shoulder height for a standard mid-chest crossover. Attach a single-grip handle to each pulley. Grasp the handles with palms facing forward or down. Step forward with one foot in a staggered stance for stability and walk far enough away from the stack that there is constant tension on the cables in the start position. Start with your arms out to the sides, slightly in front of your body, with a soft bend in your elbows. Keeping that elbow bend locked in, bring your hands together in front of your chest in a sweeping arc, leading with your elbows. Squeeze your chest hard at the bottom for a one-second peak contraction. Hands can meet, cross slightly, or stop just short depending on shoulder comfort. Slowly return the handles to the start position under control, feeling a stretch across your chest. Do not let the weight stack slam down. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Set the pulleys low to bias the upper chest, or high to bias the lower chest.
Benefits: Provides constant tension on the chest throughout the entire range of motion; Allows you to target the upper or lower chest by adjusting pulley height; Easier on the shoulders than dumbbell flys for many lifters; Excellent finishing exercise after compound chest pressing; Lets you train the chest without holding heavy free weights overhead
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (upper, middle, and lower fibers depending on pulley height); Pectoralis minor; Anterior deltoid (secondary); Serratus anterior (stabilizer)

Description: Attach a straight bar, EZ bar, or rope handle to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Step back slightly so the cable is under tension with your arms fully extended. Stand tall. Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and pin your elbows against your sides. Curl the bar up by bending only at the elbows. Keep your elbows pinned to your sides. Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps hard for one second. Lower the bar under control over two seconds. Maintain constant cable tension — do not let the weight stack touch down. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the entire range of motion; Loads the top and bottom positions better than free weights; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Multiple attachment options for different stimuli; Excellent for high-rep bicep finishing work; Easier to maintain strict form than free-weight curls
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long and short heads); Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Stand in the center of a cable crossover machine. Reach across and grab the right handle with your left hand. Reach across and grab the left handle with your right hand (arms crossed). Brace your core and keep your chest up. Hinge slightly at the hips with a small bend in the elbows. Sweep your arms out and back to your sides in a reverse fly motion. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end range. Return slowly to the crossed position.
Benefits: Builds rear delt thickness; Constant cable tension; Hits the upper back; Improves posture; Useful for shoulder balance; Strong rear delt isolation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rear deltoid; Rhomboids; Traps

Exercise Name: Cable Decline Seated Wide Grip Row
Description: Set a low or decline bench in front of a cable machine. Attach a long bar or wide-grip handle to the cable. Sit on the bench facing the cable. Grab the bar with a wide overhand grip. Lean back slightly and brace your core. Pull the bar back toward your upper chest. Lead with the elbows out to the sides at shoulder height. Squeeze the upper back hard, then return slowly.
Benefits: Builds upper back detail; Targets rhomboids and rear delts; Constant cable tension; Improves posture; Strong upper back builder; Reduces lower back stress
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rhomboids; Rear deltoid; Traps; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Attach an ankle strap to the low cable pulley and to one ankle. Get on all fours facing the cable machine. Position your hands under your shoulders and knees under your hips. Brace your core to keep a flat back. Drive the working leg back and out at a 45-degree angle. Squeeze the glute hard at the top of the kick. Pause briefly at full extension. Return slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Hits glute max and glute medius together; Sculpts the entire glute complex; Constant cable tension throughout the rep; Reduces lower back loading; Builds glute strength and shape; Useful for hip stability work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings

Description: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley. Wrap the strap around your right ankle. Face the cable machine on your hands and knees, with the cable running between your legs. Place your hands directly under your shoulders. Set your back flat. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Keep your right knee bent at roughly 90 degrees throughout the movement. Kick your right leg back and up by extending at the hip, driving your heel toward the ceiling. Lead with the heel. Continue extending until your right thigh is in line with your torso (or slightly higher). Squeeze your glute hard for one to two seconds. Lower the leg under control back to the start position. Maintain cable tension throughout. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch the strap to the left ankle.
Benefits: Direct gluteus maximus isolation; Constant cable tension throughout the entire range of motion; Excellent peak contraction at the top; Trains one side at a time, exposing imbalances; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Excellent finisher for glute workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (secondary); Erector spinae (stabilizer); Core (anti-rotation)

Description: Attach a straight bar to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Stand tall with chest up. Begin curling the bar up by bending at the elbows. As you curl, pull your elbows back behind your body. The bar should drag straight up your torso. Continue until the bar reaches your upper chest. Keep elbows back. Squeeze your biceps hard at the top. Lower under control, allowing your elbows to return to your sides as the bar lowers.
Benefits: Unique bicep stimulus through elbow path; Constant cable tension throughout; Provides variation from standard curls; Builds bicep peak; Engages the brachialis; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Set a cable pulley to a high position. Attach a V-bar or rope handle. Sit or stand facing the cable. Grip the handle. Start with arms extended toward the high cable. Row the handle down and toward your upper chest by driving your elbows back and down. Squeeze your upper back and rear delts at the end of the row. Slowly extend back to the start. Maintain upright posture throughout. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to rear delts and upper traps; Different angle than horizontal rows; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Builds upper back thickness; Useful for shoulder balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (upper and middle); Rhomboids; Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or rope handle. Face the cable. Grip the handle. Step back until the cable is taut. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back. Let the cable pull the handle forward. Lower until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings. Back flat. Drive your hips forward to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Constant cable tension at the top — unlike a barbell. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension including at the top; Teaches the hip hinge pattern; Builds glutes and hamstrings; Easy to load progressively; Less spinal loading than barbell deadlifts; Useful for hypertrophy focus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Set an adjustable bench to a decline of roughly 15 to 30 degrees and place it between two cable stations with high pulleys. Attach a single-handle (D-handle) to each high pulley. Sit on the bench and lock your feet under the leg pads. Grab one handle in each hand and lie back. Pull your shoulders down and back, plant yourself firmly against the bench, and lift your chest. Start with the handles held out to your sides at roughly chest height, arms slightly bent. The cables should be under tension at the start. Bring both handles together in a wide arc down toward your lower chest, ending with the handles touching above your sternum or just below. Squeeze your chest hard for one second at the peak. Maintain the slight elbow bend throughout. Let the handles travel back out under control over two to three seconds. Feel the stretch in your chest.
Benefits: Targets the lower (sternal) chest with constant cable tension; Long range of motion with a deep stretch at the bottom; Builds lower chest size that flat or incline work may miss; Excellent finisher for complete chest development; Easier on the shoulders than dumbbell decline flys; Easy to load in small increments
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially the sternal/lower head); Anterior deltoid (secondary); Biceps brachii (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Set an incline bench in the center of a cable crossover machine. Set both cables to a low or mid position. Stand behind the bench and grab a handle in each hand. Lean forward with your chest against the bench backrest. Allow your arms to extend out to your sides with a slight bend in the elbows. Brace your core and keep your chest pressed against the bench. Sweep your arms forward and together in front of your chest. Squeeze the chest at the meeting point and lower slowly.
Benefits: Strictest cable fly variation; Eliminates torso swing; Constant cable tension; Builds chest size and shape; Strong peak contraction; Reduces lower back stress
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Front deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable pulley to a low position behind you. Attach a single handle or rope. Face away from the cable. Hold the handle at your chest or shoulders. Step forward into a lunge against the cable tension. Lower your back knee toward the floor. Drive through your front foot to return to standing. The cable pulls you backward — brace your core to resist. Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per leg.
Benefits: Cable adds backward resistance to lunges; Challenges core anti-extension during the lunge; Constant cable tension throughout; Easy to load progressively; Builds leg strength with added core demand; Unique loading pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (anti-extension); Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Cable Floor Seated Wide Grip Row
Description: Sit on the floor in front of a low cable pulley. Attach a long bar or wide-grip handle to the cable. Plant your feet flat on the floor with knees bent. Grab the bar with a wide overhand grip and arms extended. Brace your core and sit upright. Pull the bar back toward your upper chest. Lead with the elbows out to the sides at shoulder height. Squeeze the upper back, then return slowly to the start.
Benefits: Builds upper back detail; Targets rhomboids and rear delts; No bench required; Strict floor seated form; Strong upper back builder; Beginner-friendly variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rhomboids; Rear deltoid; Traps; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle or straight bar. Stand facing away from the cable. Grip the handle between your legs or at your side. Stand tall. Brace your core. Raise the handle straight up in front of you to shoulder height with a straight arm. Squeeze your front delt at the top. Pause briefly. Lower under control over two seconds. Maintain a slight elbow bend throughout. Complete reps, then switch arms if using a single handle.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the range; Excellent front delt isolation; Easy to load progressively; Joint-friendly; Different resistance curve than dumbbells; Useful for shoulder hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (primary); Lateral deltoid (slight); Upper trapezius (slight); Pectoralis major (clavicular, slight)

Description: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle. Face away from the cable. Grip the handle behind you between your legs. Stand tall. Arm straight with slight elbow bend. Raise the handle forward to shoulder height. Squeeze the front delt. Pause briefly. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch arms (or use both arms with a bar attachment). Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the range; Superior to dumbbells for bottom-range tension; Easy to load progressively; Strict front delt isolation; Joint-friendly; Useful for shoulder hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (primary); Lateral deltoid (slight); Upper trapezius (slight)

Description: Sit at a low cable row station with feet braced on the platform. Grip a v-handle or close grip attachment with both hands. Sit tall with chest up and arms extended forward. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Row the handle to your lower chest by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Slowly extend your arms back to the starting position. Maintain an upright torso throughout. Avoid rocking back and forth.
Benefits: Builds back thickness; Constant cable tension through the range; Eliminates lower back stress; Strong lat and rhomboid engagement; Foundation rowing movement; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle and lower); Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle or straight bar. Face away from the cable. Grip the handle between your legs or at your side. Stand tall. Brace your core. Raise the handle forward to shoulder height with a straight arm. Squeeze your front delt at the top. Lower under control. Maintain slight elbow bend. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Constant cable tension for front delt isolation; Tension even at the bottom of the raise; Easy to load progressively; Strict isolation; Joint-friendly; Different resistance curve than dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (primary); Lateral deltoid (slight); Upper trapezius (slight)

Description: Set two low cable pulleys with D-handle attachments. Stand between them. Grip the right cable handle with your left hand and the left handle with your right hand (cables cross in front). Bring both handles up to your chest in a front rack position. Step forward to create cable tension. Stand tall. Brace your core. Position feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out. Sit straight down with an upright torso. Descend until your hip crease drops below your knees. Drive through your feet to stand. Keep handles at chest throughout.
