Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (especially the long head); Anconeus; Anterior deltoid (isometric); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Attach a rope handle to the low pulley of a seated row machine. Sit with feet on the platform, knees slightly bent. Lean forward, grip both ends of the rope with a neutral grip, and sit up tall. Set your start position: chest tall, shoulders down and back, core braced, arms extended. Row the rope toward your lower abdomen by driving your elbows back. Keep elbows close to your body. As the rope approaches your abdomen, split the ends apart by pulling your hands to each side of your torso. Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard at the peak. Pause briefly. Slowly extend your arms forward to the start. Feel the stretch in your lats. Do not rock. Keep your torso roughly vertical throughout.
Benefits: Neutral grip is easier on the wrists and shoulders; Rope allows a longer range of motion at the peak contraction; Splitting the rope at the top maximizes back contraction; Constant cable tension throughout the range; Excellent for high-rep mid-back volume; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip

Description: Set two cable pulleys at shoulder height. Place a bench with back support between them. Sit on the bench. Grip both D-handles with arms extended to the sides. Maintain a slight bend in your elbows throughout. Bring both handles together in front of your chest in a wide arc. Squeeze your chest hard when hands meet. Slowly open your arms back to the sides under control. Maintain constant cable tension. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through the full fly arc; Seated position provides back support; Excellent chest isolation; Easy to load progressively; Joint-friendly; Superior to dumbbell fly for constant tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Set two cable pulleys at chest height. Place a flat bench between them. Sit on the bench. Grip the D-handles at your chest, elbows at roughly 45 degrees. Press both handles forward simultaneously until arms are extended. Squeeze your chest and triceps at lockout. Slowly return the handles to your chest under control. Maintain constant cable tension — never let the weight stack rest. Keep your back pressed against the bench for support. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the press; Seated position provides back support; Easy to load progressively; Converging press path for peak contraction; Joint-friendly; Excellent for chest hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Set both cable pulleys to chest height when seated. Sit on a bench facing away from the cable stack. Grip a handle in each hand at chest level with palms facing forward. Hold the handles close together with elbows tucked. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Press both handles forward and slightly up until your arms are fully extended. Bring the handles together at the front of the press. Squeeze the triceps and inner chest, then lower with control.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through the range; Targets triceps with close grip; Seated position eliminates leg drive; Builds inner chest as well as triceps; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong lockout development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major (inner fibers); Anterior deltoid

Description: Set a cable to chest height and attach a single handle. Sit on a bench or the floor sideways to the cable stack. Reach across the body with the far hand to grip the handle. Brace your core and set the chest tall. Keep the hips facing forward and arms slightly bent. Twist the torso away from the cable pulling the handle across the body. Squeeze the obliques hard at the end range. Rotate back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Trains rotational core; Constant cable tension; Strong cable move; Useful core finisher; Builds rotational power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Sit at a cable row station. Attach a rope handle to the low cable. Grip the rope with both hands, palms facing each other. Row the rope toward your lower ribs. At the end of the row, flare the rope ends apart — pull them to the sides of your body. Squeeze your shoulder blades and rear delts at the fully flared position. Slowly return the rope forward, bringing the ends back together. The flare is the key — it adds rear delt and rhomboid activation. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Flaring action activates rear delts and rhomboids; Builds upper back thickness; Constant cable tension; Combines rowing with rear delt squeeze; Easy to load progressively; Useful for posture and shoulder balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Posterior deltoid (flare); Rhomboids (flare); Trapezius (middle); Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or EZ bar handle. Place a flat bench facing the cable. Sit on the bench. Grip the handle with an underhand grip. Arms extended toward the cable. Curl the handle toward your shoulders by bending at the elbows. Squeeze your biceps at the top. Lower under control. The seated position prevents any body swing or momentum. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Strict bicep isolation from seated position; Eliminates body english and momentum; Constant cable tension throughout; Easy to load progressively; Builds bicep strength with perfect form; Useful for hypertrophy focus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Set a cable pulley to a high position. Attach a rope handle. Sit on a bench or the floor facing away from the cable. Hold the rope behind your head with both hands near your ears. Sit up tall to start. Brace your core. Crunch forward by flexing your spine — bring your chest toward your knees. Squeeze your abs hard at the bottom of the crunch. Slowly return to the upright position under control. Keep constant cable tension. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension on the abs; Allows progressive overload beyond bodyweight; Seated position is comfortable; Easy to load progressively; Excellent for ab hypertrophy; Different angle than kneeling cable crunches
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors (slight)

Exercise Name: Cable Seated Floor One Arm Concentration Curl
Description: Set a cable to the lowest setting with a single handle. Sit on the floor in front of the cable stack. Set the feet wide and bend the knees out. Grip the handle with one hand and brace the elbow on the inner thigh. Brace your core and lean slightly forward. Curl the handle up toward the shoulder. Squeeze the bicep hard at the top. Lower back down with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong bicep peak builder; Constant cable tension; Trains unilateral biceps; Useful arm finisher; Strong cable move; Builds bicep size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Attach an ankle strap to the low cable pulley. Sit on the floor or a bench with the cable to one side. Strap the cable to the foot farther from the cable. Extend the working leg straight in front of you. Keep the knee straight and the leg still. Turn the foot outward, away from your body. Pause briefly at the end range. Return slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Strengthens the peroneal muscles; Improves lateral ankle stability; Reduces risk of ankle rolls; Useful in ankle rehab; Builds lower leg balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Peroneals; Calves; Tibialis anterior

Description: Attach an ankle cuff to a low cable pulley. Sit on a bench facing away from the pulley with the cuff on your right ankle. Position the bench so the cable runs along the side of the bench. Sit tall with chest up and grip the bench for stability. Brace your core and extend your right knee fully. Lift your shin until your leg is straight and parallel to the floor. Squeeze your quad hard at the top of the extension. Lower the leg back down with control. Complete reps, then switch legs.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through the range; Single-leg work corrects imbalances; No leg extension machine required; Builds quad size and strength; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong peak contraction
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus femoris; Vastus lateralis; Vastus medialis; Vastus intermedius

Description: Sit at a low cable row station with a v-handle or close grip attachment. Brace your feet on the platform with knees slightly bent. Grip the handle with palms facing up (underhand grip). Sit tall with chest up and arms extended forward. Brace your core. Pull the handle to your lower abdomen by driving the elbows back along your sides. Keep elbows tucked tight to the body throughout the pull. Squeeze the lats hard, then extend the arms forward with control.
Benefits: Underhand grip emphasizes lat involvement; Tucked elbow path targets lats; Builds lat thickness; Strong bicep involvement; Constant cable tension; Useful for lat specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle)

Description: Sit at a cable row station with a single bar or rope attachment at chest height. Grip the attachment with both hands and arms extended forward. Sit tall with chest up and feet braced. Brace your core. Without bending your elbows, retract your shoulder blades back and together. Allow the attachment to pull back slightly with the scapular movement. Squeeze your middle traps and rhomboids hard at the back position. Slowly extend your shoulder blades forward to the starting position.
Benefits: Strict scapular retractor isolation; Builds middle traps and rhomboids; Improves posture; Useful for shoulder health; No elbow bending isolates the shrug; Strong functional movement for posture
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Cable Seated on Floor Row with Rope
Description: Sit on the floor in front of a low cable pulley. Grip the rope ends with a neutral grip. Extend the legs forward with knees slightly bent. Sit tall with the chest up and back straight. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the rope toward the lower ribs. Flare the elbows out as the rope reaches the body. Extend the arms with control to the start.
Benefits: Long range of motion; Builds the upper back; Strong rope row; Useful floor variation; Trains the lats; Builds the biceps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Cable Seated One Arm Alternate Row
Description: Sit at a cable row station with two D-handles attached. Place your feet on the platform with knees slightly bent. Grab a handle in each hand with arms extended. Sit upright with a tall back. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Pull one handle back toward your hip. Squeeze the lat at the end of the rep, then return slowly. Pull the other handle back as the first arm extends.
Benefits: Strong unilateral back work; Trains anti-rotation core; Builds back thickness; Helps fix back imbalances; Constant cable tension; Useful for hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Core

Exercise Name: Cable Seated One Arm Concentration Curl
Description: Sit on a bench in front of a low cable pulley. Attach a single D-handle to the cable. Spread your knees and lean slightly forward. Hold the handle in one hand with palm up. Brace the back of your upper arm against the inside of your thigh. Curl the handle up toward your shoulder. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower the handle slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Strict biceps isolation; Constant cable tension; Eliminates cheating and momentum; Strong peak contraction; Allows unilateral focus; Builds biceps shape
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Forearms

Description: Set a cable to a high pulley with a single handle. Sit on a bench facing the cable station. Grip the handle with your right hand, palm facing up. Extend your arm overhead with the cable creating tension. Brace your core and keep your upper arm stationary. Curl the handle toward your head by bending only at the elbow. Squeeze the bicep hard at the peak contraction. Slowly extend your arm back overhead with control. Switch arms.
Benefits: Maximum shortened-position contraction; Builds bicep peak; Constant cable tension through the range; Different stimulus than standard curls; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong peak isolation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially short head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Set a flat bench (or a low stool) several feet in front of a high cable pulley with a straight bar or rope attachment. Sit on the bench facing the cable. Reach up and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Slide back on the bench enough that the cable is under tension with arms extended overhead. Hinge slightly forward at the hips. Set a soft, fixed bend in your elbows and lock that angle in. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down and back. Pull the bar down in a wide arc by rotating only at the shoulders. The bar should travel from overhead down to your thighs. Continue until the bar reaches your thighs. Squeeze your lats hard for one to two seconds. Slowly let the bar travel back up under control to the overhead start position. Feel the stretch in your lats at the top.
Benefits: Direct lat isolation in a seated, supported position; Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion; Provides a deep lat stretch at the top; Excellent finisher after compound back work; No lower-back demand; Easy to load progressively in small increments
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Teres major; Long head of triceps (isometric stabilizer); Posterior deltoid (secondary); Pectoralis major (sternal head, secondary)

Description: Set two cables to the lowest position. Attach D-handles. Sit on a bench between the cables. Cross the cables — right hand grips left cable, left hand grips right. Start with arms crossed in front of your body at knee level. Raise both handles out to the sides in a reverse fly arc, leading with your elbows. Squeeze your rear delts at the top. Lower under control. Maintain slight elbow bend throughout. Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Seated rear delt isolation with crossed cables; Constant cable tension throughout the arc; Eliminates body english; Easy to load progressively; Builds rear delt size and shoulder balance; Unique cable crossing pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Infraspinatus

Description: Sit on the cable row machine with your feet planted firmly on the foot platform, knees slightly bent. Lean forward and grab the attachment (typically a V-handle, neutral-grip handle, or straight bar). Sit up tall with arms extended. Set up by lifting your chest, pulling your shoulders down and back, and bracing your core. Your torso should be roughly vertical. Begin the row by driving your elbows back, pulling the handle toward your lower abdomen. Keep your elbows close to your body. At the end of the row, your hands should be at your lower abs and your shoulder blades fully retracted (squeezed together). Pause briefly. Slowly extend your arms back to the start position, allowing your shoulder blades to protract slightly at the end. Feel the stretch in your lats. Do not rock back and forth. Your torso should stay roughly vertical the entire time. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use different attachments to vary the stimulus.
Benefits: Constant tension on the back throughout the entire range of motion; Eliminates lower-back demand vs free-weight rows; Easy weight progression in small increments; Different attachments (V-bar, wide bar, rope) bias different parts of the back; Excellent volume work for mid-back hypertrophy; Easier to maintain strict form than barbell or dumbbell rows
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii and brachialis; Forearms and grip; Erector spinae (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Cable Seated Rear Delt Fly with Chest Support
Description: Set up an incline bench between two low cable pulleys. Sit chest down against the incline pad. Reach down and grab the opposite handle with each hand so the cables cross. Brace the core and keep the chest pressed to the pad. Sweep the arms out to the sides by squeezing the shoulder blades. Stop at shoulder height with the elbows slightly bent. Squeeze the rear delts at the top. Lower the arms back down with control and repeat.
Benefits: Isolates the rear delts and upper back.; Chest support eliminates body english.; Cable provides constant tension throughout.; Carryover to face pulls and pulling strength.; Builds upper back posture.; Easy to scale by adjusting cable weight.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius; Rhomboids; Infraspinatus

Description: Set a cable pulley to elbow height. Attach a D-handle. Sit sideways to the cable with your working arm closest to the cable. Grip the handle with your working hand. Pin your elbow against your side, forearm pointing toward the cable. Rotate your forearm inward across your body — away from the cable. Continue rotating until your forearm is across your stomach. Slowly let the cable pull your forearm back to the starting position. Keep your elbow pinned to your side throughout — only your forearm rotates. Use very light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Benefits: Strengthens the subscapularis (internal rotator); Essential for shoulder health and injury prevention; Constant cable tension throughout rotation; Easy to load progressively with small increments; Critical for overhead athletes and lifters; Rehabilitation and prehabilitation exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Subscapularis (primary); Pectoralis major (slight); Anterior deltoid (slight); Teres major

Description: Sit at a low cable row station with a straight bar attached. Brace your feet on the platform with knees slightly bent. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing up. Sit tall with chest up and arms extended forward. Brace your core. Pull the bar to your lower abdomen by driving the elbows back along your sides. Squeeze the lats and biceps at the back of the row. Slowly extend the arms forward to the starting position with control.
Benefits: Supinated grip emphasizes lats; Strong bicep involvement; Builds lat thickness; Different stimulus than overhand grip rows; Constant cable tension; Useful for lat and bicep training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle)

Description: Sit at a cable row station. Attach a wide lat pulldown bar or straight bar. Grip the bar wide (wider than shoulder-width) with an overhand grip. Sit upright with feet on the footplates. Row the bar toward your upper abdomen by driving your elbows out and back. Squeeze your rear delts and upper back at the end of the row. Slowly extend forward. Keep elbows wide — this shifts emphasis from lats to rear delts and traps. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to rear delts and upper back; Wide elbows target different muscles than close grip; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Builds upper back thickness and shoulder balance; Useful for posture improvement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle and upper); Rhomboids; Latissimus dorsi (slight); Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable to elbow height with a single handle attached. Stand sideways to the cable. Lift the working arm out to the side at shoulder height. Bend the elbow at ninety degrees with the forearm pointing forward. Brace your core and keep the upper arm parallel to the floor. Rotate the forearm upward by externally rotating the shoulder. Hold briefly at the rotated position. Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the rotator cuff; Strong shoulder health move; Trains external rotation; Useful for shoulder care; Builds shoulder stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Infraspinatus; Teres minor; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a cable pulley to roughly chest height. Attach a D-handle. Sit on a bench facing perpendicular to the cable machine. Cable should be on your left. Grip the handle with both hands. Extend your arms straight out in front of your chest. Sit tall with chest lifted. Brace your core. Rotate your torso to the right, away from the cable. Use your obliques to drive the rotation. Keep your arms straight and elbows locked. The handle should travel through a smooth arc. Pause briefly at the end of the rotation. Slowly return to the start. Complete all reps on one side, then switch the cable to your right side.
Benefits: Trains rotational core strength against constant tension; Smoother than Russian twists with weights; Easy to load progressively; Builds the obliques effectively; Useful for rotational sports (golf, tennis, baseball); Standing variation also possible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Erector spinae (anti-extension); Hip flexors (stabilizer)

Description: Set two cable pulleys to the lowest position. Attach D-handles. Face away from the cables. Grip both handles at shoulder height. Stand in a staggered stance for stability. Press both handles overhead to lockout. Squeeze your shoulders and triceps at the top. Constant cable tension here. Lower back to your shoulders under control. Brace your core throughout. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through full press; Tension at lockout unlike free weights; Easy to load progressively; Standing position adds core demand; Joint-friendly; Excellent for shoulder hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a cable to head height with a single handle attached. Stand sideways to the cable with the working arm closest. Lift the working arm out to the side at shoulder height. Bend the elbow at ninety degrees with the forearm pointing up. Brace your core and keep the upper arm parallel to the floor. Rotate the forearm down toward the floor. Hold briefly at the rotated position. Return with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains internal rotation; Builds the rotator cuff; Strong shoulder drill; Useful for shoulder care; Builds shoulder stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Subscapularis; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Attach a straight bar to a low cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Stand tall and step back slightly so the cable is under tension. Let the bar hang at arm’s length in front of your thighs. Keep your arms completely straight throughout. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can. Do not bend at the elbows. Squeeze your traps hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not roll your shoulders. Lower your shoulders under control. Maintain cable tension throughout — do not let the weight stack touch down. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion; Better resistance at the top contraction than free-weight shrugs; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Excellent for high-rep trap volume; Easier to maintain strict form than barbell or dumbbell shrugs; Trains grip and forearm strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (especially the upper fibers); Levator scapulae; Rhomboids (secondary); Forearms and grip

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the pulley with the cable on your right side. Grip the handle with your right hand. Pin your right elbow firmly against your right side. Bend your right elbow at 90 degrees with your forearm parallel to the floor. Step away from the pulley until the cable is under tension and your right forearm is rotated outward (palm facing right). Brace your core. Rotate your right forearm across your body, keeping your elbow pinned to your side. Continue until your right hand reaches your stomach (palm now facing your body). Slowly return to the start over two seconds. Use very light weight — the rotator cuff is small.
Benefits: Isolates the internal rotators of the rotator cuff; Balances out external rotation work; Improves shoulder stability; Useful prehab and rehab exercise; Constant cable tension; Easy to scale with light loads
Muscles Worked (Raw): Subscapularis (primary); Pectoralis major (slight); Anterior deltoid (slight); Latissimus dorsi (slight)

Exercise Name: Cable Single Arm High Scapular Row
Description: Set a cable to a high position with a single D-handle. Stand facing the cable and grab the handle with one hand. Step back to add tension to the cable. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Pull the handle back toward your shoulder with the elbow flared up. Lead with the elbow up and out to the side at shoulder height. Squeeze the rhomboid and rear delt at the end of the rep. Return slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Targets the rhomboids; Builds rear delt detail; Improves posture; Strong scapular work; Constant cable tension; Useful for shoulder health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rhomboids; Rear deltoid; Traps; Latissimus dorsi

Exercise Name: Cable Single Arm Low Scapular Row
Description: Set a cable to a low position with a single D-handle. Stand facing the cable and grab the handle with one hand. Step back to add tension to the cable. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Pull the handle back and down toward your hip. Lead with the elbow back and down. Squeeze the lower trap at the end of the rep. Return slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Targets the lower traps; Improves posture; Strong scapular control; Useful for shoulder health; Constant cable tension; Builds upper back detail
Muscles Worked (Raw): Traps (lower); Rhomboids; Rear deltoid

Description: Set a cable to a high position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your near hand at your ear. Stand tall. Feet hip-width apart. Crunch laterally away from the cable — bend your torso to the side away from the cable. Squeeze the oblique on the far side at the bottom of the crunch. Slowly return to upright. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Loaded oblique isolation; Constant cable tension throughout; Easy to load progressively; Standing position is convenient; Targets the obliques directly; Useful for core symmetry
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (opposite side from cable); Quadratus lumborum; Rectus abdominis

Description: Set a cable to a high position. Attach a D-handle. Stand facing the cable. Grip the handle with your right hand, arm extended toward the high cable. Step back for tension. Staggered stance for stability. Row the handle toward your right shoulder by driving your elbow back. Squeeze your upper back and rear delt at the end. Extend back to start under control. Complete reps, then switch arms. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Unilateral upper back work; High angle targets rear delts and upper traps; Exposes left-right imbalances; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Builds back symmetry
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (upper and middle); Rhomboids; Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your near hand at your side. Stand tall. Free hand behind your head or at your side. Bend laterally away from the cable — lean your torso to the far side. Feel the resistance through your obliques and the loaded stretch on the cable side. Return to upright under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Loaded lateral flexion with constant tension; Builds the obliques and quadratus lumborum; Easy to load progressively; Standing and convenient; Different resistance curve than dumbbells; Useful for core symmetry
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Erector spinae

Description: Attach a belt or rope to a low cable pulley. Step onto a raised platform or step near the cable. Position the belt across your hips or hold a rope handle. Stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of the step. Stand tall with knees mostly straight. Let your heels drop below the step for a deep stretch. Push through the balls of your feet to rise up onto your toes as high as possible. Squeeze your calves at the top for one second. Lower under control over two to three seconds. Return to the deep stretch. Maintain cable tension throughout — do not let the weight stack touch down. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the full range of motion; Loads the bottom stretch position better than free weights; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Builds the gastrocnemius effectively; Useful when dedicated calf machines are unavailable; Smooth resistance throughout the rep
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (medial and lateral heads); Soleus (secondary); Tibialis posterior (stabilizer)

Description: Set two cable pulleys at chest height. Attach D-handles to each. Stand between the cables with your back to the machine. Grip both handles. Step forward into a split stance — one foot forward for stability. Bring the handles to your chest with elbows bent and tucked at roughly 45 degrees. Press both handles forward simultaneously, extending your arms straight in front. Squeeze your chest hard at the lockout. Your hands should converge slightly in front. Slowly return the handles to your chest under control. Maintain cable tension throughout. Brace your core hard — the standing position demands stability.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout; Standing position adds core engagement; Functional pushing pattern; Bilateral movement allows heavier loading; Easy to load progressively; Trains chest with stability demand
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (heavy stabilizer)

Description: Stand in the center of a cable crossover with both cables set low. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing forward. Step forward slightly to add tension. Brace your core and keep your chest up. With a slight bend in the elbows, sweep one arm up and across your body. Bring the hand to about chest height in front of you. Squeeze the lower chest hard at the end range. Lower the arm slowly and alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Targets the lower chest; Constant cable tension; Alternating focus on each side; Helps fix chest imbalances; Builds chest detail; Strong lower pec isolation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (lower); Front deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a short bar attachment. Stand with your back to the cable station. Reach behind you and grip the bar with palms facing back. Step forward to create cable tension. Stand upright with the bar at hip level behind you. Allow the bar to roll down to your fingertips at the bottom of the curl. Curl the bar back up by flexing your wrists. Squeeze your forearms at the top, then lower with control.
Benefits: Trains forearm flexors through full range; Behind-the-back position frees the wrists; Constant cable tension through the range; Builds grip strength; Useful for athletes who need strong forearms; Different stimulus than standard wrist curls
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Brachioradialis; Wrist flexors

Description: Set both cable pulleys to chest height with single handles. Stand facing away from the cable stack with one handle in each hand. Hold the handles close together at chest level with palms facing forward. Step forward to create cable tension. Brace your core and stand tall. Press both handles forward until your arms are fully extended. Bring the handles together at the front of the press. Squeeze the triceps, then lower the handles back to chest level with control.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through the range; Targets triceps with close grip; Standing position adds full body engagement; Strong core stabilization demand; Useful for hypertrophy training; Functional pressing pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major (inner fibers); Anterior deltoid; Core stabilizers

Exercise Name: Cable Standing Cross Over High Reverse Fly
Description: Set both cables to a high position with single handles. Stand in the center of a cable crossover. Reach across the body to grip the opposite high cable in each hand. Cross the arms at chest height. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Pull the arms wide and back uncrossing them. Continue back until the arms are out to the sides at shoulder height. Squeeze the rear delts hard. Return with control.
Benefits: Strong rear delt builder; Constant cable tension; Trains the upper back; Builds rear delt size; Useful posture builder; Strong cable move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Trapezius

Exercise Name: Cable Standing Crossover Overhead Tricep Extension
Description: Set both cables on a crossover to low positions with single handles. Stand in the center facing away from the cables. Grip a handle in each hand and bring them up behind the head. Step forward to take tension on both cables. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Keep the upper arms vertical pointing at the ceiling. Extend both elbows pressing the handles up overhead. Lower the handles back down with control.
Benefits: Strong tricep builder; Dual cable constant tension; Trains the long head; Builds tricep size; Useful arm builder; Strong cable move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Forearm flexors

Description: Set a cable to a high position. Attach a rope handle. Face away from the cable. Hold the rope behind your head. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Crunch forward by flexing your spine. Drive your chest toward your hips. Squeeze your abs hard at the bottom of the crunch. Slowly return to standing under control. Keep constant cable tension throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Loaded standing core exercise; Constant cable tension on the abs; Requires more stability than kneeling version; Easy to load progressively; No kneeling needed; Excellent for ab hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors (slight)

Description: Set both cable pulleys to roughly chest height (or slightly higher for a high-cable fly biased toward the lower chest). Attach a single-handle (D-handle) to each pulley. Grip one handle in each hand and step forward to the center of the cable station. Stagger your stance for stability — one foot slightly forward. Lean your torso forward slightly. Start with arms out to the sides at chest height, elbows slightly bent. The cables should be under tension at the start. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down and back. Pull both handles together in a wide arc in front of your body. Keep the slight elbow bend fixed throughout — do not press. Bring the handles together in front of your chest. Squeeze your chest hard for one second. Slowly let the handles travel back out under control to the starting position. Feel the stretch in your chest at the end of each rep.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the entire range of motion; Builds chest size with a peak contraction in the center; Provides a deep stretch at the end range; Excellent finisher after compound pressing; Allows easy adjustment of pulley height to bias upper, mid, or lower chest; Easier on the shoulders than dumbbell flys for many lifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (sternal head and clavicular head depending on cable height); Anterior deltoid (secondary); Biceps brachii (stabilizer); Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a single handle or rope attached. Stand with the cable behind you, feet hip-width apart. Grip the handle with one hand and bring it in front of your thigh. Stand tall with chest up and core braced. Maintain a slight bend in the elbow. Raise the handle in an arc straight forward. Continue until your arm is at shoulder height with the handle level with your eyes. Slowly lower the handle back down to the starting position. Switch sides after the set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through the range; Resistance through the bottom of the lift; Builds front delt size and strength; Different stimulus than dumbbell raises; Useful for front delt specialization; Easy to scale by adjusting weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (clavicular head); Trapezius (upper)

Description: Attach a rope handle to a cable pulley set at roughly upper-chest or face height. Grip both ends of the rope with an overhand grip — palms facing the floor. Step back so the cable is under tension with your arms fully extended. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart in a slightly staggered stance for stability. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your torso upright throughout. Pull the rope back toward your face by driving your elbows up and out. Aim to bring the rope to roughly the level of your forehead or eyes. At the end position, your hands should be wide of your ears with thumbs pointing back behind you. Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard. Hold for one second. Slowly extend your arms back to the start position under control. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: One of the best exercises for shoulder health and rotator cuff strength; Builds the rear delts, mid traps, and rhomboids; Improves posture by strengthening the upper back muscles that resist forward shoulder rounding; Excellent warm-up before pressing exercises; Easy to perform with high frequency due to low spinal load; Helps balance the development of the front and back of the shoulder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle and lower fibers); Rhomboids; Infraspinatus and teres minor (rotator cuff); Biceps brachii (secondary); Forearms and grip

Exercise Name: Cable Standing High Cross Triceps Extension
Description: Set a cable pulley to a high position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand across your body. Start with your elbow bent, hand near your opposite shoulder. Extend your arm diagonally downward and across your body. Lock out at full extension. Squeeze your tricep. Slowly return to the start. Complete reps, then switch sides. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Unique cross-body tricep extension angle; Stretches the long head through diagonal path; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Strict isolation per arm; Different stimulus than standard pushdowns
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (long head emphasis); Anconeus

Description: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley. Strap it around your right ankle. Face the cable machine. Hold the machine for balance. Lift your right foot slightly off the floor. The cable should be under tension. Hinge slightly forward at the hips for leverage. Drive your right leg straight back behind you by squeezing your right glute. Keep the leg straight. Continue extending until your right thigh is in line with or behind your torso. Squeeze hard at the top. Slowly let the leg return forward under control. Complete all reps on the right, then switch sides.
Benefits: Direct glute isolation through hip extension; Constant cable tension throughout; Standing position requires no bench setup; Trains balance and core stability; Easy to load progressively; Targets one glute at a time
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Erector spinae (isometric); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley. Strap it around your right ankle. Face the cable machine. Hold the frame for stability. Stand on your left leg. Lean slightly forward. Kick your right leg straight back against the cable tension. Squeeze your right glute at full hip extension. Slowly return to start. Do not let the weight stack rest between reps. Complete reps, then switch legs. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Isolates the gluteus maximus with constant tension; Easy to load progressively; Excellent for glute hypertrophy; Standing position requires balance; Better tension curve than bodyweight kickbacks; Adjustable cable resistance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Erector spinae (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your hand closest to the cable. Step away slightly so the cable has tension. Curl the handle across your body toward your opposite shoulder. Keep your upper arm still. Only your forearm moves. Squeeze your bicep peak at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Emphasizes the bicep short head and peak; Cross-body path provides unique stimulus; Constant cable tension throughout; Easy to load progressively; Strict isolation — no body english; Builds the bicep peak
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially short head); Brachialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Attach an ankle strap to a low cable pulley. Wrap the strap around your right ankle. Stand facing the cable machine. Hold the machine for stability. Stand on your left leg. Slight bend in the standing knee. Keep your right thigh stationary. Curl your right heel up toward your right glute by bending only at the knee. Squeeze your hamstring hard at the top. Lower under control over two to three seconds. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout; Isolates each hamstring individually; Exposes left-right imbalances; Easy to load progressively; Standing position eliminates lower-back load; Excellent finisher for leg workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus); Gastrocnemius (secondary); Gluteus maximus (slight stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Cable Standing One Arm Hammer Curl with Rope Attachment
Description: Set a cable to low pulley and attach a rope handle. Grip one end of the rope with a neutral hammer grip. Stand tall with the cable arm at your side and elbow tucked. Brace the core and keep the upper arm fixed throughout. Curl the rope up by bending the elbow until the forearm is vertical. Squeeze the biceps and brachialis hard at the top. Lower the rope slowly back to full arm extension. Complete all reps on one side then switch arms.
Benefits: Builds the biceps and brachialis with hammer grip emphasis.; Develops grip and forearm strength through the rope.; Constant cable tension keeps the muscle loaded throughout.; Single arm work exposes and corrects strength imbalances.; Joint friendly neutral grip is easier on the wrists.; Adds variety to standard barbell or dumbbell curls.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Exercise Name: Cable Standing One Arm Triceps Extension
Description: Set the cable to a low position with a single handle. Stand facing away from the cable stack. Grip the handle in one hand and bring it up behind the head. Step forward to take tension on the cable. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Keep the upper arm vertical pointing at the ceiling. Extend the elbow pressing the handle up overhead. Lower back behind the head with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong unilateral tricep builder; Constant cable tension; Builds arm symmetry; Trains the long head; Useful arm builder; Strong cable move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Forearm flexors

Exercise Name: Cable Standing One Leg Calf Raise
Description: Attach a low cable to a belt at your waist or hold a handle in one hand. Stand on one foot facing away from the cable. Position the working foot on a small block with the heel hanging off. Lift the other foot off the floor. Hold a wall or rack for balance. Brace your core and keep the standing leg slightly bent. Press up onto your toes by lifting your heel high. Lower slowly to a deep stretch. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Targets the calves unilaterally; Constant cable tension; Trains balance; Strong calf builder; Reduces strength imbalances; Builds calf size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Soleus; Gastrocnemius

Description: Set a cable pulley to roughly chest height. Attach a straight bar, rope, or D-handle. Stand facing the cable machine with feet shoulder-width apart. Step back so the cable is under tension with your arms extended forward. Stand tall with a slight stagger in your stance for stability. Brace your core. Pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your torso upright throughout. Row the attachment toward your chest by driving your elbows back. Keep your elbows at roughly shoulder height. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the row. Pause briefly. Slowly extend your arms forward under control. Maintain cable tension throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion; Upright position reduces lower-back demand; Trains core stability and anti-extension simultaneously; Multiple attachment options for different stimuli; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Excellent for high-rep mid-back and rear-delt volume
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Latissimus dorsi (secondary); Biceps brachii; Core (anti-extension, stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Set a cable pulley to roughly elbow height. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand (the hand away from the cable). Bring your elbow to your side. Bend your elbow at 90 degrees. Place a rolled towel between your elbow and ribs. Start with your forearm across your body, hand near the opposite hip. Brace your core. Keep your elbow pinned to your side throughout. Rotate your forearm outward, away from your body, by externally rotating at the shoulder. Continue rotating until your forearm points roughly forward or as far as your range allows. Slowly return to the start. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Constant cable tension throughout the rotation; Strengthens the rotator cuff effectively; Improves shoulder stability for pressing; Helps prevent rotator cuff injuries; Easy to load progressively; Excellent warm-up before pressing exercises
Muscles Worked (Raw): Infraspinatus; Teres minor; Posterior deltoid (secondary)

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a rope or single handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the handle with both hands near your outside hip (the hip closest to the cable). Pull the handle diagonally upward across your body — from low hip to high opposite shoulder. Rotate your torso, drive through your hips, and extend your arms to the high position. Slowly return to the low position under control. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds rotational core power (low to high direction); Targets the obliques heavily; Constant cable tension throughout; Carries over to rotational sports; Easy to load progressively; Complements the high-to-low woodchop
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy); Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid; Hip rotators; Gluteus maximus

Description: Attach a single rope handle to a high or mid cable pulley. Stand in front of the cable with arms extended in front of you. Grab the rope with both hands, palms down. Keep your arms straight and elbows locked. Roll the rope up by alternating wrist flexions. Continue rolling until the rope is fully wound up. Reverse the motion to roll the rope back down with control. Repeat for time or for a set number of full rolls.
Benefits: Builds forearm strength; Improves grip endurance; Constant cable tension throughout; Useful for climbing and grappling sports; Strengthens the wrist flexors and extensors; Builds thicker forearms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms; Wrist flexors; Wrist extensors

Description: Set a cable to the lowest pulley with a short bar attachment. Stand facing the cable station with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the bar with palms facing down (overhand grip), shoulder-width apart. Step back slightly to create cable tension. Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides. Lower the bar by extending your wrists down toward the floor. Curl the bar back up by extending your wrists upward. Squeeze the forearm extensors at the top, then lower with control.
Benefits: Trains forearm extensors directly; Constant cable tension through the range; Builds back of forearm for arm thickness; Strict isolation; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong peak contraction
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm extensors; Brachioradialis; Wrist extensors

Description: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar. Face away from the cable. Grip the bar behind you with palms facing backward. Stand tall. Arms behind you, bar at glute level. Curl your wrists upward by flexing. The bar rises behind you. Squeeze your forearm flexors at the top. Lower under control. Keep your arms still — only your wrists move. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension on forearm flexors; Different resistance curve than free weights; Easy to load progressively; Builds forearm size and grip strength; Standing position is convenient; Useful for grip-intensive activities
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Flexor digitorum; Palmaris longus

Description: Sit at a cable row station with feet on the footplates. Grip the handle. Sit with your torso perfectly vertical — chest up, shoulders back and down. Maintain this exact torso position throughout. No forward lean at the start, no backward lean at the finish. Row the handle toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end of the row. Slowly extend your arms forward. Do not let your torso move. Use lighter weight than standard seated row due to the strict form. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Strict back isolation — no momentum; Eliminates lower back involvement; Builds lats and mid-traps with pure contraction; Useful for mind-muscle connection; Easy to load progressively; Excellent for hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Attach a straight bar or rope handle to a high cable pulley. Stand facing the cable machine with feet shoulder-width apart, roughly two to three feet from the machine. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Step back so the cable is under tension with arms extended overhead. Hinge slightly forward at the hips. Set a soft, fixed bend in your elbows and lock that angle in throughout. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down and back. Pull the bar down in a wide arc by rotating only at the shoulders. The bar should travel from overhead down to your thighs. Continue until the bar reaches your thighs. Squeeze your lats hard for one to two seconds. Slowly let the bar travel back up under control to the overhead start position. Maintain the slight elbow bend throughout.
Benefits: Direct lat isolation with no bicep involvement; Constant cable tension throughout the range of motion; Excellent finisher after compound back work; Easier to feel the lat than during compound rows or pulldowns; Builds a strong mind-muscle connection with the lats; Easy to load progressively in small increments
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Teres major; Long head of triceps (isometric stabilizer); Posterior deltoid (secondary); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a cable to the highest pulley with a straight bar or rope attachment. Stand facing the cable with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing down. Step back to create cable tension and lean slightly forward. Maintain straight arms throughout with a soft lock at the elbows. Pull the bar down in an arc by squeezing your lats. Continue until the bar reaches your thighs. Squeeze the lats hard, then return the bar to the starting position with control.
Benefits: Direct lat isolation; Removes biceps from the equation; Builds lat detail and width; Strong mind-muscle connection; Constant cable tension; Useful for lat specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Teres major; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a cable pulley to chest height. Attach a D-handle or rope. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with both hands at your chest. Step away for tension. Feet shoulder-width apart. Rotate your torso away from the cable, keeping your arms at your chest. Rotate as far as comfortable. Squeeze your obliques. Slowly return to the starting position. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Keep your hips stable — rotation comes from the torso. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds oblique strength with constant tension; Constant cable resistance through rotation; Easy to load progressively; Carries over to rotational sports; Functional core training; Simple setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Erector spinae

Description: Lie on your back on the floor in front of a low cable pulley with ankle straps attached. Attach the straps to your ankles. Position yourself so the cable is taut with legs extended. Brace your core. Place your hands at your sides for stability. Pull your knees toward your chest by contracting your lower abs and hip flexors. Continue until your knees are over your chest. Lift your hips slightly off the floor at the top. Squeeze your lower abs hard. Slowly extend your legs back to the start under control. Maintain cable tension. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight.
Benefits: Adds cable resistance to lower-ab training; One of the few loaded lower-ab options; Constant cable tension throughout; Builds visible lower-ab strength; Easy to load progressively; Lying position eliminates hip-flexor cheating
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially lower); Hip flexors; Obliques; Transverse abdominis

Description: Set a cable pulley to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable, with the handle on your right side. Grip with your right hand at shoulder height. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core. Press the handle up and overhead while rotating your torso to the left, away from the cable. At lockout, your right arm is fully extended overhead and your torso has rotated significantly. Reverse the motion — rotate back to start while lowering the handle to your shoulder. Complete all reps on the right, then switch sides. Use moderate weight — control through the rotation matters more than load.
Benefits: Combines pressing with rotational power; Trains the shoulders, triceps, and obliques together; Develops athletic rotational strength; Carries over to throwing and striking sports; Constant cable tension; Builds core anti-rotation control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Obliques (rotation); Core (anti-rotation, stabilizer); Upper trapezius

Description: Set a cable to chest height with a single handle. Stand sideways to the cable station with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the handle with both hands at chest level. Step away from the anchor to create cable tension. Brace your core and stand tall. Rotate your torso away from the cable, keeping arms extended. Continue rotating until you feel a strong oblique contraction. Slowly return to the starting position with control. Complete reps, switch sides.
Benefits: Trains rotational core strength; Constant cable tension through the range; Standing position adds full body engagement; Strong oblique development; Functional carryover to athletic movement; Easy to scale by changing cable resistance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis

Description: Set a cable to a high or chest-height pulley with a single handle. Stand facing the cable with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the handle with both hands or one hand at chest level. Step back to create cable tension. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Pull the handle toward your body while rotating your torso to the opposite side. Squeeze your lats and obliques at the bottom of the pull. Slowly return to the starting position with control. Complete reps, switch sides.
Benefits: Trains lats and obliques together; Strong rotational core demand; Constant cable tension through the range; Functional carryover to athletic movement; Builds back and core strength simultaneously; Useful for athletes who need rotational power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Obliques (internal and external); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable to about shoulder height. Attach a single D-handle to the cable. Stand to one side of the machine, holding the handle in the far hand. Step forward slightly to add tension. Brace your core and keep your chest up. With a slight bend in the elbow, sweep your arm across your body. Bring the hand to the centerline in front of your chest. Squeeze the chest hard at the end range. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Strict unilateral chest work; Constant cable tension; Deep stretch through the pec; Helps fix chest imbalances; Builds chest shape and detail; Strong peak contraction
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Front deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Set a cable pulley to mid-chest height. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand. Start with arm extended toward the cable, torso rotated toward the cable. Row the handle toward your hip while simultaneously rotating your torso away from the cable. Squeeze your lat and oblique at the end position. Slowly return to start — extending arm and rotating back toward the cable. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines rowing with rotational core work; Builds back and oblique strength together; Constant cable tension; Functional pulling and rotation pattern; Easy to load progressively; Useful for sport-specific conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Obliques (rotation); Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core (rotation)

Description: Set a cable pulley to a high position. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with your far hand, arm extended up toward the cable. Torso rotated toward the cable to start. Pull the handle down and across your body toward your opposite hip while rotating your torso. Squeeze your upper back and obliques at the end position. Return to start under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Diagonal pulling pattern targets upper back and obliques; Combines high row with rotation; Constant cable tension; Functional pulling pattern; Easy to load progressively; Builds shoulder and core together
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius; Latissimus dorsi; Obliques; Core (rotation); Biceps brachii

Description: Set two cables to low positions with single handles. Stand between the cables facing one stack. Grip a handle in each hand with palms facing each other. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Set the elbows up high tight against the sides. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Extend both elbows kicking the handles back behind the body. Squeeze the triceps hard at lockout. Lower with control.
Benefits: Strong tricep builder; Bilateral kickback; Constant cable tension; Brutal lockout squeeze; Useful arm finisher; Strong cable move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Posterior deltoid; Anconeus

Description: Sit at a lat pulldown station. Grip the bar with a supinated (underhand) grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Secure thighs under the pads. Arms extended overhead. Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back. Lean back slightly. Pull to your collarbone area. Squeeze your lats and biceps at the bottom. Slowly extend back overhead. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set. Use moderate weight — the underhand grip changes the loading significantly.
Benefits: Increases bicep involvement; Emphasizes the lower lats; Longer range of motion than overhand; Deeper lat contraction at the bottom; Easy to load progressively; Useful for complete back development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (lower fibers); Biceps brachii (increased); Brachialis; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids

Description: Set a cable to the lowest pulley position with a single D-handle. Stand facing the cable station with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the handle in your right hand with an underhand grip. Step back slightly to create cable tension with arm extended. Brace your core and pin your right elbow against your side. Curl the handle up by bending only at the elbow. Squeeze your bicep hard at the top. Lower the handle back down with control to full extension. Complete reps, then switch arms.
Benefits: Constant cable tension through the range; Single-arm work corrects imbalances; Allows mind-muscle focus on working bicep; Strict form enforced by cable resistance; Builds bicep size and strength; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Exercise Name: Cable Twisting Standing One Arm Chest Press
Description: Set a cable to chest height with a single handle. Stand facing away from the cable stack. Grip the handle with one hand near the chest. Set a staggered stance for stability. Brace your core and set the hips facing forward. Press the handle forward while rotating the torso. Squeeze the chest and obliques at full extension. Pull back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Combo chest and rotation move; Trains rotational power; Strong unilateral chest move; Builds the obliques; Strong cable move; Useful functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Obliques; Triceps brachii

Description: Set a cable to a high position with a straight or rope attachment. Kneel directly under the cable on both knees. Grip the attachment with both hands. Set the elbows tight against the sides. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Push the attachment straight down to the floor. Squeeze the triceps hard at full lockout. Allow the elbows to bend back to the start with control.
Benefits: Strong tricep builder; Unique kneeling angle; Strong lockout squeeze; Constant cable tension; Useful arm builder; Strong cable move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Forearm flexors

Description: Set both cable pulleys to the lowest position. Attach a D-handle to each pulley. Grip one handle in each hand. Step to the center of the station. Stagger your stance for stability. Start with handles at your sides at roughly hip level, palms facing up and forward. The cables should be under tension. Set a slight bend in your elbows and lock it in throughout. Bring both handles together in an upward arc. The path should travel from your hips up to roughly face or upper-chest height. At the top, your hands should meet in front of your upper chest or face. Squeeze your upper chest hard. Slowly lower the handles back to your sides under control. Feel the stretch in your upper chest. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight — contraction quality matters most.
Benefits: Targets the upper (clavicular) chest with constant cable tension; Low-to-high pull path is the best angle for upper-chest isolation with cables; Deep stretch at the bottom, peak contraction at the top; Excellent finisher after incline pressing; Easy to load progressively; Complements high-cable flies for complete chest development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially the clavicular/upper head); Anterior deltoid (secondary); Biceps brachii (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Set a cable to a high position. Attach a rope or straight bar handle. Stand or sit facing the cable. Grip the handle. Start with arms extended toward the high cable. Row the handle toward your face or upper chest by pulling your elbows back. Squeeze your upper back and rear delts. Slowly extend back to start. Keep upright posture throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Targets the upper back, rear delts, and traps; High cable angle provides unique stimulus; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Similar to face pull but with rowing path; Builds posture and shoulder balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (upper and middle); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Infraspinatus

Exercise Name: Cable Wide Grip Behind Neck Pulldown
Description: Sit at a cable lat pulldown machine with thighs under the pads. Attach a wide bar to the cable. Reach up and grab the bar with a wide overhand grip. Sit upright with chest up and shoulders back. Brace your core and keep your back tall. Pull the bar down behind your neck toward the upper traps. Lead with the elbows down and pinned to the sides. Squeeze the lats at the bottom, then return slowly.
Benefits: Builds upper lat width; Targets the upper traps; Old-school back-builder; Strong wide grip variation; Builds back detail; Useful for advanced lifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Traps (upper); Rhomboids; Rear deltoid

Description: Attach a long lat pulldown bar to a high cable pulley. Adjust the thigh pad so it firmly secures your legs. Reach up and grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands wider than shoulder-width — roughly where the bar bends down at the ends. Sit down with your thighs locked under the pad. Lean back slightly (about 10 to 15 degrees) and stick your chest out. Brace your core, pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Pull the bar down by driving your elbows down and out toward your hips. Lead with your elbows, not your hands. Bring the bar to your upper chest, just below your collarbones. Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom. Slowly let the bar travel back up under control until your arms are fully extended overhead. Feel the stretch in your lats. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Avoid using momentum or leaning back excessively.
Benefits: Builds the upper lats and back width more than narrow-grip variations; Excellent regression for lifters who cannot yet do pull-ups; Easy to load progressively with small weight increments; Constant cable tension throughout the entire range of motion; Trains the lats through a long stretch and full contraction; Carries over to pull-up and chin-up strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (especially the upper fibers); Teres major; Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids and middle trapezius; Biceps brachii and brachialis; Forearms and grip

Description: Attach a wide neutral-grip handle to a lat pulldown station. Sit and secure your thighs under the pads. Grip both handles with palms facing each other. Arms extended overhead. Pull the handles down to your upper chest by driving your elbows down and back. Squeeze your lats at the bottom. Slowly extend back overhead under control. Maintain upright torso throughout. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Combines wide stretch with neutral-grip comfort; Joint-friendly on the wrists and shoulders; Builds lat width; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Useful grip variation for pulldowns
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Trapezius (lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set two cable pulleys to the lowest setting. Attach D-handles to each. Stand between the cables with feet hip-width apart. Grip the right handle with your left hand and the left handle with your right hand (cables cross in front). Stand tall. Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back. Lift both arms up and out at roughly 45 degrees from your body, forming a Y shape overhead. Lead with your thumbs pointing up. Lift until your arms are overhead or as high as your range allows. Squeeze your lower traps and rear delts at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Use light weight.
Benefits: Activates the lower traps and posterior delts; Constant cable tension throughout; Improves shoulder mobility and overhead position; Excellent warm-up before pressing; Builds postural muscles; Useful for shoulder rehabilitation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lower trapezius; Posterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Rhomboids; Supraspinatus (rotator cuff)

Description: Set a cable to the lowest position. Attach a straight bar or EZ bar. Sit on a bench facing the cable. Grip the bar with palms up. Rest your forearms on your thighs, wrists hanging off your knees. Let your wrists extend (hands drop down). Curl your wrists up by flexing against the cable. Squeeze your forearm flexors at the top. Lower under control. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Constant cable tension on forearm flexors; Seated position for strict isolation; Easy to load progressively; Builds forearm size and grip strength; Different resistance curve than dumbbells; Comfortable setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Flexor digitorum; Palmaris longus

Exercise Name: Calf Raise from Deficit with Chair Supported
Description: Place a small step or weight plate on the floor. Stand on the step with the balls of the feet on the edge. Hold a sturdy chair or wall for balance. Brace the core and keep the legs straight. Allow the heels to drop down below the step level. Pause briefly at the bottom for a stretch. Press up onto the toes by extending the ankles. Squeeze the calves at the top and repeat.
Benefits: Trains the calves through a long stretch.; Deficit position increases range of motion.; No equipment needed beyond a step and chair.; Carryover to running and sprinting.; Improves ankle mobility.; Develops calf size and strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Tibialis posterior

Description: Sit at a lat pulldown station. Grip the bar with hands well outside shoulder-width. Secure thighs under the pads. Arms extended overhead. Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows down and out. Squeeze your lats at the bottom. Slowly extend overhead under control. Feel the lat stretch at the top. Maintain upright torso. Use slightly lighter weight than standard pulldown due to the wider grip. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Maximizes lat stretch at the top; Builds back width; Emphasizes the upper lats; Constant cable tension; Easy to load progressively; Different stimulus than standard-width pulldowns
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (upper fibers); Teres major; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Trapezius (lower)

Description: Step up onto the captain’s chair and place your forearms on the pads. Grip the handles firmly. Press your back firmly against the back pad. Let your legs hang straight down. Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders down and away from your ears. Lift both knees up toward your chest by contracting your abs and hip flexors. Bend at the knees and hips. For more challenge: keep your legs straight (straight-leg raise) or curl your hips up at the top. Continue lifting until your knees are at chest height or higher. Pause briefly and squeeze your abs. Lower your legs slowly under control over a count of two to three seconds back to the hanging start position. Avoid swinging or kicking. Strict reps are far more effective than sloppy momentum-driven reps.
Benefits: Direct isolation of the lower abs and hip flexors; Eliminates grip and shoulder demand vs hanging variations; Excellent for high-rep ab volume work; Easier to perform strictly than hanging exercises; Allows easy progression from bent-knee to straight-leg variations; Standard equipment in most commercial gyms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially the lower portion); Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Obliques (secondary); Transverse abdominis

Description: Grip parallel bars. Press up to lockout. Lean your torso forward about 30 degrees — more lean equals more chest. Cross your ankles behind you. Bend knees slightly. Lower by bending elbows. Flare elbows slightly wider than standard dips. Descend until you feel a stretch across your chest. Press back up. Maintain the forward lean. The forward lean is the key — it shifts load to the chest. Aim for 8 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to the chest from forward lean; Bodyweight chest pressing exercise; Builds lower chest development; Progressive with added weight; Effective mass-building exercise; Simple lean adjustment changes the target
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (lower, increased); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Get into a standard push-up position. Lower your chest toward the floor. Press up explosively — generating enough force to lift your hands off the floor. While airborne, quickly tap your chest with both hands. Return hands to the floor and absorb the landing. Immediately lower into the next rep. This is advanced — master clap push-ups first. Aim for 5 to 8 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds explosive upper-body power; Develops fast-twitch fiber recruitment; More advanced than clap push-ups; No equipment needed; Builds reactive pressing strength; Engaging and challenging
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Stand with a loaded barbell or heavy dumbbells. Use weight heavier than you can strict-curl. Use a slight lean-back and hip drive to swing the weight past the sticking point. Curl the weight to the top position using momentum. Once at the top, slow down and control the eccentric — lower over 3 to 4 seconds. The value is the heavy eccentric phase, not the concentric cheat. Use sparingly — not every set should be cheat curls. Aim for 5 to 8 reps with heavy eccentric focus. This is an advanced technique for experienced lifters.
Benefits: Allows heavier eccentric loading; Builds bicep strength beyond strict curl capacity; Advanced overloading technique; Develops eccentric bicep strength; Used by bodybuilders for advanced arm training; Should be used sparingly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (heavy eccentric); Brachialis; Forearms; Erector spinae (momentum)

Description: Set a cable pulley to chest height. Attach a D-handle. Stand sideways to the cable. Grip the handle with both hands at the center of your chest. Step away from the cable so it is taut. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core hard. Press the handle straight up overhead by extending your arms vertically. Resist the cable’s pull to the side throughout the press. Keep your torso facing forward. Hold briefly at the top with arms extended. Slowly lower the handle back to your chest under control. Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Trains core anti-rotation and anti-lateral-flexion; Builds shoulder stability under rotational load; Improves bracing for heavy compound lifts; Easy to load progressively; Excellent for athletes needing rotational stability; Functional core training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Transverse abdominis; Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid; Quadratus lumborum; Glutes (stabilizer)

Description: Hang from a pull up bar with an underhand chin up grip at shoulder width. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the body up over the bar. At the top shift the body laterally so the chin moves to one side of the bar. Continue shifting until the chin clears to the other side of the bar. Lower back down with control on the other side. On the next rep reverse direction across the bar. Continue alternating directions each rep.
Benefits: Brutal advanced chin up; Builds unilateral pull strength; Trains lateral movement; Builds the lats; Useful for advanced trainees; Builds bicep size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Brachialis

Description: Get into a standard push-up position with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Lower your chest toward the floor with control. Explode upward with maximum force. Push hard enough that your hands leave the floor. While airborne, quickly clap your hands together once. Bring your hands back to the push-up position before landing. Land softly with bent elbows to absorb the impact. Immediately drop into the next push-up. Master regular push-ups with explosive intent first. Use 3 to 8 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds explosive upper-body power; Develops fast-twitch muscle fibers; Trains the chest, triceps, and shoulders explosively; Improves athletic pressing performance; No equipment needed; Impressive bodyweight skill
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Reach up and grip a pull-up bar with an underhand (palms-toward-you) grip, hands shoulder-width apart or slightly narrower. Hang with arms fully extended. Cross your ankles. Brace your core. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down and back. Lead with your chest. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your biceps and lats hard at the top. Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang. Repeat for the desired number of reps. This is one of the easier pull-up variations for most people due to bicep involvement.
Benefits: Maximum bicep involvement of any pull-up variation; Builds the lats, biceps, and brachialis simultaneously; Often easier than wide-grip pull-ups due to bicep contribution; Excellent for arm size and back width; No equipment needed beyond a pull-up bar; Easy to load with weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (heavy involvement); Latissimus dorsi; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Trapezius and rhomboids; Forearms and grip

Description: Reach up and grip a pull-up bar with an overhand (palms-away) grip, hands roughly 6 inches apart. Hang with arms fully extended. Cross your ankles behind you. Brace your core. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down toward your hips. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Your chest should approach the bar. Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang with arms completely straight. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 5 to 10 strict reps per set. Use band assistance if you cannot complete bodyweight reps.
Benefits: Increases bicep and brachialis involvement vs wide-grip pull-ups; Builds lat width and back thickness; Trains the upper back and grip simultaneously; Useful variation for bicep development; No equipment needed beyond a pull-up bar; Easy to load with weight once bodyweight is mastered
