Exercise Name: Dumbbell Seated Tuck Crunch on Floor
Description: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet off the ground. Hold a dumbbell against your chest with both hands. Lean back slightly to balance on your tailbone. Brace your core and keep your back straight. Extend your legs out and lower your torso back partway. Crunch up by pulling your knees in toward your chest. Squeeze your abs hard at the contracted position. Extend back out to the start with control.

Description: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing forward (underhand grip). Sit tall with chest up. At the bottom, rotate your wrists back to the underhand grip. Repeat for the full set, rotating at the top and bottom.

Description: Sit on a bench with back support. Hold a dumbbell in one hand and press it overhead to lockout. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Squeeze the tricep at the top. Complete reps and switch sides.

Bend the elbow to 90 degrees so the forearm is vertical. Brace the core and keep the upper arm in place. Rotate the forearm down toward the floor by internally rotating the shoulder. Stop just before the dumbbell touches the floor. Slowly rotate back up to vertical and repeat then switch arms.

Description: Position a bench to your side. Place the top of your right foot on the bench. Step your left foot forward into a comfortable single-leg stance. Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Keep your arms straight and let the dumbbells rise with your shoulders. Do not bend at the elbows — this is not a row. Squeeze your traps hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not roll your shoulders forward or backward. Lower the dumbbells under control by relaxing your traps and letting your shoulders return to neutral. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use heavy weight and strict form for best results. Use straps for heavy loading if your grip starts to fail before your traps.

Description: Stand tall. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand at your side. Left hand behind your head or at your side. Feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Bend laterally to the right — lowering the dumbbell along your right leg. Bend as far as comfortable. Contract your left obliques to pull yourself back upright. Complete reps bending to the right (working the left obliques), then switch the dumbbell to your left hand. Keep your hips still. Move only at the waist. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.

Brace your core and lift the hips up into a side bridge. Set the top knee bent up toward the chest with the foot off the floor. Hold the side bridge with the dumbbell at the hip. Keep the body in a straight line from head to bottom foot. Hold the position. Switch sides and repeat.

Description: Lie on your right side with your forearm on the floor and elbow under your shoulder. Stack your feet on top of each other or stagger them for stability. Hold a dumbbell in your left hand resting on your top hip. Brace your core and lift your hips off the floor. Form a straight line from your head to your feet. Hold this side plank position with the dumbbell securely on your hip. Keep your hips elevated and shoulders square. Hold for time, then lower under control. Switch sides.

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Take a wide step out to the right. Toes pointing forward. Sit your hips back and bend your right knee, lowering your hips down on the right side. Keep your left leg completely straight. Both feet stay flat on the floor. Lower until your right thigh is approximately parallel to the floor. Drive through your right foot to push back to standing. Repeat on the left side. Continue alternating sides. Keep your chest up and back flat throughout.

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level. Position the dumbbells with palms facing forward. Brace your core and stand tall. Step laterally to the right with your right foot. As you land, drop into a side lunge by sitting back on your right leg. At the bottom of the lunge, press both dumbbells overhead. Lock out the press at the bottom of the lunge. Lower the dumbbells back to shoulder level as you push off your right foot to return to standing. Alternate sides.

Squeeze the rear delt at the top of the fly. Lower the dumbbell back to the hip with control. Complete reps then switch sides.

Description: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Shift your weight to your right side by bending your right knee and sitting your right hip back. Your left leg stays straight. Your right leg bends into a deep side squat. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.

Press the left dumbbell up while the right stays still. Alternate sides for the full set.

Maintain a slight bend in both elbows throughout. Brace your core hard. Lower the right dumbbell out to the side in a wide arc while the left stays extended. Squeeze the chest to bring the right dumbbell back over the chest. Repeat with the left arm, alternating sides each rep.
Benefits: Increases time under tension on each side; Strong anti-rotation core challenge; Builds chest size; Strict alternating isolation; Useful for chest specialization; Different stimulus than two-arm fly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Lie on the floor with a dumbbell in your right hand at your shoulder. Bend your knees with feet flat for stability. Left arm at your side or extended. Press the dumbbell up to lockout above your chest. Lower under control until your right elbow touches the floor. Pause briefly on the floor. Press back up to lockout. Fight rotation — maintain a flat back. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Unilateral pressing builds per-side strength; Demands core anti-rotation; Floor limits range for shoulder safety; Exposes left-right imbalances; No bench needed; Useful when only one dumbbell is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (anti-rotation)

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Single Arm Neutral Grip Front Raise
Description: Stand tall with a dumbbell in one hand at the side. Grip the dumbbell with a neutral palm facing the body. Brace your core and set the chest tall. Keep the arm slightly bent throughout. Raise the dumbbell straight up in front. Stop when the dumbbell reaches shoulder height. Pause briefly at the top. Lower the dumbbell back to the side with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong front delt builder; Trains the upper chest; Strong unilateral focus; Easy to scale loading; Useful shoulder builder; Strong dumbbell move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major; Lateral deltoid

Description: Stand tall with a dumbbell in one hand at shoulder height. Press the dumbbell straight overhead to lockout. Lock your elbow and pin your bicep close to your ear. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Begin walking forward with smooth, controlled steps. Keep the dumbbell stable directly above your shoulder. Resist any side bend or trunk rotation. Walk for distance or time, then switch arms.
Benefits: Builds shoulder stability; Brutal core challenge; Improves overhead control; Single-arm asymmetrical load; Useful conditioning work; Builds full-body bracing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Core; Obliques; Triceps brachii

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Single Arm Underhand Front Raise
Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in one hand with a supinated (palms-up) grip. Keep your arm at your side with the dumbbell in front of your thigh. Brace your core and keep your chest up. With a slight bend in the elbow, raise the dumbbell straight in front of you. Lift until your arm is parallel to the floor. Keep the palm facing up throughout the rep. Lower slowly to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Emphasizes the front deltoid; Hits the biceps short head as a synergist; New angle for shoulder development; Allows unilateral focus; Helps fix side-to-side imbalances
Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Biceps brachii; Side deltoid

Description: Sit at a preacher bench with the pad against your right armpit. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand with an underhand grip. Drape your right arm over the preacher pad with arm fully extended. Pin your chest to the pad and brace your core. Use your left hand to support yourself on the bench. Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow. Squeeze the bicep hard at the top. Lower the dumbbell back down with control to full extension. Switch arms.
Benefits: Strict single-arm bicep isolation; Eliminates body english; Allows mind-muscle focus on working arm; Corrects left-right imbalances; Strong peak contraction; Useful for breaking through bicep plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Stand tall on your right leg holding a dumbbell in your left hand (opposite the standing leg). Your left foot rests lightly behind you for balance, but most weight is on the right leg. Soft-bend your right knee and hold that fixed angle throughout. Brace your core hard. Begin the descent by hinging forward at the right hip. As you hinge, let your left leg lift behind you to counterbalance. Keep your hips square — do not let your left hip rotate up. Keep your back flat with a slight natural arch. Lower the dumbbell along the front of your right leg toward the floor. Continue until your torso and left leg form a straight line roughly parallel to the floor. Reverse the movement by squeezing your right glute and driving your hips forward to stand back up. The left leg returns to the start position. Tap the left toe down briefly between reps for balance, or hold it off the floor for more challenge. Complete all reps on the right leg, then switch and balance on the left leg with the dumbbell in the right hand.
Benefits: Builds the glutes and hamstrings unilaterally; Trains balance, ankle stability, and core control; Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances; Excellent injury-prevention exercise for athletes; Easier on the lower back than barbell deadlifts; Works at home with one dumbbell
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus and gluteus medius; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Adductor magnus; Calves (stabilizer); Core (anti-rotation, anti-lateral-flexion); Forearms and grip

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Side Lying One Hand Raise
Description: Lie on a bench on your side with the body fully supported. Hold a light dumbbell in the top hand with the arm hanging down across the body. Brace your core and keep the body still. Raise the dumbbell up away from the body in a wide arc. Keep a slight bend in the elbow throughout. Lift until the arm is roughly vertical above your shoulder. Pause briefly and squeeze the side delt. Lower with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strict side delt isolation; Deep stretch under load; Side lying angle; No leg drive cheating; Builds shoulder detail; Excellent unilateral move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Rotator cuff

Description: Stand on a step with the ball of your right foot on the edge. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand. Hold a wall or rack with your left hand for balance. Tuck your left foot behind your right ankle. Lower your right heel as far as possible for a full stretch. Press through the ball of your foot to raise as high as possible. Squeeze your calf at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per leg.
Benefits: Doubles the demand per calf; Exposes left-right imbalances; Easy to load progressively with one dumbbell; Full range with a step; No machine needed; Useful at-home calf exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (working leg); Soleus; Achilles tendon

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place a dumbbell on your right hip crease. Hold it steady with your right hand. Extend your left leg straight up toward the ceiling (or straight forward). Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up. At the top, your body should form a straight line from right knee to shoulders. Squeeze your right glute hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Repeat for the desired reps. Switch sides. Use moderate weight.
Benefits: Progressive glute loading per leg; Exposes left-right glute imbalances; Builds single-leg hip extension strength; Easy to load progressively with dumbbells; No bench needed; Excellent for glute hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Single Leg Step Up on Bench
Description: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides. Stand facing a sturdy flat bench. Place one foot fully on the bench. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Drive through the planted foot to step up. Stand tall on top with the trailing leg lifted. Step back down with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds single leg strength; Trains the quads; Strong unilateral move; Builds the glutes; Useful for balance; No barbell needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Stand in front of a box or bench, holding dumbbells at your sides. Place your right foot on the box. Drive through your right foot to step up onto the box. Stand fully on the box. Squeeze your right glute at the top. Step back down with your left foot leading. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch. Use a box height that allows a 90-degree knee bend. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per leg.
Benefits: Builds single-leg strength unilaterally; Exposes left-right imbalances; Dumbbells allow progressive loading; Easy to scale; Simple setup; Builds step-up power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (stepping leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Calves

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, a dumbbell on the floor between your feet. Bend at the hips and knees to grip the dumbbell with one hand. Keep the other arm extended out for balance. Pull your shoulders back and engage your lats. Brace your core hard. Drive through your heels to start the dumbbell moving up. As the dumbbell passes your hips, drop into a partial squat while pulling the dumbbell to your shoulder. Stand up to the lockout position with the dumbbell at your shoulder. Lower with control. Switch arms.
Benefits: Builds explosive total body power; Strong unilateral loading pattern; Develops Olympic lifting skill; Functional carryover to athletic movement; Time-efficient compound lift; Trains hip drive and shoulder catch
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid; Trapezius; Erector spinae

Description: Sit with upper back against a bench. Place a dumbbell on your right hip crease. Hold the dumbbell in place with your right hand. Bend your right knee with foot flat. Extend your left leg straight forward or up. Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up. At the top, body forms a straight line from right knee to shoulders. Squeeze your right glute hard. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Progressive glute loading per leg; Exposes glute imbalances; Builds unilateral hip extension power; Excellent for glute hypertrophy; Easier to set up than barbell hip thrusts; Useful for athletic training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand. Step one foot forward into a split stance. Fix this position for the set. Lower your back knee toward the floor by bending both knees. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor. Drive through your front foot to rise. Complete reps, then switch sides. Keep torso upright throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per leg.
Benefits: Focused loading on the front leg; No stepping or balance challenge; Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally; Easy to load progressively; Exposes left-right imbalances; Simple setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Single Spider Curl with Chest Support
Description: Set an incline bench at about 45 to 60 degrees. Lie face down on the bench with chest on the pad. Hold a dumbbell in one hand with the arm hanging straight down. Set the palm facing forward in a supinated grip. Brace your core and keep the upper arm pinned to the bench. Curl the dumbbell up by bending only the elbow. Squeeze the bicep hard at the top. Lower with control to a full stretch. Complete reps and switch arms.
Benefits: Strict bicep isolation; Single-arm focus; Builds bicep peak; Chest-supported strict form; Excellent arm-day move; Builds arm detail
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Step into a split stance — right foot forward, left foot back. Stand tall with chest up and core braced. Lower your back (left) knee straight down toward the floor by bending both knees. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor and your front thigh is parallel. Drive through your front foot to stand back up. Keep torso upright throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps on the right side, then switch. Keep the dumbbells at your sides — do not let them swing forward. Increase load progressively as you get stronger.
Benefits: Builds single-leg quad and glute strength with progressive load; Exposes left-right strength imbalances; Easier to load and balance than walking lunges; More accessible than Bulgarian split squats; Works at home with one pair of dumbbells; Trains grip as a secondary benefit
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus (front leg); Hamstrings; Adductors; Hip flexors (rear leg); Forearms and grip

Description: Stand holding a dumbbell in your right hand. Shift your weight to your left leg. Keep a very slight bend in your left knee. Hinge at the hips. Extend your right leg straight back as your torso lowers forward. Lower the dumbbell toward the floor. Keep your back flat. Continue until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Drive your left hip forward to return to standing. Squeeze your left glute at the top. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds unilateral hamstring and glute strength; Minimal knee bend maximizes hamstring involvement; Develops balance and proprioception; Exposes left-right imbalances; Simple setup; Builds hip hinge pattern on one leg
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (standing leg); Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius (balance); Erector spinae; Core (anti-rotation)

Description: Lie on a flat bench with a dumbbell in each hand at chest level. Plant your right foot flat on the floor. Place your left foot up on the bench beside your hip in a sprinter position. Hold the dumbbells with palms facing forward. Brace your core hard against the asymmetric stance. Press both dumbbells straight up to lockout, driving with the right leg. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Lower the dumbbells back to chest level. Switch leg positions partway through the set.
Benefits: Asymmetric stance creates explosive pressing power; Strong leg drive component; Builds chest, triceps, and front delts; Trains core anti-rotation; Different stimulus than standard pressing; Useful for athletic carryover
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core stabilizers

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent at 45 degrees, feet flat on the floor. Hold a dumbbell at your chest (easier) or extended overhead (harder). Brace your core. Sit up by curling your torso upward, bringing your chest toward your knees. Squeeze your abs hard at the top. Lower under control back to the floor. Anchor your feet under a heavy object if needed. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to sit-ups; Easy to scale by weight and position; Builds ab strength beyond bodyweight; No bench needed; Simple execution; Effective for ab hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques (secondary)

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart and a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body. Set your feet so toes point slightly outward. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Initiate the squat by sitting your hips back and down while bending your knees. Keep your chest tall. Allow the dumbbells to hang straight down at your sides as you descend. Squat down until your hip crease drops to or below the top of your knee (parallel or deeper). Drive through your full foot to stand back up, squeezing your glutes at the top. Keep your knees tracking in line with your toes throughout. Avoid letting them cave inward. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Increase load as form holds steady.
Benefits: Builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings with minimal equipment; Excellent regression for learning squat mechanics before adding a barbell; Easy on the lower back compared to barbell back squats; Highly portable: can be done at home with a single pair of dumbbells; Trains grip and core stability through the loaded hold; Easy to scale up by increasing dumbbell weight or adding tempo and pauses
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Erector spinae (stabilizer); Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand on your right leg. Hold dumbbells at your sides or at your chest. Extend your left leg forward. Squat down on your right leg by bending your knee and sitting back. Descend as deep as balance and strength allow. Drive through your right foot to stand. Complete reps, then switch legs. Use a box behind you to control depth if needed. Dumbbells held in front can serve as counterbalance for deeper squats.
Benefits: Adds progressive load to single-leg squats; Dumbbells as counterbalance improve depth; Builds single-leg strength; Exposes left-right imbalances; No rack needed; Develops balance and coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Calves

Description: Stand holding dumbbells at your sides. Plant your right foot firmly. Place your left foot behind you with just your toes on the floor (kickstand). The kickstand provides balance but minimal weight support. Hinge at the hips. Push your butt back. Keep back flat. Lower the dumbbells along your right leg. Feel the stretch in your right hamstring. Drive your right hip forward to stand. Squeeze your glute. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Progression toward single-leg RDL; Kickstand provides balance without much support; Most load on working leg; Builds unilateral hamstring strength; Easier balance than full single-leg RDL; Excellent teaching exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core (anti-rotation); Gluteus medius (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Split Squat Front Foot Elevated with Bosu Ball
Description: Hold a dumbbell in each hand at the sides. Place the front foot on top of a bosu ball flat side up. Set the back foot a stride length behind on the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lower the back knee toward the floor. Stop just above the floor with the front shin near vertical. Drive through the front foot to stand back up. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds single leg strength; Trains balance; Strong split squat variation; Useful for ankle stability; Builds the quads
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level. Start with palms facing your face (supinated grip), elbows tucked in front. Brace your core hard. Press the right dumbbell up while rotating your wrist outward to a pronated grip at lockout. Lock out the right arm overhead while keeping the left dumbbell stationary at the shoulder. Reverse the motion, rotating back to the supinated grip at the shoulder. Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep. Maintain a strong upright trunk throughout.
Benefits: Hits all three deltoid heads; Adds anti-lateral-flexion core challenge; Standing position adds full body engagement; Single-arm version builds stability; Corrects left-right imbalances; Strong shoulder development variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core stabilizers

Description: Stand with dumbbells held at your shoulders, palms facing each other. Feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core. Squat down to parallel or below. Drive through your feet to stand explosively. Use the standing momentum to press the dumbbells overhead. Lock out at the top. Lower the dumbbells back to your shoulders as you descend into the next squat. Move fluidly. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Full-body compound movement; Builds legs, shoulders, and core together; Excellent metabolic conditioning; Time-efficient exercise; CrossFit staple; Develops leg drive and pressing coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer); Hamstrings

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Hold two dumbbells with a neutral grip, pressing them firmly together at your chest. Maintain strong inward pressure — the dumbbells should touch each other. Press both dumbbells straight up while keeping them pressed together. Squeeze your inner chest hard at the top. Lower back down, maintaining the inward squeeze throughout. The squeeze is more important than the weight — lighter dumbbells work well. Focus on chest contraction rather than load. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Activates the inner chest fibers; Constant inward squeeze for pec adduction; Builds chest mind-muscle connection; Joint-friendly neutral grip; Excellent chest finisher; Different stimulus from standard DB press
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (inner fibers); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Alternate Hammer Curl and Press
Description: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing each other (hammer grip). Brace your core hard. Hammer curl the right dumbbell up to shoulder level. Squeeze the bicep at the top of the curl. Press the right dumbbell overhead while maintaining the neutral grip. Lock out the right arm at the top, then reverse the motion. Lower through the press and back through the curl to the starting position. Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Trains biceps and shoulders unilaterally; Time-efficient compound combo; Hammer grip targets brachialis; Strong core anti-rotation demand; Builds arm and shoulder strength; Useful for full upper body conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height. Position the dumbbells with palms facing forward. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Press the right dumbbell straight up overhead while keeping the left at shoulder level. Lock out the right arm at the top. Lower the right dumbbell back to shoulder level with control. Press the left dumbbell up while the right stays still. Alternate sides for the full set.
Benefits: Increases time under tension on each side; Builds shoulder strength unilaterally; Adds anti-lateral-flexion core challenge; Standing position adds full body engagement; Corrects left-right imbalances; Strong stability demand
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core stabilizers

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height with palms facing your body, dumbbells touching. Brace your core. Stand tall. Begin pressing the dumbbells up. As you press, rotate your wrists so palms face forward at the top. Continue pressing until arms are fully extended overhead, palms facing forward. Lower the dumbbells while reversing the rotation — palms face backward, then back to your body at shoulder height. Keep your torso upright throughout. The standing position requires extra core bracing. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight — the rotational component changes the stimulus.
Benefits: Hits all three heads of the deltoid through full rotation; Standing position adds core stability demand; Builds shoulder size and strength with greater range; Trains shoulder rotation under load; More functional than seated pressing; Works at home with one pair of dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Posterior deltoid (slight); Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Bend your elbows to 90 degrees with forearms parallel to the floor. Pin your elbows tightly against your sides. Hold the dumbbells with palms facing each other. Brace your core. Rotate your forearms outward by externally rotating at the shoulders. Continue until your forearms point out to the sides at 90 degrees. Slowly rotate back to the starting position.
Benefits: Builds rotator cuff strength; Improves shoulder health; Useful for rehab and prehab; Strict isolation of external rotators; Strong functional carryover; Easy to scale by changing dumbbell weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Infraspinatus; Teres minor; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Alternate Vertical Front Raises
Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Let the dumbbells hang at your sides in front of your thighs. Brace your core and keep your chest up. With a slight bend in the elbow, raise one dumbbell straight in front of you. Lift until your arm is parallel to the floor. Lower with control as you start to raise the other arm. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Shoulder-friendly neutral grip; Allows heavier loading; Builds front shoulder size; Alternating pattern improves focus; Even side-to-side development; Useful for shoulder hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Upper chest

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand behind your body with palms facing back. Stand upright with the dumbbells resting against the back of your thighs. Brace your core and stand tall. Allow the dumbbells to roll down to your fingertips. Curl the dumbbells back up by flexing your wrists. Squeeze your forearms hard at the top of the curl. Lower the dumbbells back down to the fingertip position with control.
Benefits: Trains forearm flexors through full range; Behind-the-back position frees the wrists; Builds grip strength; Develops wrist flexion strength; Allows progressive loading; Useful for athletes who need strong forearms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Brachioradialis; Wrist flexors

Description: Stand with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body. Brace your core and stand tall. Maintain a slight bend in the elbows throughout. Raise the right dumbbell out to the side to shoulder height. Keep the left dumbbell at the side. Squeeze the right medial delt at the top. Lower the right dumbbell back to the side with control. Raise the left dumbbell while the right stays still. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Increases time under tension on each side; Strict alternating pattern; Builds shoulder width; Adds anti-lateral-flexion core challenge; Corrects left-right imbalances; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Trapezius (upper)

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at thigh level with palms facing back. Pin your elbows against your sides. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Curl the right dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow, keeping the overhand grip. Squeeze the forearm and bicep at the top. Lower the right dumbbell back down with control. Repeat with the left arm. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Single-arm reverse curl work; Strict alternating pattern; Targets forearm extensors and brachioradialis; Corrects left-right imbalances; Builds forearm thickness; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachioradialis; Forearm extensors; Biceps brachii; Brachialis

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides, palms facing your body. Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and pin your elbows against your sides. Curl both dumbbells up at the same time, rotating your wrists outward as you lift so your palms face your shoulders at the top. Continue until the dumbbells reach shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps hard for a one-second hold. Lower both dumbbells together under control over two seconds, rotating your wrists back to neutral. Fully extend your arms at the bottom of each rep. Keep your torso completely upright — no leaning back or swinging. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Builds the biceps brachii with reliable, strict form; Forces equal effort from both arms simultaneously; Easy to load progressively over time; Trains grip and forearm strength as a byproduct; Simple enough for beginners but effective for advanced lifters; Works at home with one pair of dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (long and short heads); Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors; Anterior deltoid (minor stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Bent Arm Lateral Raise
Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand. Bend your elbows to 90 degrees with forearms parallel to the floor. Position the dumbbells in front of your body with palms facing each other. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Maintain the bent arm position throughout. Raise the dumbbells out to the sides by lifting the elbows. Continue until your upper arms are level with your shoulders. Lower the dumbbells back down with control to the starting position.
Benefits: Allows heavier loading than straight arm raises; Reduces shoulder strain; Builds side delt strength; Different strength curve than standard lateral raise; Useful for breaking through plateau; Strong side delt activation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Trapezius (upper); Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand with the balls of your feet on a step, heels hanging off. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Lower your heels as far as possible for a full stretch. Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible. Squeeze your calves at the top. Lower under control. Full range of motion on every rep. Use moderate weight. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set. Hold a wall for balance if needed.
Benefits: Simple loaded calf raise at home; No machine needed; Easy to scale by dumbbell weight; Full range with a step; Builds calf size and strength; Accessible anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Achilles tendon

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Biceps Curl To Shoulder Press
Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Use an underhand grip with palms facing forward. Brace your core hard. Curl both dumbbells up to shoulder level. Squeeze the biceps at the top of the curl. Rotate your wrists so palms face forward and continue into a shoulder press. Press the dumbbells overhead until your arms are fully extended. Reverse the motion, lowering through the press and back through the curl.
Benefits: Trains biceps, shoulders, and core in one combo; Time-efficient compound movement; Standing position adds full body engagement; Builds arm and shoulder strength; Useful for full upper body conditioning; Develops coordination across patterns
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in your right hand at shoulder level. Position the dumbbell with palm facing forward. Brace your core and shift your weight slightly to your right leg. Begin pressing the dumbbell overhead while rotating your torso to the left. Drive through your right hip and rotate your trunk through the press. Lock out the dumbbell overhead with your torso rotated to the left. Reverse the motion, lowering the dumbbell and rotating back to center. Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Benefits: Trains rotational power for athletic transfer; Links hip drive to core rotation to shoulder press; Builds explosive single-arm pressing strength; Strong functional carryover; Develops trunk rotation under load; Useful for throwing and combat sport athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Obliques; Triceps brachii; Gluteus maximus

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width. Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand with an underhand grip. Bend forward at the waist with knees slightly bent. Brace your right elbow against the inside of your right thigh, just above the knee. Allow the dumbbell to hang fully extended toward the floor. Curl the dumbbell up by bending at the elbow. Squeeze the bicep hard at the top with the dumbbell near your shoulder. Lower the dumbbell back down with control to full extension. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Strict bicep isolation; Eliminates shoulder movement; Greater range of motion than seated version; Single-arm work corrects imbalances; Strong peak contraction; Useful as a finisher for bicep day
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially short head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand. Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor. Pin your upper arms against your sides, elbows at 90 degrees. Extend both forearms straight back by straightening at the elbows. Lock out with arms fully straight behind you. Squeeze your triceps hard at the top. Slowly bend your elbows back to 90 degrees. Keep upper arms still throughout. Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Classic tricep isolation exercise; Peak contraction at lockout; Strict isolation when done correctly; Builds tricep size (especially lateral head); Simple setup; No bench needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (especially lateral head); Anconeus

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out at about 45 degrees. Press a dumbbell overhead with your right arm fully extended. Keep your eyes on the dumbbell throughout the movement. Place your left hand on your inner thigh. Brace your core hard. Push your hips back to your right side as you bend forward and to the left. Slide your left hand down your inner thigh toward the floor. Keep the dumbbell directly overhead with arm vertical. Reverse to standing. Switch sides.
Benefits: Builds hip mobility and oblique strength; Trains shoulder stability under load; Strong functional movement pattern; Develops total body coordination; Useful as a warm-up or accessory; Stretches hamstrings and adductors
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Hamstrings; Adductors; Anterior deltoid; Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing forward. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. As you curl, allow your elbows to flare slightly outward. Curl both dumbbells up to shoulder height. Continue until your forearms are roughly vertical. Squeeze the inner biceps hard at the top. Lower the dumbbells back down with control to full extension.
Benefits: Targets inner biceps and short head; Builds inner arm thickness; Different stimulus than standard curls; Useful for hypertrophy training; Pairs well with outer-grip curls; Strong peak contraction
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (short head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand pressed overhead. Position the dumbbell directly overhead with arm fully extended. Place your left hand on your hip or at your side. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Bend your right elbow to lower the dumbbell behind your head. Continue until you feel a strong stretch in the tricep. Press the dumbbell back overhead by extending the elbow. Switch arms.
Benefits: Strict single-arm tricep isolation; Strong long head emphasis; Corrects tricep strength imbalances; Builds tricep size; Strong stretch at the bottom; Useful for tricep specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (long head primarily); Triceps brachii (medial and lateral heads); Anconeus

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing One Arm Reverse Curl
Description: Stand tall. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand with a pronated (palm-down) grip. Pin your right elbow at your side. Other hand at your side. Start with arm extended. Curl the dumbbell up toward your shoulder, maintaining the pronated grip. Squeeze your forearm and brachioradialis at the top. Lower under control over two seconds. Keep your upper arm still throughout. Complete reps, then switch arms. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Targets brachioradialis and forearm extensors; Unilateral exposes imbalances; Easier on the wrists than barbell reverse curls; Builds forearm thickness; Useful for grip-intensive activities; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachioradialis (primary); Biceps brachii (reduced vs supinated); Brachialis; Wrist extensors

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing One Arm Palm In Press
Description: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in one hand at shoulder level. Set the palm facing in with the dumbbell parallel to the body. Plant your feet at shoulder-width and brace your core. Press the dumbbell straight up overhead. Keep the palm facing in throughout the press. Lock out at the top with the dumbbell over your shoulder. Resist any side lean from the load. Lower the dumbbell back to shoulder level. Complete reps and switch.
Benefits: Friendly shoulder mechanics; Trains anti-lateral flexion; Single-arm focus; Builds overhead strength; Easy on the shoulders; Useful for shoulder issues
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Lateral deltoid

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing One Arm Concentration Curl
Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width apart, soft bend in the knees. Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand. Hinge forward at the hips and rest your right elbow against your inner right thigh. Allow the dumbbell to hang at full arm extension. Place your left hand on your left thigh for support. Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower the dumbbell back down with control. Switch arms.
Benefits: Strict bicep peak isolation; Builds bicep size; No bench required; Strong stretch at the bottom; Eliminates body english; Useful for home or travel training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Forearms

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body. Pull your shoulders back and down. Brace your core. Maintain a soft (slightly bent) elbow position throughout. Lift both dumbbells out to your sides simultaneously. Lead with your elbows, not your wrists. Continue lifting until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor. Your wrists should be slightly lower than your elbows at the top. Pause briefly at the top with your shoulder blades depressed (down) — do not shrug. Lower the dumbbells under control over a count of two to three seconds back to your sides. Use moderate weight — most lifters use far too much weight on this lift, which causes upper-trap dominance and cheating. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Most direct exercise for building the lateral (side) delts; Builds shoulder width and the V-taper look; Easy to do anywhere with a pair of dumbbells; Joint-friendly when performed with strict form; Excellent finisher after compound shoulder pressing; Improves shoulder stability and posture
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid (secondary); Posterior deltoid (secondary); Trapezius (especially upper, when shrugging is allowed); Supraspinatus (rotator cuff, initial 30 degrees)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height. Position the dumbbells with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Press both dumbbells straight up overhead while maintaining the neutral grip. Bring the dumbbells together at the top of the press. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Lower the dumbbells back to shoulder height with control. Maintain the neutral grip throughout the entire set.
Benefits: Neutral grip is shoulder-friendly; Reduces shoulder strain compared to pronated grip; Builds shoulder size and strength; Strong tricep engagement; Useful for sensitive shoulders; Different stimulus than standard press
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Trapezius

Description: Stand in front of a preacher bench, leaning your chest into the pad. Drape your right arm over the pad with the upper arm fully supported. Hold a dumbbell in your right hand with an underhand grip and arm extended down. Brace your core and keep your chest pressed to the pad. Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow. Continue until your forearm is roughly vertical and the dumbbell is near your shoulder. Squeeze your bicep at the top. Lower the dumbbell with control to full extension. Complete reps, then switch arms.
Benefits: Strict single-arm bicep isolation; Standing position is more accessible than seated; Eliminates body english; Single-arm work corrects imbalances; Strong peak contraction; Builds bicep size with strict form
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at thigh level with palms facing back (overhand grip). Pin your elbows against your sides. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Curl both dumbbells up by bending at the elbows while maintaining the overhand grip. Continue until the dumbbells are near shoulder height. Squeeze the forearms and biceps at the top. Lower the dumbbells back down with control to full extension.
Benefits: Targets forearm extensors and brachioradialis; Builds forearm size and grip; Different stimulus than standard curls; Useful for thicker arms; Pairs well with regular curls for full development; Strong wrist stability work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachioradialis; Forearm extensors; Biceps brachii; Brachialis

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Single Arm Arnold Press
Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand at chin level. Start with palm facing your body, dumbbell close to your shoulder. Brace your core hard and pull your shoulder back. Press the dumbbell overhead while rotating the wrist outward. End with palm facing forward at the top. Lock out at the top with arm fully extended. Reverse the rotation as you lower back to the starting position. Switch arms.
Benefits: Hits all three deltoid heads; Strong anti-rotation core challenge; Standing position adds core engagement; Corrects shoulder imbalances; Builds total shoulder size; Useful for athletic carryover
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Posterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Front Raise Above Head
Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Use a pronated (palms-down) grip. Brace your core and keep your chest up. With a slight bend in the elbows, raise both dumbbells straight in front of you. Continue lifting past parallel and up overhead. Stop when the dumbbells are directly above your shoulders. Lower slowly back to the start.
Benefits: Trains the front delt through a long arc; Recruits upper traps and serratus; Builds front shoulder size; Improves overhead mobility; Strong full-range shoulder builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Traps; Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Single Arm Biceps Curl
Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a single dumbbell in your right hand at your side. Position the dumbbell with palm facing forward. Place your left hand on your hip or at your side. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbow. Squeeze the bicep hard at the top. Lower the dumbbell back down with control to a full stretch. Switch arms.
Benefits: Strict single-arm bicep isolation; Corrects bicep strength imbalances; Builds bicep size; Eliminates body english; Strong mind-muscle connection; Useful for arm specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a single heavy dumbbell with both hands. Press the dumbbell overhead until your arms are fully extended. Grip the top end of the dumbbell with both palms underneath. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down. Lower the dumbbell behind your head by bending only at the elbows. Keep your upper arms vertical and elbows pointed forward. Continue lowering until you feel a strong stretch in your triceps. Press the dumbbell back overhead by extending your elbows. Squeeze the triceps at lockout.
Benefits: Maximizes long head triceps stretch; Builds tricep size and strength; Standing version engages core; Different stimulus than skull crushers; Useful for tricep specialization; Strong overhead position carryover
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (long head primarily); Triceps brachii (medial and lateral heads); Anconeus

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out at about 45 degrees. Press a dumbbell overhead with your right arm fully extended. Keep your eyes on the dumbbell throughout the movement. Place your left hand on your inner thigh. Push your hips back to your right side as you bend forward and to the left. Slide your left hand down your inner thigh toward the floor. Keep the dumbbell directly overhead with arm vertical. Reverse the motion to stand back to the starting position. Complete reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds hip mobility and oblique strength; Trains shoulder stability under load; Stretches hamstrings and adductors; Strong functional movement pattern; Develops total body coordination; Useful as a warm-up or accessory
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Hamstrings; Adductors; Anterior deltoid; Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing your body. Rotate your wrists so your palms face forward. The dumbbells now hang in front of your thighs. Pin your upper arms against your sides — they should not move during the exercise. Allow the dumbbells to roll down to the tips of your fingers as you let your wrists extend backward (knuckles forward). Curl the dumbbells back up by flexing only at the wrists. Squeeze the dumbbells back into your palms as you curl up. Continue until your wrists are fully flexed (palms angled toward your forearms). Squeeze the forearms hard for one second at the top. Slowly extend your wrists back to the start position over a count of two seconds. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a light to moderate weight; reps should be in the 12 to 25 range.
Benefits: Direct isolation of the forearm flexors; Builds grip strength and visible forearm size; Easy to do at home with one pair of dumbbells; Useful accessory for any pulling exercise; Carries over to deadlifts, rows, and pull-ups; Easy to scale by changing weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Flexor carpi radialis; Flexor carpi ulnaris; Palmaris longus; Flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at thigh level with an overhand grip. Allow the dumbbells to rest against the front of your thighs. Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides. Lower the dumbbells by extending your wrists down toward the floor. Curl the dumbbells back up by extending your wrists upward. Squeeze the forearm extensors at the top of the curl. Lower back down with control.
Benefits: Trains forearm extensors directly; Builds back of forearm for arm thickness; Strict isolation; Allows progressive loading; Improves wrist strength; Useful for athletes who need strong forearms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm extensors; Brachioradialis; Wrist extensors

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Step your right foot forward two to three feet into a split stance. Keep your feet hip-width apart for balance. This is your fixed position — you will not step during the set. Lower your back (left) knee toward the floor by bending both knees. Descend until your left knee is just above the floor. Drive through your right foot to return to the top of the split stance. Complete all reps on this side, then switch which foot is forward. Keep your torso upright throughout.
Benefits: Focused loading on the front leg; No stepping or balance challenge; Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally; Easy to load progressively; Safer than walking lunges for beginners; Exposes left-right imbalances
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall holding a dumbbell in your right hand. Bend slightly forward at the waist. Press the back of your right upper arm firmly against the front of your torso. Your right arm is now braced against your body with the elbow locked in place. Curl the dumbbell up toward your right shoulder by bending at the elbow. Squeeze your bicep hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control over two to three seconds. The body brace prevents any cheating. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Ultra-strict bicep isolation; Body brace eliminates all swinging; Builds the bicep peak; No bench or preacher pad needed; Easy to load progressively; Reveals true bicep strength per arm
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially short head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Stand tall. Hold a dumbbell with both hands overhead, arms extended. Grip the inner plate. Keep upper arms vertical, pointing to the ceiling. Bend at the elbows to lower the dumbbell behind your head. Lower until you feel a deep tricep stretch. Extend your elbows to press back to lockout. Squeeze your triceps at the top. Keep elbows pointing up — do not let them flare forward. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Targets the long head of the tricep; Overhead position maximizes long-head stretch; Simple single-dumbbell setup; Builds tricep size and strength; Easy to load progressively; Classic tricep exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (especially long head); Anconeus

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Standing Single Leg Calf Raise
Description: Stand on one foot on a slightly raised step or platform. Hold a dumbbell in the same-side hand. Hold a wall or rack with the other hand for balance. Let the heel of the working foot drop below the platform. Brace your core and keep your knee straight. Press up onto the ball of the foot as high as possible. Squeeze the calf hard at the top. Lower slowly to a deep stretch. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Forces each calf to work alone; Fixes side-to-side imbalances; Builds calf hypertrophy; Improves balance and stability; Strong gastrocnemius builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Soleus; Tibialis posterior

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Step Up with Knee Raise
Description: Stand in front of a sturdy box or step, holding a dumbbell in each hand. Place one foot fully on the box. Drive through the heel of the working foot to step up onto the box. As you reach standing, drive the trailing knee up into a high knee. Raise the knee until the thigh is parallel to the floor. Pause briefly at the top with knee high. Lower the trailing leg back down and step off the box. Complete reps on one side before switching legs.
Benefits: Builds single-leg power; Combines leg and hip flexor work; Improves balance and stability; Useful for athletic training; Trains hip drive; Time-efficient combo move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hip flexors; Calves

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes. Press both dumbbells straight up to lockout overhead. Lock out with arms fully extended. Lower under control back to shoulder height. Do not use leg drive — strict press only. Keep your torso upright throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Builds bilateral overhead pressing strength; Standing position demands core stability; Dumbbells allow natural pressing path; Each arm works independently; Exposes left-right imbalances; Develops shoulder size and strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer); Upper trapezius

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Hold one dumbbell with both hands. Extend your arms straight above your chest, locked out. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Crunch up by flexing your spine. The dumbbell remains directly above your chest — arms stay straight. Lift your shoulders off the floor. Squeeze your abs at the top. Lower under control. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Long lever arm increases ab loading; Straight-arm position adds shoulder endurance; Builds ab strength with moderate weight; Simple setup; Easy to scale; Engages shoulders alongside core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary); Anterior deltoid (isometric); Hip flexors

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell above your chest with both hands, arms extended straight. Keep your arms straight (minimal elbow bend) throughout. Arc the dumbbell behind your head toward the floor. Continue until you feel a deep stretch in your lats and chest. Pull the dumbbell back over to above your chest using your lats. Squeeze at the top. The straight arms make this harder than bent-arm version — use lighter weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Longer lever arm increases lat demand; Builds the lats, chest, and serratus anterior; Deep overhead stretch; Classic bodybuilding exercise; Improves shoulder flexibility; Excellent for ribcage expansion (traditional belief)
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (increased from straight arms); Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Triceps brachii (long head); Teres major

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Straight Arm Twisting Sit Up
Description: Lie on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a dumbbell with both hands and press it straight overhead. Keep your arms long and locked out throughout. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Sit up by curling your torso off the floor. At the top, twist the torso to bring the dumbbell across to one side. Twist back through center and lower with control to the start. Alternate the twist side on each rep.
Benefits: Loaded core challenge; Hits abs and obliques; Builds trunk power; Trains rotational core; Improves bracing; Brutal ab finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs. Keep your legs as straight as possible (minimal knee bend). Back flat. Hinge at the hips, pushing your butt back. Lower the dumbbells along your legs. Continue until you feel a deep hamstring stretch. Drive your hips forward to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Maintain a flat back throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps. Only go as low as you can maintain flat back form.
Benefits: Maximizes hamstring involvement; Dumbbells allow natural hand position; Builds hip hinge strength; Develops hamstring flexibility over time; Easy to scale; Useful at-home exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Dumbbell Step Back Lunge and Row
Description: Stand tall with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Step back with your right leg into a reverse lunge. As you reach the bottom of the lunge, hinge slightly forward. Row both dumbbells up to your hips by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top of the row. Lower the dumbbells back down to arms length as you stand back up. Repeat on the other side, alternating legs.
Benefits: Trains legs and back together; Strong cardiovascular component; Time-efficient compound combo; Builds posterior chain and lat strength; Functional movement pattern; Develops coordination across patterns
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Hamstrings

Description: Place a heavy dumbbell on the floor next to your right foot. Squat down and grip the dumbbell with your right hand. Stand up tall, holding the dumbbell at your right side. Keep your left arm relaxed at your side. Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders back and down. Resist the urge to lean toward the loaded side. Stand perfectly tall. Walk forward with controlled, normal-length strides. Walk for the desired distance (20 to 50 meters) or time. Switch sides for equal work. Use heavy weight.
Benefits: Builds elite anti-lateral flexion core stability; Heavily targets the obliques; Develops grip strength; Trains posture under asymmetric load; Excellent for athletes; Time-efficient core builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy involvement); Quadratus lumborum; Core (anti-lateral flexion); Forearms and grip; Trapezius; Gluteus medius

Description: Sit on the floor and lean back slightly to form a V with the body. Extend your legs straight out and lift them off the floor. Hold a dumbbell with both hands at chest level. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Twist the torso to bring the dumbbell to one side. Tap the dumbbell to the floor next to your hip. Twist back through center to the other side. Keep legs straight and lifted throughout the set.
Benefits: Brutal oblique builder; Loaded core work; Trains hip flexor strength; Improves balance; Tough V-sit position; Strong rotational power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Hold a dumbbell vertically with both hands hanging between your legs. Hinge at the hips, sitting back as you lower the dumbbell toward the floor. Keep your back flat and chest up. Push your knees out over your toes. Lower until the dumbbell touches the floor or you feel a strong stretch in your inner thighs. Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to stand back up. Lock out by squeezing glutes at the top. Keep the dumbbell close to your body. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Targets glutes and inner thighs with the wide stance; Forces upright torso for less lower-back stress; Works at home with one dumbbell; Excellent for building glute size; Easier to load progressively than barbell sumo for many lifters; Trains the hip-hinge pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors; Quadriceps; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Forearms and grip

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your thighs. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Maintain a slight soft bend in the knees that you keep throughout the lift. Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back behind you. Lower the dumbbells along the front of your legs while keeping them close. Continue lowering until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings. Drive your hips forward to stand back up to the starting position. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top.
Benefits: Maximizes hamstring stretch and loading; Builds glute and posterior chain strength; Reinforces the hip hinge pattern; Develops lower back endurance; Less spinal compression than barbell variants; Excellent accessory for deadlift strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Lie face down on the floor with legs extended back. Hold a light dumbbell in each hand with arms extended overhead, like superman. Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes. Simultaneously lift your arms, chest, and legs off the floor — like superman flying. Lift the dumbbells as high as comfortable above the floor. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds at the top. Squeeze your back and glutes. Lower under control back to the floor. Stop just before touching down to maintain tension. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use very light dumbbells (2 to 5 lbs) — the lever arm makes this much harder than it looks.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to superman holds; Builds upper back and glute strength; Develops shoulder mobility; Useful posture corrective exercise; Easy to scale by dumbbell weight; No bench needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids

Description: Stand with feet just wider than shoulder-width, holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands by the top end. The dumbbell hangs at arm’s length between your legs. Hinge at the hips and let the dumbbell swing back between your legs. Your back stays flat and knees stay slightly bent. Brace your core hard. Set a deep “hike pass” position — chest tall, lats engaged, dumbbell behind your hips. Explosively snap your hips forward by squeezing your glutes hard. The hip drive sends the dumbbell forward and up. Let the dumbbell swing up to roughly chest or shoulder height. Your arms guide the dumbbell — they do not lift it. At the top, your body should be standing tall with hips and knees fully extended. Glutes squeezed. Let the dumbbell swing back down, hinging at the hips again as it passes your knees. Repeat for the desired number of reps in a continuous, rhythmic motion.
Benefits: Builds explosive hip extension power; Trains the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back together; Excellent conditioning effect — high heart-rate work; Time-efficient combination of strength and cardio; Carries over to athletic movements like sprinting and jumping; Works at home with one dumbbell
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Quadriceps (secondary); Anterior deltoid (guides the swing); Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Hold a dumbbell vertically with both hands by one end. Let it hang between your legs at arm’s length. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Push your knees out over your toes. Sit straight down between your heels. Keep your torso upright. Descend until your thighs are at least parallel or your hip crease is below your knees. Drive through your full foot to stand. Push your knees out. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. The dumbbell stays vertical between your legs the entire time.
Benefits: Targets the glutes and adductors more than standard squats; Easy at-home glute exercise; Forces upright torso position; Easier on the lower back than barbell squats; Beginner-friendly squat variation; Builds inner-thigh and glute size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors; Quadriceps; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold two light dumbbells together horizontally in front of your chest. Press both dumbbells inward against each other firmly with your palms — squeeze them together. Maintain this active squeeze throughout the entire exercise. Press both dumbbells straight forward by extending your arms. Continue squeezing the dumbbells together as you press out. Pause at full extension. Squeeze your chest hard. Pull the dumbbells back toward your chest under control, maintaining the squeeze. Use light weight — the Svend press is about constant tension and squeeze.
Benefits: Targets the inner chest specifically; Constant tension through active squeezing; Easy on the joints; Excellent finisher exercise; No bench needed; Builds the chest separation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially inner fibers); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior

Description: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench, roughly knee-height. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Plant your right foot fully on top of the box. Make sure your entire foot is on the surface. Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your chest tall. Drive through your right foot — pushing through the entire foot, especially the heel — to lift your body up onto the box. Stand fully tall on top of the box with both feet planted. Squeeze your right glute hard. Step the left foot back down to the floor under control. Keep most of your weight on the right leg the entire time. Once your left foot is back on the floor, follow with your right foot. That is one rep. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch. Resist pushing off the back leg — the work should come from the working leg only.
Benefits: Builds the quads, glutes, and hamstrings one leg at a time; Trains balance, ankle stability, and core control; Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances; Adjustable difficulty by changing box height; Excellent carryover to climbing, hiking, and athletic movements; Lower spinal load than back squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and gluteus medius; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (anti-rotation); Forearms and grip

Description: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench (knee-height) with a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. Step your right foot up onto the box. Drive through your right foot to stand fully on top. From standing on top of the box, step your left foot back down behind you into a reverse lunge. Lower your left knee toward the floor in the reverse lunge. Drive through your right foot to step the left foot back up onto the box. Step the right foot back down to the floor. That is one rep. Complete all reps on the right, then switch sides. Use moderate weight — the combination is more demanding than each exercise alone.
Benefits: Combines step-up and reverse lunge for unilateral leg work; Builds quad and glute strength with balance demand; Exposes left-right imbalances; Time-efficient compound exercise; Trains coordination and proprioception; Works with one pair of dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and medius; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs with palms facing your body. Set a slight, fixed bend in your knees and hold it throughout the lift. Do not bend or straighten the knees during the rep. Brace your core, pull your shoulders back, and lift your chest tall. Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt straight back. Let the dumbbells slide down the front of your legs. Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings, typically when the dumbbells reach mid-shin. Keep your back flat throughout. Reverse the movement by driving your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Stand fully tall but do not lean back at the lockout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Focus on feeling the stretch in your hamstrings, not on lifting more weight.
Benefits: Builds the hamstrings through a long, loaded stretch; Strengthens the glutes and lower back with reduced spinal load vs barbell version; Beginner-friendly entry to hip-hinge training; Excellent accessory for the conventional and Romanian deadlift; Improves hamstring flexibility and hip mobility; Highly portable — works at home with one pair of dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (semitendinosus, semimembranosus, biceps femoris); Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Hold a dumbbell in each hand above your chest, palms facing your feet. Start with arms extended at lockout. Bend your elbows and lower the dumbbells toward your chest — elbows point outward, not toward the ceiling. The dumbbells travel inward and down until they touch your chest. Extend your elbows to press back to lockout. Squeeze your triceps at the top. The movement path is different from skull crushers — elbows go wide, not back. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Unique tricep loading angle; Named after powerlifter Dave Tate; Targets the medial head of the tricep; Useful for lockout strength; Easy to set up; Different stimulus from standard extensions
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (all heads, medial emphasized); Anconeus

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Hold dumbbells at your chest with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Press the dumbbells up. As they rise, rotate your wrists so palms face forward at the top. Lock out at the top with palms facing forward. Lower back down. As you lower, rotate your wrists back to neutral. Finish at the bottom with palms facing each other. Maintain the rotation smoothly throughout each rep. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps. The rotation is continuous, not at specific points.
Benefits: Rotation recruits additional chest fibers; Builds chest through a longer activation path; Joint-friendly bottom position; Unique pressing stimulus; Builds wrist and forearm control; Engages more motor units
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Forearms (rotation)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand in front of your thighs with palms facing your body. Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and keep your chest tall. Pull both dumbbells up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out to the sides. Let the dumbbells drift slightly outward as they rise. Lead with your elbows, not your hands. Keep the dumbbells close to your body but not pressed against it. Continue pulling until the dumbbells reach roughly chest height. Your elbows should be at or slightly above shoulder height. Do not pull higher than chest level — going higher can impinge the shoulder. Pause briefly at the top, then lower the dumbbells under control back to the starting position. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight and focus on form.
Benefits: Trains the lateral delts and upper traps together; More shoulder-friendly pull path than barbell upright rows; Independent dumbbells expose left-right imbalances; Builds shoulder width and trap thickness; Easier to do at home with just dumbbells; Trains grip and forearm strength as a byproduct
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Trapezius (especially upper); Biceps brachii (secondary); Brachialis; Forearms and grip

Description: Stand tall with a single dumbbell in your right hand at your side, palm facing your body. Allow your right arm to hang fully extended. Brace your core and stand tall. Without bending your elbow, raise your shoulder blade upward toward your ear. Allow the dumbbell to rise slightly with the scapular movement. Pause briefly at the top. Lower your shoulder back down by depressing the scapula. Complete reps on one side, then switch arms.
Benefits: Trains scapular control unilaterally; Builds lower trap and serratus strength; Improves shoulder blade mechanics; Useful for shoulder health and rehab; Strong posture work; No elbow bending isolates the shrug
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower); Serratus anterior; Levator scapulae

Description: Hold a single dumbbell vertically with both hands cupping the bottom plate, palms facing up. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold the dumbbell in front of your thighs with arms extended. Brace your core and pin your elbows against your sides. Curl the dumbbell up by bending only at the elbows. Keep your wrists in the same waiter-tray position throughout. Squeeze your biceps at the top with the dumbbell near your chest. Lower the dumbbell back down with control to full extension.
Benefits: Strict bicep isolation; Locks the wrists in a fixed position; Both hands work together for stability; Eliminates wrist cheating; Builds bicep strength and size; Useful for breaking through curl plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in each hand. Bring dumbbells to shoulder height with elbows at 90 degrees. Arms form a W shape — elbows wide, palms facing forward. Pull your shoulder blades together. Chest up. Press the dumbbells up slightly and slightly out to the sides. Lock out overhead with arms nearly straight. Lower back to the W position under control. Maintain scapular retraction throughout. Use light weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Emphasizes rear delts and posture muscles; Builds scapular retraction strength; Excellent posture exercise; Combines raise with press; Useful shoulder warm-up or accessory; Builds full shoulder girdle strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Lie on a flat bench holding dumbbells above your chest with palms facing each other. Maintain a slight bend in your elbows. Lower both dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc until you feel a stretch in your chest. Pull the dumbbells back up in an arc. At the top, rotate your wrists slightly inward so the dumbbell heads touch — knuckles face down. Squeeze your inner chest hard at the peak. Lower under control back to the stretched position. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Wrist twist adds inner chest squeeze; Builds chest peak contraction; Standard fly with bonus contraction; Easy to load progressively; Different stimulus from standard fly; Engaging variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially inner fibers); Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (slight stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides. You will need open floor space ahead of you. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Keep your chest tall throughout. Step your right foot forward roughly two to three feet into a lunge stance. Lower your back (left) knee toward the floor by bending both knees together. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor. Drive through your front (right) foot and step your back (left) foot forward — past the right foot — directly into the next lunge. Lower again, this time with your left leg in front. Continue alternating, walking forward with each lunge step. Keep your torso upright and core braced the entire time.
