Do not lean forward or look down. Walk for the desired number of total steps (e.g., 20 = 10 per leg).
Benefits: Continuous tension on the working legs throughout the set; Builds the quads and glutes more aggressively than stationary lunges; Trains balance and coordination dynamically; Excellent leg-day finisher with strong conditioning effect; Exposes and corrects left-right strength imbalances; Highly portable — needs only dumbbells and floor space
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Stand tall with a light dumbbell in your right hand. Bend your right elbow to 90 degrees with your forearm pointing forward. Pin your right elbow against your right side. Place a rolled towel between your elbow and ribs if needed. Pull your shoulders back and down. Brace your core. Rotate your forearm outward (away from your body) by externally rotating at the shoulder. Keep your elbow pinned. Continue rotating until your forearm points roughly 45 to 60 degrees outward from the starting position. Slowly rotate back to the start position over two seconds. Control the descent. Complete all reps on the right, then switch. Use very light weight (2 to 8 lbs) and higher reps (15 to 25). This is a prehab exercise — do not use heavy weight. Smooth, controlled reps are the priority.
Benefits: Directly strengthens the rotator cuff (infraspinatus and teres minor); Essential for shoulder health and injury prevention; Helps prevent impingement and rotator cuff tears; Excellent warm-up before pressing exercises; Improves shoulder stability for all overhead movements; Works at home with a very light dumbbell
Muscles Worked (Raw): Infraspinatus; Teres minor; Posterior deltoid (secondary)

Description: Hold a single dumbbell with both hands above one shoulder, arms extended. Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core and pivot slightly toward the dumbbell. As you squat down, chop the dumbbell diagonally across your body to the opposite hip. Rotate your torso through the chop, keeping arms long. At the bottom, you should be in a squat with the dumbbell down by your opposite hip. Drive up through your heels while reversing the chop back to the starting overhead position. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Trains rotational core strength under load; Builds leg drive linked to core rotation; Hits obliques heavily; Strong functional carryover to throwing and rotational sports; Time-efficient combo movement; Improves hip and trunk coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand with your back against a wall. Hold dumbbells at your sides. Walk your feet out and slide down the wall until your thighs are parallel to the floor. Your knees should be at 90 degrees. Feet directly below your knees. Hold this position with the dumbbells at your sides. Brace your core. Breathe steadily. Hold for 30 to 60 seconds or until failure. To increase difficulty, use heavier dumbbells or hold them in front. Stand up by pushing against the wall.
Benefits: Builds extreme quad endurance; Loaded isometric for strength; Easy to scale with dumbbell weight; Develops mental toughness; Joint-friendly; Useful for leg conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy isometric); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (stabilizer); Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front. Heels down. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder height, palms facing forward or neutral. Sit as upright as possible. Brace your core hard. Press both dumbbells overhead to lockout. Lock out with arms fully extended. Lower the dumbbells back to shoulder height under control. No leg drive possible — pure shoulder pressing with full core demand. Use lighter weight than standing press. Aim for 8 to 10 reps.
Benefits: Eliminates all leg drive for strict pressing; Builds hip flexor and core strength; Exposes shoulder mobility limitations; Reveals true pressing strength; Named after Olympic weightlifter Zydrunas Savickas; Demanding overhead variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (heavy stabilizer); Hip flexors; Trapezius

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your shoulders with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Set your elbows just slightly in front of your body. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Sit your hips down and back into a front-rack squat. Keep your torso upright with elbows pointing forward. Descend until your hip crease drops below the top of your knee (parallel or deeper). Drive explosively through your feet to stand back up. As you reach full standing extension, use the upward momentum to press both dumbbells straight overhead. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended, dumbbells directly above your shoulders. Lower the dumbbells back to the front-rack position and immediately drop into the next squat. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Trains the entire body in one explosive movement; Combines the squat and overhead press into one lift; Brutal conditioning effect — drives heart rate up fast; Time-efficient strength-and-cardio combination; Builds full-body coordination and power; Standard CrossFit lift used in benchmarks like Fran
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Hamstrings; Upper trapezius; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead, holding a dumbbell with both hands. Extend your legs straight on the floor. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Simultaneously lift your straight legs and your torso up to meet in a V-shape. Reach the dumbbell toward your toes at the top. Squeeze your abs hard at the peak. Slowly lower back to the start position over two seconds. Keep the dumbbell controlled. Use light weight to start. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Adds loading to V-ups for progressive overload; Builds elite ab strength; Trains hip flexors; Easy to scale by dumbbell weight; Useful when bodyweight V-ups are too easy; Time-efficient core exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (entire); Hip flexors; Obliques; Quadriceps; Anterior deltoid (dumbbell hold)

Description: Stand tall holding dumbbells at your sides. Rise up onto the balls of your feet. Walk forward on your tip-toes — maintaining calf contraction throughout. Take small, controlled steps. Your heels should never touch the floor. Walk for the desired distance or time (30 to 60 seconds). Keep your torso upright. Use moderate weight. The walking fatigues the calves quickly. Set dumbbells down with control at the end.
Benefits: Builds calf endurance under walking load; Develops ankle stability; Continuous calf contraction; Unique dynamic calf exercise; Easy to scale by dumbbell weight; Engaging variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (heavy isometric and dynamic); Soleus; Ankle stabilizers; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place dumbbells across your hips just below the hip bones. Hold the dumbbells in place with both hands. Brace your core and tuck your pelvis slightly. Drive through your heels to lift your hips off the floor. Continue until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top. Lower slowly to the floor.
Benefits: Builds glute strength and size; Spares the lower back; Useful as a warm-up or main move; Easy to load progressively; Improves hip extension power; Great for home training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Hold one heavy dumbbell vertically with both hands underneath the top end. Let it hang between your legs. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Pull your shoulders back. Sit your hips back and down. Keep your chest tall throughout. Lower until the dumbbell almost touches the floor or your thighs are parallel to the floor. Keep your knees pushed wide tracking over your toes. Drive through your full feet to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired reps. Use heavy weight — the wide stance allows it.
Benefits: Heavy adductor engagement; Builds quads and glutes; Allows heavy loading with one dumbbell; No barbell needed; Easier on the lower back than back squats; Excellent for inner-thigh development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors (heavy emphasis); Hamstrings; Calves; Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Sit at a preacher bench. Place the backs of both upper arms on the pad. Hold dumbbells with a supinated (palm-up) grip, arms extended. Curl both dumbbells up toward your shoulders. At the top, rotate your wrists so palms face down (pronated). Lower both dumbbells slowly with the pronated grip — loading the forearm extensors. At the bottom, rotate back to supinated and curl up again. Use lighter weight than standard preacher curls. Aim for 8 to 10 reps per set.
Benefits: Trains biceps on concentric and forearms on eccentric; Builds both arm and forearm size; Preacher pad ensures strict isolation; Excellent complete arm exercise; Easy to load progressively; Bilateral version — balanced loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (concentric); Brachioradialis (eccentric); Brachialis; Wrist extensors (eccentric)

Description: Start in a high plank position. Arms extended, body straight. Lower your right forearm to the floor (from hand to elbow). Lower your left forearm to the floor. You are now in a forearm plank. Press back up with your right hand to extend your right arm. Press up with your left hand. You are back in a high plank. Continue alternating which arm leads. Maintain a straight body line throughout — minimize hip rocking. Aim for 8 to 12 reps (4-6 per leading arm).
Benefits: Builds tricep and shoulder endurance; Develops core anti-rotation; No equipment needed; Combines plank with pressing; Engaging variation; Builds transition strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (anti-rotation); Pectoralis major

Description: Start in a forearm plank position — elbows under shoulders, body in a straight line from heels to head. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Press your right palm into the floor and extend your right arm to high plank. Press your left palm into the floor and extend your left arm. You are now in a full high plank. Lower back down by bringing your right elbow to the floor, then your left elbow. You return to the forearm plank position. Repeat. Alternate which arm leads each rep for balanced loading. Maintain a perfectly straight body line throughout — no hip rocking or sagging.
Benefits: Heavy tricep engagement through partial range; Tremendous anti-rotation core demand; Trains the transition between forearm and high plank; No equipment needed; Builds core strength and stability; Excellent finisher for upper body or core workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major; Core (anti-rotation, anti-extension); Serratus anterior

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing forward (underhand grip). Pull your shoulders back, brace your core, and pin your elbows against your sides. Curl both dumbbells up to shoulder height with the underhand grip, just like a standard bicep curl. At the top of the curl, rotate your wrists 180 degrees so your palms now face down (overhand grip). Lower the dumbbells under control over a count of three to four seconds with the overhand grip. Once your arms are fully extended at the bottom, rotate your wrists back to the underhand grip for the next rep. Keep your elbows pinned and torso upright the entire time. Use lighter weight than standard curls — the overhand descent is much harder than it looks.
Benefits: Trains biceps and forearms in a single movement; Heavily develops the brachioradialis and forearm extensors during the descent; Builds grip strength as a byproduct; Time-efficient combination of two exercises; Great accessory for grip-demanding sports; Builds visible forearm size that pure bicep curls miss
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (concentric); Brachialis; Brachioradialis (heavy on eccentric); Forearm extensors (eccentric); Forearm flexors (grip)

Description: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Hands behind your head. Sit up fully while rotating — bring your right elbow toward your left knee. Touch or come as close as possible. Lower back down. Sit up and twist the other way — left elbow to right knee. Continue alternating. Move with control. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines sit-up with oblique rotation; Builds abs and obliques together; No equipment needed; Full range of motion; Classic core exercise; Builds rotational strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Description: Place a strong pole or broomstick across two chairs about shoulder width apart. Set a third chair to elevate your feet at hip height. Lie face up under the pole and elevate your feet on the third chair. Reach up and grip the pole with hands shoulder width apart. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes to keep the body straight. Pull your chest up to the pole by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds back strength using only chairs and a pole.; Elevated feet increase loading on the back.; Trains horizontal pulling without spinal compression.; Excellent at home alternative to cable rows.; Develops grip and core stability.; Easy to scale by adjusting body angle.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Stand with hands behind your head. Lift right knee while rotating left elbow toward it. Crunch to make contact or come close. Return to standing. Switch sides. Continue alternating at a brisk pace. Rotate your torso with each crunch. Aim for 15 to 20 total reps. Useful warm-up or circuit exercise.
Benefits: Standing oblique exercise — no floor needed; Cardiovascular conditioning; No equipment needed; Quick and accessible; Builds coordination; Useful for circuits
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Elevated Inverted Underhand Grip Row Between 3 Chairs
Description: Place a strong pole or broomstick across two chairs about shoulder width apart. Set a third chair to elevate your feet at hip height. Lie face up under the pole with feet elevated on the third chair. Reach up and grip the pole with an underhand shoulder width grip. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes to keep the body straight. Pull your chest up to the pole by driving the elbows back along your sides. Squeeze the lats and biceps at the top of the pull. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds back strength using only chairs and a pole.; Underhand grip emphasizes the biceps.; Elevated feet increase the loading on the back.; Trains horizontal pulling without weights.; Excellent at home alternative to chin ups.; Develops grip and core stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Brachioradialis

Exercise Name: Elbow to Knee Side Plank Crunch
Description: Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor. Stack the feet and legs straight. Brace your core and lift the hips into a side plank. Place the top hand behind the head with the elbow flared. Lift the top knee up toward the top elbow. Crunch the elbow down to meet the knee. Pause briefly at the contracted position. Extend back to start. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Loads the obliques; Strong side plank variation; Builds the core; Useful for core size; Trains the side abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Core; Gluteus medius

Description: Sit on a bench or chair with feet flat on the floor. Place a sturdy block or plate in front of you. Rest the balls of both feet on top of the block. Let your heels hang below the level of the block. Brace your core and keep your back upright. Press through the balls of the feet to lift the heels as high as possible. Squeeze the calves hard at the top. Lower with control back to a deep heel stretch.
Benefits: Targets the soleus; Full range of motion; Deep calf stretch; No machine required; Easy to load with weight on lap; Useful for calf detail
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Soleus; Gastrocnemius

Description: Position a sturdy box or bench behind you. Place your feet on the box and your hands on the floor in a high plank position. Set your hands shoulder-width apart with elbows extended. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Continue down until your chest nearly touches the floor. Press back up by extending your elbows. Squeeze your chest at the top.
Benefits: Targets upper chest and shoulders; Harder than standard push ups; Builds chest, triceps, and front delts; No equipment beyond a box; Stepping stone to advanced push up variations; Develops core strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (upper fibers); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core stabilizers

Description: Stand on a low box or step (4 to 8 inches high). Step your right foot off the box to the right side, down to the floor. Bend your right knee into a lateral lunge as your right foot lands. Keep your left foot on the box, left leg relatively straight. Drive through your right foot to push back up onto the box. Complete reps, then switch sides. The elevation increases the range of motion at the bottom. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Greater range of motion from elevated start; Increased adductor loading from deficit; Builds lateral movement strength; Develops hip mobility; No weights needed; Progressive from flat side lunges
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (stepping leg); Adductors (increased from deficit); Gluteus maximus; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench. Place your right foot flat on the floor, knee bent at 90 degrees. Extend your left leg straight forward or up toward the ceiling. Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up. At the top, your body forms a straight line from right knee to shoulders. Squeeze your right glute hard. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Full range from bench elevation; Doubles glute demand per leg; Exposes left-right imbalances; No weights needed for effective glute training; Builds hip extension strength per leg; Excellent glute builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae

Description: Stand on a box or step on your right leg. Left leg hangs off the edge. Squat down on your right leg. Your left leg drops below box level — this increases the range of motion. Descend as deep as your strength and mobility allow. Drive through your right foot to stand. Complete reps, then switch legs. Higher boxes allow greater range. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per leg.
Benefits: Greater range of motion than floor pistol squats; Free leg drops below box level for deeper squatting; Builds single-leg squat strength through full range; Adjustable difficulty by box height; No weights needed; Develops balance and control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with the balls of your feet on a step edge. Heels hanging off. Hold a wall or railing for balance. Lower your heels as far as possible for a deep calf stretch. Press through the balls of your feet to raise as high as possible. Squeeze your calves at the top. Lower under control. Full range every rep. Aim for 20 to 30 reps with bodyweight. Add dumbbells for progressive overload.
Benefits: Full range of motion from step elevation; Deep calf stretch at the bottom; No weights needed for effective training; Available on any staircase; Builds calf size and strength; Easy to add weight with dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Achilles tendon

Exercise Name: Elevated Standing Single Leg Calf Raise
Description: Stand with the ball of one foot on a step or block. Allow the heel to hang off the edge. Lift the other foot off the floor by bending the knee. Hold a wall or rail for balance support. Brace the core and keep the working leg straight. Lower the heel down for a deep calf stretch. Press up onto the toes as high as possible. Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds the gastrocnemius through a deep range.; Works one calf at a time for symmetry.; Bodyweight load is joint friendly.; Improves ankle mobility.; Useful for runners and athletes.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Set up in a forearm plank with both elbows on a stability ball. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace the core hard and squeeze the glutes. Keep the hips level and square to the floor. Lift one arm forward off the ball and reach up. Hold the arm overhead briefly. Lower with control to the start. Alternate arms for the working set.
Benefits: Trains the core for anti-rotation.; Builds shoulder stability.; Stability ball adds challenge.; Useful for athletic carryover.; Improves total body control.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Anterior deltoid; Core

Exercise Name: Exercise Ball Back Extension with Arms Extended
Description: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball. Set the feet wide on the floor for stability. Reach the arms straight out overhead. Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start. Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back. Continue lifting until the body forms a straight line. Squeeze the lower back and glutes at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the lower back.; Trains the glutes.; Extended arms add lever load.; Joint friendly back work.; Useful for posture.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Exercise Name: Exercise Ball Back Extension with Hands Behind Head
Description: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball. Set the feet wide on the floor for stability. Place the hands behind the head with elbows wide. Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start. Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back. Continue lifting until the body forms a straight line. Squeeze the lower back and glutes at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the lower back.; Trains the glutes.; Hands behind head adds challenge.; Joint friendly back work.; Useful for posture.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Exercise Name: Exercise Ball Back Extension with Knees Off Ground
Description: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball. Walk the feet back so the legs are straight. Set the toes wide on the floor with the knees off the ground. Place the hands by the ears or crossed on the chest. Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start. Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back. Squeeze the glutes and hamstrings hard at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the lower back.; Hammers the glutes and hamstrings.; Knees off floor adds load.; Joint friendly back work.; Useful for posterior chain.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Exercise Name: Exercise Ball Back Extension with Rotation
Description: Lie face down with the hips supported on a stability ball. Set the feet wide on the floor for stability. Place the hands behind the head. Brace the core and keep the body relaxed at the start. Lift the chest off the ball by extending the back. Rotate the torso to one side at the top. Lower with control and alternate sides each rep. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the lower back.; Trains the obliques.; Adds rotational stability work.; Useful for athletes.; Joint friendly back work.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Obliques; Gluteus maximus

Description: Place the forearms on a stability ball. Set the body in a high plank position with feet on the floor. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding an EZ bar with an underhand grip. Grip the bar at the inner curves of the EZ bar. Stand tall with elbows tucked at your sides. Press the bar back up by extending at the elbows. Focus on contracting the triceps. Lock out at the top. Re-rack the bar after the final rep. Use moderate weight — the close grip is more demanding than standard bench.
Benefits: Targets the triceps with secondary chest involvement; EZ grip is easier on the wrists than a straight barbell; Allows heavier loading than dumbbell tricep work; Excellent compound tricep mass builder; Useful for lifters with wrist issues on standard close-grip bench; Carries over to bench press strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (heavy emphasis); Pectoralis major (sternal head, secondary); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Get into a push-up position. Instead of flat palms, support yourself on your fingertips. Spread fingers wide for stability. Arch your fingers like claws. Perform push-ups from this fingertip position. Lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up. Maintain straight body line. Start with fewer fingers (all five) and progress to fewer over time. Begin with incline fingertip push-ups if full floor version is too hard. Aim for 5 to 10 reps. Build up gradually to protect your fingers.
Benefits: Builds extreme finger and hand strength; Popular in martial arts training; Develops grip strength from a unique angle; Advanced push-up variation; No equipment needed; Impressive demonstration of hand strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Finger flexors (extreme); Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Forearms; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie on the floor in front of a flat bench. Place the feet up on top of the bench with knees bent. Set the hands lightly behind the head. Brace your core and keep the lower back on the floor. Curl the head and shoulders up off the floor. Squeeze the abs hard at the top. Hold briefly at the peak. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the core; Strong basic crunch; Useful for beginners; Trains the abs; No equipment needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Core

Description: Sit on a bench. Place your forearms on the bench with wrists hanging off the edge, palms up. Hold a barbell with an underhand grip. Open your fingers and let the bar roll down to your fingertips. Once at your fingertips, curl your fingers back to bring the bar back into your palms. Then curl your wrist up for additional flexion. Slowly reverse — extend your wrist, then let the bar roll back to your fingertips. The finger roll is the key — most of the work is the finger flexors. Use light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Builds the forearm flexors (extreme); Develops crushing grip strength; Targets finger flexors directly; Useful for climbing, grappling, and lifting; Easy to load progressively; Excellent grip exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Flexor digitorum (finger flexors); Wrist flexors; Forearm flexors; Grip muscles

Description: Place a small towel under each hand on a smooth floor. Begin in a high plank position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line. Slide both hands out wide to the sides at the same time. Continue sliding until the chest lowers toward the floor. Stop with the arms in a wide fly position. Squeeze the chest to slide the hands back together. Return to the start at the top.
Benefits: Brutal chest builder; No equipment beyond towels; Trains core stability; Builds the chest; Useful chest builder; Easy at-home setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Hold an EZ bar across your chest with an overhand grip. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Sit up by curling your torso off the floor. As you reach the top of the sit-up, press the EZ bar straight overhead. Pause briefly with arms locked out. Lower the bar back to your chest as you reverse the sit-up. Lower with control to the floor.
Benefits: Trains abs and shoulders together; Builds core strength; Develops shoulder stability; Time-efficient combo move; Improves coordination; Useful for athletic conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Hip flexors

Description: Stand tall holding an EZ bar with a shoulder-width underhand grip. Let the bar hang at your thighs. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Curl the bar by pulling your elbows backward, dragging the bar up your torso. Keep the bar in contact with or close to your body the entire time. Lift until the bar reaches your lower chest. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower the bar slowly to the start.
Benefits: Maximum biceps isolation; Wrist-friendly EZ bar grip; Removes front delt involvement; Builds biceps peak and thickness; Strong mind-muscle connection; Useful for biceps hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Forearms

Description: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor. Hold an EZ bar with an underhand (palms-up) grip. Rest your forearms on your thighs with wrists hanging just past the knees. Let the bar roll down to your fingertips. Curl your fingers and wrists up to lift the bar. Keep your forearms pressed against your thighs. Squeeze the forearms hard at the top. Lower the bar slowly back to the start.
Benefits: Isolates the forearm flexors; Wrist-friendly EZ bar grip; Builds grip strength; Develops forearm size; Useful for grip-intensive sports; Easy to set up and execute
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Forearms; Grip

Description: Set up flat on a bench with chains attached to dumbbells or cables. Lie back and hold the dumbbells over your chest with palms facing in. Keep a slight bend in the elbows. Brace your core and pin your shoulder blades to the bench. Lower the weights out to your sides in a wide arc. Stop when you feel a strong stretch across your chest. Squeeze your chest to bring the weights back together over your chest. Pause briefly at the top before the next rep.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance overloads the chest; Matches the natural strength curve; Builds chest size and strength; Develops chest mind-muscle connection; Strong stretch through the chest; Useful for plateau busting
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Front deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Bend your knees slightly. Swing your arms back. Jump forward by extending at the hips, knees, and ankles. Land softly on both feet. Immediately hop forward again. Continue hopping for the desired distance or number of hops. Land softly each time — absorb through the knees. Aim for 10 to 20 hops or 20 to 40 feet.
Benefits: Builds explosive lower-body power; Develops ankle reactivity; Cardiovascular conditioning; No equipment needed; Develops jumping mechanics; Useful for athletic warm-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Calves; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Floor Twisting Crunch Feet on Bench
Description: Lie flat on the floor with the lower legs resting on a bench. Knees should be bent at 90 degrees with calves parallel to the floor. Place your hands lightly behind your head with elbows wide. Brace the core and exhale as you crunch up. As you lift, twist the torso so one elbow points toward the opposite knee. Squeeze the obliques hard at the top of the twist. Lower back to the floor with control and untwist to neutral. Alternate sides on each repetition for the full set.
Benefits: Targets the obliques through controlled rotation.; Hits the upper abs with the crunching motion.; Bench position protects the lower back from strain.; No equipment beyond a bench needed.; Easy to scale with hand position changes.; Improves rotational core control.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended out to the sides. Position your arms in a T shape at shoulder height. Place your hands palm-down on the floor. Brace your core and keep your forehead resting on the floor. Squeeze your shoulder blades together. Raise both arms straight up off the floor. Lift as high as you can with full retraction. Lower the arms slowly back to the floor.
Benefits: Strengthens the rear delts; Builds the rhomboids and lower traps; Improves posture; No equipment required; Useful for desk workers; Bodyweight rear delt work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rear deltoid; Rhomboids; Traps (lower)

Description: Lie on your back. Press lower back into the floor. Hands under hips or at sides. Raise both legs 6 to 12 inches off the floor. Alternately kick legs up and down in small, rapid motions (about 6 inches). Keep legs straight and off the floor throughout. Continue for 20 to 30 seconds or 20 to 30 kicks per leg. If lower back arches, raise legs higher. Breathe steadily. Classic military PT exercise.
Benefits: Builds lower ab and hip flexor endurance; Sustained tension throughout the set; No equipment needed; Classic conditioning exercise; Develops core endurance; Simple and effective
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors; Quadriceps (leg hold)

Description: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended forward and legs straight. Keep your gaze toward the floor. Engage your core. Lift your chest, arms, and legs off the floor by contracting your lower back and glutes (Superman position). Continue lifting until you feel a strong contraction in your lower back. Squeeze hard for one to two seconds at the top. Lower under control back to the floor. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set. Move with control — no jerking or bouncing.
Benefits: Strengthens the lower back with no equipment; Builds the entire posterior chain; Improves spinal extensor endurance; Useful for posture and rehabilitation; Works anywhere with no equipment; Easy to scale with arm or leg variations
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Posterior deltoid (arm lift); Trapezius (arm lift)

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard. Step one hand forward keeping the body steady. Step the other hand forward to match. Continue walking the hands forward step by step. Keep the hips level and the body in a straight line throughout. Walk the hands back to the start to finish the rep.
Benefits: Brutal core builder; Trains anti-extension; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Useful core finisher; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Forward to Side to Rear Lunge
Description: Stand tall with feet hip width apart in an athletic stance. Step forward with one leg into a forward lunge. Drive back to standing with control. Step the same leg out to the side into a lateral lunge. Push the hips back and bend the lunging knee while the other leg stays straight. Drive back to the start. Step the same leg back into a rear lunge and lower the back knee. Return to standing and repeat the three direction sequence then switch legs.
Benefits: Trains the legs through forward, lateral, and rear movement patterns.; Builds glute strength in all three planes of motion.; Improves balance and single leg stability.; Strengthens the inner and outer hips through the side lunge.; No equipment needed and travel friendly.; Excellent dynamic warm up for lower body training.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Adductors; Hamstrings; Gluteus medius

Description: Lie on your back. Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out to the sides. Place your hands behind your head or across your chest. Press your lower back into the floor. Crunch up by lifting your shoulders off the floor. Squeeze your abs at the top. Lower under control. The butterfly leg position minimizes hip flexor cheating. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Reduces hip flexor involvement; Isolates the abs more effectively; Butterfly position opens the hips; No equipment needed; Beginner-friendly; Useful for anyone with tight hip flexors
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary)

Description: Sit with your upper back against a bench. Bring the soles of your feet together. Let your knees fall open to the sides — your feet form a triangle shape. Keep the soles of your feet pressed together throughout the entire exercise. Brace your core. Tuck your chin slightly. Drive through the outside edges of your feet and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips. Continue until your hips are fully extended. Your knees stay splayed out wide. Squeeze glutes hard at the top for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Biases the upper gluteus maximus; External hip rotation increases glute activation; Direct glute isolation with no leg loading; Easy to perform with just a bench or even on the floor; Excellent finisher for glute workouts; Can be progressed with weight plate on hips
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (especially upper); Gluteus medius; Adductors (stretched)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hands on hips or at sides. Step your right foot forward roughly 2 to 3 feet into a lunge stance. Lower your back (left) knee straight down toward the floor. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor. Your front thigh should be parallel. Drive through your front (right) foot to push back to the starting position. Step back to your starting stance. That is one rep. Repeat with the left leg stepping forward. Continue alternating. Keep your torso upright. Track your knee over your toes.
Benefits: Builds quad, glute, and hamstring strength; Trains balance and coordination; Exposes left-right imbalances; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Foundational single-leg pattern; Easy to scale by adding load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a barbell at upper-chest height in a power rack. Step under the bar and place it across your front deltoids — high on your shoulders, just below your collarbone. Extend both arms straight forward at shoulder height, palms down. Do not grip the bar. Brace your core hard. Stand tall. Step back from the rack. Set your feet shoulder-width apart. Sit your hips straight down with a perfectly upright torso. Descend until your hip crease drops below your knees. Drive straight up through your full feet. Maintain perfect upright posture or the bar drops. Use light weight.
Benefits: Excellent technique drill for front squats; Forces perfect upright torso position; Builds quad-dominant squatting; Develops core bracing; Reveals torso-lean tendencies; Useful for Olympic lifting prep
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy emphasis); Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid (bar support); Core (heavy bracing); Upper trapezius; Erector spinae

Description: Hang from a bar with straight arms. Engage your lats and core. Raise your body toward horizontal (front lever position). Continue until your body is as close to horizontal as your strength allows. Lower under control back to the dead hang. Continue for reps. Start with tucked front lever raises and progress to full. This is extremely demanding — 3 to 5 reps is an accomplishment. Progressions: tuck → advanced tuck → straddle → full.
Benefits: Builds dynamic front lever strength; Develops lat power through the raising motion; Harder than static front lever holds; Advanced calisthenics exercise; Builds extraordinary core and back strength; Progressive with tuck variations
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (extreme); Core (extreme anti-extension); Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid; Forearms and grip

Description: Lie on your back. Bring soles of your feet together, knees wide (butterfly). Extend arms overhead on the floor. Sit up by swinging your arms forward and crunching up. Touch your toes or the floor in front of your feet. Lower back to the floor with arms overhead. The butterfly position reduces hip flexor cheating. Move with control — do not use excessive momentum. Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Reduces hip flexor involvement during sit-ups; Isolates the abs more effectively; Butterfly position opens the hips; No equipment needed; Full sit-up range of motion; Popular in CrossFit (butterfly sit-up)
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary); Hip flexors (reduced)

Description: Start in a high plank position. Jump both feet forward to the outside of your hands, landing in a deep squat. Your feet land wide, hands still on the floor between your feet. Jump your feet back to the plank position. Continue jumping forward and back at a brisk pace. Move explosively on each jump. Maintain a straight body in the plank position. Aim for 10 to 15 reps or work for time.
Benefits: Builds explosive hip power; Excellent cardiovascular conditioning; Develops core strength through transitions; No equipment needed; Dynamic and engaging; Useful for circuit training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hip flexors (jump forward); Quadriceps; Core (transitions); Anterior deltoid (plank); Cardiovascular system

Description: Place your hands on the floor shoulder-width apart (or on parallettes). Turn fingers outward. Squat down and place your knees on the backs of your elbows or just inside them. Lean forward, shifting your weight onto your hands. Lift your feet off the floor, balancing your tucked body on your hands alone. Protract your shoulders (push the floor away). Lock your arms straight. Hold for 10 to 30 seconds. Focus on keeping your hips as high as your shoulders. Build up to longer holds. Progress toward advanced tuck (hips higher, back flatter). Then progress to straddle planche by gradually extending the legs.
Benefits: First true planche hold in the progression; Builds shoulder, chest, and core strength for harder planches; Relatively achievable with consistent training; No equipment needed (parallettes recommended); Develops balance and body control; Gateway to advanced calisthenics
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (heavy); Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Core (heavy); Triceps brachii; Wrist flexors

Description: Set up in a forearm plank with elbows under shoulders and feet hip width apart. Brace your core and keep your hips level with your shoulders. Lift one foot slightly off the floor and tap it out to the side. Keep the hips square and avoid rocking side to side. Return the foot to the starting position under control. Repeat the tap with the other foot to the opposite side. Continue alternating taps while holding a strong plank position. Maintain steady breathing throughout the entire set.
Benefits: Strengthens the deep core and obliques under anti rotation demand.; Builds hip abductor strength through repeated leg taps.; Improves shoulder stability in a long lever plank position.; Reinforces a neutral spine while limbs move dynamically.; Requires no equipment and can be done anywhere.; Carryover to running, lifting, and athletic balance.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Gluteus medius; Anterior deltoid

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard and keep the hips level. Tap one foot out wide to the side. Bring it back to the start. Tap the other foot out wide to the other side. Bring it back to the start. Continue alternating side toe taps with control.
Benefits: Trains the glute medius; Strong oblique builder; No equipment needed; Builds shoulder stability; Useful core finisher; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Obliques; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hinge at the hips and place your hands on the floor in front of your feet. Walk your hands forward one at a time. Continue walking forward until you reach a high plank position. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Hold the plank briefly with body in a straight line. Walk your hands back toward your feet. Stand back up and repeat.
Benefits: Builds core stability through motion; Strong shoulder endurance challenge; Develops body control; No equipment required; Useful for warmups; Total body coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major; Hip flexors

Description: Get into a standard front plank position on your forearms and toes. Body straight from heels to head. Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes. Lift your right leg off the floor by about 6 inches. Squeeze your right glute. Keep your hips perfectly level — do not let them rotate or tilt. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower your right leg under control. Lift your left leg with the same form. Continue alternating. Perform 8 to 12 lifts per leg per set.
Benefits: Adds anti-rotation core demand to the standard plank; Engages the glutes in addition to the core; Trains hip stability under planking conditions; More challenging than a static plank; No equipment needed; Excellent finisher for core workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques (anti-rotation); Gluteus maximus and medius; Erector spinae

Description: Get into a high plank position on your hands and toes. Hands directly under shoulders. Body straight from heels to head. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Slowly lift your right hand off the floor and reach it forward at shoulder height. Keep your hips perfectly level. Do not let them rotate or tilt. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower your right hand back to the floor under control. Lift your left hand with the same form. Continue alternating. Perform 6 to 10 lifts per arm per set. Move with control.
Benefits: Adds significant anti-rotation core demand; Engages the shoulders and serratus anterior; Trains hip and core stability; More challenging than a static plank; No equipment needed; Excellent core finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (anti-rotation); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Gluteus maximus and medius; Triceps brachii (supporting arm)

Exercise Name: Forward Pulse Lunge with Hands Overhead
Description: Stand tall and step forward into a long lunge stance. Lower into a deep lunge with the back knee close to the floor. Raise both arms straight overhead with biceps near the ears. Brace the core and keep the chest tall. Pulse a few inches up and down within the lunge bottom range. Keep the front shin vertical and the torso upright through every pulse. Maintain the overhead arm position throughout the pulses. Complete all pulses on one side then switch legs.
Benefits: Smokes the quads and glutes through repeated pulses.; Challenges core stability with arms overhead.; Improves shoulder mobility and overhead control.; Builds isometric leg strength in the lunge bottom.; Improves single leg balance and coordination.; No equipment needed.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Hamstrings; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Lie face down on the floor with your forearms flat on the ground, elbows directly under your shoulders. Tuck your toes under and lift your body off the floor, supporting your weight on your forearms and the balls of your feet. Form a straight body line from your heels to the top of your head. No sagging at the hips, no piking up. Pull your shoulders down and away from your ears. Brace your core hard — imagine bracing against an incoming punch. Squeeze your glutes and quadriceps to keep your body rigid. Tuck your chin slightly so your head is in line with your spine. Hold this position for the desired duration. Breathe normally. To finish, lower your knees to the floor under control. Aim for 30 to 90 seconds per set, building duration over time.
Benefits: Builds anti-extension core strength; Foundational exercise for all core training; Improves posture and lower-back health; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Trains the entire trunk to stay rigid under load; Carries over to all heavy compound lifts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Internal and external obliques; Erector spinae (isometric); Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Serratus anterior (shoulder stabilizer); Trapezius and rhomboids

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard and keep the hips level. Hop both feet to one side together. Land softly with the feet still together. Hop both feet back through center to the other side. Continue the side-to-side hopping motion at speed. Keep the upper body steady throughout.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Adds cardio to plank; Trains the hip flexors; No equipment needed; Useful core finisher; Builds shoulder stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Adjust the seat and thigh pad so you are locked in firmly with arms reaching up to the handles. Grip the handles with an overhand or neutral grip, depending on the machine design. Sit tall with chest lifted. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Pull the handles down by driving your elbows down toward your hips. Lead with your elbows. Bring the handles to roughly chest level. Squeeze your lats hard for one second. Slowly let the handles return up under control. Feel the stretch in your lats at the top. Stop just before the weight stack touches down. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Guided motion allows pure lat focus without stabilizer demand; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Excellent for beginners learning the lat pulldown pattern; Allows safe training to failure; Useful for high-rep volume work; Constant tension throughout the range of motion
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Teres major; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip

Description: Hang from a bar or rings with straight arms. Engage your lats and core. Pull your body up to horizontal — face down, body parallel to the ground. Hold the horizontal position with arms straight above you. Start with a tucked front lever (knees to chest) and progress. Progressions: tuck → advanced tuck → straddle → full. Hold for 5 to 15 seconds at each progression. This requires months or years of dedicated training. Supplementary exercises: front lever rows, dragon flags, straight-arm pulldowns.
Benefits: One of the most impressive bodyweight skills; Builds elite lat and core strength; Develops straight-arm pulling power; Foundational gymnastics strength; Progressive skill with clear steps; Builds extraordinary body control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (extreme); Core (extreme anti-extension); Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (straight-arm); Forearms and grip; Erector spinae

Description: Grip a pull-up bar with palms facing you and hands shoulder-width. Hang from the bar with arms fully extended. Brace your core and lean back from the bar. Pull hard while keeping the lean back through the rep. Continue pulling until your lower chest touches the bar. Tilt the head back at the top to drive the chest higher. Squeeze the lats hard at the top. Lower with control to the full hang.
Benefits: Brutal lat contraction; Old-school pull-up variation; Builds upper back thickness; Strong bodyweight builder; Useful back-day move; No equipment beyond a bar
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Begin in a forearm plank position — elbows under shoulders, body in a straight line, core braced. Hold the front plank for 2 to 3 seconds. Rotate your body to the right, lifting your right arm toward the ceiling and stacking your feet for a side plank on your left elbow. Hold the side plank for 2 to 3 seconds. Keep your hips lifted. Rotate back to the front plank position. Then rotate to the left side for a side plank on your right elbow. Continue alternating sides through the front plank. Perform for time (30 to 60 seconds) or for a target number of rotations.
Benefits: Trains anti-extension and anti-lateral-flexion in one movement; Builds well-rounded core strength; Develops shoulder stability through transitions; Time-efficient core exercise; No equipment needed; Excellent for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (front plank); Obliques (side plank); Quadratus lumborum; Transverse abdominis; Anterior deltoid (transitions); Gluteus medius (side plank)

Description: Master all planche progressions first: lean planche, frog/tuck planche, straddle planche. Position your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor or parallettes. Turn fingers out to protect wrists. Protract your shoulders hard (push the floor away). Lock your arms straight. Lean forward until your feet leave the floor. Extend both legs straight back, together, keeping them parallel to the floor. Your body should be completely horizontal with only your hands touching the floor. Hold for as long as possible. A 5-second hold is an elite achievement. This is a multi-year goal for most athletes. Consistent progressive training is essential.
Benefits: Elite-level bodyweight strength demonstration; Builds extraordinary shoulder and chest strength; Develops world-class core bracing; Impressive calisthenics skill; No equipment needed (parallettes recommended); Ultimate horizontal pushing strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (extreme demand); Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Core (extreme demand); Triceps brachii; Wrist flexors and extensors; Lower back (stabilizer)

Description: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips into a standard glute bridge position — straight line from knees to shoulders. Hold the bridge at the top. Keep your hips perfectly level. Lift your right foot off the floor by driving your right knee up toward your chest. Hold briefly. Keep your hips level throughout — do not let them drop or rotate. This is the most important cue. Lower your right foot back to the floor. Immediately lift your left foot up in the same fashion. Continue alternating legs in a controlled “marching” pattern while holding the bridge. Perform the desired number of total reps (e.g., 20 = 10 per leg). Lower your hips to the floor to finish.
Benefits: Trains anti-rotation core strength while building the glutes; Develops the gluteus medius and hip stabilizers; Builds balance and single-leg stability; Excellent warm-up for squats and deadlifts; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Useful rehabilitation exercise for hip and lower-back issues
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius (hip stability); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation, obliques); Hip flexors (lifting leg)

Description: This is an elite gymnastics skill requiring years of progressive training. Master: support hold, iron cross, planche on floor, straddle maltese on rings — in that order. Hang from gymnastic rings with arms extended to the sides at shoulder height (cross position). Lean forward slowly, lowering your body toward horizontal while keeping arms wide. Continue leaning until your body is fully horizontal with arms out to the sides. Legs together and straight behind you, parallel to the floor. Hold for any duration. Even one second is extraordinary. Train under qualified gymnastics coaching with progressive overload.
Benefits: Most difficult static hold in gymnastics; Builds extraordinary shoulder and chest strength; Elite-level demonstration of strength; Requires years of progressive training; Combines cross and planche demands; Pinnacle calisthenics achievement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (extreme demand); Anterior deltoid (extreme demand); Biceps brachii (extreme isometric); Core (extreme demand); Serratus anterior; Forearms

Exercise Name: Glute Ham Developer Sit Up and Russian Twist
Description: Set up on a glute ham developer with the feet locked in. Set the hips against the pad with the torso extended back. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Sit up by curling the torso forward. Continue until the torso is upright. Twist the torso to one side at the top. Twist back through center to the other side then lower.
Benefits: Hammers the abs and obliques.; GHD allows full range sit up.; Twist adds rotational core work.; Brutal core finisher.; Useful for athletes.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Description: Achieve a full planche hold — body horizontal, supported only on the hands, legs extended behind. From the planche, bend your elbows to lower your body toward the floor. Press back up to the full planche position. Maintain the horizontal body position throughout. This requires extreme straight-arm strength, pressing power, and core stability. Progress through: pseudo planche push-ups → tuck planche → straddle planche → full planche holds → full planche push-ups. This progression takes years. Even 1 rep is an elite-level achievement.
Benefits: One of the most difficult bodyweight exercises; Requires extreme pressing and straight-arm strength; Elite calisthenics achievement; Builds extraordinary shoulder and core strength; Impressive demonstration of strength; Progressive skill with clear milestones
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (extreme); Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Core (extreme anti-extension); Serratus anterior; Biceps brachii (straight-arm)

Description: Set up on a glute ham developer (GHD). Hook the feet under the foot pads with the hips against the pad. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace your core and lower the torso forward. Extend the back to lift the torso to a straight line with the body. At the top twist the torso to one side. Twist back through center to the other side. Lower the torso back down. Continue alternating twists.
Benefits: Strong posterior chain and oblique combo; Trains rotational core; Builds the lower back; Useful back move; Builds the glutes; Strong combo move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Spinal erectors; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Hamstrings

Description: Set up on a GHD machine. Knees on the pad, feet locked under the foot pads. Hips on the front pad. Start upright with torso perpendicular to the floor. Lower your torso forward by extending at the knees and hips. Continue until your body is roughly horizontal or below. Pull yourself back up using your hamstrings (knee flexion) and glutes (hip extension). Return to the upright starting position. Use slow, controlled movement. No momentum. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per set. This is very demanding.
Benefits: Combines knee flexion and hip extension in one movement; One of the best hamstring exercises available; Builds the hamstrings through full range; Develops posterior chain strength; Prevents hamstring injuries; Builds eccentric hamstring control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (heavy — both knee flexion and hip extension); Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Calves (foot anchor); Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Glute Ham Raise with Extended Arms
Description: Set up on a glute ham developer with the feet locked in. Set the thighs against the pad with the knees just behind it. Reach the arms straight out in front of the chest. Brace the core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the torso forward by bending at the knees. Lower until the body is parallel to the floor. Pull the body back up by curling the heels toward the glutes. Finish at the top with the body upright.
Benefits: Brutal hamstring builder.; Trains the glutes.; Extended arms add lever difficulty.; Builds posterior chain strength.; Useful for sprinters.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Calves

Description: Set up on a glute ham developer (GHD) facing up. Hook the feet under the foot pads with the hips against the pad. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace your core and lower the torso back below parallel. Reach the arms back behind the head at the bottom. Curl the torso up by contracting the abs. Sit all the way up to vertical. Lower back down with control.
Benefits: Strong abs builder; Full range sit up; Trains hip flexors; Builds the rectus abdominis; Useful core builder; Strong machine move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Set up on a glute ham developer with thighs on the pad. Hook your feet in the pad supports. Extend your body so it forms a straight line from head to heel. Place your hands behind your head or across your chest. Hold the extended position with the core braced. Rotate the torso slowly to one side. Return to center and rotate to the other side. Continue alternating rotations with control.
Benefits: Loads the lower back rotators; Strong oblique builder; Trains posterior chain; Strong GHD variation; Builds rotational strength; Useful core finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Spinal erectors; Obliques; Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus

Description: Set up on a hyperextension bench. Hook one foot under the foot pad. Let the other leg hang to the side. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Hinge at the hips to lower the torso down. Drive the glute and hamstring to lift back up. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains each side; Builds the posterior chain; Strong unilateral move; Useful for athletes; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Good Morning on the Hack Squat Machine
Description: Set up under a hack squat machine with the shoulder pads on your traps. Plant the feet shoulder width on the platform. Stand up tall to unrack the weight. Brace the core and set the back flat. Hinge at the hips by pushing the hips back. Allow a slight bend in the knees and lower the torso. Stop when the torso is roughly parallel to the floor or hamstring tension caps the range. Drive the hips forward to stand back tall and repeat.
Benefits: Builds hamstring and erector strength under a fixed path.; Hack squat support reduces balance demands compared to barbell good mornings.; Carryover to deadlifts and squats.; Trains the hip hinge under load.; Easier to load heavy than free weight versions.; Saves the spine from bar pressure on the neck.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Adductors

Description: Lie face down on a glute ham developer. Set the hips on the pad and the chest forward. Let the legs hang down off the back. Hold the front handles for stability. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lift the legs up to parallel with the floor. Squeeze the glutes and hamstrings at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the posterior chain; Strong GHD variation; Trains the glutes; Useful for athletes; Builds the hamstrings
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hands behind your head or at your chest. Hinge at the hips — push your butt back, lowering your torso forward (good morning). At the bottom of the hinge, bend your knees and sit into a squat. From the squat bottom, stand up by extending hips and knees. That is one rep. Continue flowing: stand → hinge → squat → stand. Maintain a flat back during the hinge portion. Move smoothly between patterns. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Trains both hinge and squat patterns; Builds hamstring, quad, and glute strength; Time-efficient compound movement; Develops pattern transitions; No equipment needed; Useful for warm-up or conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (hinge phase); Quadriceps (squat phase); Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Bridge your hips up. Maintain the bridge position throughout. Lift your right foot 2 to 4 inches off the floor. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds. Return it to the floor. Lift your left foot. Hold. Continue alternating — marching in place from the bridge. Keep your hips level — do not let them drop when one foot lifts. Aim for 10 to 15 marches per side.
Benefits: Builds glute activation and endurance; Develops single-leg hip stability; Anti-rotation core demand from alternating; Beginner-friendly; No equipment needed; Excellent warm-up for lower-body training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (bridge hold); Gluteus medius (hip stability); Core (anti-rotation); Hamstrings

Description: Get into a push-up position. As you lower, bring your right knee across your body toward your left elbow. Press back up while returning your right leg to the start. On the next rep, bring your left knee toward your right elbow. Continue alternating. The cross-body knee drive adds oblique and hip flexor work. Maintain body control throughout. Aim for 8 to 12 total reps.
Benefits: Adds rotational core demand to push-ups; Develops hip mobility and coordination; No equipment needed; Engaging push-up variation; Builds oblique strength during pressing; Similar to Spiderman push-up but across body
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Obliques (cross-body knee); Hip flexors; Core (rotation)

Description: Lie on your back. Soles together, knees wide (butterfly). Hands behind head or across chest. Crunch up — lift shoulders off the floor. Squeeze abs at the top. Lower under control. Butterfly position reduces hip flexor cheating. Aim for 15 to 20 reps. Focus on the ab contraction.
Benefits: Reduces hip flexor involvement; Better ab isolation than standard crunches; Open hip position is comfortable; No equipment needed; Beginner-friendly; Effective for ab development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary)

Description: Stand on the hack squat machine foot plate with only the balls of your feet on the lower edge. Heels hang off. Position the shoulder pads on your shoulders. Brace your core. Unlock the safety catches and support the weight with straight legs. Lower your heels as far as possible for a deep calf stretch. Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible. Squeeze your calves hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Full range of motion on every rep. Use moderate to heavy weight. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Benefits: Allows heavy, progressive calf loading; Back support reduces lower-back stress; Full range of motion with deep stretch; Targets the gastrocnemius (standing position); Easy to load progressively; Useful when no dedicated calf raise machine is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (medial and lateral heads); Soleus; Achilles tendon

Description: Set up in a hack squat machine with the pads on the shoulders. Place one foot on the platform with the heel hanging off. Lift the other leg off the platform. Brace your core and keep the working leg straight. Lower the heel below the platform for a stretch. Press up onto the ball of the foot to a full calf raise. Squeeze the calf hard at the top. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Loads single leg calf; Strong unilateral calf; Builds calf size; Trains each side; Useful machine variation; Builds the calves
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Step onto the platform of the hack squat machine. Position your back against the sliding pad with shoulder pads above your shoulders. Set your feet shoulder-width apart on the platform. Grip the handles and unrack the safety. Brace your core and pull your back tight to the pad. Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back slightly. Continue until your thighs are parallel to the platform or deeper. Drive up through your heels to stand back to the starting position. Re-rack the safety.
Benefits: Heavy quad loading with back support; Eliminates balance demands; Allows progressive heavy weight; Builds quad size and strength; Different stimulus than free squats; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hamstrings

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Place your hands across your chest or behind your head with elbows wide. Brace your core. Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Curl your upper body off the floor by contracting your abs. Lift your head, neck, and shoulder blades. Stop when your shoulder blades clear the floor — do not sit all the way up. Squeeze your abs hard at the top. Hold for one second. Lower under control back to the floor. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Targets the rectus abdominis with reduced hip flexor involvement; Easier on the lower back than full sit-ups; Beginner-friendly ab exercise; No equipment needed; Easy to scale by adding weight to chest; Useful as a warm-up or cool-down
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially upper portion); Obliques (secondary); Transverse abdominis

Description: Grip a pull-up bar with an underhand grip. Pull up until your chin clears the bar. At the top, raise your knees toward your chest (or legs straight for harder). Hold briefly with chin above bar and knees raised. Lower your legs, then lower your body. Repeat. This is very demanding — combines two exercises. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Benefits: Combines pulling with ab work; Time-efficient compound exercise; Builds back, biceps, and abs together; Advanced bodyweight exercise; Develops hanging body control; Impressive skill
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Forearms

Exercise Name: Hammer Grip Pull Up on Dip Cage
Description: Stand under a dip cage with parallel bars at the top. Grip the bars with palms facing each other. Hang from the bars with arms fully extended. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Pull the chest up toward the bars. Drive the elbows down to the sides. Squeeze the lats and biceps at the top. Lower with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Builds the lats; Trains the biceps; Hammer grip variation; Strong neutral grip pull; Builds the brachialis; Useful pull variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Set the arms at the sides. Brace your core and lift one knee up. At the same time lift the opposite shoulder off the floor. Reach the same side hand across to touch the opposite knee. Squeeze the obliques hard at the top. Lower back to the start with control. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; No equipment needed; Beginner friendly; Trains rotational core; Easy to do anywhere; Useful core finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Hold a hand spring grip device in one hand. Wrap your fingers around the moving handle. Position the fixed handle against the heel of your palm. Brace your forearm and keep it relaxed. Squeeze the device closed by closing your fingers. Continue until the handles touch. Slowly release the squeeze to open back to start. Maintain the same forearm position throughout. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Builds grip endurance; Strengthens the forearms; Portable and easy to use; Improves crushing grip; Useful for climbers and lifters; Builds finger flexor strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms; Wrist flexors; Finger flexors

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Bend your elbows to lower your entire chest to the floor. Pause briefly with your chest fully on the ground. Lift your hands off the floor briefly. Place your hands back down under your shoulders. Press through your hands to drive back up. Lock out the elbows at the top.
Benefits: Eliminates bounce or momentum; Forces full range of motion; Standard military fitness move; Builds true pressing strength; No equipment required; Excellent push-up progression
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Description: Start in a downward-facing dog or pike position. Place your hands shoulder-width apart on the floor about two feet from a wall. Walk your feet up the wall behind you, building hand-strength tolerance gradually. For free-standing handstand: kick up to inverted position by stepping one foot up and kicking the other up to meet it. Once inverted, stack your body in a vertical line: hips over shoulders, ankles over hips. Engage your core hard. Press your shoulders up away from the floor. Squeeze your glutes and point your toes for full body tension. Make small balance corrections with your fingers and wrists, not big body shifts. Practice against a wall first. Bail by cartwheeling out to the side.
Benefits: Builds elite shoulder strength and stability; Develops body awareness and balance; Strengthens the core, wrists, and forearms; Foundational gymnastic skill; Counteracts forward-rounded posture; Improves spatial awareness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (heavy isometric); Trapezius and serratus anterior; Triceps brachii; Core (entire trunk); Forearms and wrists; Gluteus maximus

Description: Stand facing a wall. Place your hands on the floor about 6 inches from the wall, shoulder-width apart. Kick one leg up against the wall, then bring the other leg to meet it. Use a controlled, confident kick. Once inverted, press your hands firmly into the floor and lock out your arms. Keep your body in a straight line from wrists to feet. Engage your core hard. Tuck your butt slightly. Pull your ribs down. Squeeze your glutes and quads. Look at the floor between your hands or slightly forward. Hold for 15 to 60 seconds. Build up duration gradually. To exit, kick one leg down and then the other.
Benefits: Builds tremendous shoulder strength and stability; Develops inversion confidence; Trains the core in an inverted position; Foundational for freestanding handstand; Progresses toward handstand push-ups; Improves wrist strength and stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Trapezius; Serratus anterior; Core (entire trunk); Forearms and wrists

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width and toes pointed slightly out. Lower into a half squat with thighs at a 45-degree angle to the floor. Keep your chest up and back flat. Hold the half squat position throughout. Reach your right hand down to your right foot, bending sideways at the waist. Return to upright while staying in the half squat. Reach your left hand down to your left foot. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Combines leg and core work; Builds isometric leg strength; Hits the obliques and side core; Useful as a warm-up or finisher; No equipment required; Improves squat endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Adductors

Description: Kick up into a handstand against a wall. Hands shoulder-width apart, about 6 inches from the wall. Body fully inverted. Core tight. Lower your head toward the floor by bending at the elbows. Descend until the top of your head touches the floor (or use an abmat for range). Press back up to lockout. Maintain balance against the wall. Master pike push-ups and wall walks first. Aim for 3 to 10 reps.
Benefits: Most demanding bodyweight shoulder press; Presses full bodyweight overhead; Builds extreme shoulder and tricep strength; Impressive calisthenics skill; No equipment beyond a wall; Progressive with deficit or freestanding versions
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (primary); Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Core (balance)

Description: Stand below a hangboard mounted overhead. Reach up and grip an edge with your fingertips. Set your fingers in a half crimp with the second knuckles bent. Engage your shoulders and pull them down away from the ears. Lift your feet off the ground to hang from the edge. Hold the half crimp position with the body steady. Keep the core braced and avoid swinging. Lower your feet back down with control.
Benefits: Builds climbing grip strength; Trains finger tendons; Useful for rock climbers; Strong forearm builder; Develops crushing grip; Climbing-specific carryover
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Forearms; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Reach up and grab a hangboard with both hands. Use a deep edge or jug for the grip. Pull up so the elbows form a 135 degree angle. Brace the core and keep the body still. Hold the position with the slight arm bend. Engage the lats and biceps to maintain the hold. Continue the isometric for the working time. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds grip strength.; Trains the lats and biceps near full extension.; Climbing specific drill.; Useful for pulling endurance.; Builds the upper back.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Trapezius

Description: Reach up and grab a hangboard with both hands. Use a deep edge or jug for the grip. Pull up halfway so the elbows form a 90 degree angle. Brace the core and keep the body still. Hold the position with the elbows locked at 90 degrees. Engage the lats and biceps to maintain the hold. Continue the isometric for the working time. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds grip strength.; Trains the lats and biceps isometrically.; Climbing specific drill.; Useful for pulling endurance.; Builds the upper back.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Trapezius

Description: Set up a hangboard at a doorway or wall. Reach up and grip the holds with an open hand grip. Keep the fingers straight rather than crimped. Brace your core and keep the shoulders engaged. Hang from the holds with feet off the floor. Hold the hang with arms slightly bent. Lower the feet to the floor when needed. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Builds finger strength; Trains the forearms; Useful for climbing; Strong grip drill; Builds grip endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Brachioradialis; Wrist extensors

Description: Stand below a hangboard with sloping holds. Reach up and place the fingers on the slope. Set the fingers flat with an open hand grip. Engage your shoulders and pull them down. Lift your feet off the ground to hang from the slope. Press the fingers into the slope to hold the grip. Keep the body steady and avoid swinging. Lower your feet back down with control.
Benefits: Builds friction grip; Trains open hand strength; Useful for climbers; Strong forearm builder; Develops grip endurance; Climbing-specific work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Forearms; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Hang from a pull up bar with both hands shoulder-width apart. Bring your knees up to 90 degrees in a tucked hang position. Brace your core hard. Release one hand from the bar and reach forward. At the same time, extend the opposite leg straight out. Hold the contralateral position briefly. Return the hand to the bar and tuck the leg back to start. Switch sides on the next rep.
