Benefits: Advanced core stability work; Builds anti-rotation core strength; Challenges grip strength; Strong lat engagement to hang; Develops total body control; Useful for advanced ab training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with straight arms. Raise your legs to about 90 degrees (L-position). Rotate your legs to one side — lowering them toward that side. Return to center. You can alternate sides or work one side at a time. The “half” means you only go to one side rather than full windshield wiper side-to-side. Maintain straight arms throughout. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds hanging oblique strength; Develops grip endurance; Advanced hanging core exercise; Progression toward full windshield wipers; Builds rotational core power; Develops body control while hanging
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy); Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Grip a pull-up bar with palms facing forward. Hang from the bar with arms fully extended. Brace your core hard. Keep the legs straight in front of you slightly. Kick one leg up and the other down in alternating fashion. Continue alternating in a flutter pattern. Avoid swinging the body. Stop the flutter and lower the legs with control.
Benefits: Loads the lower abs; Builds hanging core control; Trains hip flexors; Useful ab finisher; Strong bodyweight builder; No floor space needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your shoulders down and back. Engage your lats by pulling slightly down on the bar. Round your upper back slightly. Pull your ribs down toward your hips. Bring your legs slightly forward of vertical — your body should form a gentle curve (the “hollow” position). Squeeze your glutes and quads. Point your toes. Hold this position for the desired duration (20 to 60 seconds). Breathe normally. Do not swing. Maintain the hollow position rigidly. Lower yourself when you can no longer maintain the position.
Benefits: Builds anti-extension core strength in a hanging position; Develops lat engagement and shoulder depression; Foundational gymnastics position; Improves body control and awareness; Builds grip endurance; Excellent warm-up for advanced hanging exercises
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi (isometric); Forearms and grip; Quadriceps (keeping legs forward)

Description: Hang from a pull up bar with hands at shoulder width. Brace your core hard. Raise the knees up toward the chest. Begin tracing a circular motion with the knees. Move the knees up to one side then around to the bottom. Continue around to the other side and back to the top. Complete a full circle with the knees. Reverse direction for the next rep.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Trains rotational core; Builds the abs; Useful core finisher; Builds the rectus abdominis; Strong hanging move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Hang from a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your shoulders down and back. Engage your lats by pulling down on the bar. Brace your core. Keep your body in a slight hollow position. Initiate the movement by pulling your knees up toward your chest. As they rise, simultaneously pull yourself up slightly so your shoulders move back. Continue pulling your knees up until they touch your elbows (or as close as you can get). At the peak, your knees should be at your elbows and your hips should be fully flexed. Lower your legs slowly under control back to the hanging start position. If you cannot reach knees to elbows, work on hanging knee raises and hanging leg raises first to build strength.
Benefits: Builds elite-level core strength; Trains the lower abs through full range of motion; Heavily engages the lats through the lat pulldown component; Improves grip and shoulder stability; Standard CrossFit benchmark exercise; Excellent test of relative core strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Latissimus dorsi; Obliques; Forearms and grip; Posterior deltoid (stabilizer)

Description: Hang from a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your shoulders down and back to engage your lats. Brace your core. Keep your legs straight (or slightly bent if you cannot do it with straight legs). Lift your legs up toward your chest by contracting your hip flexors and abs. As your thighs approach parallel to the floor, continue the movement by curling your hips up and back. Your tailbone should rotate up toward your chest. At the peak, your hips should be flexed and your lower back rounded. Squeeze your lower abs hard. Lower your legs slowly under control over two to three seconds back to the hanging start position. Avoid swinging. If you cannot do strict reps, regress to bent-knee versions or hanging knee raises until you build the strength.
Benefits: Builds the lower abs more effectively than floor-based exercises; The hip curl forces real ab work, not just hip flexor work; Trains grip and shoulder stability through the hang; Excellent advanced core exercise; Improves overall body control and coordination; Strong predictor of relative core strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially the lower portion); Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Obliques; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (isometric); Shoulders (stabilizer)

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms extended. Overhand grip. Raise your legs in front of you — bent knees (easier) or straight legs (harder). Lift to at least horizontal. Lower under control. Do not swing. Add a hip curl at the top for maximum lower ab activation. If swinging occurs, use shorter range or bent knees. Aim for 10 to 15 reps. Builds grip alongside ab strength.
Benefits: One of the best ab exercises; Hanging prevents cheating; Builds grip alongside abs; Scalable by leg position (bent vs straight); Progressive toward toes-to-bar; Develops hanging core control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors; Obliques; Forearms and grip

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your shoulders down and back. Brace your core. Keep your body still. Pull your knees up and to the right by contracting your left oblique and hip flexors. Continue until your knees are at roughly hip height on the right side. Squeeze your oblique. Lower your legs under control back to the hang. Pull your knees up and to the left on the next rep. Continue alternating sides. Avoid swinging — strict reps are essential. Repeat for the desired total reps (e.g., 20 = 10 per side).
Benefits: Builds the obliques and rotational core strength while hanging; Develops grip and shoulder stability simultaneously; Trains anti-rotation and rotation control; More challenging than floor-based oblique work; Excellent accessory for complete core development; Carries over to sports requiring rotational power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (isometric)

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar. Arms extended. Raise both straight legs upward past horizontal. Continue until your toes approach or touch the bar. Lower under control all the way back to the dead hang. The compression past horizontal is what makes this advanced. No swinging — strict form only. Aim for 5 to 10 reps. Master hanging straight leg raises first.
Benefits: Extreme ab compression strength; Harder than standard hanging leg raises; Builds toward toes-to-bar and windshield wipers; Develops advanced hanging core control; Builds grip endurance; Advanced calisthenics exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (extreme); Hip flexors (extreme); Obliques; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Reach up and grab a pull-up bar with an overhand, shoulder-width grip. Hang from the bar with arms straight. Allow the shoulders to relax and rise slightly toward the ears. Brace your core and keep your legs still. Pull your shoulder blades down and back without bending the elbows. Squeeze the lower traps and lats. Pause briefly at the top of the shrug. Lower slowly back to the relaxed hang.
Benefits: Teaches scapular control; Strengthens the lower traps; Builds the lats; Improves pull-up performance; Builds grip endurance; Useful as a pull-up warm-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Traps; Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Pull your shoulders down and back. Engage your lats. Brace your core. Lift both straight legs up by contracting your abs and hip flexors. Continue until your legs are at hip height (parallel to the floor) or higher. At the top, press your toes upward by lifting your hips slightly. This is the hip raise component. Hold the top position briefly. Squeeze your lower abs hard. Lower your legs slowly under control back to the hang position. Avoid swinging — strict reps only. Aim for 5 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds elite lower-ab strength; The hip raise component fully engages the lower abs; Develops grip and shoulder stability simultaneously; More demanding than standard hanging leg raises; Carries over to advanced core skills; Highly portable — needs only a pull-up bar
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially the lower portion); Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Obliques; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (isometric); Quadriceps (keeping legs straight)

Exercise Name: Hanging Straight Twisting Leg Hip Raise
Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with a shoulder width grip. Allow the body to hang in a straight line. Brace the core and keep the legs together. Lift the straight legs up and across to one side. Continue lifting until the toes pass the opposite hip. Squeeze the obliques hard at the top. Lower with control to the start. Alternate sides each rep or work one side at a time.
Benefits: Hammers the lower abs and obliques.; Builds advanced core strength.; Trains grip endurance.; Improves shoulder stability.; Brutal core finisher.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Forearm flexors

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with arms extended. Keep both legs straight. Raise your legs in front of you to at least horizontal (90 degrees). Control the movement — no swinging. Lower under control. Stop before legs swing behind you. Straight legs are much harder than bent-knee raises. If you swing, the weight is too heavy for strict form — try bent-knee version. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Advanced hanging core exercise; Straight legs increase difficulty significantly; Builds lower ab and hip flexor strength; Develops grip endurance; Progression from hanging knee raises; Builds toward toes-to-bar
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors (heavy); Obliques; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (anti-swing)

Description: Hang from a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands just outside shoulder-width. Pull your shoulders down and back. Engage your lats by pulling slightly down on the bar. Start with a slight hollow-body position. Brace your core hard. Initiate the movement with a slight lat pulldown, then lift your legs up by contracting your abs and hip flexors. Keep your legs straight (or slightly bent) and continue lifting until your toes touch the bar between your hands. At the top, your feet should contact the bar. Your body will be in a compressed pike position. Lower your legs slowly under control back to the hanging start position. If strict reps are too difficult, build up through hanging knee raises, hanging leg raises, and toes-near-bar progressions.
Benefits: Builds elite core and hip-flexor strength; Trains the lats and shoulders through the hanging position; Develops body control and coordination; Standard CrossFit benchmark movement; Improves grip strength heavily; One of the best tests of relative core strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Obliques; Latissimus dorsi (engagement); Forearms and grip; Shoulders (stabilizer)

Description: Lie flat on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Lift your toes off the floor. Keep only your heels in contact with the ground. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor. Continue lifting until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes and hamstrings hard at the top for one to two seconds. Lower under control back to the floor. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Increases hamstring activation vs standard glute bridge; Builds the glutes and hamstrings together; No equipment needed; Easy to scale by adding weight or single-leg variation; Useful warm-up before deadlifts; Reduces quad involvement vs standard bridge
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (increased involvement); Adductor magnus; Erector spinae (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with the balls of both feet on a step edge, heels hanging off. Rise up onto your toes using both legs. Shift your weight to your right leg. Lift your left foot. Slowly lower your right heel below the step level over 3 to 5 seconds. This slow lowering is the eccentric contraction that heals the tendon. Rise back up using both legs (not just the working leg). Repeat on the same side for the desired reps, then switch. Aim for 15 reps per leg, 2 to 3 sets. Perform twice daily for tendon rehab.
Benefits: Gold-standard for Achilles tendinopathy rehabilitation; Builds eccentric calf strength; Promotes tendon healing and remodeling; Simple and accessible; Clinically proven effective; Preventive calf health exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (eccentric); Soleus (eccentric); Achilles tendon (primary target)

Description: Set a barbell in a power rack at chest height. Stand under the bar and grip it with hands shoulder-width apart. Walk your feet forward until the body forms a slight diagonal. Brace your core and squeeze your shoulder blades down. Pull your chest toward the bar by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row. Lower with control until the arms are straight again. Keep the body in a straight line throughout.
Benefits: Upright body angle is easier; Great inverted row regression; No advanced equipment needed; Builds back and biceps; Easy to scale by foot position; Useful for beginners
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Middle trapezius

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat on the floor hip-width apart. Arms at your sides, palms down. Drive through your heels to lift your hips up. At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds. Lower under control. Do not hyperextend your lower back. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Most basic glute activation exercise; Foundational for all hip thrust variations; No equipment needed; Builds glute activation awareness; Supports lower back health; Beginner-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Erector spinae

Exercise Name: High Knee Lunge on Bosu Ball
Description: Place a Bosu ball about a stride length behind you. Step the back foot onto the dome of the Bosu. Lower into a deep lunge with the front shin vertical. Brace the core and keep the chest tall. Drive through the front foot to stand up tall. Lift the back leg through into a high knee. Pause briefly with the knee high and the body upright. Lower the back leg back onto the Bosu and repeat then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds single leg strength on an unstable surface.; Trains balance and proprioception.; Hammers the glutes and quads.; Improves athletic stability.; Develops core control.; Adds variety to standard lunges.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Hamstrings; Core; Calves

Description: Lie on your side with the legs stacked. Bend the knees to about 90 degrees. Stack the feet on top of each other. Rest the head on your bottom arm. Keep the feet together as you lift the top knee. Open the knee like a clam shell to the top. Squeeze the glute medius at the top. Lower with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Activates the glute medius; Builds hip stability; Useful warm-up move; No equipment needed; Easy to add to any session; Strong hip activator
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Hip flexors

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Extend the arms overhead on the floor with palms up. Set the feet hip width apart. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Drive through the heels to lift the hips up. Extend the hips to a straight line with the body. Reach the arms long overhead at the top. Lower the hips back down with control.
Benefits: Strong glute builder; Trains the lats; No equipment needed; Builds the hamstrings; Useful glute builder; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent at 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor. Place hands behind your head. Brace your core. Lift your feet off the floor so your shins are parallel to the floor. Simultaneously crunch your upper body up and lift your hips off the floor by pressing your feet toward the ceiling. At the peak, your shoulder blades should be off the floor and your hips should be lifted. Squeeze your abs hard. Lower your shoulders and hips back to the start under control. Do not let your feet touch the floor between reps. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Focus on contracting your abs, not pulling with your neck.
Benefits: Trains upper and lower abs in one movement; Time-efficient core exercise; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Builds core strength and endurance; Easy to scale by adjusting rep count; Excellent finisher for core workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (upper and lower); Obliques (secondary); Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis

Description: Start in a forearm plank. Rotate to a side plank on your right forearm. Stack or stagger your feet. Hold the side plank for 1 to 2 seconds. Rotate back to front plank. Rotate to a side plank on your left forearm. Continue rolling front → right → front → left. Maintain body alignment through each position. Aim for 5 to 8 rolls per side.
Benefits: Trains the core through all angles; Combines front and side plank demands; Builds anti-extension and anti-lateral flexion; No equipment needed; Develops rotational transitions; Engaging dynamic plank variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (front plank); Obliques (side plank); Transverse abdominis; Quadratus lumborum; Anterior deltoid

Description: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a flat bench. Your shoulder blades should rest on the bench edge. Plant your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart, roughly 12 to 18 inches in front of you. Brace your core. Tuck your chin slightly. Keep your gaze forward. Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips off the floor. Continue until your body forms a straight line from your knees to your shoulders. Your shins should be roughly vertical at the top. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not hyperextend your lower back. Lower under control back toward the floor. Touch lightly, then drive up again. Aim for 12 to 20 reps. Progress to weighted variations once bodyweight becomes easy.
Benefits: Most effective bodyweight glute exercise; Foundation for all weighted hip thrust variations; Builds glute size and strength with no equipment; Easier on the lower back than many glute exercises; Trains glute activation for squats and deadlifts; Easy to progress to weighted versions
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Adductor magnus; Quadriceps (secondary); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie flat on your back. Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Lift your shoulders, head, and legs slightly off the floor. Reach your arms overhead alongside your ears. Keep legs straight and pointed. Round your upper back slightly. Pull your ribs down toward your hips. This is the hollow position — your body forms a gentle banana shape. Brace your core hard. Maintain this position rigidly. Hold for as long as you can while maintaining perfect form (start with 15 to 30 seconds, build to 60+). If your lower back lifts off the floor, regress by bending your knees (tuck hold) or lowering your arms. Breathe steadily — do not hold your breath.
Benefits: Foundational gymnastics core hold; Builds elite anterior core strength; Teaches rigid core bracing; Carries over to all advanced calisthenics skills; No equipment needed; Develops body control and awareness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Hip flexors; Quadriceps; Anterior deltoid (arms overhead)

Description: Lie on your back. Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Lift your shoulders, arms, head, and legs slightly off the floor. Reach your arms overhead alongside your ears. Keep your legs straight and pointed. Round your upper back slightly. Pull your ribs down toward your hips. This is the hollow position — your body forms a gentle banana shape. Brace your core hard. Maintain this position rigidly throughout the rocking. Begin gently rocking back and forth like a rocking chair, using a slight upper-body lift to drive the rock. Keep the hollow shape constant — the entire body moves as one unit. Do not break the position. Continue for 20 to 60 seconds. If you cannot maintain the hollow shape, regress to the hollow hold first.
Benefits: Builds elite anterior core strength; Foundational gymnastics movement; Teaches rigid core bracing; Carries over to all advanced calisthenics skills; No equipment needed; Develops body control and awareness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Hip flexors; Quadriceps; Anterior deltoid (arms overhead)

Description: Sit on a horizontal leg press machine with your back firmly against the pad. Place one foot on the platform in the middle area. Keep the other leg off the platform. Release the safety stops. Brace your core and grip the handles. Press the platform forward by extending the working leg. Stop just short of locking out the knee. Slowly lower the platform back to the start. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Builds single-leg strength; Fixes side-to-side imbalances; Strong unilateral leg builder; Useful for rehab; Builds quad and glute size; Reduces injury risk
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Find a sturdy vertical pole that can support your weight. Stand sideways to it. Grip the pole with both hands stacked vertically — top hand higher with overhand grip pulling down, bottom hand lower pushing the pole away. The top hand pulls toward you while the bottom hand pushes away — creating opposing forces. Brace your core hard. Engage your lats. Lift your legs off the ground and extend them out to the side, parallel to the floor. Your body forms a horizontal “flag” parallel to the ground. Hold for as long as possible — even 1 to 5 seconds is impressive at first. This is elite-level. Build up with tuck flags, single-leg flags, and progressive holds first.
Benefits: Builds elite shoulder, lat, and core strength; Develops complete body control; Impressive calisthenic skill; Trains opposing force production; Carries over to all advanced bodyweight skills; Builds mental toughness and dedication
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (heavy involvement); Anterior, lateral, and posterior deltoid; Obliques (heavy); Serratus anterior; Triceps brachii; Core (entire trunk); Forearms and grip

Description: Lie on a flat bench holding light dumbbells. Plant your feet flat. Brace your core. Start with both dumbbells touching directly above your chest at lockout, palms facing each other. From the top, lower the dumbbells out to the sides in a wide arc with a slight elbow bend. Lower until you feel a deep chest stretch — typically when your arms are level with your shoulders. Reverse the motion: sweep the dumbbells up and back together in a wide arc, focusing on squeezing your chest. Bring the dumbbells back to touching at the top. Squeeze your chest hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Use lighter weight than standard flys. Form is everything.
Benefits: Greater chest activation than standard flys; Targets the inner chest fibers; Longer time under tension; Builds chest size; Provides unique stimulus; Useful variation for plateau breaking
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially inner fibers); Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (slight stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms at your sides. Hinge forward at the hips and place both hands on the floor in front of your feet. Bend your knees if needed. Walk your hands forward, one at a time, until you reach a high plank position. Hold the plank briefly. Brace your core. Walk your feet forward toward your hands, taking small steps. Continue walking your feet forward until you return to the standing forward fold. Stand up tall. That is one rep. Perform 5 to 10 reps as part of a warm-up.
Benefits: Mobilizes the hamstrings dynamically; Warms up shoulders and core; Excellent full-body warm-up; Builds endurance and conditioning; No equipment needed; Engaging and active
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (stretched); Calves; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (heavy stabilizer); Erector spinae

Description: Hang from a straight bar with an overhand grip. Pull yourself up (like a pull-up). As your chest reaches the bar, lean forward and transition your body over the bar. Push down into a dip position above the bar. Lower back below the bar in a controlled reverse of the movement. The transition from below to above is the “impossible” part. This requires significant pulling and pushing strength. Master muscle-ups before attempting. Aim for 1 to 3 reps.
Benefits: Advanced calisthenics skill; Combines pulling and pushing in one movement; Builds transition strength; Develops full upper-body control; Impressive demonstration of strength; Progression from muscle-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (pull phase); Pectoralis major (transition); Triceps brachii (dip phase); Anterior deltoid; Core (transition); Biceps brachii

Description: Set up on a 45-degree hyperextension bench. Adjust the pad so it sits just below your hip bones, with your feet locked under the foot pads. Cross your arms over your chest or place your hands behind your head. Brace your core. Start with your torso angled up so your body forms a roughly straight line from heels to head. Hinge forward at the hips by lowering your torso toward the floor. Keep your back flat — do not round. Lower until your torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings. Reverse the movement by squeezing your glutes and hamstrings to bring your torso back up. Stop at the position where your body forms a straight line. Do not hyperextend (overarch) the lower back at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Add load by holding a weight plate against your chest as you get stronger.
Benefits: Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings; Excellent rehabilitation and warm-up exercise; Builds endurance in the spinal erectors; Easy to scale by adding load; Improves the hip-hinge pattern; Useful accessory for the deadlift and squat
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae (lower back); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductor magnus; Trapezius and rhomboids (when hands behind head)

Description: Lie head down on an incline bench. Grip the top of the bench behind the head. Lift both legs straight off the bench. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Kick one leg up while the other goes down. Alternate the legs in small flutter kicks. Keep the legs straight throughout. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Loads the lower abs; Strong incline variation; Trains the hip flexors; Useful core builder; Builds the core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip Flexors; Core

Description: Place hands close together on a bench or box — 6 to 12 inches apart. Set your body in a straight line from heels to head. Lower your chest toward the bench by bending elbows. Keep elbows close to your body. Press back up to lockout. The incline reduces difficulty; the narrow grip targets triceps. Progress toward floor close-grip push-ups. Aim for 10 to 15 reps. Maintain straight body line throughout.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly tricep push-up; Incline reduces total load; Narrow grip targets the triceps; No equipment beyond a bench; Progressive toward floor version; Builds tricep pressing strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (increased); Pectoralis major (inner); Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Place hands on a bench or box at chest height. Set feet back in a push-up position. Lower your chest toward the bench. Press up explosively — generate enough force to briefly lift your hands off the surface. Land softly back on the bench and immediately lower into the next rep. The incline makes this easier than floor plyo push-ups. Maintain a straight body line throughout. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set. Progress toward floor-level plyo push-ups over time.
Benefits: Plyometric pressing regression (easier than floor); Builds explosive upper-body power; Accessible for developing pressing explosiveness; No equipment beyond an elevated surface; Progressive — decrease incline for more difficulty; Builds fast-twitch pressing strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Place your hands on a sturdy elevated surface (bench, box, or counter) slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers pointing forward. Step your feet back so your body forms a straight line from heels to head. Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your hips level. Lower your chest toward the surface by bending at the elbows. Tuck your elbows at roughly 45 degrees from your torso. Lower until your chest lightly touches or comes within an inch of the surface. Press back up by extending at the elbows, driving your hands into the surface. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Maintain the straight body line throughout. Progress to a lower surface as you get stronger. Eventually transition to floor push-ups.
Benefits: Effective progression step toward full push-ups; Easily scalable by changing surface height; Builds the chest, triceps, and shoulders with reduced load; Trains core stability through the plank position; No equipment needed beyond a sturdy surface; Excellent warm-up for experienced lifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Place your hands on a bench or box at chest height, fingers pointing toward your feet (reverse grip). Set your body in a straight line from heels to head. Lower your chest toward the bench by bending at the elbows. Press back up to lockout. The reverse grip naturally tucks your elbows. The incline makes it easier than floor reverse grip push-ups. If wrists are uncomfortable, try a wider hand position. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis toward lower chest; Natural elbow tuck reduces shoulder stress; Incline makes it accessible; No equipment beyond an elevated surface; Unique grip variation; Builds chest from a different angle
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (lower fibers); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid (reduced); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Place your hands on a sturdy bench or against a wall. Walk your feet back to a high incline push-up position. Keep your arms straight throughout the entire movement. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Allow your shoulder blades to squeeze together (retract). Your chest will dip slightly toward your hands. Push through your hands to spread the shoulder blades apart (protract). Round your upper back at the top of each rep.
Benefits: Strengthens the serratus anterior; Improves scapular control; Beginner-friendly variation; Useful for shoulder health; Builds pressing stability; No equipment beyond a bench
Muscles Worked (Raw): Serratus anterior; Front deltoid; Pectoralis major

Description: Set an incline bench at about a 30 to 45 degree angle. Lie face down on the bench with your hips at the lower edge. Allow your legs to hang straight down off the bench. Grip the bench with your hands for stability. Brace your core and keep your legs straight. Lift both legs up and back until they are roughly in line with your torso. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top. Lower slowly to the start.
Benefits: Builds glute and hamstring strength; Strengthens the lower back; Increased range from incline angle; Spinal-friendly compared to traditional hyper; No equipment beyond a bench; Useful as a posterior chain accessory
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Place your hands on a sturdy box or bench. Step the feet back to a plank position. Brace your core hard and keep the body in a straight line. Squeeze the glutes to keep the hips stable. Lift one hand off the surface and tap the opposite shoulder. Hold the tap briefly without letting the hips rotate. Plant the hand back down and repeat with the other hand. Continue alternating taps with control.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly plank tap; Trains anti-rotation; Builds shoulder stability; Useful regression move; No special equipment needed; Strong core builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Obliques; Core

Description: Lie on a decline bench with feet hooked under the pads. Hands behind your head. Sit up and rotate — bring your right elbow toward your left knee. Return to the decline position. Sit up and rotate the other way — left elbow to right knee. Continue alternating. Control both the sit-up and the rotation. Use bodyweight or hold a plate for added resistance. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines decline ab loading with oblique rotation; Builds abs and obliques together; Greater resistance than flat twisting sit-ups; Simple setup; Easy to add weight; Complete core exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Inverted Chin Curl with Bent Knee Between Chairs
Description: Place a sturdy bar across two chairs about shoulder width apart. Test the setup carefully to confirm it can hold your weight. Lie face up under the bar with a close underhand grip. Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor. Brace the core and keep the back relatively straight. Curl your chest up to the bar by bending the elbows hard. Squeeze the biceps and lats at the top. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds biceps strength using only chairs and a bar.; Bent knees scale the difficulty.; Underhand grip targets the lats and biceps.; No spinal compression like with curls.; Develops grip and forearm strength.; Excellent at home biceps option.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Latissimus dorsi; Brachialis; Forearm flexors

Exercise Name: Inverse Leg Curl with Bench Pads
Description: Kneel on a pad behind a flat bench. Hook the feet under the lower edge of the bench pads. Set the shins flat on the floor with the feet locked. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the body forward by extending the knees. Control the descent using the hamstrings. At the bottom catch with the hands on the floor. Push up with the arms and pull with the hamstrings to return.
Benefits: Brutal hamstring builder; Trains eccentric strength; Builds posterior chain; No machine needed; Useful hamstring builder; Strong bench move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves

Description: Set a bar at about hip height. Lie underneath and grip with overhand grip. Extend your body in a straight line from heels to head. Heels on the floor. Pull your chest toward the bar by driving elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control. Adjust body angle for difficulty — more horizontal is harder. Aim for 8 to 15 reps. Progress toward pull-ups by lowering the bar height over time.
Benefits: Primary bodyweight back exercise; Counterpart to the push-up; Adjustable difficulty by body angle; Builds pulling strength toward pull-ups; No pull-up bar height needed; Accessible for all levels
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Inverted Row Bent Knee Under Table
Description: Find a sturdy table that can support your full bodyweight. Lie face up underneath with your chest below the edge. Reach up and grip the edge of the table with both hands. Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor. Brace the core and keep the back straight from shoulders to knees. Pull your chest up to the table edge by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds back strength with only a sturdy table needed.; Bent knees make it accessible for beginners.; Trains horizontal pulling without spinal compression.; Strengthens the lats, mid back, and biceps.; Develops grip and core stability.; Travel friendly with zero special equipment.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a bar at about hip height. Lie underneath it and grip with an overhand grip. Bend your knees at 90 degrees with feet flat on the floor. Pull your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control. The bent knees make this significantly easier than straight-leg rows. Progress to straight-leg inverted rows as you get stronger. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Easiest inverted row regression; Builds pulling strength for beginners; Shorter lever reduces difficulty; Progresses to straight-leg rows; Minimal equipment needed; Safe and controlled
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Place two sturdy chairs facing each other a few feet apart. Lay a strong stick or pole across the chair seats. Make sure the setup is stable before getting under it. Slide under the bar and grip it with hands shoulder-width apart. Walk your feet out so the body hangs from the bar. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Pull your chest toward the bar by bending the elbows. Lower with control to the start. Make sure the chairs do not move.
Benefits: Home back option with no rack; Builds back and biceps; Travel-friendly idea; Easy to scale by foot position; Useful when no bar is available; No gym required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Middle trapezius

Description: Set a bar at about hip height. Place a bench nearby for your feet. Lie underneath the bar. Grip with an overhand grip. Place your heels on the bench. Body forms a straight line from heels to head. Pull your chest toward the bar. Squeeze your shoulder blades together. Lower under control. The elevated feet make this harder than flat-foot rows. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Increased difficulty from elevated feet; Greater pulling demand per rep; Progressive from flat-foot inverted rows; Builds toward weighted rows and pull-ups; Simple setup; Develops back pulling strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a barbell in a power rack at about waist height. Lie on the floor underneath the bar. Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, palms facing away. Position your body in a straight line with heels on the floor. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Pull your chest up to the bar by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Builds back strength with bodyweight; Accessible to lifters who cannot do pull-ups; Strong rhomboid and lat engagement; No weights required; Strong core engagement to maintain plank; Easy to scale by adjusting bar height
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a barbell in a power rack at about waist height. Place sliders or towels under your heels on a smooth floor. Lie on the floor underneath the bar with feet on the sliders. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing away. Position your body in a straight line. Pull your chest up to the bar while letting feet slide forward slightly. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower yourself back down as your feet slide back to the starting position.
Benefits: Adds dynamic stability work to inverted rows; Builds back strength with bodyweight; Strong core engagement; Develops body control through the rep; Accessible to lifters who cannot do pull-ups; Useful variation for breaking up training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Biceps brachii; Core

Description: Set up under a low bar with sliders under the heels. Grip the bar with an overhand grip slightly wider than shoulder width. Set the body in a straight line. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the chest toward the bar. Let the heels slide forward as you pull up. Squeeze the upper back at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the back; Trains the biceps; Strong inverted row; Adds hamstring work; Useful bodyweight move; Builds upper back size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Hamstrings

Description: Choose a sturdy table that can support your full body weight without tipping. Test it carefully first. Lie on your back underneath the table with your chest below the edge. Reach up and grip the edge of the table with both hands, slightly wider than shoulder-width. Position your body so your arms are fully extended. Keep your body straight from heels to head. Brace your core. Pull your shoulders down and back. Pull your chest up to touch the underside of the table by bending at the elbows and squeezing your shoulder blades. Lower under control back to a fully extended position. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Bend your knees if the straight-body version is too difficult.
Benefits: Excellent at-home bodyweight back exercise; Builds the lats, mid-back, and biceps; No gym equipment required; Good progression toward pull-ups; Trains core stability through the plank position; Easy to scale by adjusting body angle
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid; Core (anti-extension); Forearms and grip

Description: Anchor the middle of a sturdy bed sheet in a closed door. Grip the sheet ends with both hands. Lean back with the arms straight and feet planted. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the chest toward the door by bending the elbows. Squeeze the lats and upper back at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: No equipment needed; Strong home option; Builds the back; Trains the biceps; Useful for travel; Builds upper back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with straight arms, overhand grip. Start in a passive hang — shoulders shrugged up near your ears. Without bending your elbows, pull your shoulder blades down and back (depress). Your body will rise 1 to 2 inches. Squeeze your lower traps. Release back to passive hang. Continue for the desired reps. This is a small but important movement. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds lower trap strength; Develops scapular depression control; Essential for proper pull-up mechanics; Prevents shoulder injury during hanging; Simple concept with big carryover; Useful warm-up before pull-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower fibers); Latissimus dorsi (slight); Serratus anterior; Forearms and grip (hanging)

Exercise Name: Inverted Row with Bent Knee Between Chairs
Description: Place a sturdy pole or broomstick across two chairs about shoulder width apart. Test the setup by hanging cautiously to make sure it holds your weight. Lie face up under the pole with the chest below the bar. Reach up and grip the pole with hands shoulder width apart. Bend your knees and place your feet flat on the floor. Pull your chest up to the pole by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the upper back at the top. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds back strength with only chairs and a pole needed.; Bent knee position makes it beginner friendly.; Trains horizontal pulling without weights.; Develops grip and core control.; Easy to scale by adjusting body angle.; Excellent at home substitute for cable rows.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set a barbell in a power rack at about waist height. Lie on the floor underneath the bar. Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width, palms facing away. Position your body in a straight line with heels on the floor. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Pull your chest up to the bar by leading with the elbows out wide. Squeeze your shoulder blades together hard at the top. Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang.
Benefits: Wide grip emphasizes upper back; Strong rear delt and rhomboid engagement; Builds back strength with bodyweight; No weights required; Different stimulus than standard inverted row; Useful for posture work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle and upper); Posterior deltoid; Latissimus dorsi

Exercise Name: Inverted Underhand Grip Row Between Chairs
Description: Place a sturdy pole across two chairs about shoulder width apart. Test the setup by hanging cautiously to confirm it holds your weight. Lie face up under the pole with the chest below the bar. Reach up and grip the pole with an underhand shoulder width grip. Set your feet on the floor with legs straight or slightly bent. Pull your chest up to the pole by driving the elbows back along your sides. Squeeze the lats and biceps at the top. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Hits the lats hard with the underhand grip.; Builds biceps strength through bodyweight pulling.; No spinal compression like with bent over rows.; Develops grip and forearm strength.; At home alternative to chin ups and seated cable rows.; Easy to scale by adjusting body angle.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Brachioradialis

Description: Set a bar at hip height. Grip the bar with a wide overhand grip. Hang under the bar with the body angled. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the chest toward the bar with wide grip. Lower then move the hands narrow and row again. Continue alternating wide and narrow grip rows.
Benefits: Trains multiple angles; Builds the back; Strong row variation; Useful for back size; Trains the biceps; No weights needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set TRX straps or rings to roughly hip height. Grip the handles with both hands. Walk your feet forward until your body forms a leaning angle. Set your body in a straight line from heels to head. Brace your core. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Row your chest up toward your hands by driving your elbows back and down. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control to a full hang with arms extended. Steeper body angle (more upright) is easier; more horizontal angle is harder.
Benefits: Builds the back and biceps with bodyweight; Suspension instability adds core demand; Easily scalable by adjusting body angle; Excellent at-home back exercise; Builds shoulder stability; Useful when no pull-up bar is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Lie face down on the floor. Extend both arms straight out to the sides at shoulder height. Press through your palms and toes to lift your body off the floor into a plank. Your body should be straight from heels to head — arms extended wide. Hold this position. The wide arms make it extremely demanding. Breathe steadily. Maintain the plank. Start with 10 to 15 seconds and build up. If too difficult, start with hands slightly closer than full cross. Maintain a flat back — do not let hips sag.
Benefits: Extreme chest and shoulder demand from wide arm position; Builds isometric chest and core strength; Advanced plank progression; No equipment needed; Develops shoulder stability; Builds mental toughness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (heavy isometric); Anterior deltoid; Core (anti-extension); Serratus anterior; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand or sit tall. Bring your hands to your chest with palms together (prayer position). Press your palms together as hard as possible. Squeeze your chest hard. You should feel the pectorals contract. Hold the maximum squeeze for 5 to 10 seconds. Relax briefly, then squeeze again. Perform 5 to 10 reps with 5- to 10-second holds. Try at different angles — hands at chest, hands lower, hands higher — to engage different chest fibers. Keep elbows slightly elevated for better engagement.
Benefits: Strong isometric chest contraction; Excellent chest activation warm-up; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Useful for chest mind-muscle connection; Safe for rehabilitation; Quick and easy to perform
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially clavicular and sternal heads); Pectoralis minor; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with straight arms. Raise both legs to roughly horizontal (L-sit or beyond). Rotate your legs to one side — like a windshield wiper frozen in position. Hold this rotated position for 10 to 20 seconds. Return to center. Rotate to the other side and hold. Maintain straight arms throughout. This requires significant grip, core, and oblique strength. Aim for 3 to 5 holds per side.
Benefits: Extreme oblique isometric challenge; Builds hanging core control; Advanced calisthenics exercise; Develops oblique strength through isometric holds; Builds grip endurance; Impressive body control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy isometric); Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (hanging)

Description: Place the shins or feet on top of a stability ball. Set up in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to feet. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Pull the knees forward toward the chest. Roll the ball forward as the knees come in. Pause briefly at the tucked position. Extend the legs back to the start.
Benefits: Loads the core; Strong ab builder; Trains stability; Builds the abs; Useful core move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Core; Hip Flexors

Description: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart, body in a straight line from heels to head. Brace your core hard. Keep your hips stable. Jump both feet out wider than your hips simultaneously. Immediately jump both feet back together to the start position. Continue jumping your feet in and out rapidly. Maintain the plank position throughout — only your legs move. Do not let your hips bounce up and down or sag toward the floor. Perform for 20 to 45 seconds per set.
Benefits: Builds core stability with cardio demand; Develops shoulder endurance; Excellent HIIT exercise; Trains hip stability under movement; No equipment needed; Time-efficient core/cardio combo
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core (heavy stabilizer); Anterior deltoid; Adductors and abductors; Hip flexors; Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii

Description: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Simultaneously lift your torso and your straight legs upward, reaching your hands toward your feet. Meet at the top in a V-shape with your fingers reaching toward your toes. Squeeze your abs hard at the top. Lower under control back to the start with arms overhead and legs extended. Stop just before your hands and heels touch the floor to maintain tension. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use bent knees if too difficult.
Benefits: Trains upper and lower abs simultaneously; Builds core strength and endurance; No equipment needed; Time-efficient core exercise; Excellent finisher for ab workouts; Develops body control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (upper and lower); Hip flexors; Obliques (secondary); Quadriceps (keeping legs straight)

Description: Lie flat on your back on the floor. Extend your arms overhead and your legs straight. Brace your core hard. Lift your legs and torso off the floor at the same time. Reach the hands toward the toes in a V shape. Pause at the top with the body folded. Lower the legs and torso back down with control. Avoid letting the lower back arch off the floor.
Benefits: Strong full ab builder; No equipment needed; Trains hip flexors; Easy to scale; Useful core finisher; Builds abdominal strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Stand on a low box on one leg. Extend the other leg straight in front of you. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Lower yourself into a single-leg squat on the working leg. Continue down until your butt is below your knee. Drive up explosively through the working leg, jumping off the box. Land on the same leg with the knee soft to absorb the impact. Step back onto the box and reset. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Builds single-leg explosive power; Develops vertical jump; Strong progression toward pistol squats; Hits the quads and glutes hard; Improves balance and stability; Useful for athletic training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Calves

Description: Lie on your back, knees bent at 90 degrees. A partner holds your calves or you hook your heels under a bar. Actively pull your heels back (contracting hamstrings) throughout the sit-up. Squeeze your glutes simultaneously. Sit up by flexing your spine. The hamstring activation reduces hip flexor cheating. Lower under control while maintaining the heel pull. The active hamstring contraction is the key — it reciprocally inhibits the hip flexors. This makes the sit-up much harder on the abs. Aim for 8 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Reduces hip flexor involvement in sit-ups; Forces the abs to do more work; Named after Dr. Vladimir Janda; Builds true ab strength; Uses reciprocal inhibition principle; Advanced sit-up technique
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (increased); Obliques; Hamstrings (isometric, reciprocal inhibition); Gluteus maximus (isometric)

Description: Start in a deep lunge with one foot forward and the back knee near the floor. Set your front foot flat with knee tracking over the toe. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Drive through the front foot to jump straight up. Bring the back leg up under you in the air. Land softly back on the same front foot in a lunge. Sink back down into the deep lunge position. Complete reps on one side before switching legs.
Benefits: Builds explosive single-leg power; Trains balance and stability; Strong conditioning effect; No equipment needed; Useful for athletes; Improves jump strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Calves

Description: Clean two kettlebells to the front rack position. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Press the right kettlebell overhead to lockout while keeping the left in the rack. Lower the right KB to the rack. Press the left kettlebell overhead while the right rests in the rack. Continue alternating for the desired reps. Maintain an upright torso throughout. Do not lean away from the pressing side. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per arm.
Benefits: Builds shoulder endurance through alternating pattern; Develops anti-lateral flexion core strength; Exposes left-right pressing imbalances; Extended time under tension; Useful for conditioning; Foundational kettlebell pressing variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (anti-lateral flexion); Upper trapezius

Description: Lie on your back on the floor with a kettlebell in each hand. Position the kettlebells at your sides with elbows on the floor. Hold both kettlebells with palms facing each other (neutral grip). Brace your core and press your back to the floor. Press the right kettlebell up over your chest while the left stays at your side. Lower the right kettlebell back to the starting position. Press the left kettlebell up while the right stays at the side. Continue alternating sides for the full set.
Benefits: Shoulder-friendly chest work; Floor protects the shoulders; Strong anti-rotation core challenge; No bench required; Useful for home training; Time under tension on each side
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Lie on your back with arms at your sides, legs extended straight up toward the ceiling. Press your palms into the floor. Brace your core. Exhale and use your core to lift your hips off the floor, rolling your legs overhead toward the floor behind your head (rollover). Once your toes touch the floor (or as close as your flexibility allows), inhale. Exhale and lift your legs straight up toward the ceiling, balancing on your shoulders. Pause briefly with legs vertical and torso supported by your shoulders. Slowly roll back down one vertebra at a time, lowering your legs back to vertical. Repeat for 3 to 6 reps. Do not perform if you have neck or upper-back issues.
Benefits: Builds extreme core control; Stretches the hamstrings and entire posterior chain; Develops shoulder and upper-back strength; Advanced Pilates exercise; Decompresses the spine; Trains controlled spinal articulation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (rolling control); Hip flexors; Hamstrings (stretched); Erector spinae (stretched); Core stabilizers

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out at 45 degrees. Press a kettlebell overhead with your right arm in the bottoms-up position. Stabilize the kettlebell carefully with bell pointing up. Keep your eyes on the kettlebell throughout. Place your left hand on your inner thigh. Push your hips back to your right side as you bend forward and to the left. Slide your left hand down your inner thigh toward the floor. Reverse the motion to stand back up. Complete reps, switch sides.
Benefits: Extreme shoulder stability demand; Builds hip mobility and oblique strength; Develops total body coordination; Strong functional movement pattern; Useful for advanced lifters; Trains rotator cuff and shoulder control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Hamstrings; Adductors; Anterior deltoid; Rotator cuff

Description: Lie flat on your back. Arms extended overhead, legs extended. Simultaneously raise your torso and legs, reaching your hands toward your toes. Your body forms a V at the top. Touch or reach toward your toes. Lower everything back to flat under control. That is one rep. Move with control — do not use momentum. Aim for 10 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Works upper and lower abs simultaneously; Full range of motion core exercise; No equipment needed; Challenging and effective; Builds ab strength through complete range; Develops coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (full range); Hip flexors; Obliques (secondary)

Description: Lie on your back with legs extended together and arms at your sides. Brace your abs hard. Crunch your shoulders off the floor. At the same time, split your legs out wide to either side. Reach your hands toward the outside of your legs. Squeeze the abs at the top. Lower your shoulders back down as you bring the legs back together. Continue at a steady pace.
Benefits: Combines crunch with leg split; Strong full ab engagement; No equipment required; Builds adductor strength; Different stimulus than standard crunches; Useful for ab training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Adductors

Description: Place two kettlebells on the floor shoulder-width apart. Get into a high plank with each hand gripping a KB handle. Set your feet wider than hip-width for stability. Brace your core hard. Maintain a straight body line from heels to head. Row the right KB up to your right hip by driving your elbow back. Keep your hips perfectly still — do not rotate. Lower the right KB to the floor under control. Row the left KB. Continue alternating. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines back rowing with core anti-rotation; Builds shoulder stability under unilateral load; Time-efficient compound exercise; Develops grip strength; Useful for full-body conditioning; Engaging challenging variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Core (heavy anti-rotation); Anterior deltoid (plank hold); Trapezius; Forearms and grip

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a KB in each hand. Hinge at the hips until torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor. Back flat. Let both KBs hang with arms extended. Row the right KB up while keeping the left hanging. Lower the right, then row the left. Continue alternating in a smooth rhythm. Maintain the hinge position throughout. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Continuous back tension through alternating pattern; Extended time under tension; Builds back endurance; Core anti-rotation from unilateral pulling; Easy to set up; Engaging rowing variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Anchor a resistance band to the floor in front of you. Loop the band through the handle of a kettlebell. Stand with feet slightly wider than shoulder-width. Grip the kettlebell handle with both hands. Hinge at the hips and swing the kettlebell back between your legs. Drive your hips forward explosively to swing the kettlebell up. The band tension will increase as the kettlebell rises. Allow the kettlebell to swing back through your legs and repeat the swing.
Benefits: Forces harder hip drive at the top; Combines kettlebell load with band tension; Builds explosive hip power; Trains the posterior chain; Accommodating resistance through the swing; Useful for breaking through swing plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a KB in each hand at your sides (or in the front rack). Step your right foot back two to three feet behind you. Lower your right knee toward the floor by bending both knees. Descend until your right knee is just above the floor. Drive through your front (left) foot to return to standing. Alternate legs or complete all reps on one side. Keep your torso upright. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per leg.
Benefits: Easier on the knees than forward lunges; Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally; KB handles demand grip engagement; Easy to scale by adjusting weight; Exposes left-right imbalances; Useful at-home leg exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Exercise Name: Kettlebell Bent Arm Pullover with Knees Bent
Description: Lie on your back on a flat bench or the floor. Bend your knees and place feet flat on the surface. Hold a kettlebell with both hands by the handle above the chest. Bend the elbows so the forearms are roughly parallel. Brace the core and keep the lower back pressed down. Lower the kettlebell back over your head with bent elbows. Feel the stretch in the lats and chest at the bottom. Pull the kettlebell back over the chest by squeezing the lats and repeat.
Benefits: Hits the lats hard through the overhead stretch.; Builds chest size with the pullover motion.; Strengthens the long head of the triceps.; Improves shoulder mobility through full overhead range.; Bent knees protect the lower back.; Easy to load progressively.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Kettlebell Bent Over Alternate Twist Row
Description: Stand holding a kettlebell in each hand at the sides. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and slight knee bend. Let the kettlebells hang down with palms facing each other. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Row one kettlebell up to the hip while rotating the torso slightly. Squeeze the lat hard at the top. Lower with control while rotating the torso back to neutral. Row the other kettlebell while rotating to that side. Alternate sides.
Benefits: Combo back and core move; Trains rotational strength; Builds lat thickness; Strong unilateral row; Useful back-day move; Builds rotational core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Obliques; Biceps brachii

Description: Hold a kettlebell in each hand. Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees from horizontal. Let the kettlebells hang at arm’s length. Brace your core. Lock in your back angle. Row both kettlebells up by driving your elbows back along your sides. Pull the kettlebells to your lower ribs. Squeeze your shoulder blades together. Pause briefly at the top. Squeeze your back hard. Lower under control. Maintain your torso angle throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use straps for heavy loading if needed.
Benefits: Builds the back with a different stimulus than dumbbells; Thick KB handle builds grip strength; Trains the lats, mid-traps, and rear delts; Easier setup than barbell rows; Allows heavy loading at home; Carries over to all pulling strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip; Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Clean a KB to the front rack. Palm faces your body. Elbow down. Stand tall. Brace your core. Begin pressing upward. As the KB rises, rotate your wrist outward so your palm faces forward at lockout. Lock out overhead with arm fully extended, palm facing forward. Reverse the motion — rotate your palm back inward as you lower to the rack. Complete reps, then switch sides. The rotation should be smooth and continuous throughout the press. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Engages all three deltoid heads through rotation; Builds complete shoulder development; Unique pressing angle from KB handle position; Unilateral — exposes imbalances; Develops shoulder mobility under load; Named after Arnold Schwarzenegger
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Posterior deltoid (slight at bottom); Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Position a bench or box behind your standing position. Stand near a stable wall, post, or rack for hand support. Hold a kettlebell in your right hand and place your left hand on the support. Place the top of your left foot on the bench behind you. Stand tall with most of your weight on the front leg. Brace your core and lower into a split squat by bending the front knee. Use the support hand for light balance assistance as needed. Drive through the front foot to stand back to the starting position. Switch sides.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly Bulgarian split squat; Reduces balance demands; Allows focus on the strength pattern; Stepping stone to free-standing version; Builds single-leg strength; Useful for rehab or movement re-education
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Exercise Name: Kettlebell Bottom Up One Arm Bench Press
Description: Lie on a flat bench with a kettlebell beside you on the floor. Pick up the kettlebell with your right hand and balance it bottom-up with the bell pointing up. Position the kettlebell at chest level with the wrist locked. Brace your core hard against the asymmetric load. Press the kettlebell straight up while maintaining the bottom-up balance. Lock out at the top with the kettlebell still balanced upside down. Lower the kettlebell back to chest level with control. Maintain the bottom-up position throughout the entire set. Switch arms.
Benefits: Extreme stability and balance demand; Builds chest and tricep strength; Strong forearm and grip work; Develops shoulder stability; Useful for athletes who need stability; Functional carryover to overhead positions
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Forearm flexors; Rotator cuff

Exercise Name: Kettlebell Bottoms Up Clean From the Hang Position
Description: Stand over a kettlebell with feet shoulder-width apart. Hinge at the hips and grip the kettlebell handle with one hand. Clean the kettlebell up to shoulder height by driving through your hips. As the bell reaches shoulder height, catch it in the bottoms-up position — bottom of the bell pointing to the ceiling. Grip the handle extremely hard to keep the bell balanced upside down. Brace your core. Keep your wrist neutral and forearm vertical. Hold the bottoms-up position for 1 to 2 seconds, then lower under control. Use a much lighter kettlebell than standard cleans. Grip strength is the limiter.
Benefits: Builds extreme grip strength; Develops shoulder stability; Trains wrist stability and proprioception; Excellent for shoulder health; Unique and challenging; Carries over to all kettlebell work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms and grip (extreme); Rotator cuff (heavy stabilizer); Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer); Biceps brachii

Exercise Name: Kettlebell Bottoms Up to Knee Turkish Get Up
Description: Lie on the back with one arm extended overhead holding a kettlebell upside down. Bend the same side knee with the foot flat. Brace the core and lock the working shoulder. Roll up onto the opposite forearm then to the opposite hand. Press through the floor and lift the hips. Sweep the straight leg under and back to a kneeling position. Pause at the half kneel with the bell still inverted overhead. Reverse the steps to return to the start.
Benefits: Brutal shoulder stability drill.; Builds grip strength.; Trains the core for total body control.; Useful for athletic carryover.; Bottoms up grip is humbling.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Forearm flexors; Core; Trapezius

Description: Clean a KB to the right front rack. Stand with feet wider than hip-width. Turn your feet to the left (about 45 degrees). Begin bending your torso to the left. At the same time, extend your right arm upward. The KB stays roughly in place while your body lowers under it. Continue bending until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor with the KB locked out overhead. Look up at the KB throughout. Stand back up with the KB overhead by reversing the lateral bend. Use light weight until technique is solid. Aim for 3 to 5 reps per side.
Benefits: Old-time strongman skill; Builds extraordinary lateral core and shoulder strength; Develops overhead mobility under lateral bend; Tests total-body control and flexibility; Allows pressing very heavy weight overhead; Impressive demonstration of strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy); Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (heavy stabilizer); Hamstrings and hip flexors (lateral bend); Erector spinae

Description: Stand tall holding a kettlebell in your right hand at your side. Grip the handle. The bell will rest against the back of your wrist when curled up. Pin your right elbow against your side. Pull your shoulders back. Brace your core. Curl the kettlebell up toward your shoulder by bending only at the elbow. Keep your wrist neutral — do not let it bend backward. Continue until the kettlebell reaches your shoulder. Squeeze your bicep hard. Lower under control over two seconds. Switch arms or curl simultaneously with two kettlebells.
Benefits: Different feel than dumbbell curls; Challenges grip and forearm stabilizers; Builds the biceps; Useful when only kettlebells are available; Easy to scale by kettlebell weight; Engaging variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearms (heavy stabilizer)

Description: Sit on a bench with feet wide. Hold a KB in your right hand. Place the back of your right upper arm against your right inner thigh. Start with arm extended, KB hanging. Curl the KB up toward your shoulder by bending at the elbow. Squeeze your bicep at the top. Hold briefly. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch arms. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps.
Benefits: Strict bicep isolation; Thigh brace eliminates cheating; KB handle provides unique grip challenge; Builds the bicep peak; Easy to load progressively; Simple setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially short head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Clean the kettlebell to the front-rack position using hip drive. Stand tall with the bell at your shoulder. Brace your core. Dip by bending only at the knees (4 to 6 inches). Keep torso vertical. Reverse the dip explosively. As legs extend, drive the bell overhead. Drop slightly under the bell and catch it locked out overhead. Stand fully tall to complete the jerk. Lower the bell back to the rack, then swing it between your legs for the next clean. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Builds maximum overhead power with leg drive; Allows heavier loading than the clean and press; Develops full-body coordination and timing; Standard kettlebell sport competition event; Excellent conditioning exercise; Trains the entire body in one movement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Hamstrings; Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Trapezius; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, kettlebell on the floor between your feet. Squat down and grip the kettlebell with your right hand. Drive through your feet and explode upward, swinging the kettlebell up and rotating your wrist around to land it in the front rack position (resting on your forearm at shoulder height). Stand tall in the front rack. Brace your core hard. Press the kettlebell straight up overhead by extending at the elbow. Lock out at the top with arm fully extended above your shoulder. Lower the kettlebell back to the front rack, then back to the floor or hold for the next rep. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Builds full-body power and strength; Combines clean and press in one movement; Excellent metabolic conditioning; Develops shoulder stability under load; Time-efficient compound exercise; Foundational kettlebell exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Trapezius; Core (heavy stabilizer); Quadriceps

Description: Place a kettlebell on the floor between your feet, with the handle aligned with your mid-foot. Stand with feet just wider than shoulder-width and toes pointed slightly outward. Push your hips back, bend your knees slightly, and reach down to grip the kettlebell handle with both hands using an overhand grip. Lift your chest, pull your shoulders back and down, and brace your core. Your back should be flat with a slight natural arch. Take a deep breath, then drive your feet through the floor and stand up tall, lifting the kettlebell straight up between your legs. Lock out at the top by squeezing your glutes — your body should form a straight standing line. Reverse the movement by hinging at the hips first, then bending the knees once the kettlebell passes them. Set the kettlebell back on the floor between your feet under control. Reset and repeat.
Benefits: Teaches the hip-hinge pattern with light, forgiving loading; Builds the glutes, hamstrings, and lower back without the spinal load of a barbell; Foundational drill before learning the kettlebell swing; Trains grip strength through the loaded hold; Highly portable — needs only one kettlebell and a small space; Excellent rehabilitation and warm-up exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Trapezius (stabilizer); Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer); Quadriceps (secondary)

Description: Stand tall holding a light kettlebell at your chest with both hands (goblet position). Squat down deeply. Tuck your tailbone and roll backward onto your upper back. Briefly touch your back to the floor with the kettlebell still at your chest. Use momentum to roll forward, planting your feet flat on the floor in a deep squat position. Maintain control of the kettlebell at your chest throughout. Drive through your feet to stand up explosively from the deep squat. Lock out at the top, then immediately roll backward into the next rep. Use light weight to start. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds full-body coordination; Develops core strength and rolling agility; Excellent metabolic conditioning; Improves squat depth and mobility; No equipment needed besides a kettlebell; Engaging variation on standard squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (heavy involvement); Hip flexors; Anterior deltoid (kettlebell hold)

Description: Place two kettlebells on the floor about shoulder-width apart with horns up. Get into a high plank position gripping the horns of the kettlebells. Set your feet hip-width apart for stability. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Lower your chest between the kettlebells, going below the hand level. Continue lowering until you feel a strong stretch in your chest. Press back up to the high plank position by extending your arms. Squeeze your chest at the top.
Benefits: Extended range maximizes chest stretch; Builds chest size and strength; Strong tricep and shoulder engagement; Develops mobility through the chest; Useful for breaking through push up plateaus; No bench required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Set a sturdy box behind you at a height that allows your thighs to reach parallel when you sit down (typically 12 to 18 inches). Stand in front of the box with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly. Hold a kettlebell at your chest with both hands underneath the bell (goblet position). Brace your core. Lift your chest. Sit your hips back and down toward the box. Keep your chest tall throughout. Lightly touch your butt to the box without fully sitting or rocking back. Drive through your full feet to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
