Description: Place the kettlebell on the floor about a foot in front of your toes. Stand with feet just outside shoulder-width apart. Hinge at the hips and reach for the bell, keeping your back flat and your knees softly bent. Tilt the bell toward you so the handle is angled. “Hike” the bell back between your legs like a football snap, with your forearms making contact high on your inner thighs. Your hips should be loaded and your back flat. Snap your hips forward explosively, squeezing your glutes hard. The arms stay relaxed; the bell floats up to about chest height as a result of hip drive, not arm lifting. At the top, your body forms a straight standing plank: glutes squeezed, quads tight, core braced. Do not lean back. Let the bell fall back down on the same arc, catching it with another hip hinge as it passes between your legs. Stand tall and snap again for the next rep. Finish a set by parking the bell back on the floor with a final hinge, not by catching it with your arms.
Benefits: Builds explosive hip-extension power in the glutes and hamstrings; Improves cardiovascular conditioning with minimal equipment and space; Reinforces a strong hip-hinge pattern that protects the lower back in other lifts; Develops grip strength and shoulder stability; Highly time-efficient: a few minutes of hard swings deliver real conditioning work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae (lower back); Core (rectus abdominis and obliques); Forearms and grip; Lats (stabilizers)

Exercise Name: Kettlebell Turkish Get Up to Hand
Description: Lie on your back with a kettlebell pressed up over the chest with one arm. Bend the same side knee and plant the foot flat on the floor. Extend the opposite arm and leg out at about 45 degrees. Brace the core and keep the kettlebell pressed straight up. Roll up onto the off side elbow while keeping the bell vertical. Press up further onto the off side hand with the arm extended. Pause briefly in the up to hand position with the kettlebell overhead. Reverse the motion to lower back to the floor and complete all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds shoulder stability through the overhead carry.; Improves total body coordination.; Strengthens the core and obliques through the rolling motion.; Trains hip mobility through the leg drive.; Develops the deep stabilizers around the shoulder.; Excellent warm up or shoulder health drill.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Obliques; Triceps brachii; Core; Hip flexors

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart holding a KB in each hand. Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor. Let the KBs hang with arms extended. Back flat. Row both KBs toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control. Maintain a flat back throughout. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Bilateral back loading with kettlebells; KB handles demand extra grip engagement; Builds lats, mid-traps, and rhomboids; Easy to set up; Useful at-home back exercise; Develops hinge posture strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip; Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Clean two kettlebells to the front-rack position (or hold one in a goblet grip). Feet shoulder-width apart. Sit into a deep squat — hip crease below knees. Keep torso upright and elbows up. Drive explosively through your feet to stand. Use the upward momentum to press the kettlebells overhead to lockout. Lower the kettlebells back to the front-rack and immediately drop into the next squat. Keep the movement continuous and rhythmic. Each rep flows into the next. Brace your core throughout. Use moderate weight for high reps. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Full-body strength and conditioning in one movement; Builds quads, glutes, and shoulders together; Brutal cardiovascular conditioning effect; Time-efficient compound exercise; Carries over to all pressing and squatting strength; Highly portable — needs only kettlebells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Place two kettlebells between your feet. Hinge at the hips and grip both kettlebells. Swing both bells back between your legs. Drive your hips forward explosively. As the bells rise, rotate your wrists and catch both bells in the front rack. Absorb the catch with a slight dip. Stand tall with both bells in the rack. Lower and repeat. Use moderate weight until technique is solid.
Benefits: Builds bilateral hip drive and clean mechanics; Entry point for double KB pressing and jerking; Develops explosive power; Trains symmetrical technique; Excellent conditioning exercise; Full-body movement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Forearms and grip; Anterior deltoid (catch); Core (stabilizer); Trapezius

Description: Pick up a heavy kettlebell with one hand. Stand tall with the bell at your side. Brace your core hard against the load pulling you sideways. Keep your shoulders level and your torso vertical. Walk forward with normal stride length. Maintain a tight grip on the kettlebell handle. Walk for the desired distance. Switch hands and complete reps on the other side.
Benefits: Builds grip strength; Trains core anti-lateral flexion; Builds total-body strength; Carries over to lifts and sports; Useful for athletes; Strong functional move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms; Obliques; Traps; Core

Description: Clean two kettlebells to the front rack — one in each hand at shoulder height. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Press both kettlebells straight overhead simultaneously by extending your elbows. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Lower both kettlebells back to the front rack under control. No leg dip or leg drive — pure pressing strength. Use moderate weight. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set. Maintain upright torso throughout.
Benefits: Builds bilateral overhead pressing strength; Strict form with no leg drive; Develops core stability under bilateral load; Trains shoulder mobility; Useful for kettlebell sport training; Builds shoulder size and strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Core (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Description: Stand in a wide sumo stance with feet 1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width apart, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Hold a kettlebell by the handle with both hands. Let it hang between your legs at arm’s length. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Push your knees out over your toes. Sit straight down between your heels by bending at the knees and hips. Descend until the kettlebell nearly touches the floor or until you reach full depth. Drive through your full feet to stand back up. Push knees out. Squeeze glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a heavier kettlebell over time to progressively overload.
Benefits: Targets the glutes and adductors with wide-stance loading; Easy to set up — needs only one kettlebell; Allows deep squatting without the back-loaded barbell position; Builds inner thigh and glute strength; Forces upright torso position; Useful at home or in the gym
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors; Quadriceps; Hamstrings (secondary); Core (stabilizer); Forearms and grip

Description: Hold a kettlebell in front of you at hip height with both hands gripping the handle. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Pull the kettlebell straight up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out. Continue pulling until the kettlebell reaches chest height. Do not pull higher. Keep the kettlebell close to your body throughout. Squeeze your traps and lateral delts at the top. Lower the kettlebell slowly back to the start under control. Use moderate weight. Stop immediately if you feel shoulder discomfort.
Benefits: Builds the traps and lateral delts; Easy to set up at home; Two-hand grip is shoulder-friendly; Develops grip strength; Easy to load progressively; Useful when no barbell is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (upper); Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (secondary); Forearms (grip)

Description: Press a KB overhead with your right arm. Lock out. Feet slightly wider than hip-width, left foot turned out 45 degrees. Push your right hip out to the right side. Slowly hinge at the hips to the left, sliding your left hand down your left leg toward the floor. Keep the KB locked out overhead. Look up at the KB throughout. Continue until your left hand touches the floor (or as low as flexibility allows). Reverse the motion by driving your right hip forward to stand back up. Complete reps, then switch sides. Use light weight. Aim for 5 to 8 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds overhead stability under lateral hinge; Develops lateral hip mobility; Strengthens the obliques and core; Improves hamstring flexibility; Unique multi-planar movement; Excellent for shoulder health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Anterior deltoid (overhead hold); Gluteus medius; Hamstrings (stretched); Core (stabilizer); Erector spinae

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out. Place a kettlebell on the floor in front of each foot, inside your stance. Bend at the hips and knees to grip a kettlebell in each hand. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Drive your knees out and push the floor away to stand. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Lower the kettlebells back to the floor with control.
Benefits: Sumo stance emphasizes glutes and adductors; No barbell required; Builds posterior chain strength; Useful for home training; Strong adductor stretch at the bottom; Easy to scale by changing kettlebell weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hamstrings; Quadriceps; Erector spinae

Description: Set up on hands and knees in a quadruped position. Place the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips. Keep one knee bent at ninety degrees. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Kick the bent leg up toward the ceiling. Drive the heel up so the sole faces the ceiling. Squeeze the glute hard at the top. Lower with control. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the glutes; Strong glute isolator; Trains the hamstrings; Useful for glute shape; No equipment needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Kick up into a wall-supported handstand. Hands about shoulder-width apart. Lower your head toward the floor by bending at the elbows. At the bottom, tuck your knees slightly toward your chest. Explosively extend your hips and legs upward while pressing with your arms. The hip kip assists the pressing phase. Lock out at the top. This allows more reps than strict HSPUs. Master strict HSPUs first for shoulder safety.
Benefits: Higher rep output than strict HSPUs; Develops overhead pressing endurance; CrossFit competition exercise; Builds explosive pressing power; Develops kipping mechanics; Conditioning benefit from high rep sets
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Hip flexors (kip); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Lower your chest to the floor in a controlled push-up. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Lift the right hand and kick the right leg under your body to the left side. Pivot on your left foot and right hand briefly off the floor. Return to the push-up position. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Builds full-body coordination; Trains core control and stability; Combines strength and conditioning; No equipment required; Useful for athletic training; Strong calorie burner
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Core; Front deltoid; Obliques

Description: Sit on a bench. Hold a light KB in your right hand. Rest your right forearm on your right thigh, wrist hanging off the knee. Let the KB hang with your wrist extended (hand hanging down). Curl the KB up by flexing your wrist. Squeeze your forearm flexors at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch. Use light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds forearm flexor strength; KB handle provides a unique grip challenge; Easy to load progressively; Useful for grip-intensive activities; Simple setup; Builds wrist health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors (flexor carpi radialis, flexor carpi ulnaris); Flexor digitorum; Palmaris longus

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Arms relaxed at your sides or extended forward for balance. Stand on your left leg with a slight knee bend. Drive your right knee up toward your chest as high as comfortable. Use your hands to gently pull the knee closer if you can reach. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds at the top. Lower your right foot back to the floor. Repeat with the left knee. Continue alternating for 10 to 15 reps per side as a warm-up.
Benefits: Activates the hip flexors; Builds standing balance; Excellent pre-workout warm-up; Improves hip mobility; No equipment needed; Quick and accessible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris); Quadriceps; Core (stabilizer); Gluteus medius (standing leg, balance)

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar. Initiate a kipping swing (arch-to-hollow). At the peak of the forward swing, pull explosively while driving your hips toward the bar. Use the kip momentum to get your chest above the bar. Transition over the bar into a dip position. Press to lockout. Swing back to initiate the next rep. Master strict muscle-ups or aggressive kipping pull-ups first. Aim for 3 to 10 reps in competition settings.
Benefits: Higher rep output than strict muscle-ups; CrossFit competition standard; Develops explosive pulling power; Builds kipping mechanics; Conditioning benefit from high rep sets; Develops rhythm and timing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Pectoralis major (transition); Triceps brachii (dip); Hip flexors (kip); Core; Forearms; Muscle-Up (strict); Pull-Up; Kipping Handstand Push-Up; Ring Muscle-Up; Chest-to-Bar Pull-Up; Weighted Muscle-up; Band Assisted Muscle Up

Description: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat. Arms at your sides or resting on your thighs. Crunch up, sliding your hands along your thighs toward your knees. Continue until your fingers touch or pass your kneecaps. Squeeze your abs at the top. Lower under control. The hand position guides consistent crunch height. Slightly easier than hands-behind-head crunches. Aim for 15 to 25 reps.
Benefits: Guided crunch height through hand position; Slightly easier than hands-behind-head crunches; Beginner-friendly; No equipment needed; Builds ab contraction awareness; Simple and accessible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary)

Description: Lie on your side with the legs straight. Stack the legs and bend the knees slightly. Place the hand behind the head with elbow pointed up. Set the bottom arm out for support. Brace your core hard. Tuck the knees up while crunching the elbow down to meet them. Squeeze the obliques hard at the top. Lower back to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Side crunch isolation; No equipment needed; Builds the obliques hard; Useful core finisher; Easy to do anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Hip flexors

Description: Set up on hands and knees in a quadruped position. Place the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips. Keep the back flat and head neutral. Brace your core and inhale to expand the belly. Exhale and pull the navel up toward the spine. Hold the draw in position briefly. Release and let the belly expand naturally. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the deep core; Trains the transverse abdominis; Strong core activation; Useful for posture; Builds core control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core; Rectus abdominis; Obliques

Description: Set a sturdy bar at chest height. Kneel on the floor under the bar. Reach up and grip the bar with an underhand chin up grip. Set the body in a straight line from knees to head. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the chest up toward the bar using the legs to assist. Slide the knees along the floor as you pull up. Lower back down with control to the start.
Benefits: Beginner friendly chin up; Builds the lats; Trains the biceps; Useful chin up progression; No high bar needed; Builds back size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids

Description: Kneel on a pad with knees roughly hip-width apart. Tops of feet flat on the floor behind you. Sit your hips back toward your heels (hip-flexed position). Keep your torso upright. Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes. Drive your hips forward by extending at the hips. Squeeze your glutes hard. Continue until your hips are fully extended and your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders (tall kneeling position). Squeeze glutes for one to two seconds at the top. Sit your hips back toward your heels under control. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Direct glute activation without leg or back loading; Useful for rehabilitation and beginner glute training; Teaches hip extension separate from knee extension; Easy to perform anywhere with no equipment; Excellent warm-up before squats and deadlifts; Can be progressed with bands or weights
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Kneel on a pad in front of a sturdy bench. Place the hands on the edge of the bench at shoulder width. Walk the knees back so the body forms a slight diagonal. Set the upper arms at an angle. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the body partway by bending the elbows. Stop at the halfway point with the elbows at 90 degrees. Press back up to extension by extending the elbows.
Benefits: Beginner friendly tricep move; No equipment beyond a bench; Trains the triceps; Strong starter move; Useful for travel; Builds the chest
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Get on hands and knees with hands directly below shoulders and knees below hips. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Lift your right foot off the floor and bring the knee toward your chest. Press your right leg back and up by extending the hip and knee. Continue pressing until your leg is straight and slightly above hip level. Squeeze your glute hard at the top. Bring your knee back to your chest with control. Complete reps on one side, then switch legs.
Benefits: Direct glute isolation; Quadruped position eliminates lower back stress; No equipment required; Builds glute size and strength; Useful for rehab or beginners; Strong peak contraction
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Core

Description: Get into a kneeling push-up position with knees on the floor. Place your hands under your shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to knees. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Lower your hips to the floor and arch your upper back. Lift your chest up off the floor in a cobra position. Lower the chest back down and return to the push-up start.
Benefits: Combines push-up with back extension; Trains chest and spine; Beginner-friendly hybrid move; Improves spinal mobility; No equipment required; Useful warm-up combination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Spinal erectors; Triceps brachii

Description: Begin in a high plank position from the knees. Set the hands under the shoulders and the body in a straight line. Brace your core and keep the hips level. Lift one hand off the floor. Tap the opposite shoulder with the hand. Place the hand back on the floor. Repeat with the other hand to tap the opposite shoulder. Continue alternating shoulder taps.
Benefits: Beginner friendly plank move; Trains anti-rotation core; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Useful core builder; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Anterior deltoid

Description: Begin on hands and knees with hands wider than shoulders. Push the hips up high into a kneeling pike position. Bend the elbows and dive the chest forward and down. Sweep the chest close to the floor as you flow forward. Continue forward as the chest rises toward an upward dog. Lock out the arms with the chest up and hips low. Press back through the flow to the start. Continue the flowing push up motion.
Benefits: Beginner friendly hindu push up; Trains shoulder mobility; Builds the chest; Useful for beginners; Strong yoga inspired move; Builds the triceps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Get into a quadruped position on hands and knees. Position your hands shoulder-width apart and knees under hips. Lift your right knee up and back behind you, knee bent at 90 degrees. Press the heel up toward the ceiling. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Lower the leg slightly without touching the floor. Pulse the leg up and down in short controlled motions. Maintain constant glute tension. Switch sides after the set.
Benefits: Maximum glute time under tension; Burnout finishing exercise; Builds glute size; No equipment required; Strong mind-muscle connection; Useful for glute specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings

Description: Get into a kneeling push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to knees. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Rotate your body to one side, lifting one arm up to the ceiling. Form a side plank position briefly. Rotate back to the push-up start position. Complete another push-up and rotate to the other side.
Benefits: Combines chest and core rotation; Beginner-friendly variation; Builds the obliques; No equipment required; Strong core work; Useful for full-body training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Obliques; Front deltoid; Core

Description: Get into a kneeling push-up position with hands under shoulders. Keep your arms straight throughout the entire movement. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to knees. Allow your shoulder blades to squeeze together (retract). Your chest will dip slightly toward the floor. Push through your hands to spread the shoulder blades apart (protract). Round your upper back at the top of each rep. Move only the shoulder blades, not the elbows.
Benefits: Strengthens the serratus anterior; Improves scapular control; Beginner-friendly version; Useful for shoulder health; Builds pressing stability; No equipment required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Serratus anterior; Front deltoid; Pectoralis major

Description: Get into a high plank on your knees. Hands under shoulders. Lift your right hand and tap your left shoulder. Return your right hand to the floor. Lift your left hand and tap your right shoulder. Continue alternating. Minimize hip rocking. The kneeling position makes this easier than full plank taps. Brace your core throughout. Aim for 10 to 15 taps per side.
Benefits: Beginner regression for shoulder taps; Builds anti-rotation core strength; Kneeling position reduces difficulty; No equipment needed; Develops body control; Progresses to full plank shoulder taps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core (anti-rotation); Anterior deltoid; Obliques

Description: Kneel on the floor on a soft surface (mat or carpet) with your feet behind you. Place your hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers pointing forward. Lean forward into a high-plank position with your knees down. Your body should form a straight line from your knees to your head. Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulders down and back. Keep your hips level — do not let them sag or pike up. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending at the elbows. Keep your elbows tucked at roughly 45 degrees from your torso, not flared out wide. Lower until your chest is just above the floor. Press back up by extending at the elbows, driving your hands into the floor. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Maintain the straight body line throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Progress to incline push-ups, then full push-ups as you get stronger.
Benefits: Effective regression for building toward a full push-up; Builds the chest, triceps, and shoulders with reduced load; Allows beginners to learn proper push-up form without failing reps; Trains core stability through the plank position; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Higher rep range possible than full push-ups for volume work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set up on hands and knees with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Brace the core and keep the back flat. Lift one leg out to the side with the knee bent. Kick the foot out laterally to extend the leg. Hold briefly at the extended kick position. Bend the knee back to the lifted side position. Lower the knee back to the start. Complete all reps on one side then switch.
Benefits: Targets the gluteus medius for hip stability.; Strengthens the side glutes and hip abductors.; Improves hip mobility and control.; No equipment needed.; Excellent prehab for runners and athletes.; Adds variety to standard fire hydrant moves.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Hip flexors; Core

Description: Get into a push-up position on closed fists. Wrists straight and neutral. Place fists shoulder-width apart. Knuckles on the floor. Perform push-ups from this fist position. Lower your chest between your fists. Press back up. The neutral wrist position is often more comfortable. Use a mat or folded towel under your fists for comfort. Maintain straight body line. Aim for 10 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Neutral wrist position reduces wrist pain; Conditions the knuckles for martial arts; Slightly deeper range from fist height; No equipment needed; Useful for people with wrist flexibility issues; Builds forearm strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Forearms (wrist stabilization); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie face down on a mat. Prop yourself up on your forearms with elbows directly under shoulders. Bend your knees and lift your hips so you support your weight on your forearms and knees. Form a straight line from your knees to your shoulders. Tuck your hips slightly. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Keep your head in line with your spine. Hold the position for the desired duration — start with 20 to 30 seconds and progress over time. Breathe normally throughout the hold. Progress to a full front plank when you can hold a kneeling plank for 60+ seconds with good form.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly plank progression; Builds core endurance with reduced difficulty; Reduces lower-back strain compared to full plank; Useful for rehabilitation and post-injury; No equipment needed; Easy progression toward full front plank
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Erector spinae (isometric); Anterior deltoid (light)

Description: Begin in a high plank position from the knees. Set the hands under the shoulders and the body in a straight line. Brace your core hard. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Press back up to lockout. At the top lift one hand and tap the opposite shoulder. Place the hand back down. Repeat with the other hand on the next rep.
Benefits: Beginner friendly chest move; Trains anti-rotation core; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Useful chest builder; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid

Description: Get into a kneeling push-up position. Place one hand under your shoulder. Place the other hand slightly forward or to the side. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line from head to knees. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. The hand that is forward will bear more load. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Switch hand positions partway through and complete reps on each side.
Benefits: Builds unilateral chest strength; Beginner archer push-up progression; No equipment required; Helps fix chest imbalances; Builds shoulder stabilizers; Useful push-up variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Description: Kneel on a padded surface and have a partner hold your ankles (or use a fixed anchor). Lift one leg off the ground behind you. Brace your core and keep your hips and shoulders aligned. Use the working hamstring to slowly lower your body forward toward the floor. Maintain a straight line from knees to head. Catch yourself with your hands when your strength fails. Push back up using your hands and the working hamstring. Complete reps on one side before switching legs.
Benefits: Brutal eccentric hamstring work; Builds single-leg strength; Reduces hamstring injury risk; Useful for sprinters; Strong unilateral builder; Improves knee flexion strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves

Description: Set up a landmine. Grip the end of the bar with both hands at chest level. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Extend your arms. Lift the bar overhead and to one side of your body. Sweep the bar in an arc over your head to the other side of your body. Use your hips and core to power the rotation — not just your arms. Continue alternating sides in a sweeping rhythm. Maintain straight arms (slight elbow bend) throughout the arc. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 sweeps per side.
Benefits: Builds explosive rotational core power; Develops shoulder mobility under load; Trains hip-to-shoulder force transfer; Engaging full-body exercise; Useful for rotational athletes; Builds anti-extension and rotational strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy); Anterior and lateral deltoid; Core (heavy); Hip rotators; Gluteus maximus; Forearms and grip

Description: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment, loaded with weight. Stand facing the loaded end with feet wider than shoulder-width. Pick up the free end with both hands and extend your arms forward. Position the bar in front of your body at chest height. Brace your core and pivot from the hips and feet. Swing the bar down and across to your right hip in a 180-degree arc. Swing the bar back up and over to your left hip in the opposite arc. Continue alternating sides at a controlled pace.
Benefits: Builds rotational core power; Strong oblique engagement; Develops shoulder stability; Time-efficient compound movement; Athletic carryover; Useful for core specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Landmine Floor One Arm Chest Fly
Description: Lie on the floor next to a landmine setup. Grab the end of the landmine bar with one hand. Position the working arm out to the side with a slight elbow bend. Brace the core and press the back flat to the floor. Sweep the bar end across the body in an arc. Stop when the working hand reaches the centerline of the chest. Squeeze the pec hard at the top. Lower with control to the start and repeat for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates one side of the chest.; Floor stops the range to protect the shoulder.; Trains anti-rotation core stability.; Useful chest accessory.; Builds the pectorals.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Lift your legs straight in front of you to form an L-shape with your body. Hold them there throughout. Brace your core hard. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down. Maintain the L-position the entire time. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats at the top. Lower under control to a full hang, maintaining the L-position. If you cannot hold a full L-sit, start with a tuck L-pull-up (knees bent). Repeat for low reps (3 to 8 per set). Quality matters more than volume.
Benefits: Builds elite core, lat, and hip-flexor strength simultaneously; Foundational gymnastics strength skill; Trains the abs isometrically under extreme demand; Builds pulling strength with an added anti-extension challenge; Excellent test of relative strength; Highly portable — needs only a pull-up bar
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rectus abdominis (isometric L-hold); Hip flexors (isometric L-hold); Biceps brachii; Trapezius and rhomboids; Forearms and grip; Quadriceps (keeping legs straight)

Description: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front of you. Place your hands flat on the floor directly beside your hips, fingers pointing forward. Press down through your palms and straighten your arms to lift your body off the floor. Your butt and legs should both clear the floor. Keep your legs extended straight in front of you, parallel to the floor, forming an “L” shape with your torso. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your quads to keep your legs straight. Point your toes forward. Pull your shoulders down and back. Avoid shrugging. Hold for the desired duration — even a few seconds is an accomplishment. Build up to 15 to 30 seconds. If the full version is too difficult, start with tucked knees (tuck L-sit) or lift one leg at a time. Using parallettes or raised surfaces makes this easier by giving more hand clearance.
Benefits: Builds elite core, hip-flexor, and tricep strength; Foundational gymnastics skill; Trains the abs isometrically through a long lever arm; Develops shoulder depression and scapular control; No equipment needed (or use parallettes for easier version); Excellent test of relative strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris); Triceps brachii (pressing into floor); Quadriceps (keeping legs straight); Serratus anterior and shoulder depressors; Forearms and wrists

Description: Sit on the floor with legs extended straight in front. Place your hands flat on the floor next to your hips. Press your hands into the floor and lift your butt and legs off the ground simultaneously. Keep your legs straight and parallel to the floor — body forms an “L” shape. Press through your shoulders. Lock out your arms. Keep your shoulders pulled down away from your ears. Engage your quads to keep your legs straight and pointed. Hold for 5 to 30 seconds. Breathe steadily. Lower with control. If full L-sit is too hard, regress: tucked L-sit (knees bent), single-leg L-sit, or floor-supported L-sit.
Benefits: Builds elite anterior core strength; Develops hip flexor and quad strength; Strengthens triceps and shoulders isometrically; Foundational gymnastics skill; Progresses toward V-sit and advanced calisthenics; No equipment needed (or use parallettes)
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris); Quadriceps; Triceps brachii (heavy isometric); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Begin in a high plank position from the knees. Set the hands wider than shoulder width. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line from knees to head. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Stop just before the chest touches the floor. Press back up to lockout. Squeeze the chest hard at the top. Lock out at the top before the next rep.
Benefits: Beginner friendly wide chest move; Trains the outer chest; No equipment needed; Builds the chest; Useful chest builder; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand in front of a bar at hip height, facing away from it. Grip the bar behind you with both hands. Arms behind your body. Lift your feet off the floor. Support yourself on the bar behind you. Lower your body by bending at the elbows — the bar stays behind you. Descend until you feel a deep stretch in your chest and shoulders. Press back up to lockout. This requires excellent shoulder extension mobility. Start with very small range and progress gradually. Aim for 5 to 8 reps.
Benefits: Extreme chest and shoulder stretch; Advanced calisthenics exercise; Builds shoulder extension strength and mobility; Unique dip angle targets the chest differently; Develops body control; Impressive calisthenics skill
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (deep stretch); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid (extreme extension); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment. Load the free end with weight plates. Stand facing the landmine end. Hold the loaded end of the bar at your chest with both hands cupped underneath. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly turned out. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Stand tall. Sit your hips straight down with a perfectly upright torso. Descend until your hip crease drops below your knees. Drive straight up through your feet. Squeeze your glutes at the top. The bar weight pulls you forward and down — the landmine angle keeps you upright.
Benefits: Eliminates need for perfect front rack mobility; Forces upright torso position; Builds quad-dominant squatting; Joint-friendly alternative to barbell front squats; Easy to scale by adjusting weight; Works at home with a landmine attachment
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy emphasis); Gluteus maximus; Core (heavy bracing); Anterior deltoid (bar support); Upper trapezius; Erector spinae

Description: Set a barbell in a landmine attachment. Load the free end if needed. Stand facing away from the landmine. Hold the free end at your chest or on one shoulder. Feet shoulder-width apart, slightly forward of the bar for balance. Brace your core. Squat down by bending at the knees and hips. Descend until thighs are parallel or deeper. Keep torso upright. Drive through your full foot to stand back up. Squeeze quads at the top. The angled resistance shifts emphasis to the quads and reduces back strain. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Quad-dominant squat without a hack squat machine; Angled resistance reduces lower-back involvement; Forces upright torso position; Easy to set up with a landmine and barbell; Useful when no leg machines are available; Builds quad size effectively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy emphasis); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (secondary); Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Landmine Kneeling One Arm Shoulder Press
Description: Anchor a barbell in a landmine attachment. Kneel in a half kneeling position with one knee down. Grip the loaded end with the same side hand. Bring the bar up to the shoulder. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Press the bar up and across the body. Squeeze the shoulder hard at full extension. Lower with control. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the shoulders; Strict press form; Trains core stability; Strong landmine variation; Useful for shoulder size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core

Description: Set up a landmine. Kneel on the floor facing the free end of the barbell. Grip the end of the barbell between both palms at chest height, squeezing inward. Kneel tall with core braced. Press the barbell end forward and slightly up by extending your arms. Maintain the inward squeeze throughout the press — this activates the inner pec. Lock out at full extension. Squeeze your chest and triceps. Slowly pull the barbell back to your chest. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Targets the inner chest fibers; Squeeze component activates pec adduction; Kneeling position removes leg drive; Unique landmine loading pattern; Builds chest definition; Easy to set up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (inner fibers); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a barbell in a landmine. Stand sideways to the landmine. Grip the free end of the bar with the far hand (the hand away from the landmine). Start with the bar in front of your body at hip level. Set a slight bend in your elbow and lock it in. Lift the bar out to your side in a wide arc. Lead with your elbow. Continue until your arm is roughly parallel to the floor. Pause briefly at the top. Lower under control. Complete all reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Unique resistance curve — tension increases at the top; Different stimulus than dumbbell or cable raises; Builds the lateral deltoid effectively; Easy to set up with a landmine; Useful variation for breaking through side-delt plateaus; Trains core stability asymmetrically
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid (secondary); Supraspinatus (initial range); Core (anti-lateral-flexion)

Description: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment. Load the free end with weight plates. Kneel on both knees facing the loaded end. Pick up the free end and bring it to your chest with both hands. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Sit your hips back slightly while keeping your torso upright. Drive your hips forward and press the bar up and away from your chest. Lower the bar back to chest level under control.
Benefits: Combines hip drive with overhead press; Tall kneeling base limits leg drive; Strong core and glute engagement; Builds shoulder power; Different stimulus than standing thrusters; Useful for athletic conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Gluteus maximus; Core

Description: Set up a landmine. Hold the free end of the barbell at chest height with one or both hands. Stand with feet staggered, facing the landmine. Press the barbell end forward and upward along its natural arc. Lock out at the top. Lower under control back to chest height. The angled path is easier on the shoulders than vertical pressing. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps. Single-arm pressing adds core anti-rotation demand.
Benefits: Shoulder-friendly pressing arc; Natural bar path reduces shoulder impingement risk; Versatile — standing, kneeling, single-arm, double; Builds pressing strength; Easy to set up; Useful for shoulder rehab
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (upper); Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer); Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Landmine One Leg Stiff Leg Deadlift
Description: Anchor a barbell in a landmine attachment. Stand on one leg facing the loaded end. Grip the loaded end with the opposite hand. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Hinge at the hip and lift the back leg behind you. Lower the bar toward the floor as the back leg rises. Keep the back flat and the hips square. Stand back up. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the posterior chain; Trains balance; Loads single leg hinge; Strong landmine variation; Useful functional move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi

Exercise Name: Landmine One Arm Bent Over Bench Row
Description: Anchor a barbell in a landmine and load the working end with weight. Stand to the side of the bar and place one hand on a flat bench. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and the bench arm extended. Grip the end of the bar with the free hand using a neutral grip. Brace the core and keep the spine neutral. Pull the bar up to your hip by driving the elbow back. Squeeze the lat hard at the top of the row. Lower the bar slowly back to full extension and repeat all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds unilateral back strength with the landmine arc.; Bench support reduces lower back load.; Hits the lats and rhomboids hard.; Constant load through the natural arc of the bar.; Develops grip and biceps strength.; Joint friendly for athletes with back issues.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Landmine One Arm Bent Over Row
Description: Anchor a barbell in a landmine and load the working end with weight. Stand straddling the bar with feet shoulder width apart. Grip the end of the bar with one hand using a neutral grip. Hinge at the hips into a strong bent over position with a flat back. Place the free hand on your knee or hip for support. Brace the core and pull the bar up toward your hip. Drive the elbow back and squeeze the lat at the top. Lower the bar slowly back to full extension and repeat all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds back thickness through the landmine arc.; Hits the lats, rhomboids, and rear deltoids.; Trains anti rotation as the body resists the bar pull.; Easy to scale with bumper plates of any size.; Develops grip and biceps strength.; Carryover to bent over barbell rows and deadlifts.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment or wedged in a corner. Load the free end with weight plates. Pick up the free end and bring it to chest level with both hands. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Step back with your right leg into a reverse lunge. Lower until your back knee almost touches the floor. Push through the front foot to drive back to standing. Alternate legs.
Benefits: Loaded reverse lunge with stable bar path; Easier on wrists than barbell front rack; Builds glute and quad strength; Strong core engagement; Develops single leg stability; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Set up a landmine. Hold the free end at shoulder height with your right hand. Stand in a staggered stance, right foot slightly forward. Press the barbell end upward along its arc with your right arm. Lock out at the top. Core braced to prevent rotation. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch arms. The single-arm loading demands anti-rotation core strength. Use moderate weight. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per arm.
Benefits: Unilateral pressing with anti-rotation core demand; Shoulder-friendly arc path; Exposes left-right imbalances; Builds pressing strength per arm; Easy to set up; Versatile — can be done standing, kneeling, or half-kneeling
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (upper); Triceps brachii; Core (anti-rotation); Serratus anterior

Description: Set up a landmine. Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench. Place the end of the barbell on your right hip crease. Bend your right knee with foot flat. Extend or lift your left leg. Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up against the bar. Squeeze your right glute at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. The landmine guides the weight path for stability.
Benefits: Guided bar path stabilizes the load; Builds single-leg glute strength; Easier to manage than free weights on single-leg thrusts; Exposes left-right glute imbalances; Easy to load progressively; Excellent glute isolation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae

Description: Set up a landmine. Stand facing the free end on your right leg. Grip the end of the barbell with your left hand (contralateral). Hinge at the right hip, pushing your left leg behind you. Lower the barbell toward the floor along its arc while keeping a flat back. Continue until you feel a deep hamstring stretch. Drive through your right hip to stand back up. Complete reps, then switch sides. The landmine arc guides the bar path for easier balance.
Benefits: Guided bar path easier to balance than free weights; Builds single-leg hamstring and glute strength; Excellent single-leg RDL regression; Develops balance and hip stability; Contralateral loading is natural; Easy to set up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core (anti-rotation); Gluteus medius (balance)

Description: Anchor a barbell in a landmine and load the working end. Stand at the side of the bar holding the end with one hand. Shift weight onto the same side leg. Brace the core and lift the opposite leg slightly off the floor. Hinge at the hips by pushing the hips back. Lower the bar end down toward the floor with a flat back. Keep the working leg slightly bent and feel the hamstring stretch. Drive through the heel to stand back tall and complete all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds unilateral hamstring and glute strength.; Landmine arc helps balance compared to free weight RDL.; Trains anti rotation and core stability.; Carryover to single leg deadlifts.; Joint friendly with the fixed bar path.; Improves hip hinge mechanics.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Adductors

Description: Set up a barbell in a landmine attachment (or wedge the end into a corner). Stand facing the barbell, holding the free end with both hands at hip height. Feet hip-width apart. Set a soft, fixed bend in your knees. Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back. Lower the bar along the guided arc. Keep your back flat and the bar close to your body. Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings. Drive your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Guided bar path reduces balance demand vs standard RDL; Constant tension through the angled resistance; Builds the hamstrings and glutes effectively; More accessible for beginners learning the RDL; Easy to set up with a landmine or corner; Good variation for lifters with balance issues
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a barbell in a landmine. Stand over the free end in a wide sumo stance, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Hold the free end of the bar with both hands, letting it hang between your legs. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Push your knees out over your toes. Sit straight down between your heels. Keep torso upright. Descend until hip crease is below knees or as deep as you can go. Drive through your full foot to stand. Push knees out. Squeeze glutes at top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Adjust stance width to bias different muscles.
Benefits: Targets the glutes and adductors with guided resistance; Easier on the lower back than standard sumo squats; Easy to set up with a landmine attachment; Forces upright torso position; Good variation for home gyms; Builds inner thigh and glute strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors; Quadriceps; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall holding a towel taut between both hands at hip level. Set your feet at shoulder-width and brace your core. Pull outward on the towel to create tension. Maintain that pull throughout the entire set. Raise your arms out to the sides while keeping the towel taut. Lift until your arms reach shoulder height. Pause briefly and squeeze the side delts. Lower the arms back to the start while maintaining tension.
Benefits: Builds side delt detail; No hardware needed; Constant tension method; Travel-friendly; Old-school technique; Useful at-home move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Upper trapezius

Description: Anchor a barbell in a landmine and load the working end. Drop into a half kneeling position with the bar end at one shoulder. Brace the core and keep the chest tall. Drive through the front heel to stand up tall. As you rise, lift the back leg up into a high knee. Press the bar overhead at the top. Lower the bar back to the shoulder and step back into the kneeling start. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds full body power and coordination.; Trains the legs, core, and shoulders together.; Improves single leg balance and stability.; Develops the ability to transition under load.; Carryover to athletic explosiveness.; Adds variety to standard kneeling presses.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Anterior deltoid; Core; Hip flexors

Description: Lie on your right side. Place your right forearm on the floor, elbow under your shoulder. Stack your feet or stagger them. Lift your hips off the floor until your body forms a straight line. Hold this position for the desired time. Keep hips elevated — do not let them sag. Breathe steadily. Hold for 20 to 45 seconds per side. Switch sides.
Benefits: Builds anti-lateral flexion core strength; Targets the obliques and quadratus lumborum; No equipment needed; Foundational core exercise; Builds hip stability; Recommended by Dr. McGill for core health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius (hip stabilizer); Transverse abdominis

Description: Set up a landmine with the barbell end at chest height. Hold the end with both hands at your chest. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. The bar is vertical or slightly angled in front of you. Squat down while holding the bar at your chest. Descend to parallel or below. Drive through your feet to stand explosively. As you reach standing, use the momentum to press the barbell end up and forward in an arc. Lock out at the top. Lower the bar back to your chest as you descend into the next squat.
Benefits: Full-body compound movement; Angled bar path is shoulder-friendly; Builds legs, shoulders, and core together; Excellent conditioning exercise; Easier to learn than barbell thrusters; Unique landmine loading pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set gymnastic rings just out of reach overhead from a seated position. Sit under the rings and grip them overhead. Place the feet flat on the floor in front. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Pull the chest up toward the rings using the legs to assist. Bend the elbows and rotate the wrists naturally as you pull. Squeeze the lats hard at the top. Lower back down with control to the start.
Benefits: Beginner friendly pull up; Builds the lats; Allows natural ring rotation; Useful pull up progression; Builds back size; Strong upper body builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set up sideways to a flat bench. Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor. Place the top foot up on the bench. Stack the bottom foot on the floor. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Lift the hips up off the floor. Squeeze the obliques and glutes hard at the top. Hold for the working set then switch sides.
Benefits: Loads the obliques; Strong side plank variation; Builds the core; Useful for core size; Trains the side abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Core; Gluteus medius

Description: Start in a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart on the floor. Turn your hands outward slightly (fingers pointing to the sides) to protect your wrists. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Protract your shoulders (push the floor away). Lean your body forward by shifting weight onto your hands — your shoulders should pass over or beyond your wrists. Maintain straight arms and a straight body line. Hold the forward-leaned position for 10 to 30 seconds. Increase the forward lean gradually over weeks. Your feet will become lighter. Eventually, they begin to lift as you approach planche balance.
Benefits: Foundational planche progression; Builds extreme anterior deltoid strength; Develops wrist and forearm conditioning; Builds core bracing under forward lean; No equipment needed; Essential stepping stone to full planche
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (heavy); Pectoralis major; Serratus anterior; Core (heavy); Wrist flexors and extensors; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand beside a box or step. Place your inside foot on the box. Drive through that foot to step up onto the box. Stand fully on the box. Step back down to the side. Complete reps, then switch sides. Keep torso upright. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds lateral movement strength; Develops frontal-plane single-leg power; Useful for lateral-sport athletes; No weights needed; Develops hip control; Accessible variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and medius; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Walk one hand and the same-side foot to the side. Bring the other hand and foot to meet them. Perform another push-up. Continue walking sideways with each rep.
Benefits: Combines chest and conditioning; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment required; Strong calorie burner; Useful for full-body workouts; Adds variety to push-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Front deltoid; Triceps brachii; Core

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Continue down until your entire body is flat on the floor. Briefly relax with arms by your chest. Place your hands back under your shoulders. Press through your hands to drive your body back up. Lock out the elbows at the top.
Benefits: Eliminates momentum; Forces full range of motion; Builds true pressing strength; No equipment required; Strong push-up progression; Excellent for strength building
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Description: Sit on the leg extension machine and adjust the seat back so the back of your knees rests against the edge of the seat pad. Adjust the ankle pad so it sits comfortably across your shins, just above your feet. Grip the handles or sides of the seat firmly. Sit upright with your back pressed against the pad. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Extend both knees by lifting the pad up. Keep your hips planted on the seat — do not lift them. Continue extending until your legs are fully straight (or nearly so). Squeeze your quads hard for one second at the top. Lower the pad under control over a count of two to three seconds back to the starting position. Stop just before the weight stack touches down to maintain tension on the quads.
Benefits: The most direct isolation exercise for the quadriceps; Constant tension throughout the entire range of motion; Allows safe, comfortable training to muscular failure; Useful for finishing the quads after compound leg work; Easy to load progressively in small increments; Trains the rectus femoris (hip flexor + quad) effectively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius)

Exercise Name: Leg Lift to Chest Front Plank
Description: Set up in a forearm plank with elbows under shoulders. Brace the core and keep the body straight from heels to head. Lift one foot off the floor and pull the knee toward your chest. Tuck the knee in tight while keeping the hips level. Pause briefly at the top of the tuck. Extend the leg back to the plank position with control. Repeat with the opposite leg. Continue alternating knee tucks for the full set.
Benefits: Strengthens the deep abs and hip flexors.; Trains core stability under dynamic leg movement.; Improves shoulder endurance in the plank position.; No equipment needed.; Easy to scale by slowing or speeding the tempo.; Builds carryover to running and athletic core control.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Cross one ankle over the opposite knee. Place the arms at the sides palms down. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Drive through the planted heel to lift the hips. Squeeze the glute hard at the top. Lower with control to the start. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds single leg glute; Strong glute isolator; Trains each side; Useful warm-up; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core

Description: Get into a forearm plank. Body straight, core braced. Lift your right leg straight up about 6 to 12 inches. Keep it straight. Squeeze your right glute. Hold for 2 to 3 seconds. Lower your right leg. Lift your left leg. Continue alternating. Minimize hip rotation — keep hips level. Set feet wider for easier balance. Aim for 8 to 12 lifts per leg.
Benefits: Adds glute activation to planks; Increases anti-rotation core demand; No equipment needed; Builds hip extension from plank position; Engaging plank variation; Develops body control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core (anti-rotation); Gluteus maximus (lifting leg); Hamstrings; Anterior deltoid (support)

Description: Lie on a flat bench. Reach overhead and grip a sturdy support behind the head. Pinch the shoulder blades and brace your core hard. Lift the entire body up by driving the legs straight up. Keep the body in a straight line from feet to shoulders. At the top the body should be vertical with weight on upper back. Lower the body back down slowly keeping it straight. Stop just above the bench. Repeat without touching down.
Benefits: Elite abs builder; Trains full body tension; Builds full ab strength; Useful for advanced trainees; Strong calisthenic move; Builds core size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Sit on the end of a flat bench facing forward. Grip the sides of the bench behind your hips. Lean back slightly and extend the legs out straight in front. Brace the core and keep the feet just off the floor. Pull the knees in toward the chest by bending the hips and knees. Squeeze the abs hard at the top. Extend the legs back out to the start position with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hammers the lower abs and hip flexors.; Builds core strength through the pull in motion.; Easy to scale by changing leg position.; Bench position keeps the back supported.; Carryover to hanging leg raises.; Develops anterior core endurance.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Quadriceps

Description: Lie flat on your back with legs extended straight. Place your hands under your glutes or at your sides. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Lift both straight legs up to vertical (90 degrees) — this is the leg raise portion. Once your legs are vertical, press your feet toward the ceiling by lifting your hips off the floor. This is the hip lift. Squeeze your lower abs hard at the top of the hip lift. Lower your hips back to the floor, then slowly lower your legs back toward the floor under control. Stop just before your heels touch. Repeat for the desired number of reps. If your lower back lifts off the floor during the leg-lowering phase, reduce range of motion.
Benefits: Combines the leg raise and hip lift for deeper lower-ab work; The hip lift forces the lower abs to contract fully; Builds lower-ab strength beyond what standard leg raises provide; No equipment needed; Excellent progression from lying leg raises; Trains core anti-extension control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially the lower portion); Hip flexors; Obliques (secondary); Transverse abdominis

Description: Lie on your back with arms by your sides or under your hips. Keep your legs together with a slight bend in the knees. Brace your core and press your lower back into the floor. Lift both legs up toward the ceiling. Continue until your hips start to lift off the floor. Twist your legs together down to one side. Stop just before your legs touch the floor. Twist back up to center, then alternate sides on each rep.
Benefits: Combines lower abs and obliques; Builds lower abdominal strength; Time-efficient ab combo; No equipment required; Strong oblique builder; Useful for waist trimming
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Obliques; Hip flexors

Description: Set up a T-bar with one end anchored in a landmine attachment or corner. Load the free end with weight plates and grip the handles. Stand over the bar with feet hip-width apart. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Maintain a slight soft bend in the knees. Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back behind you. Lower the T-bar along the front of your legs while keeping it close. Drive your hips forward to stand back up to the starting position.
Benefits: Hits hamstrings from a different angle than standard RDL; T-bar handles offer comfortable grip; Builds posterior chain strength; Easier on the lower back than barbell RDL for some lifters; Useful variation for hamstring development; Allows progressive loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Set up on a decline bench with the feet hooked under the pads. Lie back on the decline. Reach the arms straight overhead and keep them there. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Sit up by curling the torso forward. Keep the arms reaching forward and up throughout. Touch the hands toward the toes at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Loads the abs hard; Strong long lever variation; Builds the core; Useful for advanced lifters; Builds the rectus abdominis
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip Flexors; Obliques

Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Place the arms at the sides palms down. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lift the hips just slightly off the floor. Squeeze the glutes hard at the small lift. Lower with control nearly back to the floor. Stop just before the hips touch and lift again. Continue the small range pulses.
Benefits: Builds the glutes; High tension activation; Strong glute drill; Useful warm-up; Builds glute endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core

Description: Lie face down on the floor. Reach the arms straight overhead. Set the legs straight back. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Lift the chest, arms, and legs off the floor. Keep the arms reaching long. Squeeze the lower back and glutes hard. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the lower back; Trains the glutes; Strong superman variation; Useful for back health; Builds posterior chain
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Trapezius

Description: Lie face down on the floor. Arms at your sides or hands behind your head. Keep your legs on the floor. Lift your chest and upper body off the floor by extending your lower back. Rise as high as comfortable. Squeeze your lower back at the top. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds. Lower under control. Keep the movement controlled — no jerking. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Strengthens the erector spinae; Simple and accessible; No equipment needed; Builds lower back endurance; Useful for back health and posture; Beginner-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus (slight); Hamstrings (slight); Multifidus

Description: Set up a horizontal rope or series of overhead bars/handholds at above-head height. Grip the rope or first handhold. Lift your feet off the floor so you hang freely. Begin traversing sideways by reaching with one hand to the next handhold, then following with the other. Keep your body as horizontal as possible (like a bridge) — this reduces the lever arm on your grip. Minimize swinging. Use controlled movements. Traverse the full length, then come back. If you cannot go fully horizontal, hang vertically and traverse — it is still effective. Build up distance over time. Focus on grip endurance.
Benefits: Builds elite grip endurance; Develops lat and shoulder strength; Trains core stability under hanging load; Staple in obstacle course racing; Fun and functional; Builds pulling strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms and grip (extreme); Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Core (heavy anti-rotation); Posterior deltoid

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Extend both arms straight overhead behind your head, biceps by your ears. Keep your arms straight and in this position throughout. Crunch up by lifting your shoulders off the floor. Your extended arms rise with your torso — they do not swing forward. Squeeze your abs at the top. Lower under control. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Longer lever arm increases ab demand; Harder than standard crunches without added weight; No equipment needed; Simple progression from standard crunches; Builds ab strength effectively; Easy to learn
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques (secondary)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Place your hands on your hips or in front for balance. Step your right foot forward roughly two to three feet. Lower your back (left) knee straight down toward the floor by bending both knees together. Descend until your back knee is roughly an inch above the floor. Your front thigh should be parallel to the floor. Drive through your front (right) foot to push back up to the starting position. Step the right foot back to your starting stance. That is one rep. Repeat with the left leg stepping forward. Continue alternating until you complete the desired total reps per leg. Keep your torso upright the entire time. Progress by adding dumbbells or a barbell.
Benefits: Foundational single-leg exercise for all fitness levels; Builds quads, glutes, and balance with no equipment; Trains coordination and proprioception; Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances; Works anywhere — no equipment needed; Excellent warm-up or rehabilitation exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Arms extended in front of you or hands at your chest. Step forward into a lunge with your right foot. Lower your left knee toward the floor. At the bottom, rotate your torso to the right (toward the front leg). Return to center, then drive through your front foot to stand. Step forward with your left foot and twist to the left. Continue alternating. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines lunging with rotational core work; Builds leg and oblique strength together; Improves coordination; No equipment needed; Great warm-up exercise; Develops hip and thoracic mobility
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Core (rotation); Hip rotators

Description: Lie on your back on the floor. Bend your knees to 90 degrees with feet off the floor. Place your palms on the front of your thighs near your knees. Brace your core and engage your abs. Press your hands forward against your thighs while your thighs press back into your hands. At the same time, crunch your shoulders off the floor. Hold the isometric press for one to two seconds. Slowly release and lower your shoulders back down.
Benefits: Strong isometric ab contraction; Builds core endurance; No equipment required; Useful for ab specialization; Easy to scale by changing pressure; Develops mind-muscle connection with abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis

Description: Lie on the back with the legs straight. Place the hands at the sides palms down. Brace your core and lift the legs slightly off the floor. Bend one knee and pull the heel toward the glute. Extend the leg back out straight. Repeat with the other leg in alternating fashion. Keep both feet off the floor throughout. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Loads the lower abs; Trains the hip flexors; Strong core drill; Builds the abs; Useful core move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip Flexors; Core

Description: Lie flat on your back on the floor. Place your hands behind your head or at your sides. Lift the legs into the air with the knees bent. Brace your core hard. Pedal the legs as if riding a bicycle. Extend one leg while bringing the other knee in. Continue alternating in a smooth pedaling motion. Keep the lower back pressed into the floor.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly ab move; Trains lower abs; No equipment needed; Easy to scale; Useful core warm-up; Strong basic ab move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Set the arms at the sides. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Drive through the heels to lift the hips up into a glute bridge. Hold the bridge position with hips fully extended. Lift one knee up toward the chest. Lower that foot back down and lift the other knee. Continue alternating leg lifts while holding the bridge.
Benefits: Strong glute builder; Trains anti-rotation core; No equipment needed; Builds the hamstrings; Useful glute finisher; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Hip flexors; Core

Description: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended forward and legs straight. Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes. Lift your chest, arms, and head off the floor by contracting your lower back. Continue lifting until you feel a strong contraction in your erector spinae. Hold for one to two seconds at the top. Lower under control back to the floor. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Keep the movement small and controlled — do not hyperextend.
Benefits: Strengthens the lower back (erector spinae); Builds postural endurance; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Excellent rehabilitation exercise; Counteracts the effects of prolonged sitting; Foundation for hyperextensions and back-extension machines
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Posterior deltoid (arm lift)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step forward into a lunge with your right foot. Lower your left knee toward the floor. Drive through your right foot to stand. As you reach standing, lift your left leg straight behind you — squeeze your left glute. Hold the single-leg balance briefly. Step your left foot forward into the next lunge. Continue for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines lunging with glute activation; Builds single-leg balance; Develops glute strength through hip extension; No equipment needed; Engaging lunge variation; Improves coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus (leg lift); Hamstrings; Core (balance); Gluteus medius (standing leg)

Description: Lie face down on the floor with legs extended and arms in front. Rest your forehead lightly on the ground. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Lift your chest, arms, and legs off the floor at the same time. Continue lifting until you feel a strong contraction in the lower back. Hold the top position briefly. Lower back down with control. Reset and repeat.
Benefits: Builds lower back strength; Strengthens the posterior chain; No equipment required; Useful for home training; Reduces lower back pain over time; Improves posture
Muscles Worked (Raw): Spinal erectors; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step forward into a lunge with your right foot. Place both hands on the floor beside your front foot. Kick both feet back to a push-up position. Perform a push-up. Jump your feet back to the lunge position. Drive through your front foot to stand. Repeat leading with the left foot. Aim for 6 to 10 total reps.
Benefits: Full-body conditioning in one movement; Combines leg and pressing work; No equipment needed; Builds cardiovascular fitness; Time-efficient; Engaging and challenging
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (lunge); Pectoralis major (push-up); Triceps brachii; Gluteus maximus; Core (transitions)

Description: Lie flat on your back with arms and legs extended. Brace the core and press the lower back to the floor. Lift one leg and the opposite arm at the same time. Reach the hand toward the lifted foot at the top of the rep. Squeeze the abs and obliques. Lower the arm and leg back to the floor with control. Repeat on the other side. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Trains the abs and obliques with a crossing pattern.; Builds rotational core strength.; No equipment needed.; Easy to scale by adjusting reach height.; Carryover to athletic rotation.; Develops mind muscle connection through the core.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Quadriceps

Description: Lie flat on your back with the legs lifted and knees bent at ninety degrees. Place the hands at your sides for support. Brace the core and press the lower back to the floor. Begin tracing a figure 8 pattern with the knees in the air. Move smoothly from one loop to the other. Keep the knees bent at the same angle throughout. Control the movement with the abs and obliques. Repeat for the desired number of full figure 8 patterns.
Benefits: Trains the abs and obliques together.; Builds rotational core control.; No equipment needed.; Adds variety to standard crunches.; Carryover to athletic rotation.; Develops total core endurance.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis

Description: Lie on your back on the floor. Place the hands at the sides for support. Bend the knees with feet on the floor. Brace your core hard. Lift the bent knees up toward the chest. Continue lifting until the thighs are vertical. Curl the hips up off the floor at the top. Lower the legs back down with control.
Benefits: Beginner friendly abs move; No equipment needed; Builds the lower abs; Trains hip flexors; Useful core builder; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Lie on your back on the floor. Hold a towel with one hand at each end. Set one arm straight at the side and the other bent at the chest. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Curl the working arm up squeezing the bicep. Resist the curl with the other arm pulling against it. Squeeze the bicep hard at the top. Lower with control. Switch arms each set.
Benefits: Travel-friendly arm move; No equipment needed; Builds bicep size; Strong creative arm move; Easy to scale by tension; Useful for hotel rooms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended overhead. Make loose fists with palms facing each other. Brace your core and keep your head neutral. Lift your chest off the floor by extending the back. At the same time press your arms forward and overhead. Reach high with the hands as the chest rises. Pause briefly at the top and squeeze the back and glutes. Lower the chest and arms back to the floor with control.
Benefits: Trains back and shoulders together; Builds posterior chain; No equipment needed; Useful for posture; Combo move saves time; Easy to add to any session
Muscles Worked (Raw): Spinal erectors; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid; Lower trapezius

Exercise Name: Lying Double Legs Biceps Curl with Towel
Description: Lie flat on your back on the floor with knees bent. Loop a towel under both feet with each end held in your hands. Set the elbows close to the body with palms facing up. Press both legs gently against the towel to create tension. Curl your hands up toward the shoulders by bending the elbows. Increase or decrease leg pressure to control the load. Squeeze the biceps at the top. Lower the towel slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
