At the top of the push-up, row the right dumbbell up to your right hip by driving your elbow straight back. Squeeze your shoulder blade. Keep your hips perfectly level throughout the row — do not rotate or tilt. This is the hardest part. Lower the right dumbbell back to the floor under control. Then row the left dumbbell with the same form. That is one full rep. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use moderate weight — form matters more than load.
Benefits: Trains push, pull, and core stability in one movement; Builds the chest, back, shoulders, triceps, biceps, and core simultaneously; Develops anti-rotation core strength; Time-efficient combination of multiple exercises; Exposes left-right strength imbalances on the row; Works at home with one pair of hex dumbbells
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Latissimus dorsi; Triceps brachii; Biceps brachii; Anterior and posterior deltoid; Trapezius and rhomboids; Core (anti-rotation, anti-extension); Forearms and grip

Description: Set up on a 45-degree or horizontal hyperextension bench. Adjust the pad to sit just below your hip crease. Lock your feet under the leg pads. Hold a weight plate against your chest with both hands. Cross your arms over the plate to keep it steady. Start hinged forward at the hips. Brace your core. Extend your torso up by contracting your glutes and lower back. Stop when your body forms a straight line. Do not hyperextend. Lower under control back to the starting hinged position. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use heavier plates as you get stronger.
Benefits: Adds progressive load to bodyweight hyperextensions; Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings; Easier to load than holding a barbell; Excellent posterior chain accessory; Easy to scale by changing plate weight; Useful for high-volume back work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Get into a standard push-up position with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, body in a straight line from heels to head. Brace your core hard and pull your shoulders down and back. Lower your chest toward the floor under control by bending at the elbows. Lower until your chest is just above the floor. Pause briefly. Press up explosively with maximum force, generating enough power that your hands leave the floor at the top. If you can, add a quick clap mid-air. Keep your body line straight throughout the airborne phase. Land with soft, slightly bent elbows to absorb the impact. Immediately drop into the next descent. Repeat for low reps (3 to 8 per set) — power exercises lose effectiveness when fatigued. Use longer rests between sets.
Benefits: Builds explosive upper-body pressing power; Trains fast-twitch muscle fibers; Improves rate of force development; Carries over to athletic movements like pushing, throwing, and punching; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Excellent finisher for chest workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand a weight plate (or two plates pressed together) on the floor with the smooth side facing outward. Hinge down and grip the plate(s) between your thumb on one side and four fingers on the other. Stand up holding the plate(s) by pinch grip alone. Stand tall with the plate(s) hanging at your side at arm’s length. Hold for the desired time (30 seconds to 2 minutes) or walk a designated distance. Lower carefully back to the floor. Switch hands and repeat. Use 5 to 25 lb plates depending on your grip strength.
Benefits: Builds elite pinch grip strength; Develops thumb and finger strength; Useful for climbers, strongman athletes, and combat sports; Easy to set up with weight plates; Easy to scale by adding plates; Carries over to all gripping activities
Muscles Worked (Raw): Thumb flexors; Forearm flexors; Finger flexors; Trapezius (loaded carry)

Description: Sit or stand tall with the spine neutral. Place both hands on the back of your head. Brace your core and keep the chin slightly tucked. Push the back of the head back into the hands. Resist the push with the hands at the same intensity. Hold the static contraction without movement. Breathe normally throughout the hold. Release the press slowly.
Benefits: Builds neck strength safely; Static isometric hold; No equipment needed; Useful for athletes; Strong neck builder; Easy to scale intensity
Muscles Worked (Raw): Neck extensors; Trapezius; Spinal erectors

Description: Stand over the barbell with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Drop your hips low. Chest up. Shoulders over the bar. Pull the bar from the floor — keep it close to your body. As the bar passes your knees, explosively extend your hips and shrug. Pull yourself under the bar and catch it on your front shoulders in a quarter-squat (above parallel). Stand up from the quarter-squat to complete the lift. Lower the bar back to the floor under control. Easier to learn than the full clean. Master the hang power clean first.
Benefits: Most popular Olympic lift for athletes; Builds explosive triple extension; Easier to learn than the full clean; Carries over to jumping, sprinting, and tackling; Develops rate of force development; Excellent power exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Quadriceps; Trapezius (upper); Erector spinae; Anterior deltoid (catch); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart. Position your body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Lower your right forearm to the floor. Lower your left forearm to the floor (now in forearm plank). Press up onto your right hand to extend the arm. Press up onto your left hand to return to the high plank. Alternate which arm leads on each rep.
Benefits: Builds core stability through movement; Strong shoulder endurance challenge; Develops body control; Combines isometric and dynamic core work; No equipment required; Useful for full body conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Obliques

Description: Stand about 2 feet from a wall. Place hands on the wall at chest height. Lean into the wall by bending your elbows. Push off the wall explosively — hard enough to briefly lift your hands off. Catch yourself back on the wall as your hands return. Immediately lower and repeat. The wall angle makes this very accessible. Aim for 10 to 15 explosive reps. Progress to incline plyo push-ups, then floor plyo push-ups.
Benefits: Easiest upper-body plyometric exercise; Builds explosive pressing power for beginners; Safe — wall angle is forgiving; No equipment needed; Progressive toward harder plyo push-ups; Develops fast-twitch pressing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (slight)

Description: Attach a strap or harness to a weighted sled. Hold the strap handles or wear the harness. Face away from the sled with feet shoulder-width. Brace your core and lean back slightly. Walk backward with controlled steps. Drive through the heels and pull the sled. Continue walking backward for the working distance. Keep the back tall and chest up throughout.
Benefits: Strong quad builder; Builds conditioning; Useful for athletes; Trains posterior chain; Strong sled drill; Builds work capacity
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Calves; Hamstrings

Description: Load a prowler sled with the desired weight. Stand behind the sled and grip the high or low handles. Lean forward into the sled at roughly 45 degrees. Arms straight. Brace your core. Drive your legs by taking powerful, driving steps. Push through the balls of your feet. Keep your torso at a consistent forward lean. Do not stand upright. Drive your knees forward and up with each step. Short, powerful strides work best. Push the sled for the desired distance (20 to 50 meters) or time. Rest fully between sets. This is not a pacing exercise — each push should be near-max effort. Low handles bias a more horizontal push (more leg drive). High handles are more upright (easier).
Benefits: Builds total-body strength and conditioning simultaneously; Minimal eccentric loading means minimal muscle soreness; One of the best conditioning tools available; Develops quad, glute, and calf strength and endurance; Carries over to sprinting and athletic performance; Can be programmed for power (heavy, short) or conditioning (light, long)
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy involvement); Gluteus maximus; Calves; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Anterior deltoid and triceps (pushing)

Description: Attach a strap or rope to a power sled. Stand facing away from the sled and grip the strap behind. Walk forward to take tension on the strap. Set a slight forward lean and bend the elbows. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Extend the elbows back hard pulling the strap. As the elbows lock out the sled drags forward. Step forward to take new tension and continue the drags.
Benefits: Strong tricep builder; Adds sled conditioning; Builds tricep size; Useful arm builder; Strong sled move; Builds posterior shoulder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Posterior deltoid; Anconeus

Description: Adjust the seat so your upper arms rest flat on the pad with elbows aligned to the machine pivot. Sit with chest against the pad. Grip the handles with an underhand grip. Start with arms nearly extended. Brace your core. Curl the handles up by bending at the elbows. Keep upper arms on the pad. Continue until forearms are roughly vertical. Squeeze your biceps hard. Lower under control. Stop just before full extension to maintain tension. Stop before the weight stack touches down. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Strictest possible bicep isolation — no body english; Guided path with easy progressive loading; Allows safe training to failure; Easy to use for drop sets; Excellent for beginners learning bicep contraction; Comfortable arm-pad support
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Hold a PVC pipe or empty barbell at chest height with a wide snatch-width grip. Stand with feet at hip-width. Quickly dip and drop into a full overhead squat, pressing the bar up as your body drops down. Catch the bar overhead with arms locked out in the bottom of the overhead squat. Your feet should jump to receiving width as you drop. Stand up from the overhead squat. This is a speed and timing drill — use a PVC pipe or empty bar only. Aim for 5 to 8 reps focusing on speed.
Benefits: Teaches snatch receiving mechanics; Builds drop-under speed; Develops overhead squat stability; Olympic lifting drill; Light load focuses on technique; Builds confidence dropping under the bar
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Anterior and lateral deltoid; Core (heavy stabilizer); Triceps brachii; Trapezius

Description: Lie on your back with hands behind your head, elbows wide. Without using your hands (they stay behind your head), rise to a standing position. You may roll to one side, bring one knee up, and step up — whatever works. Stand fully upright. Lower yourself back to the floor in a controlled manner without using your hands. That is one rep. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set. This becomes harder with age and reduced mobility — track your progress.
Benefits: Functional full-body movement; Tests and builds leg strength and mobility; No equipment needed; Builds body control; Useful fitness assessment; Develops real-world functional strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Core (stabilizer); Hip flexors; Calves

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place the hands behind the head with elbows out wide. Brace your core hard. Curl the upper body off the floor. Sit up only halfway keeping the lower back on the floor. Squeeze the abs at the top of the half sit up. Pause briefly at the contracted position. Lower back to the start with control.
Benefits: Beginner friendly abs move; Protects the lower back; No equipment needed; Builds the abs; Useful core builder; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Clasp your hands behind your head, elbows pulled wide. Keep your chest tall throughout. Pull elbows back to engage upper back. Brace your core. Sit your hips back and down into a squat. Lower until your hip crease drops below your knees. Drive through your full feet to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Maintain the elbows-wide, hands-behind-head position throughout. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps.
Benefits: Demands tall, upright squat posture; Builds upper-back and core engagement; No equipment needed; Develops squat pattern; Easy to scale by adjusting tempo; Useful for warm-ups and conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (postural stabilizer); Upper back and rhomboids; Calves

Description: Lie face down on a bench or floor. Head hanging off the edge (bench) or forehead on the floor. Keep your body relaxed. Arms at your sides. Slowly lift your head by extending your neck — look forward and slightly up. Hold for 3 to 5 seconds. Lower with control. Move gently — the cervical spine is delicate. Aim for 10 to 15 reps. Stop if you feel pain or dizziness.
Benefits: Strengthens the neck extensors; Rehabilitation exercise for cervical health; Builds neck endurance; No equipment needed; Gentle and controlled; Complements chin tucks for balanced neck training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Neck extensors (splenius, semispinalis); Upper trapezius

Description: Lie face down on the floor. Set the arms at the sides or under the forehead. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lift the head and chest slightly off the floor. Hold the cervical extension position. Keep the chin tucked rather than craned back. Maintain the isometric hold. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the neck; Strong neck drill; Useful for athletes; Trains posterior neck; Builds neck endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Sternocleidomastoid; Trapezius; Erector spinae

Description: Lie face down on the floor with the legs extended. Slide both palms under the upper thighs facing down. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes. Lift the chest and shoulders off the floor by extending the spine. Press the palms gently into the thighs to reinforce the lift. Squeeze the shoulder blades together. Hold the top position briefly. Lower the chest back to the floor with control and repeat.
Benefits: Builds lower back and upper back endurance.; Hand position reinforces the spinal extension.; No equipment needed.; Excellent posture builder.; Reduces upper back stiffness.; Carryover to back squats and deadlifts.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Trapezius; Posterior deltoid; Gluteus maximus; Rhomboids

Description: Lie face down on the floor or an incline bench. Extend your right arm at about a 45-degree angle from your head (Y position). Thumb pointing up. Lift your arm off the floor as high as possible. Squeeze your lower trap at the top. Hold for 2 seconds. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch arms. Use bodyweight only or very light weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps.
Benefits: Isolates the lower trapezius; Essential for scapular health; Rehabilitation and prehabilitation exercise; Builds shoulder blade control; No equipment needed; Develops postural muscles
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower fibers); Serratus anterior; Posterior deltoid (slight)

Description: Lie face down on the floor or on an incline bench (set at 30 to 45 degrees). Extend both arms forward at a roughly 45-degree angle from your torso, forming a Y shape. Thumbs pointing up. Brace your core. Keep your forehead on the floor or hovering just above. Lift both arms straight up off the floor, leading with your thumbs. Continue lifting until your arms are level with or slightly above your head. Squeeze your lower traps and rear delts at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control back to the floor. Use no weight or very light dumbbells (1 to 5 lbs). 10 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Activates the lower traps directly; Builds postural muscles that resist forward rounding; Improves shoulder positioning for pressing and pulling; No equipment needed; Excellent warm-up before upper-body training; Useful rehab exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lower trapezius; Posterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Rhomboids; Erector spinae (slight)

Description: Get into a push-up position. Place your hands beside your hips rather than your shoulders — fingers pointing sideways or backward. Lean your body forward so your shoulders are in front of your hands. Lower your chest toward the floor while maintaining the forward lean. Press back up. The forward lean dramatically increases shoulder demand. Start with a slight lean and progress to more forward lean over time. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set. This is a planche progression exercise — requires patience.
Benefits: Key planche progression exercise; Builds anterior deltoid and chest strength; Develops straight-arm strength foundations; No equipment needed; Progressive by adjusting lean angle; Builds toward advanced calisthenics skills
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (heavy); Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Core (heavy stabilizer); Serratus anterior; Biceps brachii (straight-arm component)

Description: Reach up and grip a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width apart. Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Hang from the bar with arms fully extended and feet off the floor. Cross your ankles behind you for stability. Set your starting position by pulling your shoulder blades down and back, away from your ears. Your chest should rise slightly. Drive your elbows down and back toward your hips to pull your chest up to the bar. Avoid kipping or swinging. Continue until your chin is clearly over the bar. Pause briefly at the top with your shoulder blades pinned together. Lower yourself under control to a full hang with arms completely straight. Do not drop down; the eccentric builds strength. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Quality reps with a full range of motion are far more valuable than partial-rep volume.
Benefits: Builds size and strength in the lats, upper back, and biceps; Improves grip strength and shoulder stability; Bodyweight movement that transfers to climbing, gymnastics, and athletics; One of the strongest predictors of upper-body strength relative to bodyweight; Can be progressed indefinitely by adding weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (lower and middle fibers); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Brachialis and brachioradialis; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizers)

Exercise Name: Pull Up with Bent Knee Between Chairs
Description: Place a sturdy bar across two chairs about shoulder width apart. Test the setup carefully to confirm it can hold your weight. Sit between the chairs with the bar above your head. Reach up and grip the bar with hands shoulder width apart. Bend your knees and let your feet rest on the floor for assistance. Pull your chest up to the bar by driving the elbows down. Use the legs lightly only as needed to assist the pull. Lower yourself slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Builds pull up strength using only chairs and a bar.; Bent knees and floor contact help scale difficulty.; Trains the lats and biceps with bodyweight.; Develops grip and back strength.; Excellent at home substitute for assisted pull up machines.; Easy to progress by lifting the feet off the floor.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Forearm flexors

Description: Set up an inverted row position — hang from a bar or TRX at hip height, body in a straight line. Row yourself up to the bar so your chest is near the bar. At the top, perform small pulsing reps — lower 2 to 3 inches and pull back up. Maintain the near-top position throughout — never fully extend. Squeeze your shoulder blades together on each pulse. Continue pulsing for the desired reps or time. Maintain a straight body line throughout. Aim for 15 to 25 pulses per set.
Benefits: Constant peak tension on the back; Builds endurance and mind-muscle connection; Excellent finisher exercise; No additional equipment needed; Develops isometric back strength; Engaging variation on standard rows
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back. Extend both legs straight up toward the ceiling, perpendicular to the floor. Arms at your sides, palms down for stability. Press your lower back into the floor. Lift your hips 2 to 3 inches off the floor by contracting your lower abs — push your feet toward the ceiling. Lower your hips back to the floor. Continue pulsing. The movement is small but intense. Keep legs vertical throughout — do not let them swing. Aim for 15 to 25 pulses per set.
Benefits: Isolates the lower abs effectively; Small range of motion with high intensity; No equipment needed; Builds lower ab strength; Useful finisher exercise; Develops hip curl mechanics
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors; Obliques (slight)

Description: Stand with the loaded barbell racked across your front shoulders, hands just outside shoulder-width, elbows up. Set your feet hip-width apart with toes pointed straight ahead. Brace your core hard and lift your chest tall. Initiate the dip by bending only at the knees — about 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches). Keep your torso completely vertical. Do not bend at the hips. Reverse the dip explosively by driving through your feet and extending your hips and knees. As your legs reach full extension, press the bar straight up overhead. The leg drive does most of the work; your arms finish the lift. Lock out with the bar directly over your shoulders and head, arms fully extended. Lower the bar under control back to the front rack position. Reset your dip and drive for the next rep.
Benefits: Allows you to press significantly more weight overhead than a strict press; Builds explosive lower-body power and full-body coordination; Trains the core and lower body to transmit force through the upper body; Excellent crossover to Olympic lifting and athletic performance; Builds total-body strength and conditioning in one movement; Useful when shoulder strict press strength is the limiting factor
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Quadriceps (drive); Glutes (drive); Upper trapezius; Core (rectus abdominis, obliques)

Description: Get on your hands and knees in a tabletop position. Set the hands under the shoulders and knees under the hips. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Lift one hand off the floor. Reach the arm forward and through the gap under the body. Continue the reach to the opposite side. Pull the arm back through to the start. Repeat reaches alternating arms.
Benefits: Mobilizes the shoulders; Trains anti-rotation core; No equipment needed; Useful warm-up drill; Easy mobility move; Strong core builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core; Anterior deltoid; Obliques

Description: Get into a high plank. Hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers forward. Set your body in a straight line from heels to head. Lower your chest to the floor by bending at the elbows. Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees to your body. Touch your chest to the floor (or come within an inch). Press back up to lockout. Maintain a straight body line throughout. Aim for 10 to 25 reps per set depending on fitness level.
Benefits: Most fundamental bodyweight pressing exercise; No equipment needed; Builds chest, tricep, and shoulder strength; Develops core stability; Can be done anywhere; Endlessly scalable through variations
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (anti-extension); Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Push Up and Triceps Dip on Parallel Bars
Description: Position yourself between two parallel bars with hands gripping the handles. Walk your feet back and lower into a push up position with hands on the bars. Lower your chest toward the floor while keeping the elbows tucked. Press back up to extend the arms and then jump or step up onto the bars. Support your bodyweight with locked arms in the dip starting position. Bend the elbows and dip down until your shoulders pass below your elbows. Press through the palms to return to the locked out top position. Lower yourself back to the push up start and continue alternating.
Benefits: Hits the chest, triceps, and shoulders in a single fluid combo.; Builds upper body endurance under continuous tension.; Develops bodyweight control and shoulder stability.; Functional carryover to gymnastic and calisthenic skills.; Adds variety to push and dip routines.; Strengthens stabilizers around the elbow and shoulder joints.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid

Description: Start kneeling on the floor with hips back on your heels. Reach your arms forward and let your chest lower toward the floor. This is the child pose start position. Slide your body forward by straightening the hips and bringing the chest near the floor. Plant your hands and shift weight onto them. Push up to a full plank position with elbows locked. Lower into a push up with elbows tucked. Reverse the movement back into the child pose to finish the rep.
Benefits: Combines strength and mobility; Opens hips and shoulders; Builds upper body control; Useful warm-up flow; No equipment required; Improves movement quality
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core

Exercise Name: Push Up Close Grip Off Dumbbell
Description: Place a dumbbell on the floor in front of you. Set the hands close together on top of the dumbbell. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Lower the chest down toward the dumbbell. Keep the elbows tight to the sides. Press back up to lockout. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Trains the triceps; Builds the inner chest; Strong push up variation; Useful tricep finisher; Builds the upper arms
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anconeus

Description: Place a medicine ball on the floor. Get into a high plank position with one hand on the ball and the other on the floor (or both hands on the ball for advanced). Brace your core hard. Form a straight body line from heels to head. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending at the elbows. The ball will want to wobble — control it. Lower until your chest is just above the floor. Press back up to lockout, controlling the ball throughout. For variation: switch which hand is on the ball each rep, or roll the ball under your chest between reps. Use moderate tempo — control matters more than speed. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set. Progress to both hands on the ball as control improves.
Benefits: Heavy stabilizer engagement from instability; Builds rotator cuff stability; Demands strong core engagement; Develops shoulder stability under load; Time-efficient advanced push-up; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Rotator cuff (heavy stabilizer); Serratus anterior; Core (anti-rotation)

Description: Place a Bosu ball on the floor with the flat side down (rounded side up). Grip the sides of the rounded surface with both hands. Walk your feet back into a high plank position with hands on the Bosu. Brace your core hard. Form a straight body line from heels to head. Lower your chest toward the Bosu by bending at the elbows. Lower until your chest is just above the Bosu. Press back up to lockout, controlling the unstable surface throughout. Maintain straight body line. The Bosu will wobble — control it with strong stabilizers.
Benefits: Heavy stabilizer engagement from instability; Builds rotator cuff stability; Demands strong core engagement; Develops shoulder stability under load; Engaging push-up variation; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Rotator cuff (heavy stabilizer); Serratus anterior; Core (anti-rotation)

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Press back up to lockout. Pike the hips up high into a downward dog position. Reach one hand back to touch the opposite ankle. Return to plank. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Combo full body builder; Stretches the hamstrings; Trains rotational core; Builds the chest; Useful conditioning combo; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Hamstrings; Obliques; Anterior deltoid

Description: Perform a push-up. At the top, rotate into a side plank — extend one arm to the ceiling. Hold the side plank briefly. Return to push-up position. Perform another push-up. Rotate to the other side. Continue alternating. Maintain body alignment during transitions. Aim for 8 to 12 total reps.
Benefits: Combines pressing with core rotation; Builds shoulder stability in rotation; No equipment needed; Develops oblique strength; Engaging full-body variation; Builds thoracic rotation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Obliques (side plank); Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Lower the chest toward the floor in a push up. Press back up to lockout. Lift one hand and tap the opposite knee. Return the hand to the floor and repeat the push up. Alternate the tapping hand each rep.
Benefits: Builds the chest; Adds core work; Trains shoulder stability; Strong push up variation; Useful combo move; Builds the triceps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Core; Anterior deltoid

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. At the bottom drive one knee toward the chest. Return the foot to the start. Press back up to lockout. Repeat with the other knee on the next rep.
Benefits: Combo chest and core builder; Trains hip flexors; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Useful conditioning combo; Strong push up variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Anterior deltoid

Description: For incline (easier): Place hands on the chair seat. Feet on the floor. Perform push-ups. For decline (harder): Place feet on the chair seat. Hands on the floor. Perform push-ups. Ensure the chair is stable and will not slide. Use a wall behind the chair. Maintain a straight body line throughout. Lower your chest toward the chair (incline) or floor (decline). Press back up. Incline targets less chest load; decline targets more upper chest. Aim for 10 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Adjustable difficulty with common furniture; No gym equipment needed; Incline is beginner-friendly; Decline targets upper chest; Easy to set up at home; Progressive by switching from incline to decline
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Get into a high plank. Hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, fingers forward. Set your body in a straight line from heels to head. Lower your chest to the floor by bending at the elbows. Keep your elbows at about 45 degrees to your body. Touch your chest to the floor (or come within an inch). Press back up to lockout. Maintain a straight body line throughout. Aim for 10 to 25 reps per set depending on fitness level.
Benefits: Most fundamental bodyweight pressing exercise; No equipment needed; Builds chest, tricep, and shoulder strength; Develops core stability; Can be done anywhere; Endlessly scalable through variations
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (anti-extension); Serratus anterior

Description: Perform a standard push-up — lower to the floor and press up to lockout. At lockout, push further by driving your shoulder blades apart (protracting). Your upper back rounds slightly as your shoulder blades spread wide. Hold the protracted position for 1 second. Allow your shoulder blades to come back together (retract). Lower into the next push-up. The “plus” is the extra push at the top — it is small but important. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Activates the serratus anterior; Builds scapular protraction strength; Important for shoulder health; Used in physical therapy; Easy addition to standard push-ups; Prevents winging scapula
Muscles Worked (Raw): Serratus anterior (primary focus); Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Bend your elbows to lower your chest toward the floor. Press back up to the top of the push-up. Pike your hips up high toward the ceiling. Reach the right hand back and touch your left foot. Return to the push-up position. Repeat the push-up, then touch the other side.
Benefits: Combines strength and conditioning; Builds core control; Improves hamstring flexibility; No equipment required; Strong calorie burner; Useful for full-body training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Core; Front deltoid; Hamstrings

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard. Perform a standard push up lowering and pressing back up. At the top move one hand forward. Move the other hand forward to match. Perform another push up. Continue alternating push ups with hand walks forward.
Benefits: Combo chest and core builder; Trains coordination; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Useful core builder; Strong push up variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid; Rectus abdominis

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Place a PVC pipe or broomstick across your upper traps (like a back squat). Grip the pipe with both hands. Stand tall. Brace your core. Push your hips straight back while keeping your back flat. Bend your knees slightly. Your torso should hinge forward until it is roughly parallel to the floor. Feel the stretch through your hamstrings. Drive your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Maintain a flat back throughout — if your back rounds, the hinge is too deep. Repeat for 10 to 15 reps as a warm-up or movement drill.
Benefits: Teaches the good morning hinge pattern safely; No load — pure movement learning; Develops hamstring flexibility; Builds awareness of flat-back position; Excellent warm-up before deadlifts or good mornings; Prevents lower-back rounding under load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hold a PVC pipe or broomstick vertically behind you. The pipe should touch three points: the back of your head, your upper back (thoracic spine), and your tailbone. Hold the pipe with one hand behind your neck and one hand at your lower back. Push your hips straight back while keeping all three contact points on the pipe. Bend your knees slightly. Keep your back completely flat. Continue hinging until you feel a stretch in your hamstrings. Drive your hips forward to stand back up, maintaining all three contact points. Repeat 10 to 15 times as a pattern drill before deadlifting.
Benefits: Gold standard drill for teaching hip hinge mechanics; Instant feedback on spinal position; Develops proper deadlift and RDL pattern; No weight needed — pure movement learning; Excellent warm-up before hinge exercises; Prevents lower-back rounding under load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae (maintaining flat back); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Hold a PVC pipe with a wide snatch-width grip overhead. Lock out your arms. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Squat down while keeping the PVC locked overhead. The pipe should stay directly over your midfoot. Descend as deep as mobility allows. Stand back up with the pipe still overhead. If the pipe drifts forward, your thoracic or shoulder mobility needs work. Aim for 10 to 15 reps as a warm-up or assessment.
Benefits: Lightest overhead squat for mobility assessment; Reveals shoulder, thoracic, hip, and ankle mobility issues; Used as warm-up before loaded overhead squats; Minimal equipment needed; Foundational movement screening tool; Builds overhead squat mechanics safely
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Deltoids (overhead hold); Core (stabilizer); Thoracic extensors

Description: Get on all fours — hands under shoulders, knees under hips. Extend your right leg straight behind you, parallel to the floor. Curl your right heel toward your right glute by bending at the knee. Squeeze your hamstring at the top. Extend back out. Continue for desired reps, then switch legs. Use a band around the ankle for added resistance. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per leg.
Benefits: Isolates the hamstring through knee flexion; No equipment needed; Useful for activation and warm-up; Easy to add band resistance; Beginner-friendly; Builds hamstring mind-muscle connection
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus (leg hold); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Press back up to lockout. At the top lift one leg up and kick it through across the body. Bring the leg back to the start. Repeat the push up and kick the other leg on the next rep.
Benefits: Combo chest and core builder; Trains rotational core; Builds the glutes; Strong push up variation; Useful core builder; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Obliques; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid

Description: Get into a standard push up position with hands under shoulders. Set your feet wider than shoulder-width for balance. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Press back up to the top with arms straight. At the top, rotate the body and raise one arm out to the side. Reach the arm up toward the ceiling in a side plank. Plant the hand back down and repeat with the other arm.
Benefits: Brutal anti-rotation challenge; Builds chest and core; Improves shoulder stability; Trains balance; Combo strength move; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Obliques; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie flat on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place your hands behind your head or across your chest. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Lift your shoulder blades only slightly off the floor. Stop at about a quarter range, with the lower back still in contact with the floor. Hold and squeeze the upper abs briefly. Lower with control. Maintain tension throughout the set.
Benefits: Maximizes upper ab tension; Constant tension throughout; Reduces hip flexor involvement; No equipment required; Great high-rep ab finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Core

Description: Get into a standard push up position with hands under shoulders. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Lift one leg straight off the floor a few inches. Squeeze the glute on the lifted leg to keep it up. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Press back up to the top with arms straight. Keep the leg lifted throughout all reps on one side. Switch legs and complete reps on the other side.
Benefits: Builds chest and triceps; Trains anti-rotation core; Adds glute engagement; Easy progression; No equipment needed; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Gluteus maximus; Core

Description: Lie on your back on the floor. Place both feet on a step, bench, or box. Arms at your sides, palms down. Drive through your heels to thrust your hips up. The elevated feet create a greater range of motion. At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Greater range of motion from elevated feet; Increased glute demand through extended range; No equipment needed beyond a step; Bodyweight exercise — easy to do at home; Builds glute strength and activation; Useful progression from flat bridges
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Rear Delt Fly with Bed Sheet
Description: Loop a bed sheet around a fixed anchor point at chest height. Stand facing the anchor. Grab the ends of the sheet with both hands held in front. Step back to create tension on the sheet. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Pull the hands out to the sides while squeezing the rear delts. Stop when the arms reach a T position. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Trains the rear delts at home.; No equipment required.; Builds the upper back.; Useful for travel.; Improves posture.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius; Rhomboids

Exercise Name: Rear Delt Row with Bed Sheet
Description: Anchor the middle of a sturdy bed sheet in a closed door. Grip the sheet ends with both hands. Lean back with the arms straight and feet planted. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Pull the sheet toward the chest with elbows flared wide. Squeeze the rear delts hard at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Targets the rear delts; No equipment needed; Strong home option; Builds upper back; Useful for travel; Trains the back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius

Description: Stand on a small platform or step with both feet. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Step backward with one foot off the platform. Lower into a deep lunge with the back knee toward the floor. Allow the front leg hip to sink lower than the platform top. Feel a deep stretch in the front leg glute and hamstring. Drive through the front heel to step back to standing. Alternate legs each rep.
Benefits: Deep glute and hamstring stretch; Longer range of motion; Builds leg strength; Trains balance; No barbell required; Strong unilateral leg work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Grip a pull-up bar with a wide overhand grip. Pull yourself up, leaning your head slightly forward. Continue until the bar touches the back of your neck. Lower under control. This requires excellent shoulder external rotation mobility. Stop immediately if you feel shoulder pain. Use only if you have good shoulder health. Aim for 5 to 10 reps. Use lighter body angle (feet assisted) to learn.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to mid-traps and rhomboids; Different lat activation angle; Builds upper back thickness; Requires shoulder mobility; Advanced pull-up variation; Used in bodybuilding for back width
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Teres major; Biceps brachii

Description: Stand on a low platform or weight plate. Set the feet hip width apart on the deficit. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Step one foot back off the platform. Lower the back knee toward the floor. Stop just above the floor with the front shin near vertical. Drive through the front foot to return to the platform. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Loads the front leg; Longer range than flat; Builds the quads; Strong lunge variation; Trains the glutes; Useful for balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point. Loop the other end across the upper back behind the neck. Set up on a 45 degree hyperextension bench. Hook the heels under the foot pads and the hips against the pad. Brace your core and start with the torso angled down. Extend the hips lifting the torso to a straight line with the body. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top. Lower the torso back down with control.
Benefits: Strong posterior chain builder; Adds resistance to back extension; Builds the glutes; Useful back move; Strong band move; Builds the hamstrings
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Anchor a resistance band at ankle height to your side. Loop the band around your front (right) thigh just above the knee. Step the right leg forward into a split stance. Position the left leg behind in lunge position. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Lower into a split squat by bending both knees. Resist the band pulling your right knee outward by activating the adductors. Drive up through the front foot to standing. Switch sides after the set.
Benefits: Strong adductor engagement; Builds inner thigh strength; Trains knee tracking; Different stimulus than standard split squat; Useful for hip stability work; Adds variety to leg training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Adductors; Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Anti Rotation Dead Bug
Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to one side. Lie on the back perpendicular to the anchor. Press the hands together with arms extended toward the ceiling. Hold the band handles with both hands. Brace the core and press the lower back into the floor. Lower one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg. Resist the band pulling toward the anchor side. Return to the start and alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Trains anti-rotation core strength.; Loads the obliques and deep core.; Builds total core stability.; Useful for athletes.; Improves spinal control.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Core; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Assisted Nordic Hamstring Curl
Description: Anchor a resistance band high to a sturdy point. Kneel on a pad with the feet locked under a sturdy support. Grip the band with both hands at chest height. Brace your core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the body forward by extending the knees. Control the descent using the hamstrings. At the bottom catch with the hands on the floor. Use the band assistance to pull back up to vertical.
Benefits: Builds eccentric hamstring strength; Beginner friendly nordic regression; No machines needed; Useful hamstring builder; Strong band move; Builds posterior chain
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Bent Over Neutral Grip Row
Description: Stand with the resistance band looped under both feet. Grip the band ends with a neutral hammer grip. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and the chest tall. Let the arms hang straight down toward the floor. Brace the core and pull the band ends up toward your hips. Drive the elbows back and keep them tucked close. Squeeze the lats and mid back at the top. Lower the band slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Constant band tension keeps the back loaded throughout.; Neutral grip is easier on the shoulders and elbows.; Builds back thickness without weights.; Engages the brachialis along with the biceps.; Travel friendly and joint friendly.; Easy to scale by stepping wider for more tension.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Brachialis; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Bent Over Rear Delt Fly
Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends of the band. Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly parallel to the floor. Let the band hang straight down with arms extended. Raise both arms out to the sides in a fly motion until they are parallel to the floor. Squeeze your rear delts and shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control. Keep a slight bend in your elbows throughout. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Targets the rear delts with constant tension; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful for shoulder balance and posture; No bench needed; Builds mid-traps and rhomboids
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid (primary); Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Infraspinatus

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends of the band. Hinge at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees to the floor. Let the band hang straight down with arms extended. Brace your core. Keep your back flat. Row both ends of the band up toward your lower ribs by driving your elbows back along your sides. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control over two seconds. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Effective at-home back row; Constant band tension throughout; Builds lats, mid-traps, and rhomboids; Highly portable; Teaches proper hinge position; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Anchor a resistance band low or loop it around your hips connected to a stable point. Stand facing away from the anchor with feet shoulder-width apart. Step forward to create band tension at the hip. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back. Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor. Drive up against the increasing band tension to stand. Lock out at the top with hips fully extended.
Benefits: Accommodating resistance gets harder at lockout; Builds lockout strength; Strong glute development; Useful for home training; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Functional movement pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with the balls of your feet. Heels hang off the edge or are flat on the floor. Hold both ends of the band at your shoulders. Stand tall. Brace your core. Rise up onto the balls of your feet by pressing through your toes. Squeeze your calves at the peak. Lower under control. If standing on a step, lower heels below the step for a full stretch. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Benefits: Adds load to calf raises at home; Increasing tension at peak contraction; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no machines are available; Builds calf size and strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Achilles tendon

Description: Place a mini band around both thighs just above your knees. Lie on your right side with knees bent at 90 degrees, feet together. Keep your feet together throughout. Open your left (top) knee upward against the band, like a clamshell opening. Keep feet touching. Open as far as possible. Squeeze your left glute at the top. Slowly close your knee back to the start. Complete 15 to 20 reps, then switch sides. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Gold-standard glute medius activation; Used in physical therapy worldwide; Builds hip stability and knee tracking; Prevents knee valgus; Highly portable; Excellent warm-up before lower-body training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius (primary); Gluteus minimus; Deep hip rotators

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Deadlift with Single Arm Row
Description: Stand on a resistance band with feet at hip-width. Hold each end of the band with arms hanging down. Hinge at the hips and bend the knees to grip the band low. Drive through the heels and stand up to lock out the deadlift. At the top, row one band end to your ribs by pulling the elbow back. Squeeze the back at the top of the row. Lower the band back down and reset. Hinge back down to repeat. Alternate the rowing arm each rep.
Benefits: Trains posterior chain and back; Combo move saves time; Builds hip hinge skill; Improves back strength; Travel-friendly equipment; Constant band tension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii

Description: Set the feet on a low box or step. Loop a resistance band across the hips with both ends anchored to the floor on each side. Lie on your back with the feet on the box. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Drive through the heels to lift the hips up. Extend the hips to a straight line with the body. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top against the band. Lower the hips back down with control.
Benefits: Strong glute builder; Adds band tension at top; Trains the glutes through full ROM; Useful glute builder; Strong band move; Builds the hamstrings
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Get on hands and knees in tabletop position. Loop a resistance band around your right hand and left foot. Brace your core. Keep your back flat. Simultaneously extend your right arm forward and left leg back against the band tension. Squeeze your glute and core at full extension. Hold for 1 to 2 seconds. Return to start under control. Complete reps on this side, then switch band to left hand and right foot. Use a light to moderate band. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Adds resistance to the bird dog; Builds anti-rotation core strength; Develops glute and shoulder stability; Excellent rehab and core exercise; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core (anti-rotation); Gluteus maximus (extending leg); Anterior deltoid (extending arm); Erector spinae; Hamstrings

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a sturdy point at elbow height. Stand sideways to the anchor with the band on your right side. Grip the band with your right hand. Pin your right elbow against your right side, bent at 90 degrees. Step away from the anchor until the band is under tension. Forearm starts pointing across your body. Brace your core. Keep your right elbow pinned to your side. Rotate your forearm outward away from your body, pulling the band. Continue until your forearm is pointing forward (or as far as comfortable). Slowly return to start. Use light resistance — this is a rotator cuff exercise, not a power lift.
Benefits: Strengthens the rotator cuff; Improves shoulder stability; Helps prevent shoulder impingement; Useful for athletes and lifters; Highly portable; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Infraspinatus; Teres minor; Posterior deltoid

Description: Sit on the floor with one leg straight in front. Loop a resistance band around the working foot. Anchor the other end to a stable point on the inside. Brace your core and keep the leg still. Rotate the foot outward against the band. Squeeze the outside of the lower leg at the end range. Return the foot to the start with control. Complete reps and switch feet.
Benefits: Strengthens the peroneals; Builds ankle stability; Useful for runners; No major equipment needed; Strong rehab move; Easy to add to a warm-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Tibialis anterior; Forearms

Description: Sit on the floor with one leg straight in front. Loop a resistance band around the working foot. Anchor the other end to a stable point on the outside. Brace your core and keep the leg still. Rotate the foot inward against the band. Squeeze the inside of the lower leg at the end range. Return the foot to the start with control. Complete reps and switch feet.
Benefits: Strengthens the inner ankle; Builds ankle stability; Useful rehab move; No major equipment needed; Strong for runners; Easy to add to a warm-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Tibialis anterior; Forearms

Description: Sit on the floor with the legs extended. Anchor a resistance band to the inside of the working foot. Loop the band around the ball of the foot. Brace your core and keep the back straight. Rotate the foot outward against the band tension. Hold briefly at the rotated position. Return with control to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds ankle stability; Trains the peroneals; Strong rehab drill; Useful for ankle health; Builds lower leg strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Tibialis anterior; Gastrocnemius

Description: Sit on the floor with the working leg extended. Loop a resistance band around the ball of the foot. Hold the band ends with both hands. Brace your core and keep the leg straight. Point the foot downward against the band tension. Squeeze the calf hard at full plantar flexion. Return with control to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains plantar flexion; Builds the calves; Strong rehab drill; Useful for ankle health; Builds lower leg
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Gastrocnemius; Soleus

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Front Plank with Single Arm Pulldown
Description: Anchor a resistance band to a sturdy point overhead. Set up in a high plank facing away from the anchor. Grab the band with one hand keeping the arm extended overhead. Brace the core and keep the body in a straight line. Pull the band down toward the same side hip by driving the elbow back. Resist rotation through the torso as you pull. Return the arm overhead with control. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains the lats and core together.; Builds anti rotation strength.; Plank position improves shoulder stability.; Carryover to athletic performance.; Develops total body coordination.; Easy to scale by adjusting band tension.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Posterior deltoid

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Place a mini band around your thighs above your knees. Push your knees outward against the band tension throughout the exercise. Brace your core. Tuck your pelvis. Drive through your full feet and lift your hips up off the floor. Continue lifting until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Maintain band tension by pushing knees out throughout.
Benefits: Activates the gluteus medius along with maximus; Excellent for total glute development; Easy to set up at home; Highly portable; Useful warm-up before squats and deadlifts; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus and medius; Hamstrings; Adductors (slight); Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Half Kneeling Face Pull
Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height. Kneel in a half kneeling position with one knee down. Grip the band ends with both hands. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Pull the band toward the face with elbows high. Squeeze the rear delts hard at the back. Drive the elbows out and back. Return with control to the start.
Benefits: Targets the rear delts; Builds the upper back; Strong shoulder health move; Trains core stability; Useful warm-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius; Rhomboids; Infraspinatus

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet hip-width apart. Grip both ends with a neutral grip — thumbs pointing up, palms facing each other. Pin your elbows at your sides. Curl the band up by bending at the elbows, maintaining the neutral grip. Squeeze at the top. Lower under control over two seconds. Use a thicker band for more resistance. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per set.
Benefits: Targets the brachialis and brachioradialis; Builds upper arm thickness; Highly portable; Easy to scale; Joint-friendly neutral grip; Useful when no dumbbells are available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Biceps brachii

Exercise Name: Resistance Band High Knee Lunge with Single Arm Row
Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height and hold the handle in one hand. Step back into a split stance facing the band anchor. Lower into a lunge by dropping the back knee toward the floor. Keep the chest tall and the front shin vertical at the bottom. Drive through the front foot and lift the back leg into a high knee. Pull the band toward your hip as the knee comes up. Squeeze the back muscles and tuck the elbow close to the side. Lower back into the lunge with control and repeat for all reps.
Benefits: Develops single leg strength in the quads and glutes.; Builds back thickness through unilateral rowing tension.; Improves balance and coordination between upper and lower body.; Trains anti rotation as the band pulls across the body.; Joint friendly resistance from the band protects the spine.; Adds explosive hip drive into a back exercise for athletic carryover.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Core

Description: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench, feet flat on the floor, knees bent at 90 degrees. Loop a resistance band across your hip crease and anchor both ends under your feet. Place your feet hip-width apart. Adjust the band until it is taut. Drive through your heels and thrust your hips up toward the ceiling. At the top, your body should form a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard. The band provides maximum tension at this top position. Lower your hips back down under control. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Adds load to hip thrusts at home; Maximum band tension at peak glute contraction; Highly portable; Excellent for glute development; Useful when no barbell is available; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Sit on the floor with upper back against a bench. Loop a resistance band across your hip crease and anchor both ends under your feet. Bend your knees at 90 degrees. Feet flat, hip-width apart. Drive through your heels to thrust your hips up. At the top, your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard. The band tension is highest here — at peak glute contraction. Lower under control. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Progressive glute loading at home; Maximum tension at peak glute contraction; Highly portable; Excellent glute builder; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no barbell is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Hip Thrusts on Knees
Description: Anchor a resistance band low to a sturdy point behind you. Loop the band around the hips at the front of the pelvis. Kneel on a pad with knees hip width apart. Sit the hips back to the heels in a kneeling start. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Thrust the hips forward driving the body up to a tall kneeling position. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top against the band. Sit back to the heels with control.
Benefits: Strong glute builder; No bench needed; Trains hip extension; Builds the hamstrings; Useful glute builder; Strong band move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Anchor a resistance band at chest height to one side. Stand far enough away to put tension on the band. Hold the handle at the center of your chest with both hands. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core hard against the band pull. Press the handle straight out from your chest to full extension. Resist the band trying to rotate you toward the anchor. Pause briefly, then bring the handle slowly back to your chest.
Benefits: Trains anti-rotation core; Builds trunk stability; Useful for athletes; Easy to set up at home; Strengthens the obliques; Carries over to lifts and sports
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis

Description: Set up a bar at hip height (in a power rack or sturdy table). Loop a resistance band across your chest (over your back, under the bar). Hang from the bar with arms extended, body in a straight line from heels to head. Row your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows down and back. The band adds resistance, making the row harder especially at the top. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to inverted rows; Builds back strength beyond bodyweight alone; Constant tension with band resistance; Useful for advanced at-home trainees; Easy to scale by band thickness; No additional equipment beyond a bar and band
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band overhead. Kneel down with the knees hip-width apart. Grab the band with both hands at the head or neck. Brace your core hard. Crunch the torso down toward the floor. Pull the band along with the torso. Squeeze the abs hard at the bottom. Return to the upright position with control.
Benefits: Loaded ab crunch; Continuous band tension; Builds ab strength; No bench needed; Useful core finisher; Strong band ab move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Kneeling Leg Half Circle on Bench
Description: Loop a resistance band around one foot. Anchor the band end to a low fixed point. Set up on hands and knees with the chest supported on a bench. Brace the core and keep the back flat. Lift the banded leg off the floor with the knee bent. Press the foot back and up against the band. Sweep the leg out to the side in a half circle. Return with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds the glute through multiple ranges.; Loads extension and abduction.; Bench keeps the back stable.; Useful glute accessory.; Joint friendly drill.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings

Description: Anchor a resistance band high above shoulder height. Kneel sideways to the anchor with the knee closer to the band on the floor. Grab the band with both hands at the high side. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Pull the band diagonally across the body to the low far hip. Rotate through the obliques as you chop. Squeeze the core at the end range. Return to the start with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong rotational core builder; Trains the obliques; Stable kneeling base; Builds power transfer; Useful core move; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low point in front of you. Lie face down on the floor with legs extended toward the anchor. Loop the band around both ankles. Move away from the anchor until the band is taut with legs extended. Curl both heels toward your glutes by bending at the knees. Squeeze your hamstrings at the top of the curl. Slowly extend your legs back to the start under control. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Isolates the hamstrings at home; Mimics the lying leg curl machine; Constant band tension throughout; Highly portable; Useful for hamstring rehab or activation; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus); Gastrocnemius (secondary)

Description: Sit on a chair or bench. Anchor a resistance band to a low point behind you. Loop the band around your right ankle. Sit tall with your right thigh on the bench, knee at 90 degrees. Extend your right knee by straightening your leg forward against the band tension. Squeeze your quadriceps hard at full extension. Slowly bend your knee back to 90 degrees under control. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Isolates the quadriceps at home; Mimics the leg extension machine; Constant band tension throughout; Highly portable; Useful for quad activation or rehab; Easy to scale by band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (all four heads)

Description: Anchor a resistance band to a low point behind your head (bed frame, pole). Lie on your back. Loop the band around both ankles. Move away from the anchor until taut. Lie flat with arms at your sides. Press your lower back into the floor. Lift both legs up toward the ceiling, keeping them straight. Continue until your legs are vertical (or as high as your core can maintain lower-back contact). Lower under control. Stop just before your feet touch the floor. Repeat. Use a thinner band for more reps or thicker for strength. If your lower back arches, bend your knees slightly.
Benefits: Adds resistance to lying leg raises; Targets the lower abs and hip flexors; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Progressive overload beyond bodyweight; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors (iliopsoas); Obliques; Quadriceps (keeping legs straight)

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with your right foot. Hold both ends at shoulder height. Step your left foot back into a lunge stance. Lower your left knee toward the floor by bending both knees. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor. Drive through your right foot to stand back up against the band tension. The band tension increases as you stand — loading the glute lockout. Complete reps on one side, then switch which foot stands on the band. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Adds progressive resistance to bodyweight lunges; Increasing tension at the top loads the lockout; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Useful when no weights are available; Builds single-leg strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Resistance Band One Arm Bent Over Row
Description: Stand with one foot on the resistance band. Grip the band end with the same side hand. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Place the free hand on the knee for support. Let the working arm hang straight down with band tension. Pull the band up toward your hip by driving the elbow back. Squeeze the lat hard at the top. Lower the band slowly back to full arm extension and repeat all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds unilateral back strength with constant tension.; Reveals and corrects strength imbalances.; Joint friendly resistance from the band.; Travel friendly with minimal equipment.; Trains anti rotation as the body resists twisting.; Easy to scale band tension by adjusting stance width.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Stand on the middle of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a handle in each hand at shoulder level. Use a pronated grip with palms facing forward. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Press both handles straight overhead. Lock out the arms with hands meeting above your head. Pause briefly at full extension. Lower the handles slowly back to shoulder level.
Benefits: Builds shoulder strength; Increasing tension at lockout; No bar or rack needed; Easy to scale by changing band tension; Joint-friendly variation; Strong home shoulder builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Triceps brachii; Traps

Description: Stand on the center of a resistance band with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold both ends overhead with arms locked out. Hands wider than shoulder-width. Brace your core. Keep arms directly overhead (in line with ears). Squat down while keeping the band locked out overhead. Descend as deep as mobility allows. Drive through your feet to stand against the band tension. Maintain the overhead position throughout. Use a lighter band — this is a mobility exercise as much as a strength exercise.
Benefits: Demands and develops overhead mobility; Builds core stability under overhead load; Band tension loads the top of the squat; Highly portable; Excellent warm-up before overhead pressing or snatching; Exposes mobility weaknesses
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior and lateral deltoid; Core (heavy stabilizer); Trapezius

Description: Stand tall. Hold a resistance band in front of you at chest height with both hands, arms extended. Start with hands about shoulder-width apart. Pull the band apart by spreading your arms to the sides. Keep arms straight. Continue until the band touches your chest and your arms are fully spread. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the end position. Slowly return to the starting position under control. Move the grip narrower for more resistance or wider for less. Maintain straight arms throughout (slight elbow bend only). Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds rear delts and upper back posture muscles; Highly portable — the most popular band exercise; Excellent warm-up before pressing; Counteracts forward-rounded shoulders; Easy to scale by grip width or band thickness; Joint-friendly and accessible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle fibers); Infraspinatus; Erector spinae (slight)

Description: Anchor a resistance band at a low point behind you (base of squat rack, door anchor, or low hook). Face away from the anchor. Step over the band and grip it between your legs with both hands. Walk forward until the band is under tension. Stand with feet slightly wider than hip-width. Hinge forward at the hips, letting the band pull your hands back between your legs. Keep your back flat. Feel a stretch in your hamstrings. Brace your core. Snap your hips forward by squeezing your glutes. Stand tall at the top. The band tension should peak at the lockout, loading the glutes maximally at full hip extension. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Effective at-home glute and hamstring exercise; Teaches the hip-hinge pattern effectively; Band tension peaks at lockout for maximum glute loading; No heavy equipment required; Useful for learning the hip hinge before progressing to deadlifts; Easy to scale by changing band thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Loop a resistance band across your upper back, under your armpits. Hold both ends of the band under your palms as you set your hands on the floor in push-up position. Get into a high plank. The band should be taut at the top position. Lower your chest to the floor. The band tension decreases as you lower. Press back up. The band tension increases as you rise, loading the lockout. Lock out at the top. The band is at maximum tension here. Continue for the desired reps. Use a thicker band for more resistance.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to push-ups; Increasing tension at the top loads the lockout; Mimics accommodating resistance from powerlifting; Highly portable; Easy to scale by band thickness; Builds chest, tricep, and shoulder strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Anchor a resistance band at roughly chest height (door frame, pole, or rack). Grip both ends of the band. Step back so the band is under tension with arms extended. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core. Row the band toward your face by driving your elbows up and out to the sides. At the peak, your elbows should be at or above shoulder height, hands at ear level. Squeeze your rear delts and mid-traps hard. Hold one second. Slowly extend forward under control. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Benefits: Targets the rear delts and mid-traps; Highly portable — needs only a band and anchor; Improves shoulder health and posture; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Useful warm-up before pressing; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Trapezius (middle fibers); Rhomboids; Infraspinatus; Biceps brachii (secondary)

Description: Stand tall. Hold a resistance band in front of you at chest height with both hands, arms extended. Palms facing down. Pull the band apart by spreading your arms to the sides. Lead with the backs of your hands. Keep arms straight. Continue until the band touches your chest. Squeeze your rear delts and shoulder blades together. Slowly return to start. Move grip narrower for more resistance. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per set.
Benefits: Isolates the rear delts with constant tension; Highly portable; Excellent warm-up for pressing; Builds shoulder balance and posture; Easy to scale; Joint-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Infraspinatus

Description: Anchor a band at a low point. Loop the other end around your feet. Lie on your back with your head away from the anchor. Bend your knees to 90 degrees. The band should be under tension at the start. Place your hands at your sides for stability. Brace your core. Pull your knees toward your chest by curling your hips off the floor. At the peak, your knees should be near your chest and your hips lifted slightly. Squeeze your lower abs hard. Lower under control back to the starting position. Maintain band tension throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Adds progressive resistance to the reverse crunch; Targets the lower abs effectively; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Highly portable; Useful when no cable machine is available; Constant tension throughout the range
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially lower); Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis; Obliques (secondary)

Exercise Name: Resistance Band Reverse Hyper with Stability Ball on Flat Bench
Description: Place a stability ball on top of a flat bench. Lie face down with the hips supported on the ball. Loop a resistance band around both ankles. Anchor the band end to a low fixed point in front. Hold the bench for stability. Brace the core and keep the back flat. Lift both legs back behind the body against the band. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top then return with control.
Benefits: Builds the glutes and hamstrings.; Trains the lower back.; Band tension grows through the lift.; Useful posterior chain accessory.; Joint friendly drill.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Loop a resistance band around both ankles. Anchor the other end of the band at a low point in front of the bench (under the bench or to a low hook). Lie face down on a flat bench with your hips at the edge so your legs hang off freely. Grip the bench for stability. The band should be under tension with your legs hanging straight down. Lift your legs up against the band tension by squeezing your glutes and hamstrings. Continue until your legs are parallel to the floor or slightly higher. Squeeze hard at the top for one second. Lower under control back to the hanging position. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Builds the glutes and hamstrings without spinal compression; Mimics a reverse hyper machine with portable equipment; Excellent for at-home training; Decompresses the lumbar spine; Easy to scale by changing band thickness; Useful rehabilitation exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Sit on a bench or chair with feet on the middle of a resistance band. Hold a handle in each hand with palms facing forward. Sit upright with your back tall.
