Brace your core and stand tall. Lower into a single-leg squat by bending your left knee. Descend until your left thigh approaches parallel to the floor. Drive up through your left heel to stand back to the starting position. Complete reps on one side, then switch the bench to your other side.
Benefits: Hits adductors and inner quad; Trains lateral hip stability; Single-leg loading corrects imbalances; Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally; Different stimulus than standard Bulgarian split squat; Improves lateral movement performance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hip stabilizers

Description: Lie on your right side. Place right forearm on floor, elbow under shoulder. Stack or stagger your feet. Lift hips until body forms a straight line. Hold for the desired time. Keep hips elevated. Breathe steadily. Switch sides. Start with 10 to 20 seconds and build to 45 to 60 seconds. One of McGill’s “Big Three” for back health.
Benefits: McGill’s recommended core exercise for back health; Builds anti-lateral flexion endurance; Develops oblique and quadratus lumborum strength; No equipment needed; Promotes spine stability; Evidence-based for back pain prevention
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius; Transverse abdominis

Description: Get into a side plank on your right forearm. Lift your left (top) leg up about 12 to 18 inches. Hold briefly. Lower under control. Continue for desired reps while maintaining the plank. Switch sides. Keep hips elevated throughout. Aim for 10 to 15 lifts per side. Builds obliques and glute medius together.
Benefits: Combines side plank with hip abduction; Builds obliques and gluteus medius together; No equipment needed; McGill-style core exercise progression; Develops hip stability; Engaging side plank variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Gluteus medius (top leg); Quadratus lumborum; Core

Description: Lie on your side with the legs stacked. Set your bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder. Stack the feet and press up into a side plank. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Reach the top arm straight up overhead in line with the body. Hold the long position with the core braced. Lower the arm back down then drop down. Switch sides.
Benefits: Advanced side plank; Builds strong obliques; Trains shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Strong core builder; Useful core finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius; Anterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Side Bridge with Arm Leg Swing
Description: Set up in a side plank with elbow under shoulder and feet stacked. Lift the hips so the body forms a straight line. Brace the core and keep the bottom side strong. Lift the top arm and the top leg into the air. Swing both the arm and leg forward toward each other. Then swing both back away from the body. Keep the hips lifted and the core braced through every swing. Complete all swings on one side then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains elite obliques and lateral core strength.; Challenges balance through dynamic limb movement.; Builds shoulder stability in the side plank position.; Improves hip mobility through the leg swings.; No equipment needed.; Carryover to athletic balance and rotational sports.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Gluteus medius; Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie on your side with the bottom knee bent and the top leg extended. Place the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder. Stack the shoulders and hips in line. Brace the core and squeeze the obliques. Lift the hips off the floor by pressing the forearm down. Form a straight line from the head through the top leg. Hold the position for the desired duration. Lower the hips and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds oblique and lateral core strength.; Bent knee setup makes the side plank accessible.; No equipment needed.; Excellent foundation for the full side plank.; Carryover to spine stability.; Develops anti lateral flexion strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius; Rectus abdominis

Description: Lie on your side with the legs extended and stacked. Place the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder. Stack the shoulders, hips, and feet in line. Brace the core and squeeze the obliques. Lift the hips off the floor by pressing the forearm down. Form a straight line from the head to the feet. Hold the position for the desired duration. Lower the hips and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds full oblique and lateral core strength.; Trains the glute medius for hip stability.; No equipment needed.; Excellent foundation for advanced plank work.; Carryover to spine stability.; Develops anti lateral flexion strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius; Rectus abdominis; Adductors

Description: Lie on your back, knees bent. Drop both knees to the right side. Hands behind your head. Crunch straight up — the rotated leg position targets the left obliques. Squeeze at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps, then drop knees to the left and crunch for the right obliques. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side. Alternatively, lie on your side and crunch laterally.
Benefits: Directly targets the obliques; Simple floor exercise; No equipment needed; Builds oblique definition; Easy to learn; Accessible for all levels
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis (secondary)

Description: Lie on your back on the floor. Bend both knees with feet flat on the floor. Drop both knees together to your right side. Place your hands behind your head with elbows wide. Brace your abs hard. Crunch your left obliques by lifting your shoulders off the floor. Lift the left shoulder higher than the right toward the ceiling. Squeeze the obliques at the top, then lower with control. Switch sides after the set.
Benefits: Direct oblique isolation; No equipment required; Builds oblique strength; Easy to scale by adjusting range; Useful for oblique specialization; Strong mind-muscle connection
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Rectus abdominis; Core

Exercise Name: Side Crunch with Hands on Chest
Description: Lie on your side with legs stacked and slightly bent. Cross both hands over your chest. Place the bottom arm under the torso for support if needed. Brace the obliques and lift the top shoulder off the floor. Crunch the side body to lift the rib cage toward the hip. Squeeze the obliques hard at the top. Lower the shoulder back to the start with control. Complete all reps on one side then switch sides.
Benefits: Isolates the obliques without using the arms or neck.; Beginner friendly side core exercise.; Builds lateral core strength.; Improves rotational core control.; No equipment needed.; Easy to scale by changing leg position.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand tall. Hold a wall for balance. Shift weight to your left leg. Lift your right leg straight out to the right side. Lift to about 30 to 45 degrees. Keep torso upright. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side. Add an ankle weight for progression.
Benefits: Targets the gluteus medius; Builds hip abductor strength; No equipment needed; Useful for warm-up and rehab; Improves hip stability; Accessible for all levels
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius and minimus; Tensor fasciae latae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Sit on a hip adduction machine with the back flat against the pad. Set the inner thighs against the leg pads. Grip the handles for stability. Brace your core and set the feet on the foot platforms. Squeeze the legs together pressing the pads inward. Hold the squeeze hard at the bottom. Pause briefly at the contracted position. Return to the start with control.
Benefits: Strong adductor builder; Constant lever resistance; Easy to scale loading; Builds inner thigh strength; Useful adductor isolation; Strong machine move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Adductors; Gracilis; Pectineus

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step your right foot out wide to the right. Sit your hips back and bend your right knee, keeping your left leg straight. Lower as deep as your mobility allows. Drive through your right foot to push back to standing. Alternate sides or complete all reps on one side. Keep your torso upright. Chest tall. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds lateral movement strength; Develops adductor flexibility; Improves hip mobility; No equipment needed; Useful for athletes in lateral-movement sports; Builds frontal-plane leg strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (bending leg); Adductors (both legs); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your right side on the floor. Stack your hips and shoulders directly on top of each other. Bend your knees to roughly 45 degrees. Stack your left leg directly on top of your right leg. Rest your head on your right arm or a pillow. Place your left hand on your left hip to feel the muscle work. Brace your core gently. Keep your hips stacked — do not roll backward. Keep your feet pressed together. Lift your top (left) knee away from your bottom knee by externally rotating at the hip. Continue lifting until you feel the contraction in your upper outer glute. Do not roll your hips back to lift higher. Pause briefly at the top, then lower your knee under control back to the starting stacked position. Complete all reps on one side, then roll over and repeat on the other side. Add a resistance band around the knees for more challenge.
Benefits: Direct activation of the gluteus medius; Improves hip stability and balance; Excellent warm-up before squats and deadlifts; Helps prevent IT band issues and knee pain; Useful for rehabilitation and return-to-training; No equipment needed — works anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus minimus; Piriformis (deep external rotator); Other deep hip rotators

Exercise Name: Side Lying Diagonal Backward Leg Raise
Description: Lie on one side on the floor. Set the bottom leg bent for stability. Keep the top leg straight. Rest the head on the bottom arm. Brace the core and keep the hips stacked. Lift the top leg back and up at a diagonal angle. Squeeze the glute hard at the top. Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates the glute medius.; Trains the outer glute.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for hip stability.; Builds glute size.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Lie on your side with legs straight and stacked. Set the bottom arm under the head for support. Place the top hand on the hip. Brace your core hard. Lift both feet up off the floor together. Continue lifting until the legs are at an angle to the floor. Squeeze the obliques and glute medius at the top. Lower with control. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Trains glute medius; No equipment needed; Builds hip stability; Useful core builder; Easy to do anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Gluteus medius; Quadratus lumborum

Description: Lie on your right side. Stack your hips. Rest your head on your right arm. Bend your left knee and place your left foot flat on the floor in front of your right thigh. Keep your right (bottom) leg straight. Flex the right foot. Brace your core. Lift your right leg straight up toward the ceiling as high as comfortable. Squeeze your inner thigh at the top. Lower the right leg under control back toward the floor. Stop just before it touches. Repeat for 12 to 20 reps. Switch sides and repeat.
Benefits: Direct inner-thigh isolation with no equipment; Helps prevent groin strains; Builds adductor strength for squats and deadlifts; Useful rehabilitation exercise; Works at home; Easy to scale with ankle weights
Muscles Worked (Raw): Adductor magnus, longus, brevis; Gracilis; Pectineus

Description: Lie on your right side with legs stacked and straight. Support your head with your right hand. Lift your left (top) leg straight up toward the ceiling. Lift to about 30 to 45 degrees. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Keep your hips stacked — do not let the top hip roll back. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Benefits: Most basic gluteus medius isolation; Standard physical therapy exercise; No equipment needed; Builds hip abductor strength; Improves hip stability; Beginner-friendly
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius and minimus; Tensor fasciae latae; Gluteus maximus (slight)

Description: Lie on your side with the knees bent at forty five degrees. Stack the hips and shoulders in line. Keep the feet together throughout the movement. Brace the core and engage the glutes. Lift the top knee away from the bottom knee. Stop when the hips begin to rotate backward. Squeeze the glute at the top of the rep. Lower with control and repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Trains the glute medius and hip abductors.; Improves hip stability for running and lifting.; No equipment needed.; Excellent warm up before squats and deadlifts.; Carryover to single leg balance.; Reduces knee valgus on heavy squats.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Tensor fasciae latae; Obliques

Description: Lie on your right side with legs extended and stacked. Support your head with your right hand. Lift your top (left) leg up. As you lower it, lift your bottom (right) leg up. Continue alternating in a scissor pattern. The top leg works the abductors; the bottom leg works the adductors. Move with control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 15 to 20 scissors per side.
Benefits: Works both hip abductors and adductors; No equipment needed; Engaging side-lying exercise; Builds hip stability; Useful warm-up or rehab; Develops coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius (top leg); Hip adductors (bottom leg); Obliques (stabilizer); Core

Description: Lie on your right side with your right forearm flat on the floor, elbow directly under your shoulder. Stack your left foot on top of your right foot, with legs straight. Brace your core hard and lift your hips off the floor by pressing through your right forearm and the side of your right foot. Form a straight line from your head to your heels. Your body should look like a sideways plank from any angle. Pull your right shoulder away from your ear — do not let it shrug up. Place your left hand on your hip or extend it straight up. Hold this position for the desired duration. Breathe normally throughout. To finish, lower your hips back to the floor under control. Switch sides and repeat. Aim for 20 to 60 seconds per side, building duration as you get stronger.
Benefits: Builds the obliques and lateral core strength; Trains the core to resist sideways collapse (anti-lateral-flexion); Improves hip stability and shoulder stability; Carries over to all lifts and athletic movements; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Excellent for lower-back health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius (top hip stabilizer); Transverse abdominis; Serratus anterior (supporting shoulder); Adductors (top leg)

Description: Get into a side plank on your right forearm. Stack your feet. Cross your top (left) foot in front of or behind your bottom (right) foot and place it on the floor for stability. Your bottom (right) leg is now free. Lift your bottom right leg upward toward the ceiling. Squeeze your right inner thigh (adductor) at the top. Lower under control. Continue for 10 to 15 reps, then switch sides. Maintain the side plank throughout.
Benefits: Targets the inner thigh (adductors) of the bottom leg; Builds core anti-lateral flexion simultaneously; Unique side plank variation; No equipment needed; Useful for adductor strengthening; Develops hip stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Adductors (bottom leg); Obliques (side plank hold); Quadratus lumborum; Gluteus medius (top leg, stabilizer); Core

Description: Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor. Bend the bottom knee for support. Stack the hips and shoulders. Brace your core and lift the hips into a side plank. Extend the top leg straight. Lift the top leg up toward the ceiling. Squeeze the glute medius at the top. Lower with control. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Loads the obliques; Trains the glute medius; Strong side plank variation; Useful for athletes; Builds the core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Gluteus medius; Core

Description: Lie on your right side with legs stacked. Prop yourself up on your right forearm with elbow under shoulder. Position your feet stacked or staggered. Place your left hand on your hip or extend it overhead. Brace your core hard. Lift your hips off the floor into a side plank position. Hold a straight line from head to heels. Hold for the duration. Lower hips down with control. Switch sides.
Benefits: Builds isometric oblique strength; Strong shoulder stability work; No equipment required; Develops anti-lateral flexion strength; Easy to scale by adjusting time; Useful for core training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Quadratus lumborum; Anterior deltoid

Description: Get into a side plank on your right forearm. Body in a straight line. Extend your left arm toward the ceiling. Reach your left arm under your body — threading it between your torso and the floor. Pull your left arm back up and open to the ceiling by rotating your torso. Continue the reach-and-pull for the desired reps. Maintain the side plank throughout. Complete reps, then switch sides. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines side plank with rotational movement; Builds oblique strength with thoracic mobility; Develops anti-lateral flexion core; No equipment needed; Engaging dynamic plank variation; Improves thoracic rotation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (anti-lateral flexion); Rectus abdominis; Posterior deltoid and trapezius (pulling motion); Gluteus medius (hip stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your right side. Wrap your right arm across your chest. Place your left hand on the floor in front of your chest. Press your torso up off the floor by extending your left arm. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. The range of motion is limited but effective for triceps. Keep your hips on the floor — only your torso lifts. Aim for 12 to 20 reps per side.
Benefits: Simple floor tricep exercise; No equipment needed; Isolates one arm at a time; Accessible for all levels; Useful when standard push-ups are too hard; Builds basic pressing strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (slight)

Description: Get into a side plank on your right forearm. Body straight. Lift your left (top) leg straight up about 12 to 18 inches. Hold briefly at the top. Lower under control. Continue for the desired reps while maintaining the plank. Switch sides. Keep hips elevated and stacked throughout. Aim for 10 to 15 lifts per side.
Benefits: Combines side plank with hip abduction; Builds obliques and gluteus medius together; No equipment needed; Engaging side plank variation; Develops hip and core stability; Builds the outer hip
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (plank hold); Gluteus medius (top leg lift); Core (anti-lateral flexion); Quadratus lumborum

Description: Lie on your right side. Stack your legs. Anchor your feet or have a partner hold them. Place your left hand behind your head. Laterally flex your spine — lift your torso off the floor sideways. Rise as high as possible. Squeeze your left oblique. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. This is a direct oblique exercise through lateral flexion. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Direct oblique loading through lateral flexion; Isolates one side at a time; No equipment needed; Builds oblique strength and definition; Simple and effective; Develops lateral core power
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (working side); Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand in a very wide stance. Toes pointed slightly out. Shift your weight to the right. Bend your right knee deeply. Keep your left leg completely straight. Left heel stays on the floor. Lower as deep as possible — ideally your right hamstring contacts your right calf. Drive through your right foot to return to center. Repeat on the left side. Keep your torso upright or lean slightly forward. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per side.
Benefits: Builds extreme adductor flexibility; Develops deep lateral squat mobility; Tests and builds hip mobility; No equipment needed; Useful for martial artists and dancers; Develops frontal-plane leg strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (bending leg); Adductors (both legs); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (straight leg, stretched); Calves (ankle mobility)

Description: Stand in a wide stance — 1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width. Toes slightly out. Shift your weight to the right. Bend your right knee, sitting into that hip. Keep your left leg relatively straight. Lower as deep as your mobility allows. Drive through your right foot to return to center. Shift to the left side. Repeat. Keep torso upright throughout. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Targets quads and adductors unilaterally; Builds lateral movement strength; Develops hip mobility; No equipment needed; Stationary stance is easier to balance than stepping; Useful for warm-up or conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (bending leg); Adductors; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core hard and keep the hips level. Step one hand and the same side foot out wide to one side. Step the other hand and foot to follow. Continue side stepping in the same direction. Keep the body in a straight line throughout. Reverse direction and side step back.
Benefits: Brutal core and shoulder builder; Trains the gluteus medius; Builds lateral stability; No equipment needed; Useful core finisher; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Gluteus medius; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Raise your right arm overhead and place your left hand on your hip. Brace your core and stand tall. Lean to the left, reaching the right arm over your head. Feel a stretch in your right obliques. Crunch laterally back to the right by contracting the right obliques. Squeeze the obliques as you return upright. Repeat for desired reps, then switch sides.
Benefits: Combines stretch and contraction; Builds oblique strength; Improves lateral mobility; No equipment required; Useful for waist and oblique training; Strong oblique engagement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (internal and external); Quadratus lumborum; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Loop a resistance band around both legs above the knees. Anchor a second band at chest height and grip a handle in each hand. Step back to take tension on the chest band. Set a quarter squat stance with feet hip width. Brace your core and pinch the shoulder blades. Take a side step out wide while rowing the elbows back. Squeeze the rear delts and glute medius at the top. Step back together. Continue side stepping in one direction.
Benefits: Combo glute and back move; Trains the gluteus medius; Builds rear delts; Useful warm-up move; Strong band combo; Builds shoulder posture
Muscles Worked (Raw): Posterior deltoid; Gluteus medius; Rhomboids; Trapezius

Description: Get into a side plank on your right forearm. Left hand behind your head. Body in a straight line from heels to head. Bring your left elbow and left knee toward each other by crunching at the waist. Squeeze your left oblique at the crunch. Extend back to the straight side plank position. Continue for the desired reps. Switch sides and repeat. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines static and dynamic oblique loading; Builds oblique strength and definition; No equipment needed; Engaging side plank variation; Develops hip and shoulder stability; Useful for core development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (primary); Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors (knee drive); Gluteus medius (bottom leg stabilizer); Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand tall with feet together and arms at your chest for balance. Step one foot wide out to the side. Plant the foot and immediately drop into a wide squat. Sit your hips back and keep your chest up. Continue until your thighs are parallel to the floor. Drive up and step the foot back to center. Stand tall briefly. Step out to the other side and squat. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Builds the adductors; Trains lateral movement; Combines strength and conditioning; No equipment required; Useful for athletes; Strong leg builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Hamstrings

Description: Hang from a pull up bar with an underhand shoulder width grip. Engage the lats and brace the core. Pull yourself up toward the bar. Near the top, shift your body to one side so that side bears more load. Pause briefly at the shifted top position. Lower yourself slowly back to a full hang. Pull up again and shift to the opposite side. Continue alternating sides for all reps.
Benefits: Builds unilateral lat and biceps strength.; Challenges grip and forearm endurance.; Develops control and stability at the top of the chin.; Carryover to harder pulling progressions like one arm chins.; Hits the upper back hard.; Bodyweight loading scales naturally with strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Forearm flexors

Description: Get into a push-up position. Place feet wider than shoulder-width for stability. Remove one hand — place it behind your back. Lower your chest toward the floor using only the support arm. Press back up to lockout. Fight rotation — keep your hips as level as possible. Switch arms. This is extremely advanced. Progress through archer push-ups first. Aim for 1 to 5 reps per arm.
Benefits: Elite unilateral pressing strength; Extreme core anti-rotation demand; One of the most impressive bodyweight exercises; No equipment needed; Builds pressing power per arm; Tests total-body control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (pressing arm); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core (extreme anti-rotation); Obliques

Exercise Name: Single Arm Push Up on Medicine Ball
Description: Place a medicine ball on the floor. Set up in a high plank with one hand on the ball and the other on the floor. Spread the feet wide for added stability. Brace the core and keep the body in a straight line. Lower the chest toward the hands by bending the elbows. Stop when the chest is just above the hands. Press back up to the start position. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds unilateral chest and triceps strength.; Med ball adds instability for core engagement.; Trains anti rotation through the torso.; Carryover to one arm push up progressions.; Improves shoulder stability.; Develops total upper body coordination.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Obliques; Rectus abdominis

Description: Lie on your side with the legs stacked. Set the bottom forearm on the floor under the shoulder. Stack the feet and press up into a side plank. Set the body in a straight line. Brace your core and squeeze the glutes. Lift the top leg high while holding the side plank. Hold the elevated position briefly. Lower the leg with control. Drop down then switch sides.
Benefits: Strong glute medius builder; Trains the obliques; Combo side plank move; No equipment needed; Useful for athletes; Strong hip stability move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Obliques; Quadratus lumborum

Exercise Name: Single Arm Side Straight Arm Lat Pulldown
Description: Set a cable handle at high height. Stand sideways to the cable with the working arm closer. Grab the handle with a slight elbow bend. Step back to set tension and stand tall. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Pull the handle down across the body to the hip. Squeeze the lat hard at the bottom. Return with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates the lat.; Single arm focus exposes weakness.; Trains the back without bicep involvement.; Useful lat finisher.; Builds back width.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Teres major; Triceps brachii

Exercise Name: Single Arm Push Up Supported Wall
Description: Stand facing a sturdy wall about an arms length away. Place one hand flat on the wall at chest height. Tuck the other arm behind your back. Step the feet back so your body angles forward toward the wall. Brace the core and keep the body straight from heels to head. Bend the working elbow and lower your chest toward the wall. Press through the palm to push back to full arm extension. Complete all reps on one arm then switch.
Benefits: Trains unilateral pushing strength with reduced load.; Beginner friendly progression toward one arm push ups.; Builds chest, triceps, and shoulder stability.; No equipment beyond a wall.; Trains anti rotation as the body resists twisting.; Easy to scale by stepping closer or farther from the wall.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core

Exercise Name: Single Dumbbell Decline Overhead Sit Up
Description: Lie back on a decline bench with feet secured under the pads. Hold a dumbbell with both hands directly over your chest. Press the dumbbell up so the arms are straight overhead. Brace the core and keep the arms locked straight throughout. Sit up by curling the upper body toward the knees. Keep the dumbbell tracking straight overhead the whole way up. Lower back down to the bench with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hammers the abs through the loaded sit up.; Decline angle increases the demand on the core.; Trains shoulder stability with the overhead hold.; Builds full body strength through coordination.; Easy to scale weight up or down.; Carryover to overhead lifting and athletic core.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Stand on one leg with a slight bend in the knee. Lift the opposite foot just off the floor. Bring the hands up into a guard position. Brace the core and engage the glute on the standing leg. Throw a cross punch with one hand by rotating the torso. Bring the hand back to the guard. Throw a cross punch with the other hand. Continue alternating for the desired duration then switch standing legs.
Benefits: Builds single leg balance and core stability.; Trains rotational power through the punches.; No equipment needed.; Carryover to athletic performance.; Improves total body coordination.; Easy to scale by holding light weights.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Gluteus medius; Anterior deltoid; Rectus abdominis; Quadriceps

Description: Stand on your right leg in front of a bench, facing away from it. Extend your left leg forward. Squat down on your right leg until your glutes touch the bench. Lightly sit — do not fully relax. Drive through your right foot to stand back up on one leg. Complete reps, then switch legs. Adjust bench height for difficulty — lower is harder. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per leg.
Benefits: Excellent pistol squat regression; Bench provides safety and consistent depth; Builds single-leg squat strength; Adjustable difficulty by bench height; No weights needed; Develops balance and control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Calves

Exercise Name: Single Leg Bridge with Hip Flexion
Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Pull one knee toward the chest and hold it there. Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes. Place the arms at the sides palms down. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Drive through the planted foot to lift the hips. Squeeze the working glute hard at the top. Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates one glute.; Hip flexion of the off leg increases load.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for glute imbalances.; Builds glute strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Single Leg Calf Raise Off Step
Description: Stand on a step with the ball of your right foot on the edge. Heel hanging off. Tuck your left foot behind your right ankle. Hold a wall for balance. Lower your right heel as far as possible for a deep stretch. Press through the ball of your foot to raise as high as possible. Squeeze your calf at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per leg.
Benefits: Full range of motion from step; Doubles calf demand per leg; Exposes left-right calf imbalances; No weights needed for effective training; Available on any staircase; Builds calf size and strength unilaterally
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (working leg); Soleus; Achilles tendon

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Extend your left leg straight up toward the ceiling (or straight forward). Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up. Squeeze your right glute at the top. Body forms a line from right knee to shoulders. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs. Keep your hips level — do not let the unsupported side drop. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per leg.
Benefits: Doubles glute demand per leg; Exposes left-right imbalances; Builds single-leg hip extension strength; No equipment needed; Develops core anti-rotation; Progresses to weighted single-leg bridges
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Single Leg Bridge with Outstretched Leg
Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Extend one leg straight out at hip level. Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes. Place the arms at the sides palms down. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Drive through the planted foot to lift the hips. Squeeze the working glute hard at the top. Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates one glute.; Straight leg increases instability.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for glute imbalances.; Builds glute strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Single Leg Deadlift with Knee Lift
Description: Stand on one leg with a slight knee bend. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Hinge at the hip and lift the back leg behind you. Lower the torso toward parallel with the floor. Stand back up to the starting position. Drive the back knee up high in front of you. Pause briefly at the high knee position. Lower the knee. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds balance; Strong combo move; Trains the hamstrings; Builds the glutes; Useful functional move; Trains the core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Hip Flexors; Core

Exercise Name: Single Leg Glute Bridge with External Rotation
Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Lift one foot off the floor and rotate the knee out to the side. Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes. Place the arms at the sides palms down. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Drive through the planted foot to lift the hips. Squeeze the working glute and side glute at the top. Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates one glute.; External rotation loads the side glute.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for hip stability.; Builds the glute medius.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings

Exercise Name: Single Leg Glute Bridge with Knee to Chest
Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Pull one knee tight to the chest with both hands. Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Drive through the planted foot to lift the hips. Squeeze the working glute hard at the top. Lower the hips with control to the start. Continue for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Isolates one glute.; Knee to chest fixes the off side.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for glute imbalances.; Builds glute strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Hip flexors

Description: Sit with your upper back against a bench and feet flat on the floor. Lift your right leg off the floor and extend it straight in front of you, parallel to the floor. Plant your left foot firmly. This is your working leg. Drive through your left heel and squeeze your left glute to lift your hips. Continue until your body forms a straight line from your left knee to your shoulders. Keep your right leg lifted. Squeeze your left glute hard at the top for one to two seconds. Keep hips level — do not let the right side drop. Lower under control. Complete all reps on the left, then switch. If too difficult, place the non-working foot lightly on the floor for assistance.
Benefits: Builds unilateral glute strength; Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances; More challenging than two-legged thrusts at the same bodyweight; Trains anti-rotation core stability; Carries over to single-leg athletic performance; No equipment needed beyond a bench
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Gluteus medius (hip stability); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Hip flexors (lifted leg, isometric)

Description: Set a low box or sturdy chair behind you. Stand on one leg in front of the box. Extend the other leg forward off the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Sit back and squat down to lightly tap the box with the hips. Keep the working knee tracking over the toe. Drive through the working heel to stand back up. Lock out at the top. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Strong unilateral builder; Box ensures consistent depth; Trains balance and stability; No equipment beyond a box; Builds the glutes; Useful pistol squat progression
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Lie on your back with one knee bent and the foot flat on the floor. Extend the other leg straight out. Place the arms at your sides for support. Brace the core and squeeze the glute on the working side. Drive the hips up powerfully through the planted heel. Allow the planted foot to leave the floor at the top of the bridge. Land softly back into the bridge position. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds explosive glute power.; Single leg setup trains unilateral strength.; No equipment needed.; Carryover to sprinting and jumping.; Improves hip extension force.; Develops total posterior chain strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Adductors

Description: Stand on one leg in front of a low seat or box. Lift the other leg slightly off the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Lower the hips back and down. Tap the seat lightly with the glutes. Drive through the planted foot to stand back up. Keep the lifted leg off the floor throughout. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds single leg strength; Strong pistol progression; Useful for athletes; Builds the quads; Trains balance; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Stand with your right foot on a box or step (12 to 18 inches). Left foot on the floor. Drive explosively through your right foot to jump upward. Extend your right hip, knee, and ankle to generate maximum height. Land softly back on the box with your right foot. Left foot taps down for stability if needed. Reset and repeat. Complete reps, then switch legs. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per leg.
Benefits: Builds single-leg explosive power; Develops jumping and sprinting ability; Exposes left-right power imbalances; Plyometric training for athletes; Simple setup with a box; Builds reactive strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Calves; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand on one leg with the other foot on a slider. Set the working leg with a slight knee bend. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Slide the slider foot back behind you. Hinge slightly at the hip as the foot slides back. Pull the slider foot back to the start by engaging the glute. Squeeze the glute hard at the top. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the hamstrings; Trains balance; Strong glute builder; Useful for athletes; Trains single leg control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Core

Exercise Name: Single Leg Sliding Floor Bridge Curl on Towel
Description: Place a small towel under one heel on a smooth floor. Lie on your back with both knees bent. Lift the hips into a glute bridge position. Lift the non working foot off the floor. Brace the core and keep the hips lifted. Slide the working heel out away from your body by extending the knee. Pull the heel back toward the hips by bending the knee. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds unilateral hamstring strength.; Bridge position keeps the hips active throughout.; No equipment needed beyond a towel.; Excellent at home alternative to single leg curls.; Improves hamstring eccentric control.; Carryover to running and sprinting.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves; Erector spinae

Description: Stand facing a sturdy vertical pole, doorway, squat rack upright, or TRX handle. Grip the support with both hands at chest height. Lift your right leg straight forward, parallel to the floor. Stand on your left leg. Slowly lower into a single-leg squat by sitting your hips back and bending your standing knee. Use your hands on the support to assist with balance. Pull lightly only as needed. Descend as low as comfortable while keeping the lifted leg extended. Drive through your standing foot to push back to standing. Switch sides.
Benefits: Builds toward unassisted pistol squat; Allows deeper squat depth than unassisted; Builds single-leg strength progressively; Trains balance gradually; Joint-friendly; Useful for rehabilitation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and medius; Hamstrings; Calves; Hip flexors (extended leg); Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Single Straight Leg Glute Bridge Hold
Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Extend one leg straight out at hip level. Keep the other foot planted close to the glutes. Place the arms at the sides palms down. Brace the core and drive through the planted foot. Lift the hips to full extension. Hold the bridge position isometrically. Continue for the working time then switch sides.
Benefits: Isolates one glute.; Isometric hold builds endurance.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for glute activation.; Builds glute strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Sit on the floor with upper back on a bench. Place one foot flat on the floor in front of you. Lift the other leg straight off the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Drive the hips up explosively through the planted heel. Let the planted foot leave the floor at the top. Land soft with the foot back on the floor. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds glute power; Strong explosive move; Useful for athletes; Trains the glutes; Builds single leg strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Quadriceps

Description: Stand on one leg on a box or step (12 to 20 inches high). Extend your free leg forward off the edge of the box. Squat down on your standing leg slowly and with control. Continue until the heel of your free leg lightly touches the floor. Drive through your standing foot to stand back up. Complete reps, then switch legs. Adjust box height for difficulty — taller box means more range. Aim for 6 to 10 reps per leg.
Benefits: Excellent pistol squat progression; Controlled range of motion via box height; Builds single-leg squat strength; Develops balance and control; No equipment needed besides a box; Scalable by adjusting box height
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (standing leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Calves

Description: Stand in front of a box or step. Place your right foot on top. Drive through your right foot to step up. Stand fully on the box. Step back down with your left foot leading. Complete reps, then switch legs. Do not push off with the back foot — let the front leg do the work. Keep torso upright. Box height determines difficulty — higher is harder. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per leg.
Benefits: Builds single-leg strength with bodyweight; Develops balance and coordination; No weights needed; Adjustable difficulty by box height; Exposes left-right imbalances; Progresses to weighted step-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (stepping leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Single Leg Stand on Bosu Ball
Description: Place a bosu ball dome side up on the floor. Step one foot onto the center of the dome. Lift the other foot off the floor. Set the arms out to the sides for balance. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Hold the single leg balance position. Continue for the working time. Switch sides and repeat.
Benefits: Trains ankle stability.; Builds core stability.; Useful for athletes.; Improves balance.; Joint friendly drill.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Core; Gluteus medius; Tibialis anterior

Exercise Name: Single Leg Step Up on Bench
Description: Stand facing a bench with one foot on top. Place the other foot flat on the floor behind. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Drive through the bench foot to step up. Bring the trail foot up to meet the lead. Stand tall on top of the bench briefly. Step the trail foot back down to the floor. Continue for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the quads and glutes.; Trains balance and unilateral strength.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for athletes.; Improves leg drive.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Calves

Description: Stand tall holding a sturdy support (squat rack pole, wall, or chair) with one hand for balance. Rise up onto the balls of your feet. Bend your knees and let them travel forward as you lean your torso backward, keeping your hips in line with your knees and shoulders. Maintain a straight line from your knees through your hips to your shoulders. Lower as deep as comfortable — your knees will travel far forward. Drive through the balls of your feet to stand back up. Squeeze your quads hard at the top. Repeat for 8 to 12 reps. Use light load to start — this is intense.
Benefits: Isolates the quadriceps; Stretches the rectus femoris under load; Builds quad size and definition; No equipment needed beyond support; Useful for quad-focused leg days; Different stimulus than standard squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy isolation); Hip flexors (rectus femoris); Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand on your right leg. Bend your left knee behind you so your left foot hovers behind. Extend your arms forward for counterbalance. Squat down on your right leg — sitting back and down. Lower until your left knee lightly touches the floor (or a pad). Drive through your right foot to stand back up. Complete reps, then switch legs. Place a pad behind you for the rear knee to touch for depth reference. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per leg.
Benefits: Single-leg squat without hip flexor flexibility demands; Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally; Requires less flexibility than pistol squats; No equipment needed; Develops balance and control; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Calves

Description: Stand in front of a sturdy chair or bench with your back to it. Feet shoulder-width apart. Cross your arms in front of your chest, or extend them forward for balance. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Sit your hips back and down toward the chair. Lower until your butt lightly touches the chair (do not fully sit — touch and go). Immediately drive through your feet to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for 10 to 20 reps. Use a higher chair for an easier version.
Benefits: Beginner-friendly squat pattern; Chair provides depth control; Builds confidence in the squat; Excellent rehabilitation exercise; Useful for elderly fitness; No equipment needed besides a chair
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat. Anchor feet or leave free. Hands behind your head, across your chest, or extended forward. Sit up by flexing your spine. Rise to a full upright seated position. Lower under control back to the floor. Do not pull on your neck if hands are behind your head. Move with control — do not use momentum. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set. Classic ab exercise used since the beginning of fitness training.
Benefits: Classic ab exercise — simple and effective; Full range of spinal flexion; No equipment needed; Builds rectus abdominis strength; Universally known and accessible; Progressive with weight or decline
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques (secondary)

Exercise Name: Sit Up with Arms on Chest
Description: Lie on the back with the knees bent and feet flat. Cross the arms over the chest. Brace the core and keep the chin tucked slightly. Lift the upper body up off the floor. Continue lifting until the elbows reach the thighs. Squeeze the abs hard at the top. Lower with control to the start. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the abs.; Trains the hip flexors.; Hands on chest removes momentum.; Bodyweight move.; Useful for core size.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Exercise Name: Sled 45 Degrees Narrow Stance Leg Press
Description: Sit in a 45 degree leg press machine. Place the feet close together on the platform. Set the toes pointing slightly out. Brace your core and grip the handles. Release the safeties. Lower the platform until the knees are deep. Press the platform back up through the heels. Stop just short of locking the knees.
Benefits: Targets the outer quads; Loads the legs heavy; Strong quad builder; Useful for leg size; Builds the legs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Sit on the leg press machine with your back firmly against the pad. Place your feet on the platform shoulder-width apart, roughly in the center. Release the safety handles and straighten your legs to take the weight. Do not lock your knees fully at the top. Brace your core and keep your lower back pressed firmly against the pad throughout. Lower the sled by bending at the knees and hips. Allow your knees to travel toward your chest. Descend until your thighs reach roughly 90 degrees or until your lower back begins to round off the pad — stop before rounding. Drive the sled back up by pressing through your full foot. Do not lock your knees at the top. Adjust foot position: higher on the platform biases glutes/hamstrings, lower biases quads, wider biases adductors. Re-engage the safety handles before exiting the machine.
Benefits: Allows extremely heavy quad and glute loading in a guided path; Removes balance demand and upper-body involvement; Reduced lower-back stress compared to squats; Foot position adjustments bias different muscles; Allows safe training to failure with the safety stops; Easy to load progressively with plates
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (secondary); Adductors (wider stance); Calves (secondary)

Description: Sit on an angled leg press sled with the back flat against the pad. Place one foot on the platform centered with the hip. Set the other foot off to the side. Grip the handles for stability. Brace your core and unrack the sled. Lower the sled by bending the working knee. Continue lowering until the knee is near the chest. Press the sled back up to extension. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Strong unilateral leg builder; Heavy load capacity; Builds the glutes; Useful for leg symmetry; Strong machine move; Builds quad size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Exercise Name: Sled Calf Press on Leg Press
Description: Sit on a leg press machine with the back flat against the pad. Set the platform load with the appropriate weight. Place the balls of the feet on the bottom edge of the platform. Set the heels hanging off the edge. Press the sled to extend the legs to almost lockout. Brace your core and unrack the safeties. Let the heels drop below the platform to stretch. Press the platform up by rising onto the toes squeezing the calves.
Benefits: Heavy calf builder; Easy to overload; Builds calf size; Useful calf builder; Strong machine move; Trains the gastrocnemius
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Exercise Name: Sled 45 Degrees Wide Stance Leg Press
Description: Sit in a 45 degree leg press machine with your back against the pad. Place your feet on the platform in a wide stance with toes turned out. Unrack the safeties and lower the platform under control. Bend the knees toward your shoulders while keeping the lower back pinned. Lower until your thighs nearly touch the chest or you reach end range. Press through the heels to drive the platform back up. Stop just before the knees lock to keep tension on the legs. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hits the adductors and inner thighs with the wide stance.; Builds glute and quad strength simultaneously.; Loads the legs without spinal compression.; Easy to load heavy with sled stability.; Trains a strong squat pattern variation.; Excellent leg builder for hypertrophy.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Adductors; Hamstrings

Description: Hang from a set of gymnastic rings or a pull-up bar with arms extended. Engage your core. Lift your knees up toward your chest in a tuck. Continue tucking — bring your knees up between your hands and through your arms. Continue rotating backward by extending your hips up and back. Allow your body to rotate fully into an inverted hang behind your hands. At the bottom, your body is upside down with arms extended overhead behind you. Hold briefly. Reverse the motion: tuck your knees back through your arms and unroll forward to the start hang. This is an advanced skill. Build up with assisted versions and shoulder mobility work first.
Benefits: Builds elite shoulder mobility; Develops grip and core strength; Foundational ring skill; Trains full-body control; Useful for advancing to other ring skills; Stretches the chest and shoulders deeply
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (stretched); Pectoralis major (stretched); Anterior deltoid (stretched); Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip; Core (heavy involvement); Hip flexors

Description: Step into the hack squat sled and place your shoulders against the pads. Position your feet on the platform with feet close together. Release the safety handles and brace your core. Lower yourself by bending the knees. Sit your hips back as you descend. Continue down until your thighs are at or just below parallel. Drive through your heels and the balls of your feet to stand. Lock the safeties at the top after the final rep.
Benefits: Targets the outer quad sweep; Builds the vastus lateralis; Stable, guided machine path; Easy to load progressively; Reduces lower back strain; Useful for quad development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (vastus lateralis); Quadriceps (vastus medialis); Gluteus maximus

Exercise Name: Sled One Leg Calf Press on Leg Press
Description: Set up on a leg press machine and unrack the safeties. Place the ball of one foot near the bottom edge of the platform. Remove the other foot from the platform. Press the platform up by extending the ankle of the working foot. Stop at full plantar flexion and squeeze the calf. Lower the platform by bending the ankle for a stretch. Continue for all reps without locking the knee. Switch sides and repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Trains the calves and soleus unilaterally.; Long stretch position builds calf size.; Carryover to running and sprinting.; Easy to load heavy on the leg press.; Improves single leg ankle strength.; Adds variety to standing calf raises.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Tibialis posterior

Description: Load a power sled and grip the handles. Lean forward into the sled with arms extended. Place the feet hip width apart with the heels down. Brace your core and keep the legs straight. Press up onto the balls of the feet. Squeeze the calves hard at the top. Lower with control to the floor. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Loads the calves; Strong sled variation; Builds the calves; Useful conditioning; Trains calf endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Step onto the hack squat machine and place your back flat against the pad. Position your shoulders under the shoulder pads. Place your feet on the platform shoulder-width apart. Lower foot positions bias the quads more; higher positions bias glutes more. Release the safety handles and straighten your legs to take the weight. Keep a slight bend in your knees at the top. Brace your core and keep your back pressed firmly against the pad throughout. Lower the sled by bending at the knees. Your knees should track over your toes. Descend until your thighs are at least parallel to the platform or deeper if your flexibility allows. Drive the sled back up by pressing through your full foot. Do not lock your knees at the top. Re-engage the safety handles before exiting.
Benefits: Allows heavy quad-dominant squatting with full back support; Removes balance and spinal-stability demand; Excellent for building quad size and strength; Allows deep squatting safely with guided path; Easy to train to failure with safety stops; Useful for lifters with lower-back issues
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy emphasis); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (secondary); Adductors; Calves (secondary)

Description: Lie on your back on a vertical leg press machine. Place both feet on the platform overhead, shoulder-width apart. Release the safety stops. Brace your core and grip the handles for stability. Press the platform up by extending your legs. Stop just short of locking out the knees. Slowly lower the platform back down toward your chest. Allow your knees to come close to your chest at the bottom.
Benefits: Allows deep range of motion; Heavy leg loading; Builds quad and glute size; Strong hypertrophy move; Reduces lower back stress; Excellent for legs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Step into the hack squat sled and place your shoulders against the pads. Position your feet on the platform wider than shoulder-width. Point your toes slightly out. Release the safety handles and brace your core. Lower yourself by bending the knees and sitting your hips back. Continue down until your thighs are at parallel. Drive through your heels to stand back up. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top.
Benefits: Targets the inner thighs and glutes; Adductor builder; Stable, guided machine path; Easy to load progressively; Reduces lower back strain; Useful for glute development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Quadriceps

Description: Set up on hands and knees in a quadruped position. Place a slider under one foot with the toes down. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Reach the opposite arm forward. Slide the foot back along the floor as the leg extends. Continue until the leg is fully extended. Slide the foot back to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the core; Trains the glutes; Strong bird dog variation; Useful warm-up; Builds posterior chain
Muscles Worked (Raw): Core; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae

Exercise Name: Sliding Floor Bridge Curl on Towel
Description: Lie on your back on a smooth floor with knees bent and feet flat. Place a small towel under each heel. Lift your hips up into a strong glute bridge. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes throughout. Slide the feet away from your body to extend the legs. Keep the hips lifted as the legs slide out. Curl the feet back toward your hips by squeezing the hamstrings. Repeat the slide and curl while keeping the bridge held high.
Benefits: Hammers the hamstrings with sliding eccentric load.; Strengthens the glutes through the bridge hold.; No equipment beyond towels and a slick floor.; Joint friendly hamstring training option.; Builds hip extension and posterior chain strength.; Excellent home alternative to a hamstring curl machine.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves; Erector spinae

Description: Lie on the back support of a horizontal leg press sled. Place your feet on the platform shoulder-width apart. Grip the handles for stability. Unrack the safety and brace your core. Lower the platform by bending your knees toward your chest. Continue until your thighs reach a comfortable depth without rounding the lower back. Drive through your heels to extend your legs back to the starting position. Re-rack the safety when finished.
Benefits: No spinal compression; Heavy quad and glute loading; Allows safe heavy loading; Useful for lifters with back issues; Builds leg size and strength; Strong hypertrophy stimulus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Calves; Adductors

Description: Kneel on the floor with towels under both hands. Set the hips back over the heels. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Slide the hands forward as the torso lowers. Stop with the arms fully extended overhead. Pull the hands back toward the hips by driving the elbows down. Squeeze the lats hard as the hands return. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: No equipment needed; Trains the lats; Strong floor variation; Useful for travel; Builds the back; Trains the biceps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Teres major

Exercise Name: Sliding Leg Curl on Floor with Towel
Description: Lie on your back on a smooth floor with knees bent and feet flat. Place a small towel under each heel. Press your hips up slightly to lift the back off the floor. Brace the core and engage the glutes. Slide both feet away from your body until the legs are nearly straight. Maintain hip lift through the slide. Pull the feet back toward your hips by curling the hamstrings. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hammers the hamstrings through the curl motion.; Trains the glutes with isometric hold.; No equipment beyond towels and a slick floor.; Builds posterior chain strength at home.; Easy to scale by adjusting hip lift height.; Joint friendly with smooth sliding tempo.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Calves; Erector spinae

Description: Position an upright bench inside the Smith machine so the bar tracks just behind your head when seated. Sit with your back against the pad. Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Brace your core. Plant your feet. Twist the bar to unrack. Lower the bar behind your head to roughly ear level — do not go deeper than ear level. Press the bar back up to lockout directly above your shoulders. Keep the descent controlled — the behind-neck position is harder on the shoulders under speed. Use lighter weight than front pressing. Shoulder safety is the priority. Stop immediately if you feel any shoulder discomfort. This exercise is not suitable for everyone.
Benefits: Shifts more emphasis to the lateral deltoid vs front pressing; Builds the side shoulders with a different stimulus; Guided bar path provides safety on a demanding exercise; Useful for advanced lifters with excellent shoulder mobility; Builds shoulder width with heavy loading; Can be a useful variation in a periodized program
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid (increased emphasis); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Serratus anterior

Description: Set up a Smith machine with bands attached to each end of the bar and anchored low. Step under the bar and place it across your upper back. Unrack the bar and step into your squat stance. Brace your core and squat down through a deep range below parallel. The bands should be slack at the bottom of the deep squat. Drive up explosively against the increasing band tension. Lock out at the top with hips and knees fully extended. The bands should reach maximum tension at the top.
Benefits: Deep range maximizes quad development; Accommodating resistance gets harder at lockout; Smith machine fixed path eliminates balance demands; Forces explosive drive; Builds lockout strength; Useful for breaking through squat plateaus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Position a flat bench inside the Smith machine so the bar lowers to your mid-chest. Lie flat on the bench. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Unrack the bar by rotating the safety catches. Lower the bar to your mid-chest under control over two seconds. Press the bar straight up by extending your elbows. The Smith guides the path. Lock out at the top. Squeeze your chest. Lower and repeat for the desired reps. Re-rack by rotating the safety catches at the top. Set safety stops at chest height.
Benefits: Guided bar path allows solo training safely; Allows heavier loading than free-weight for some lifters; Built-in safety catches; Removes stabilization demand — isolates chest more; Easy to set up; Useful for beginners or hypertrophy focus
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Set up a smith machine bar at upper chest height. Step under the bar and place it on the upper back. Unrack the bar and step back. Set the feet shoulder width with knees softly bent. Brace your core and set the chest tall. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Lower until the torso is parallel to the floor. Drive the hips forward to stand back up squeezing the glutes.
Benefits: Strong posterior chain builder; Fixed bar path is easy to learn; Trains the hip hinge; Builds the hamstrings; Strong machine move; Useful for beginners
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Spinal erectors

Description: Set up a Smith machine bar at thigh level. Stand in front of the bar with the bar behind your legs. Squat down and grip the bar with palms facing back, hands wider than shoulder-width. Stand up with the bar held behind your body. Position the bar against the back of your thighs. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Squeeze the traps hard at the top, then lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Different angle than standard shrug; Builds upper traps and rear delts; Wide grip adds rear delt work; Smith machine allows safe loading; Strong shoulder blade retraction; Useful for trap training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (upper); Trapezius (middle); Posterior deltoid; Rhomboids

Exercise Name: Smith Bent Over Narrow Pronated Grip Row
Description: Set the Smith machine bar at about knee height. Stand close to the bar with feet hip width apart. Grip the bar with a close overhand grip. Unrack the bar and step back slightly. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and the chest tall. Pull the bar up to your lower chest by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the upper back at the top of the row. Lower the bar slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Hits the upper back with the close pronated grip.; Fixed bar path of the Smith reduces stabilization demand.; Builds rhomboids and rear deltoids.; Easy to load heavy with bar safety hooks.; Trains horizontal pulling strength.; Smith path keeps form consistent on heavy sets.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at hip level. Stand with your back to the bar. Reach behind you and grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, palms facing back. Stand tall with the bar resting against the back of your thighs. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Hold the squeeze for one count, then lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Targets lower traps and rhomboids; Behind-the-back position changes pull angle; Fixed bar path removes balance demands; Allows progressive heavy loading; Builds full trap development; Useful for posture work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (lower and middle fibers); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Lie on a flat bench inside the Smith machine with your eyes under the bar. Grip the bar with hands roughly shoulder-width apart or slightly narrower. Wrap your thumbs. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Plant feet firmly. Brace your core. Twist the bar to unrack. Lower the bar under control to your lower chest or sternum area. Keep your elbows tucked tight against your sides throughout the descent. Press the bar back up by extending at the elbows, focusing on squeezing the triceps. Lock out at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack on the final rep. Use safety stops for failure training.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis heavily onto the triceps; Fixed bar path allows safe training to failure; Often allows heavier loading than dumbbell tricep work; Excellent compound tricep mass builder; Useful for high-rep and drop-set training; Easier to set up than barbell close-grip bench
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (heavy emphasis); Pectoralis major (sternal head); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Place a bench, box, or sturdy chair behind you inside the Smith machine. Set the bar at upper-chest height. Step under, rack across upper traps, twist to unrack. Feet shoulder-width apart, slightly forward of the bar. Brace core. Sit back and down toward the chair. Keep chest tall and knees tracking over toes. Lightly touch the chair with your glutes — do not sit down or relax. Drive through your feet to stand back up immediately upon contact. Twist to re-rack when finished. Lower the chair height as mobility and strength improve. Progress to no-chair squats.
Benefits: Consistent depth target builds confidence and teaches squat depth; Guided bar removes balance demand; Excellent for beginners learning to squat; Adjustable box height scales difficulty; Useful for rehabilitation and returning from injury; Builds the squat pattern without overloading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at the lowest position. Load it with weight. Stand with feet hip-width apart underneath the bar. Bar should be roughly over your mid-foot. Squat down and grip the bar with hands just outside your knees, overhand grip. Set your back flat. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Drive through your full feet and stand up. The bar travels straight up. Stand tall at the top with shoulders pulled back. Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips first, then bending your knees. Use moderate weight. The fixed path eliminates the slight forward sweep of a real deadlift.
Benefits: Eliminates balance demand; Useful for beginners learning the deadlift pattern; Easier to load progressively; Allows higher reps for hypertrophy; Reduces lower back stress; Useful when no barbell is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Trapezius; Quadriceps; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (stabilizer)

Description: Set the Smith machine bar to roughly knee height. Stand inside the machine with feet hip-width apart. Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees from horizontal. Grip the bar with hands just outside your knees using an overhand or underhand grip. Twist the bar to unrack. Let it hang at arm’s length. Brace your core and lock in your back angle. Row the bar to your lower chest or upper abdomen by driving your elbows up and back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Pause briefly. Lower the bar under control back to the start. Maintain the same torso angle throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack when finished.
Benefits: Fixed bar path allows focus on pulling without horizontal stabilization; Allows heavy loading for serious back development; Easier to maintain strict form than free-weight rows; Multiple grip options (overhand, underhand, wide, narrow); Excellent for high-rep hypertrophy work; Useful for lifters learning the bent-over row pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Erector spinae (isometric); Forearms and grip

Description: Position a decline bench (15 to 30 degrees) inside a Smith machine so the bar tracks over your lower chest. Lock your feet under the leg pads. Lie back with the bar above your lower chest. Grip slightly wider than shoulder-width. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Brace your core. Twist the bar to unrack. Lower under control to your lower chest, elbows at 45 to 70 degrees. Press back up to lockout, exhaling as you press. Twist to re-rack on the final rep. Set the safety stops just above chest contact for failure training. The decline angle may allow heavier loading than flat or incline Smith pressing.
Benefits: Targets the lower chest with guided safety; Allows training to failure without a spotter; Reduces anterior deltoid involvement vs flat pressing; Often allows heavier loading than flat pressing; Excellent for drop sets and high-rep work; Useful for lifters with shoulder issues on flat pressing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially the sternal/lower head); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid (reduced); Serratus anterior

Exercise Name: Smith Bent Over Narrow Supinated Grip Row
Description: Set the Smith machine bar at about knee height. Stand close to the bar with feet hip width apart. Grip the bar with a close underhand grip. Unrack the bar and step back slightly. Hinge at the hips with a flat back and the chest tall. Pull the bar up to your lower abdomen by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the lats and biceps at the top. Lower the bar slowly back to full arm extension and repeat.
Benefits: Hits the lats hard with the underhand grip.; Builds biceps strength through the supinated pull.; Smith path keeps the bar moving in a fixed line.; Easy to load heavy on the Smith machine.; Carryover to chin ups and underhand pulls.; Trains horizontal pulling strength.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Brachialis; Posterior deltoid

Description: Position a Smith machine bar over a flat bench at hip level. Sit on the floor with your upper back against the bench. Position the bar across your hips with a foam pad for comfort. Bring the soles of your feet together with knees flared out wide. Brace your core and pull your shoulders into the bench. Drive your hips up by squeezing your glutes hard. Continue until your hips are fully extended at the top. Hold the squeeze for one count, then lower the hips back down with control.
Benefits: Frog stance maximizes glute activation; Removes quad and hamstring contribution; Smith machine allows safe heavy loading; Builds glute size with progressive overload; Forces strong glute squeeze; Useful for glute specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Adductors

Description: Set a decline bench inside a smith machine. Lie back with the bar over your lower chest. Grip the bar with an underhand (palms-up) grip at shoulder width. Unrack the bar and brace your core. Lower the bar to your lower chest with control. Keep your elbows tucked toward your sides. Press the bar back up to the start. Lock out at the top before the next rep.
Benefits: Hits the lower and upper chest fibers; Stable smith machine path; Reverse grip recruits triceps; Reduces shoulder strain; Easy to load progressively; Useful for chest variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at hip height. Stand directly underneath the bar. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, underhand (supinated) grip. Stand tall. Pull your shoulders back. Brace your core. Curl the bar up by bending at the elbows. As you curl, drag the bar up close to your body — bar should slide up along your torso. Allow your elbows to travel backward as you curl, instead of forward. Continue until the bar reaches roughly chest height. Squeeze your biceps hard. Lower under control back to the start. Use moderate weight.
Benefits: Biases the long head of the biceps; Removes momentum from the curl; Smith machine simplifies the dragging motion; Builds bicep peak; Easy to load progressively; Different stimulus than standard curls
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii (especially long head); Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Posterior deltoid (slight, due to elbow travel); Forearms

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at hip level. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, bar at thigh level. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Bend at the hips and knees to lower the bar to a hang position. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Drive through your heels and explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles. Pull the bar up while shrugging hard and dropping under it. Catch the bar in the front rack position with elbows high. Lower with control.
Benefits: Builds explosive power and hip drive; Fixed bar path simplifies hang clean technique; Develops front rack catching strength; Trains triple extension; Useful for athletes new to Olympic lifting; Strong total body conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Trapezius; Anterior deltoid; Erector spinae

Description: Set up a flat bench under the Smith machine bar. Lie back on the bench with the bar over your chest. Grip the bar with both hands very close together — about 6 inches apart, almost touching. Unrack the bar by twisting it. Hold it above your chest with arms extended. Brace your core. Press your hands actively toward each other against the bar. Lower the bar slowly to your chest, maintaining the inner squeeze. Press the bar back up to lockout, continuing to squeeze your hands together. Squeeze your chest hard at the top. Use moderate weight. Aim for higher reps focused on the squeeze.
Benefits: Targets the inner chest specifically; Smith machine eliminates balance demand; Active inner-squeeze creates constant chest tension; Builds chest separation; Easier on the shoulders; Useful chest finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially inner fibers); Triceps brachii (heavy involvement from close grip); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior

Description: Position an adjustable bench at 30 to 45 degrees inside a Smith machine so the bar tracks over your upper chest. Lie back with your eyes directly under the bar. Plant both feet firmly on the floor. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Pull your shoulder blades down and back into the bench. Lift your chest. Brace your core. Twist the bar to unrack it and bring it over your upper chest with arms extended. Lower the bar under control to your upper chest, allowing elbows to flare to about 45 to 70 degrees. Press the bar back up to lockout, exhaling as you press. Twist the bar to re-engage the hooks on your final rep. Use the safety stops for failure training.
