Benefits: Fixed path allows pure upper-chest focus without stabilizer demand; Safety hooks allow training to failure without a spotter; Useful for beginners learning the incline press pattern; Allows heavier loading than dumbbell incline pressing for many lifters; Easy to set up and adjust; Excellent for drop sets and high-rep hypertrophy work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (especially the clavicular/upper head); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior

Description: Set an incline bench inside a smith machine. Lie back with the bar over your upper chest. Grip the bar with an underhand grip at shoulder width. Unrack the bar and brace your core. Lower the bar to your upper chest with control. Keep your elbows tucked toward your sides. Press the bar back up to the start. Lock out at the top before the next rep.
Benefits: Maximally targets the upper chest; Stable smith machine path; Reverse grip recruits triceps; Reduces shoulder strain; Easy to load progressively; Best move for upper chest activation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (clavicular); Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Description: Position a flat bench horizontally inside the Smith machine. Set the bar at a height that allows you to sit on the floor with the bar across your hips. Sit on the floor with your upper back against the bench. Roll or position the Smith bar across your hip crease. Use a barbell pad for comfort. Plant your feet hip-width apart, roughly under your knees when at the top of the thrust. Brace your core. Twist the bar to unrack. Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips. Continue until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Your shins should be roughly vertical. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not hyperextend your lower back. Lower your hips under control. The bar follows the guided path. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack when finished.
Benefits: Guided bar path eliminates lateral stabilization demand; Allows heavy glute loading with easier setup than barbell hip thrust; Safety hooks provide built-in failure protection; Builds the glutes directly with peak contraction at the top; Easier to set up solo than barbell version; Allows easy progressive loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductor magnus; Quadriceps (secondary); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at a low height appropriate for hip thrusts. Position a bench under the bar perpendicular to the rack. Sit on the floor with your upper back against the bench. Position the bar across your hips. Use a pad if needed for comfort. Plant your feet flat with knees bent. Brace your core and pin your shoulders to the bench. Drive your hips up by squeezing your glutes hard. Lower your hips back down with control.
Benefits: Heavy glute loading; Smith fixed bar path provides stability; Easier setup than barbell hip thrust; Builds glute size and strength; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong hip extension work
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Position a Smith machine bar at hip height. Kneel on the floor below the bar with knees on a pad. Pull the bar down across your hips and use a foam pad. Sit your hips back so your butt rests on your heels. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Drive your hips forward by squeezing your glutes hard. Continue until your hips are fully extended and body is upright. Lower your hips back to the starting position with control.
Benefits: Different hip extension pattern than standard hip thrust; Strong glute engagement; Smith machine allows safe loading; Develops kneeling hip drive strength; Useful variation for glute training; Builds glute and hamstring strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae

Description: Set an incline bench inside a smith machine. Lie back with the bar above your face. Grip the bar with a shoulder-width overhand grip. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Lift the bar straight up in a front-raise arc. Continue until your arms are straight overhead. Squeeze the front delts hard at the top. Lower the bar back down with control.
Benefits: Targets the front delts; Stable smith machine path; Builds front shoulder size; Reduces stabilization demand; Easy to load progressively; Useful for shoulder variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Upper chest

Description: Set the smith machine bar low and load with light weight. Kneel on all fours under the bar. Position the bar across the back of one foot near the heel. Hold the foot flexed to keep the bar in place. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Drive the foot up and back to lift the bar. Squeeze the glute hard at the top of the kick. Lower with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Loaded glute builder; Smith machine support; Single-leg focus; Easy to load heavy; Strong unilateral move; Excellent glute hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Lower back

Description: Place a step-up box to the side of a smith machine. Position the smith bar on your upper back. Stand sideways to the box with the foot closest to it. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Step onto the box with the foot closest to it. Drive through that heel to lift your body up onto the box. Stand fully on the box at the top. Step back down with control. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Hits the gluteus medius; Builds unilateral leg strength; Stable smith machine loading; Improves hip stability; Useful for athletic training; Develops side-to-side balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings

Description: Set the Smith bar at upper-chest height. Step under and rack it across your front shoulders, arms crossed over the bar. Twist to unrack. Step your feet slightly forward of the bar. Feet shoulder-width apart, toes slightly out. Brace core. Lift chest. Sit straight down with an upright torso. Descend until hip crease is below knee top. Drive through full foot to stand. Keep elbows up and chest tall. Twist to re-rack when finished. The fixed path allows you to shift feet further forward for more quad bias. Use lighter weight than back squats — the front-loaded position is more demanding.
Benefits: Guided bar removes front-rack mobility demands; More quad-dominant than back squat variations; Forces upright torso for less lower-back stress; Allows safe training to failure with safety hooks; Useful when wrist or shoulder mobility limits free-weight front squats; Easy to adjust foot position for different biases
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy emphasis); Gluteus maximus; Adductors; Core (stabilizer); Erector spinae (isometric)

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at upper back height. Step under the bar and position it across your traps. Walk your feet slightly forward of the bar so they are in front of your shoulders. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists and standing up. Brace your core and slowly squat down through a deep range. Continue lowering until your hips are below parallel. Drive up through your heels to stand back to the starting position. Lock out the bar and rotate to re-rack when finished.
Benefits: Fixed bar path removes balance demands; Deep range maximally stretches quads; Allows focus on leg drive without form concerns; Heavier loading possible for many lifters; Beginner-friendly squat variation; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at hip height. Stand perpendicular to the bar with your right side toward it. Grip the bar with your right hand and step back into a bent over position. Plant your left hand on a bench or your left thigh for support. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Row the bar up by driving your right elbow back toward your hip. Squeeze your right shoulder blade at the top. Lower the bar back down with control. Complete reps, switch sides.
Benefits: Single-arm back work corrects imbalances; Smith fixed bar path eliminates balance demands; Builds back size and thickness; Strong lat engagement; Useful for hypertrophy training; Allows progressive heavy loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Biceps brachii; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at hip level. Stand in front of the bar and grip it with an overhand grip. Unrack the bar and step back into your stance. Stand on your right leg with your left foot lifted slightly behind you. Brace your core and lift your chest. Hinge at the right hip while extending your left leg back behind you. Lower the bar along your right leg until you feel a strong hamstring stretch. Drive your right heel into the floor to stand back up. Switch sides.
Benefits: Builds single-leg hamstring strength; Fixed bar path provides stability; Reduces balance demands; Corrects left-right imbalances; Strong glute development; Useful for rehab or beginners
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Erector spinae; Core

Description: Set the Smith bar to a low position and set the safety stops to catch the bar if needed. Lie on your back under the bar. Place your feet flat on the underside of the bar, roughly shoulder-width apart. Twist the bar to unrack. Extend your legs to push the bar up, but do not lock your knees. Bend your knees to lower the bar toward your chest. Your knees should track toward your chest. Lower until your thighs approach 90 degrees or your lower back begins to lift off the floor. Press the bar back up by extending your legs. Do not lock your knees at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack when finished. Use the safety stops — this exercise can be dangerous without them.
Benefits: Simulates a leg press without a dedicated machine; Guided bar path provides consistency; Targets the quads and glutes with adjustable foot position; Useful when no leg press machine is available; Easy to load progressively; Low spinal load since you are lying on the floor
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings (secondary); Calves (secondary)

Exercise Name: Smith One Leg Floor Calf Raise
Description: Set a smith machine bar at upper chest height. Step under the bar and place it on the upper back. Unrack the bar and step out. Lift one foot up off the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Rise onto the ball of the foot of the working leg. Squeeze the calf hard at the top. Lower the heel back down with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Strong unilateral calf builder; Heavy load capacity; Builds calf size; Useful calf builder; Strong machine move; Trains balance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Set the Smith bar at the lowest position. Stand facing the bar with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with an underhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Twist to unrack. Stand tall with the bar at arm’s length. Pin elbows to your sides. Curl the bar up along the guided track by bending only at the elbows. Continue until the bar reaches shoulder height. Squeeze your biceps hard. Lower under control over two seconds. Do not let the weight slam down. Keep elbows pinned and torso upright throughout. Twist to re-rack when finished.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Set an incline bench at 30 to 45 degrees inside a Smith machine. Position it so the bar travels over your forehead when lying down. Lie back on the incline bench. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width apart, overhand grip. Unrack the bar with arms fully extended above your chest. Bend at the elbows to lower the bar toward your forehead. Keep your upper arms still. Lower until the bar is just above or behind your forehead. Extend your arms to press the bar back up to lockout. Squeeze your triceps at the top. Use the Smith safety stops as a safety measure.
Benefits: Emphasizes the long head of the tricep; Smith bar guides the path for safety; Allows heavier loading than free-weight skull crushers; Incline position targets different angle than flat; Safety catches reduce injury risk; Builds tricep size and strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (especially long head); Anconeus

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at upper back height. Place a small platform or weight plates under the rack for elevation. Step under the bar and place it across your upper traps. Place your heels on the platform with toes hanging off. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Brace your core and stand tall. Lift your toes as high as possible by dorsiflexing your ankles. Squeeze the front of your shins at the top, then lower with control.
Benefits: Trains the tibialis anterior; Supports knee health; Improves sprinting and jumping; Smith fixed bar path eliminates balance demands; Useful for athletic conditioning; Strong shin muscle development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Tibialis anterior; Extensor digitorum longus; Extensor hallucis longus

Exercise Name: Smith Reverse Grip Bent Over Row
Description: Set up a smith machine bar at knee height. Stand facing the bar with feet shoulder width apart. Grip the bar with an underhand reverse grip at shoulder width. Unrack the bar and step back. Hinge forward at the hips with a flat back. Brace your core and let the bar hang at arms length. Pull the bar up to the belly button by driving the elbows back. Squeeze the lats hard. Lower with control.
Benefits: Strong lat builder; Reverse grip biases lower lats; Trains the biceps; Builds back thickness; Useful back move; Strong machine move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid

Description: Set up a flat bench under the Smith machine bar. Lie back with eyes under the bar. Grip the bar with palms facing you (underhand grip), shoulder-width apart. Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar with control to your upper chest. Press the bar back up by squeezing the upper chest. Re-rack the bar by rotating your wrists when finished.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (clavicular head); Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at just above knee height. Load it with heavy weight. Stand with feet hip-width apart underneath the bar. Hinge forward and grip the bar with hands just outside your knees, overhand grip. Set your back flat. Brace your core hard. Lift your chest. Drive through your feet and pull the bar straight up by extending your hips and standing tall. Lock out at the top with shoulders pulled back, hips fully extended. Lower under control back to the just-above-knee starting position. Use heavy weight — the partial range allows it. Excellent for building the upper portion of the lift.

Exercise Name: Smith Seated One Leg Calf Raise
Description: Set a smith machine bar at the height of the seated thigh. Place a low block under the bar. Sit on a bench with the working foot on the block. Place the bar across the thigh just above the knee. Unrack the bar and let the heel drop below the block. Brace your core and keep the foot fixed. Rise onto the ball of the foot squeezing the calf. Lower the heel back down with control. Complete reps and switch legs.
Benefits: Strong soleus builder; Unilateral calf isolation; Heavy load capacity; Builds calf size; Useful calf builder; Strong machine move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Soleus; Gastrocnemius; Calves

Description: Set the Smith bar at roughly knee height. Stand with feet hip-width apart, facing the bar. Grip the bar with a wide overhand grip — roughly 1.5 times shoulder-width. Twist to unrack. Hinge forward at the hips until your torso is roughly 45 degrees. Let the bar hang. Brace core and lock in back angle. Row the bar up by driving elbows up and out to the sides, not back. Pull to upper chest or clavicle level. Elbows should be at or above shoulder height. Squeeze rear delts and mid-traps. Pause briefly. Lower under control. Twist to re-rack when finished.
Benefits: Guided path allows focus on rear delt contraction; High-elbow path targets rear delts over lats; Allows heavier loading than dumbbell rear delt work; Builds rear-delt thickness and mid-trap strength; Easy to set up and adjust weight; Useful for high-rep shoulder volume

Description: Position an upright bench (90 degrees) inside the Smith machine so the bar tracks in front of your face when seated. Sit with your back firmly against the pad. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Plant your feet flat. Brace your core. Twist the bar to unrack. Lower the bar under control to your upper chest, just below your chin. Press the bar straight up by extending at the elbows and shoulders. Move your head back slightly as the bar passes your face. Lock out at the top with the bar directly above your shoulders. Lower under control and repeat. Twist to re-rack on the final rep. Set safety stops at chin level for failure training.
Benefits: Guided path eliminates stabilizer demand for pure shoulder focus; Back support reduces lower-back strain; Safety hooks allow training to failure without a spotter; Useful for beginners and for high-volume shoulder work; Easy to set up and load progressively; Excellent for drop sets and mechanical drop sets
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Serratus anterior

Description: Set a flat bench inside the Smith machine. Place a step plate or block on the floor in front of the bench. Sit on the bench with the bar across your lower thighs (just above the knees). Use a pad for comfort. Place the balls of your feet on the step plate with your heels hanging off. Unrack the bar by rotating the safety catches. Lower your heels as far as possible for a deep calf stretch. Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible. Squeeze your calves hard at the top. Hold for one to two seconds. Lower under control. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Benefits: Targets the soleus specifically (seated position); Smith machine provides guided vertical loading; Easy to load progressively; Useful when no dedicated calf raise machine is available; Safe and stable; Builds lower calf thickness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Soleus (primary — seated position); Gastrocnemius (reduced in seated); Achilles tendon

Description: Set an adjustable bench inside the Smith machine. Adjust the bench to upright (90 degrees) or just below. Position the Smith bar at upper-chest height when you sit on the bench. Sit on the bench with your back firmly against the pad. Plant your feet flat. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width with an overhand grip. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Press the bar straight up by extending your elbows. Lock out at the top. Lower the bar slowly to your upper chest or just above clavicles. Re-rack at the end of the set by rotating your wrists.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Serratus anterior

Description: Set the Smith bar at mid-thigh height. Stand with feet hip-width apart, facing the bar. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Twist to unrack. Stand tall with the bar at arm’s length in front of your thighs. Keep your arms completely straight throughout. Do not bend at the elbows. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears as high as you can. Squeeze your traps hard at the top for one to two seconds. Do not roll your shoulders. Lower under control. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack when finished. Use straps for heavy loading if needed.
Benefits: Fixed bar path eliminates front-to-back drift; Allows heavy loading for serious trap growth; Easier to maintain strict form than free-weight shrugs; Easy to set up and load; Useful for drop sets and high-rep volume; Trains grip and forearm strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (especially the upper fibers); Levator scapulae; Rhomboids (secondary); Forearms and grip

Description: Position a flat bench about two feet behind the Smith machine bar. Step under the bar with it across your upper traps. Place the top of your left foot on the bench behind you. Position your right foot about two feet forward of the bar. Unrack the bar. Brace your core. Lower by bending your right knee until your left knee is just above the floor. Drive through your right foot to stand back up. Complete reps on one side, then switch.

Description: Set the Smith bar at upper-chest height. Step under and rack it across your upper traps. Step one foot forward and one foot back into a split stance. Your front shin should be close to vertical when you lunge down. Twist the bar to unrack. Brace your core and lift your chest. Lower your body by bending both knees. Your back knee should descend toward the floor. Descend until your back knee is roughly an inch above the floor or your front thigh is parallel. Drive through your front foot to press back up. Keep your torso upright. Complete all reps on one side, then switch legs. Twist to re-rack when finished. Adjust foot position forward to bias quads or further under the bar to bias glutes.

Description: Set the safety stops on the Smith machine just below where you would be at the bottom of your squat. Set the bar at upper-chest height. Step under the bar and rest it across your upper traps. Twist the bar to unrack it. Set your feet shoulder-width apart, with your feet positioned slightly forward of the bar — typically 6 to 12 inches in front of where they would be in a free squat. This setup biases the quads and protects the lower back. Brace your core, take a deep breath, and pull your chest tall. Bend at the knees and hips together, descending until your hip crease drops below the top of your knee. Drive through your full foot to stand back up, keeping the bar moving along the fixed track. At the top of the final rep, twist the bar to re-engage the safety hooks before stepping out. Adjust foot position forward to bias the quads or directly under the bar to bias the glutes and hamstrings.

Description: Stand in a smith machine with the bar set behind you at hip height. Grip the bar behind your back with an underhand grip. Stand tall with arms straight at your sides. Brace your core and keep your shoulders pulled back. Curl the bar up and back by flexing your wrists. Squeeze the forearms hard at the top. Lower the bar back down with control. Maintain a tall posture throughout.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Forearms; Brachioradialis

Exercise Name: Smith Standing Behind Head Military Press
Description: Set up a smith machine bar at shoulder height. Stand under the bar with feet shoulder-width. Grip the bar wider than shoulder-width with palms forward. Unrack the bar and lower it to the back of the neck. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Press the bar straight up overhead. Lock out the elbows at the top. Lower the bar back behind the head with control.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at upper chest height. Stand under the bar with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Position the bar at the front of your shoulders. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Press the bar straight up overhead until your arms are fully extended. Lower the bar back to the front rack position with control.

Description: Position a small block or plate under the smith machine. Step under the bar with the bar across your upper traps. Place the balls of your feet on the block with heels hanging off. Unrack the bar by twisting the safety hooks. Brace your core and stand tall. Press up onto your toes by lifting your heels as high as possible. Squeeze the calves hard at the top. Lower slowly to a deep calf stretch.

Exercise Name: Smith Single Arm Bent Over Row
Description: Set up a smith machine bar at knee height. Stand sideways to the bar with feet hip width apart. Grip the bar with one hand near the center. Unrack the bar and step back into a hinged position. Hinge forward with a flat back and brace the other hand on a support. Let the bar hang at arms length. Pull the bar up to the side of the body by driving the elbow back. Squeeze the lat hard. Lower with control. Switch sides and repeat.

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at upper chest height. Stand under the bar with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Position the bar at the front of your shoulders with palms forward. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Press the bar straight up overhead until your arms are fully extended. Lower the bar back to the front rack position with control.

Description: Set the Smith bar at mid-thigh height. Stand with feet hip-width apart, facing the bar. Grip the bar with an overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Twist to unrack. Set a slight, fixed bend in your knees. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Hinge forward at the hips by pushing your butt back. Let the bar slide down along the guided track. Lower until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings. Keep your back flat. Drive your hips forward to stand back up. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack when finished. The fixed path is less forgiving of bar drift — focus on the hip-hinge pattern.

Description: Set the Smith bar at upper-chest height. Step under and rack it across your upper traps. Twist to unrack. Step your feet out to a wide sumo stance — 1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width. Toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Brace core. Lift chest. Push knees out over toes. Sit straight down, keeping torso upright. Descend until hip crease is below knees. Drive through full foot to stand. Push knees out. Squeeze glutes at top. Twist to re-rack when finished. The fixed path allows foot position adjustments without balance concerns. Use moderate weight and focus on depth and glute contraction.

Description: Set the Smith bar at the lowest position or on the floor stops. Stand with a wide sumo stance inside the machine, toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Grip the bar shoulder-width apart with hands inside your knees. Twist to unrack. Set your back flat, chest tall, and knees pushed out over your toes. Drive through your feet and extend your hips and knees to stand up. Keep the bar close to your body along the guided track. Lock out by standing tall with glutes squeezed. Do not lean back. Lower the bar under control by hinging at the hips and bending the knees. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Twist to re-rack when finished. Adjust stance width and toe angle to find your strongest position.

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at upper back height. Place a small platform or weight plates under the rack for elevated foot position. Step under the bar and place it across your upper traps. Place the balls of your feet on the platform with heels hanging off. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Brace your core and stand tall. Lower your heels below the platform level for a stretch. Raise your heels as high as possible by pushing through the balls of your feet. Squeeze the calves at the top.

Description: Set up a flat bench under the Smith machine bar. Lie back with eyes directly under the bar. Grip the bar wider than your normal bench press grip. Plant your feet flat and pull your shoulder blades back into the bench. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar with control to your upper chest. Press the bar back up to lockout, squeezing your chest. Re-rack the bar by rotating your wrists when finished.

Description: Set a decline bench under the Smith machine bar. Lie back with feet secured on the foot pads, eyes under the bar. Grip the bar wider than your normal bench press grip. Pull your shoulder blades back into the bench. Unrack the bar by rotating your wrists. Lower the bar with control to your lower chest. Press the bar back up to lockout, squeezing your chest. Re-rack the bar by rotating your wrists when finished.

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width. Hold a single dumbbell with both hands in front of your body. Rotate your torso to the right, swinging the dumbbell to the right side at hip or chest height. Pivot on your left foot as you rotate. Reverse the motion. Rotate your torso to the left, swinging the dumbbell to the left side. Pivot on your right foot. Continue alternating sides in a smooth rhythmic motion. Keep your arms roughly straight with a slight bend. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 swings per side.

Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy rotation); Rectus abdominis; Hip rotators; Anterior deltoid; Core (rotation)

Description: Stand over the barbell with feet hip-width apart. Grip the bar with a wide snatch grip (index fingers on the outer rings). Drop your hips low. Chest up. Back flat. Pull the bar from the floor by extending your legs. As the bar passes your knees, explosively extend your hips, knees, and ankles. At full extension, shrug your shoulders hard and pull the bar up with your elbows high. The bar rises to about chest or upper-chest height. Lower the bar back down. Aim for 3 to 5 reps per set.

Description: Get into a high plank position on your hands and toes. Hands directly under shoulders. Brace your core. Body straight from heels to head. Bring your right knee up and out toward your right elbow. The knee tracks outside your right arm. Touch (or come close to) your right elbow with your right knee. Return your right foot to the starting position. Bring your left knee up and out toward your left elbow. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps or time. Move with control. Keep your hips low — do not pike up.

Description: Start in a push-up position. As you lower into a push-up, bring your right knee to your right elbow. Simultaneously step your left hand forward. Press up while stepping into the next position. On the next push-up, bring your left knee to your left elbow and step your right hand forward. Continue crawling forward with each push-up. Move low to the ground like a spider crawling. Aim for 10 to 20 feet of crawling or 5 to 8 reps per side.

Description: Place a foam roller behind you on the floor. Stand in front of the roller in a split stance. Place the top of your back foot on the roller. Position your front foot a comfortable stride forward. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Lower your body by bending both knees. Continue until your back knee is just above the floor. Drive up through the front heel. Complete reps on one side before switching.

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder width and toes pointed forward. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Shift the hips back and to one side bending that knee. Lower into a deep lateral squat with one leg straight and the other bent. Keep the back flat and the chest up. Smoothly roll the hips through center to the other side. Lower into a deep lateral squat on the other side. Continue alternating sides with smooth flow.
Benefits: Trains hip mobility; Strong adductor builder; Builds the quads; Useful warm-up; Strong functional pattern; Builds the glutes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Adductors; Gluteus maximus

Description: Step into a split stance — right foot forward, left foot back, roughly 2 to 3 feet apart. Stand tall with chest up. Place hands on hips or in front for balance. Brace your core. Both knees should bend roughly 90 degrees at the bottom. Lower your back (left) knee straight down toward the floor. Descend until your back knee is roughly an inch above the floor. Drive through your front foot to stand back up. Keep torso upright. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch legs. Adjust foot position: closer stance is more quad-dominant; longer stance is more glute-dominant.
Benefits: Builds single-leg strength without complex balance demands; Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances; Easier to load progressively than lunges; Regression from Bulgarian split squats; No equipment needed; Carries over to all single-leg athletic movement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus (front leg); Hamstrings; Adductors; Hip flexors (rear leg, stretched); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step one foot forward into a split stance. This is your fixed position. Lower your back knee toward the floor. Descend until the back knee is just above the floor. Drive through your front foot to rise. Complete reps, then switch feet. Keep torso upright. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per leg.
Benefits: Foundational single-leg squat pattern; No stepping required; Builds single-leg strength; Beginner-friendly; No equipment needed; Progresses to loaded split squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Step one foot forward into a long split lunge stance. Set the front foot flat with knee tracking the toe. Keep the back leg long with the back heel lifted. Stand tall with chest up and core braced. Bring one arm forward and the other arm back, like a sprinter pose. Sink into a tall lunge position with hips squared forward. Hold the position and feel the hip flexor stretch on the back leg. Switch sides and repeat with the opposite stance.
Benefits: Mobilizes the hip flexors; Trains sprint posture; Useful for runners; No equipment required; Builds single-leg balance; Easy to add to any warm-up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hip flexors; Hamstrings

Description: Lie flat on your back with arms at your sides and legs extended straight. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Explosively sit up while simultaneously driving your right knee toward your chest and swinging your left arm forward (like a sprint). Your left elbow should approach your right knee. Your right arm swings back naturally. Pause briefly in the crunch position, then lower back to the flat starting position. On the next rep, drive your left knee and right arm forward. Continue alternating for the desired total reps. Move explosively but with control. Do not slam down on the descent.
Benefits: Trains the abs, obliques, and hip flexors dynamically; Athletic movement pattern with sports carryover; Builds core power and coordination; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Excellent finisher for core or conditioning workouts; More engaging than static crunches
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors; Transverse abdominis

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly (5 to 15 degrees). Extend your arms forward at shoulder height for balance, or place them at your chest. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Look straight ahead. Initiate the squat by sitting your hips back, then bending your knees. Lower your body until your hip crease drops below your knees (or as deep as your mobility allows). Keep your knees tracking over your toes. Do not let them collapse inward. Drive through your full foot to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Foundation for all squat variations; Builds the squat movement pattern; Improves hip and ankle mobility; Builds quad, glute, and hamstring endurance; No equipment needed; Universally beneficial for all fitness levels
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold your arms out for balance or place hands on hips. Squat down until your thighs are parallel to the floor. Hold the parallel squat position throughout the set. Raise both heels off the floor, lifting onto the balls of your feet. Squeeze your calves hard at the top of the raise. Lower your heels back down with control. Continue raising and lowering your heels while holding the squat.
Benefits: Trains calves and quads simultaneously; Builds isometric quad endurance; Forces calves to work under squat fatigue; No equipment required; Develops balance and proprioception; Useful as a warm-up or finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Squat down to parallel or below. Drive through your feet to stand. At the top, immediately rise onto your toes (calf raise). Hold the calf raise briefly. Squeeze your calves. Lower your heels and descend into the next squat. Continue fluidly. Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Combines squatting with calf raises; Builds quads, glutes, and calves together; Time-efficient leg exercise; No equipment needed; Develops balance on toes; Engaging and challenging
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Gastrocnemius and soleus (calf raise); Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Start with the barbell in the front rack position — bar across your front shoulders, elbows up. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core hard. Dip slightly by bending only at the knees (4 to 6 inches). Keep torso upright. Reverse the dip explosively — drive the bar up using leg drive. As the bar leaves your shoulders, drop straight down into a full overhead squat to catch the bar. Catch the bar with arms locked out overhead, in a full squat position. Stand up from the squat with the bar overhead to complete the lift. This is an elite-level Olympic lift — work with a qualified coach to learn it.
Benefits: Builds explosive overhead power; Develops overhead squat strength and mobility; Allows heavier loads than split jerks for some lifters; Used in elite Olympic weightlifting; Excellent full-body power exercise; Trains rate of force development
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior and lateral deltoid; Triceps brachii; Trapezius; Core (heavy stabilizer); Calves

Description: Stand inside the Smith machine. Position the bar at hip height. Grip the bar with hands shoulder-width or slightly wider apart, overhand grip. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core. Pull the bar straight up the front of your body by driving your elbows up and out. Continue pulling until the bar reaches chest height. Do not pull higher. Squeeze your traps and lateral delts at the top. Lower the bar slowly under control to the starting position. Use moderate weight. Use a wider grip to reduce shoulder impingement risk.
Benefits: Stable bar path allows focus on the muscles; Builds the traps and lateral delts; Easier to control than free-weight versions; Useful for high-rep work; Wide grip reduces shoulder risk; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid; Trapezius (upper); Anterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (secondary); Forearms (grip)

Description: Set the Smith machine bar at hip level. Stand under the bar with feet shoulder-width apart. Grip the bar with a wide overhand grip, well outside the shoulders. Unrack the bar and stand tall with arms straight. Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. Shrug your shoulders straight up toward your ears. Hold the contraction at the top for one count. Lower the bar back down slowly with control.
Benefits: Wide grip increases middle trap and rhomboid engagement; Fixed bar path eliminates balance demands; Builds upper trap mass; Allows heavy progressive loading; Strong forearm engagement; Useful for hypertrophy training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius (upper and middle fibers); Rhomboids; Levator scapulae; Forearm flexors

Description: Kneel on the floor with a stability ball in front of you. Place your forearms on the ball. Brace your core hard. Squeeze your glutes. Keep your body in a straight line from knees to head. Slowly roll the ball forward by extending your arms and reaching forward. Continue rolling out as far as you can while maintaining a straight body line. Do not let your hips sag. Pause briefly at the end position. Pull the ball back toward you by contracting your abs and pulling your forearms toward your knees. Return to the starting kneeling position. Repeat for 6 to 12 reps. Quality over quantity.
Benefits: Builds extreme core anti-extension strength; Softer progression than ab wheel rollouts; Trains the abs to resist spinal extension under load; Excellent for building deep core strength; Useful step toward the ab wheel; Trains shoulder stability simultaneously
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (heavy); Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi (isometric); Anterior deltoid (extending arms); Gluteus maximus (anti-arching)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Arms at your sides. Squat down into a deep bodyweight squat — hip crease below knees if possible. From the bottom, drive through your feet to stand back up explosively. As you reach standing, sweep both arms overhead. Reach as high as possible. Lower your arms and immediately squat again. Continue for 10 to 15 reps as part of a warm-up. Move with control and rhythm. Breathe deeply. For more intensity, jump at the top instead of just reaching.
Benefits: Mobilizes hips, ankles, and shoulders in one movement; Elevates heart rate as a warm-up; No equipment needed; Excellent pre-workout warm-up; Builds coordination; Easy to scale by adding a jump
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps and glutes (squat); Deltoids (overhead reach); Hip flexors and adductors; Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Exercise Name: Squat to Overhead Reach With Twist
Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Arms at your sides. Squat down into a deep bodyweight squat — hip crease below knees if possible. Stand up explosively. As you rise, reach one arm up and overhead while rotating your torso to that side. Fully extend overhead and twist. Look up at your hand. Return to standing, then squat again. On the next rep, reach and twist to the opposite side. Continue alternating for the desired number of reps. Move smoothly and rhythmically. This is a warm-up, not a max-effort exercise.
Benefits: Mobilizes hips, thoracic spine, and shoulders in one movement; Elevates heart rate as a warm-up; Combines squat depth with rotational mobility; Excellent pre-workout warm-up for any training session; No equipment needed; Builds coordination and body awareness
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps and glutes (squat); Obliques (rotation); Deltoids (overhead reach); Thoracic spine rotators; Hip flexors and adductors

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Squat down and place your hands on the floor in front of you. Kick both feet back to land in a plank position. Immediately jump your feet back to the squat position. Stand up. That is one rep. Continue at a brisk pace. No push-up or jump needed — just the squat-plank-squat-stand cycle. Aim for 10 to 20 reps per set or work for time.
Benefits: Full-body conditioning without impact from jumping; Builds cardiovascular endurance; Easier than burpees; No equipment needed; Develops speed and agility; Useful for circuit training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Core (transitions); Hip flexors; Anterior deltoid (plank); Cardiovascular system

Description: Place a Bosu ball on the floor with the rounded side down (flat side up). Carefully step onto the flat side of the Bosu with both feet hip-width apart. Find your balance. Brace your core hard. Slowly squat down, sitting your hips back and bending your knees. Descend only as low as you can maintain balance — typically not as deep as a stable squat. Drive through your feet to stand back up. Maintain balance throughout. Use slow, controlled movement. Step off carefully when finished. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per set.
Benefits: Builds ankle and foot stability; Improves balance and proprioception; Useful for rehabilitation; Trains core engagement under unstable load; Engaging variation for balance work; Limited equipment needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and medius; Hamstrings; Calves and ankle stabilizers; Core (heavy stabilizer); Foot intrinsic muscles

Description: Place a stability ball against a wall at your lower back height. Lean your back against the ball. Walk your feet forward 12 to 18 inches. Lift your left foot off the floor, extending it forward. Squat down on your right leg by bending your right knee. The ball rolls down the wall. Descend until your right thigh is parallel to the floor (or as deep as you can manage). Drive through your right foot to stand back up. The ball rolls up. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Use bodyweight or hold dumbbells for added load.
Benefits: Develops single-leg squat strength; Wall support provides stability; Builds quad and glute strength unilaterally; Easy to scale by adjusting depth; Useful progression toward pistol squats; Low-impact exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (working leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer); Calves

Description: Lie on the side with the bottom forearm on the floor. Stack the bottom leg straight under the body. Place the top foot in front of the bottom foot on the floor. Brace your core and keep the body straight. Lift the hips up off the floor into a side plank. Squeeze the obliques and glutes hard. Hold the position for the working set. Finish then switch sides.
Benefits: Loads the obliques; Strong side plank variation; Builds the core; Useful for core size; Trains the side abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Core; Gluteus medius

Description: Start seated on the floor in a wide straddle with hands on the floor between your legs. Lean forward onto your hands, shifting your weight onto your palms. Using hip flexor and shoulder strength, lift your hips up while keeping your legs in a straddle. Continue pressing upward, stacking your hips over your shoulders. As your hips rise above your hands, begin closing your legs together overhead. Press all the way up to a full handstand. This requires elite flexibility, compression, and pressing strength. Train with parallettes for extra clearance and handstand press progressions.
Benefits: Builds elite pressing and compression strength; Demands extreme hamstring flexibility; Foundational gymnastics skill; Develops body control and balance; Impressive calisthenics achievement; No equipment needed (parallettes help)
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Hip flexors (extreme compression); Core (heavy); Serratus anterior; Adductors (straddle hold); Hamstrings (extreme flexibility)

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Bend your knees slightly. Extend both arms forward at chest height with palms together (or hold a light weight). Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back. Rotate your torso to the right as far as comfortable. Keep your hips facing forward. Pause briefly at the end of the rotation. Rotate back through center and continue to the left. Continue alternating side to side rhythmically. Keep the rotation in your thoracic spine — not your lumbar spine.
Benefits: Builds oblique strength; Trains rotational control; Warms up the thoracic spine; Useful for athletes; No equipment needed; Quick and accessible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Transverse abdominis; Erector spinae; Quadratus lumborum

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Hands behind your head. Lift your right knee while crunching your left elbow toward it. Touch or bring them as close as possible. Return to standing. Lift your left knee while crunching your right elbow toward it. Continue alternating at a brisk pace. Rotate your torso with each crunch. Aim for 15 to 25 reps total or work for time.
Benefits: Standing oblique and ab exercise; Cardiovascular conditioning; No equipment needed; No floor space needed; Engaging and dynamic; Builds coordination
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Cardiovascular system

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart on a flat surface, or stand with the balls of your feet on the edge of a step or weight plate to allow a full stretch at the bottom. Stand tall with knees mostly straight (a slight unlocked bend is fine). Pull your shoulders back and brace your core. If using a step, let your heels drop below the level of the step to feel a stretch in your calves. Push through the balls of your feet to rise up onto your toes as high as possible. Squeeze your calves hard at the top for one second. Try to get your heels as high as your range allows. Lower under control over a count of two to three seconds. If on a step, return to a deep stretch at the bottom. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Use a wall or pole for balance as needed. Add load by holding dumbbells, wearing a weighted vest, or progressing to a calf raise machine.
Benefits: Direct isolation of the calf muscles; Standing position with straight knees emphasizes the gastrocnemius; Easy to scale up by adding load; Highly portable — needs only a step or flat surface; Improves ankle stability and lower-leg endurance; Carries over to running, jumping, and athletic performance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (medial and lateral heads); Soleus (secondary); Tibialis posterior (stabilizer); Foot intrinsics

Description: Stand facing a wall or sturdy support. Place the hands on the support at chest height. Set the feet hip width apart. Brace your core and keep the legs straight. Press up onto the balls of the feet. Squeeze the calves hard at the top. Lower with control to the floor. Continue for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the calves; Easy balance; Useful for beginners; No equipment needed; Strong calf basic
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Stand tall with feet together, holding onto a wall, chair, or pole for balance. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Keep your supporting leg slightly soft (not locked). Slowly lift your right leg out to the side by abducting at the hip. Keep your knee straight and your toes pointing forward. Lift your leg to roughly 30 to 45 degrees from your body. Stop when you feel the contraction in your upper outer glute. Avoid leaning your torso to the opposite side — keep your body upright. The work should come from the hip, not from leaning. Pause briefly at the top, then lower the leg under control back to the start position. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch to the left. Add load by attaching ankle weights or a resistance band around the ankles for more challenge.
Benefits: Direct gluteus medius and minimus activation; Improves hip stability and balance; Helps prevent knee and lower-back issues; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Excellent warm-up exercise; Builds the upper outer glute
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius; Gluteus minimus; Tensor fasciae latae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a barbell at upper-chest height in a power rack. Step under the bar and place it across your upper traps behind your neck. Grip the bar slightly wider than shoulder-width. Step back from the rack. Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Brace your core. Press the bar straight up by extending at the elbows. Move your head slightly forward as the bar passes. Lock out at the top with the bar directly above your shoulders. Lower the bar slowly behind your head — only as low as your mobility allows. Stop at ear level or slightly lower. Press back up to lockout. Repeat for the desired reps. Use lighter weight than front pressing. Stop immediately if you feel shoulder discomfort.
Benefits: Shifts emphasis to the lateral deltoid; Reduces anterior deltoid involvement; Builds shoulder width; Useful variation for advanced lifters; Trains shoulder mobility under load; Different stimulus than front pressing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Lateral deltoid (increased emphasis); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Upper trapezius; Serratus anterior

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Press up onto the balls of both feet. Hold the high position with weight balanced on the toes. Slowly rotate both ankles in a circular motion outward. Continue circling for several rotations at the top. Reverse direction and circle the ankles inward. Lower the heels back to the floor with control.
Benefits: Builds calf strength; Trains ankle mobility; Improves balance; No equipment needed; Useful warm-up move; Hits the small ankle stabilizers
Muscles Worked (Raw): Calves; Soleus; Gastrocnemius

Description: Position yourself in the standing leg curl machine with the platform under your standing foot. Place the back of your right calf against the roller pad. Grip the handles in front of you for stability. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Curl your right heel up toward your glute by bending the knee against the pad. Squeeze your hamstring at the top of the curl. Lower the leg back down with control to a fully extended starting position. Complete reps on one leg, then switch.
Benefits: Single-leg hamstring isolation; Constant machine resistance; Builds hamstring size and strength; Corrects left-right imbalances; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong peak contraction
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings; Gluteus maximus; Gastrocnemius

Exercise Name: Standing Single Leg Calf Raise with Support
Description: Stand on one foot near a wall or rail. Hold the wall or rail for balance support. Lift the other foot off the floor by bending the knee. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Allow the heel to drop slightly toward the floor. Press up onto the toes by raising the heel. Squeeze the calf hard at the top. Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds the calf.; Trains one calf at a time for symmetry.; Support removes balance demand.; Useful for calf focus.; Joint friendly drill.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Calves

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Place your hands behind your head with elbows wide. Lift your right knee up toward your right elbow while crunching your right side. Bring your right elbow down toward your right knee. The two should meet near hip height. Squeeze your right oblique at the top of the crunch. Return to standing. Repeat with the left side — left elbow to left knee. Continue alternating sides at a controlled pace. Stay tall through the spine — do not collapse forward. Perform 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Engages the obliques and core; Combines core work with light cardio; Standing position is functional; No equipment needed; Easy on the lower back; Practical and accessible
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques (heavy involvement); Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Quadratus lumborum; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall. Hold a wall or chair for balance. Shift weight to your left leg. Lift your right leg straight out to the side. Lift to about 30 to 45 degrees. Keep your torso upright — do not lean away. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch legs. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side.
Benefits: Targets the gluteus medius; Builds hip abductor strength; Simple and accessible; Useful for warm-up and rehab; Improves hip stability; No equipment needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius and minimus; Tensor fasciae latae; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding an ab wheel on the floor in front of your toes. Bend at the hips to reach the wheel. Grip the handles. Brace your core extremely hard. Tuck your pelvis (posterior tilt). Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your body. Continue rolling until your body is nearly horizontal — arms overhead, body straight. Do NOT let your lower back arch at any point. If it arches, you have gone too far. Pull yourself back to standing by contracting your abs and lats. Master the kneeling rollout for sets of 15+ before attempting standing.
Benefits: One of the hardest core exercises in existence; Builds elite anti-extension strength; Develops lat and shoulder strength; Benchmark calisthenics core exercise; No equipment needed besides an ab wheel; Progresses from kneeling rollouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (extreme demand); Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi (heavy); Anterior deltoid; Hip flexors

Exercise Name: Standing Single Leg Calf Raise Balance
Description: Stand on one foot with the other foot lifted. Set the arms at the sides for balance. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Allow the heel to drop slightly toward the floor. Press up onto the toes by raising the heel. Squeeze the calf hard at the top. Lower with control to the start. Continue for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the calf.; Trains ankle stability.; No equipment required.; Improves balance.; Useful for athletes.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius; Soleus; Tibialis posterior

Description: Place a sturdy chair against a wall for stability. Stand facing the chair. Step your right foot onto the chair seat. Drive through your right foot to step up. Stand fully on the chair. Step back down with your left foot leading. Complete reps on one side, then switch. Ensure the chair is stable and will not tip. Use a wall for the chair back. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per leg.
Benefits: At-home leg exercise with no gym equipment; Builds single-leg strength; Easily accessible — just need a chair; Develops balance and coordination; Beginner-friendly; Progresses to weighted step-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (stepping leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Calves; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set a cable to the highest pulley with a wide bar attachment. Grip the bar with an overhand grip wider than shoulder-width. Stand facing the cable station and hold the bar overhead with arms extended. Step back two or three steps to create a slight angle in the cable. Brace your core and lean back slightly. Pull the bar down to your upper chest by driving your elbows back and down. Squeeze your lats hard at the bottom of the pull. Slowly return to the starting position with arms extended overhead.
Benefits: Standing pulldown alternative; Stepback creates a strong lat-emphasizing angle; Constant cable tension through the range; Builds lat size and strength; Useful when no pulldown bench is available; Strong lat isolation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius (middle); Posterior deltoid

Description: Stand on a box, step, or platform that is 6 to 18 inches tall. Stand on your right leg with the left leg hanging off the side of the box. Hold your arms out for balance or place hands on hips. Brace your core and stand tall. Slowly lower yourself by bending your right knee. Allow your left foot to extend toward the floor. Tap your left heel to the floor lightly without putting weight on it. Drive up through your right heel to stand back to the starting position. Complete reps, then switch legs.
Benefits: Builds eccentric single-leg strength; Strong knee stability work; Develops quad and glute control; Useful for rehab and prehab; No equipment beyond a box; Easy to scale by changing box height
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Gluteus medius; Hamstrings

Description: Adjust the standing leg curl machine so the roller pad sits behind your right ankle when standing. Stand facing the machine. Position the back of your right ankle against the roller pad. Stand on your left leg. Hold the machine handles for stability. Brace your core. Stand tall with hips facing forward. Curl the roller pad up by bending at the right knee. Squeeze your hamstring. Continue until your knee is fully bent and your heel is near your glute. Lower under control over two to three seconds. Complete reps on one side, then switch.
Benefits: Isolates each hamstring individually; Exposes left-right strength imbalances; Easy to load progressively; Useful for rehabilitation after hamstring strains; Standing position eliminates lower-back load; Excellent finisher for leg workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus); Gastrocnemius (secondary); Gluteus maximus (slight stabilizer)

Description: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step your right foot forward into a split stance. This is your fixed position for the set. Lower your back (left) knee toward the floor. Descend until your left knee is just above the floor. Drive through your front foot to rise. Complete all reps in this stance, then switch feet. Keep your torso upright. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per leg.
Benefits: Simplest lunge variation; No stepping required; Builds single-leg strength; Beginner-friendly; No equipment needed; Progresses to weighted split squats
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (front leg); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand facing a sturdy box or bench, roughly knee-height. Plant your right foot fully on top of the box. Make sure your entire foot is on the surface. Stand tall with chest up and core braced. Drive through your right foot — pressing through the entire foot, especially the heel — to lift your body up onto the box. Stand fully tall on top of the box with both feet planted. Squeeze your right glute hard. Step the left foot back down to the floor under control. Keep most of your weight on the right leg. Once your left foot is back on the floor, follow with your right foot. That is one rep. Complete all reps on the right side, then switch. Resist pushing off the back leg. Progress by adding dumbbells or a barbell.
Benefits: Builds quads, glutes, and balance with no equipment; Easily scalable by changing box height; Trains coordination and ankle stability; Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances; Carries over to climbing, hiking, and athletic movements; Works anywhere — needs only a sturdy surface
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus and gluteus medius; Hamstrings; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Place a small towel under one foot on a smooth floor. Stand tall with the feet shoulder width apart. Brace the core and shift weight to the planted leg. Slide the towel foot out to the side by extending the leg. Stop when you feel a stretch in the inner thigh. Pull the towel foot back to the start by squeezing the inner thigh. Keep the planted leg slightly bent throughout. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds adductor and glute strength.; No equipment needed beyond a towel.; Excellent at home alternative to a Cossack squat.; Trains hip stability on the planted leg.; Carryover to lateral movement in sport.; Develops single leg balance.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Adductors; Gluteus medius; Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a weight plate flat between your palms at chest level. Squeeze the plate hard between your palms with fingers pointing up. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Press the plate forward away from your chest while maintaining the squeeze. Continue pressing until your arms are nearly extended. Squeeze your chest hard at the front of the press. Slowly bring the plate back to your chest while maintaining the squeeze.
Benefits: Self-resistance chest contraction; Useful warm-up or finisher; Builds chest mind-muscle connection; Easy to scale by changing plate weight; Strong inner chest engagement; Practical for home training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (inner fibers); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Set up in a high plank position with hands on a PVC stick. Hold the stick on the floor in front of you. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Press into the stick to engage the lats. Hold the isometric position with the core tight. Maintain the rigid plank. Hold for the working set.
Benefits: Loads the core; Trains isometric strength; Strong plank variation; Builds the abs; Useful core builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Core; Anterior deltoid

Description: Lie on your back. Arms extended toward the ceiling. Legs raised with knees at 90 degrees. Press your lower back into the floor. Brace your core. Slowly extend your right leg fully straight forward, lowering it toward the floor. Keep your left knee at 90 degrees. Return your right leg to start. Extend your left leg straight. Maintain lower back contact with the floor throughout. Aim for 8 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Increased anti-extension demand from straight legs; Harder than standard dead bug; Builds deep core stability; No equipment needed; Progressive from standard dead bug; Excellent for lower back health
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: This is an elite gymnastics skill. Master iron cross and straddle planche on rings first. From an iron cross position on gymnastic rings, lean your body forward. Row the bar up by driving your elbows back and slightly out. Keep elbows close to your body. Pull the bar to your lower chest or upper abdomen. Squeeze your shoulder blades together. Lower the bar under control back to arm’s length. Maintain torso angle throughout. Repeat for the desired number of reps. The neutral grip allows heavier loading than overhand barbell rows for many lifters.
Benefits: Neutral grip is comfortable on wrists and shoulders; Allows heavier loading than barbell rows for many lifters; Builds the lats, mid-traps, and rear delts; Easy to set up — no need to clean the bar from the floor; Excellent heavy back exercise; Carries over to deadlift strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Erector spinae (isometric); Forearms and grip

Description: Set a low platform or plates and stand on them. Position a loaded trap bar around you. Squat down inside the trap bar and grip the handles. Brace your core and set a flat back. Drive through the legs to lift the bar off the floor. Stand up tall locking out the hips. Squeeze the glutes hard at the top. Lower the bar back to the floor with control.
Benefits: Strong leg and back builder; Increased range of motion; Builds power off the floor; Easier on the lower back than barbell deadlift; Useful strength move; Builds posterior chain
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Place your hands on the floor behind you with fingers pointing toward your body. Position your hands shoulder-width apart. Lift your hips off the floor with arms straight. Brace your core. Lower your body by bending the elbows. Continue until your hips almost touch the floor. Press back up to the starting position by extending the arms.
Benefits: Builds tricep strength with no equipment; Useful for home or travel training; No bench or chair required; Easy to scale by changing leg position; Strong tricep activation; Develops shoulder stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major

Description: Sit on the floor with knees bent, feet flat. Place hands behind you with fingers pointing forward. Lift your hips slightly off the floor. Bend your elbows to lower your body toward the floor. Lower until your glutes nearly touch the floor. Press back up by extending your elbows. Keep your back close to your hands throughout. The floor limits range — this is easier than bench dips. Aim for 12 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Beginner regression for bench dips; No bench needed; Builds basic tricep pressing strength; Floor limits range for safety; Accessible anywhere; Progresses to bench dips
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (lower)

Description: Stand inside a loaded trap bar. Grip the side handles with a neutral grip. Step your left foot back about 12 inches behind your right, resting on the toes of the left foot. Most of your weight should be on your right (front) foot. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Hinge at the hips by pushing your butt back, lowering the trap bar along your right leg. Keep your right knee slightly bent. Your back stays flat. Descend until you feel a deep stretch in your right hamstring. Drive your hips forward to stand up. Squeeze your right glute at the top. Complete reps, then switch.
Benefits: Unilateral hip hinge with trap bar stability; Neutral grip reduces lower-back stress; Builds hamstring and glute strength per leg; Exposes left-right imbalances; More stable than single-leg RDL; Easy to load progressively
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hamstrings (front leg); Gluteus maximus (front leg); Erector spinae; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand in the middle of a loaded trap bar. Squat down and grip the handles with a neutral grip. Stand up tall with the bar at the sides. Brace your core and set the chest tall. Keep the arms straight and shoulders down. Shrug the shoulders straight up toward the ears. Squeeze the upper traps hard at the top. Lower the shoulders back down with control.
Benefits: Heavy trap builder; Neutral grip is wrist friendly; Easy to overload; Builds trap size; Useful trap builder; Strong machine free move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Trapezius; Rhomboids; Levator scapulae

Description: Load a trap bar with heavy weight on the floor. Stand inside the bar with feet hip-width apart. Squat down and grip the side handles firmly with both hands. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Drive through your feet to stand up explosively. Stand tall with the bar hanging at arm’s length at your sides. Pull your shoulders back and down. Maintain perfect upright posture. Walk forward with controlled, normal-length strides. Walk for the desired distance (50 to 100 feet) or time. Set the bar down with control at the end.
Benefits: Builds elite grip strength and endurance; Allows much heavier loading than dumbbells; Develops core stability and posture; Trains traps and upper back; Excellent full-body conditioning; Easier on the body than dumbbell carries due to balanced load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms and grip (heavy); Trapezius (entire); Core (anti-flexion stabilizer); Erector spinae; Quadriceps; Calves

Description: Mount a set of parallel dip bars by gripping them with arms locked out, supporting your full body weight. Cross your ankles behind you. Keep your torso as upright as possible — leaning forward shifts emphasis to the chest, staying upright biases the triceps. Brace your core, pull your shoulders down and back, and tuck your elbows close to your sides. Lower your body slowly under control by bending at the elbows. Keep your elbows tracking close to your body — do not let them flare out. Lower until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor or just below. Avoid going deeper unless your shoulders feel comfortable. Press back up by extending at the elbows, driving your hands down into the bars. Lock out at the top, briefly squeezing your triceps before the next rep. Add weight via a dip belt or weighted vest as you get stronger.
Benefits: One of the best bodyweight exercises for building tricep size and strength; Trains the triceps, chest, and shoulders together; Easy to scale up by adding weight or scale down by using assistance; Builds shoulder and core stability; Highly portable — needs only a set of bars; Strong predictor of relative upper-body pressing strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major (especially the lower/sternal head); Anterior deltoid; Rhomboids and trapezius (stabilizers); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Get into a high plank position with hands placed close together (shoulder-width or narrower) directly under your shoulders. Brace your core. Form a straight body line from heels to head. Tuck your elbows tight against your sides as you lower your chest toward the floor. Lower until your chest is just above the floor or hands. Press back up by extending at the elbows, focusing on squeezing your triceps. Lock out at the top with arms fully extended. Maintain the elbow tuck throughout — do not let them flare. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Emphasizes the triceps over the chest; Builds tricep size and strength with bodyweight; Easier on the shoulders than wide-grip pressing; No equipment needed; Useful for tricep development at home; Builds the chest and shoulders as secondary
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii (heavy emphasis); Pectoralis major (sternal head); Anterior deltoid; Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand inside a loaded trap bar. Grip the high or low handles with a neutral grip. Set feet shoulder-width apart. Stand up by extending your hips and knees — like a deadlift but with more knee bend (squat-like). Stand tall at the top. Lower back down by bending at the knees and hips — sitting more into a squat than a hinge. The more you bend your knees and keep upright, the more squat-like it becomes. Touch the plates to the floor and repeat. Aim for 6 to 10 reps.
Benefits: Natural neutral grip reduces shoulder stress; More upright torso than barbell back squats; Easier on the lower back; Hybrid squat-deadlift movement; Easy to learn; Builds quad and glute strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Erector spinae; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back with arms extended behind your head and legs extended straight. Brace your core and press your lower back into the floor. Simultaneously lift your upper body (reaching your hands forward) and pull your knees toward your chest. Meet in the middle with your hands reaching past your knees. Squeeze your abs hard. Slowly extend back to the start position — arms overhead and legs extended. Do not let your hands, feet, or shoulder blades touch the floor between reps to maintain tension. Control both the crunch and extension phases. No swinging or jerking. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Trains upper and lower abs simultaneously; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Time-efficient core exercise; Easy to scale by adjusting speed and range; Builds ab endurance and strength; Excellent core finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques (secondary); Transverse abdominis

Description: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs extended straight. Brace your core. In one explosive motion, sit up while pulling your knees toward your chest. Reach your hands forward to wrap around your shins or knees as you crunch up. Finish balanced on your sit bones in a tucked V-sit position — knees pulled in, chest up. Hold for one second. Reverse the motion under control — extend your legs and arms back out, lowering to the start. Do not let your hands or feet touch the floor between reps to maintain tension. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Builds dynamic core strength and explosive power; Trains hip-flexor strength; Develops balance and body control; CrossFit and gymnastics benchmark; No equipment needed; Time-efficient core exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Quadriceps (knee tuck)

Description: Lie on your side with the forearm on the floor under the shoulder. Stack the feet and press up into a side plank. Set the body in a straight line with the hips lifted. Reach the top arm up toward the ceiling. Thread the top arm under the body twisting the torso down. Reach as far through as possible squeezing the obliques. Twist back open and reach the arm up to the ceiling. Continue the twisting motion. Complete reps and switch sides.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Trains rotational core; No equipment needed; Builds shoulder stability; Useful core finisher; Adds dynamic challenge to side plank
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Anterior deltoid

Description: Get into a high plank position with hands shoulder-width apart. Brace your core hard and squeeze your glutes. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Press back up to the high plank position. At the top, rotate your torso to the right and lift your right hand off the floor. Reach your right hand up toward the ceiling, forming a side plank. Hold the side plank briefly, then return your right hand to the floor. Lower into the next push up. Alternate sides each rep.
Benefits: Trains chest and obliques together; Strong rotational core demand; Builds total body coordination; Time-efficient compound movement; Develops shoulder stability; No equipment required
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Obliques; Core stabilizers

Exercise Name: Twin Handle Parallel Grip Lat Pulldown
Description: Set up two parallel handles on a high cable pulldown station. Grab one handle in each hand with a neutral grip. Sit on the seat with the thighs locked under the pad. Brace the core and keep the chest up. Pull the handles down toward the chest. Drive the elbows down and back to the sides. Squeeze the lats hard at the bottom. Return with control to the stretched position.
Benefits: Builds the lats.; Neutral grip is wrist friendly.; Twin handles allow natural arm path.; Trains the biceps.; Useful back accessory.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Trapezius; Rhomboids

Description: Lie on your back, knees bent, feet flat (anchored or free). Hands behind your head. Sit up fully. At the top, rotate and bring your right elbow toward your left knee. Return to center and lower back to the floor. Sit up and rotate the other way — left elbow to right knee. Continue alternating. Control both the sit-up and the rotation. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Combines sit-up with oblique rotation; Builds abs and obliques together; No equipment needed; Classic core exercise; Full range of motion; Simple and effective
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hands at your chest or behind your head. Squat down to parallel. At the bottom, rotate your torso to the right. Return to center. Stand up. Squat down again and rotate to the left. Continue alternating rotation sides. Aim for 10 to 15 reps total.
Benefits: Combines squatting with rotational core work; Builds leg and oblique strength; Improves hip mobility and coordination; No equipment needed; Engaging variation on bodyweight squats; Useful for warm-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Obliques (rotation); Core; Hip rotators

Description: Sit on the floor with the legs straight in front. Lean back and lift the legs into a V sit. Set the body in a V shape with abs engaged. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Reach one hand across to tap the opposite toe. Return to the V sit position. Tap the other toe with the opposite hand. Continue alternating sides.
Benefits: Loads the core; Trains the obliques; Strong V sit variation; Builds the hip flexors; Useful core move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip Flexors; Obliques

Description: Sit on the floor with the legs straight in front. Lean back and lift the legs into a V sit. Set the body in a V shape with abs engaged. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Make fists and bring them up to chest height. Throw a cross body punch with one arm. Twist the torso toward the punch. Alternate sides at a steady pace.
Benefits: Loads the core; Trains the obliques; Strong V sit variation; Useful for core size; Builds the abs
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Core

Description: Lie flat on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes. Simultaneously lift the legs and torso into a v shape.
