Reach the hands toward the toes at the top. Clap the hands together against the feet at the peak. Hold the v shape briefly with everything tight. Lower the legs and torso back to the floor with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hammers the upper and lower abs together.; Builds explosive core strength through the clap.; Trains coordination between upper and lower body.; Improves hip flexor strength.; No equipment needed.; Excellent finisher for ab workouts.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Quadriceps

Description: Lie face down on the floor with arms extended overhead. Position your legs straight with toes pointed. Brace your core and squeeze your glutes. Lift your chest, arms, and legs off the floor in a Superman position. Hold the lifted position briefly. Twist your torso to the right while staying lifted. Return to center, then twist to the left. Lower back to the floor with control.
Benefits: Builds back extension strength; Adds rotational core work; Strong oblique engagement; Strong glute activation; No equipment required; Useful for posterior chain training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae; Gluteus maximus; Obliques; Posterior deltoid

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat on the floor. Place your hands behind your head with fingers lightly touching. Do not pull on your neck. Brace your core. Press your lower back into the floor. Curl your upper body up and rotate to the right, bringing your left elbow toward your right knee. Squeeze your oblique and abs at the top. Hold one second. Lower under control back to the floor. On the next rep, rotate to the left, bringing your right elbow toward your left knee. Continue alternating for the desired total reps.
Benefits: Trains the rectus abdominis and obliques together; Simple variation of the standard crunch; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Easy to learn and perform; Builds rotational core strength; Excellent finisher for core workouts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Internal and external obliques; Hip flexors (secondary); Transverse abdominis

Description: Lie on your back. Arms at your sides for stability. Raise both legs together, angling them slightly to the right. Lift until your legs are nearly vertical. Lower under control, maintaining the angle. Complete reps angled to the right, then switch to the left. Alternatively, raise legs straight and twist them to one side at the top. Maintain lower back contact with the floor. Aim for 10 to 12 reps per side.
Benefits: Targets obliques alongside lower abs; Adds rotational demand to leg raises; No equipment needed; Engaging ab variation; Builds oblique strength from the floor; Develops core rotation control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis (lower); Hip flexors

Description: Sit on the floor with knees bent and feet flat. Lean back slightly so you balance on your sit bones. Lift both feet off the floor. Extend your legs straight out at roughly 45 degrees. Extend both arms forward at shoulder height, parallel to your legs. Your body should form a V-shape with your torso and legs both at 45 degrees. Brace your core hard. Keep your back as flat as you can — no rounding. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds, working up to 60 seconds. If full extension is too hard, start with bent knees (tuck V-sit) or hold one leg at a time. Breathe steadily throughout the hold.
Benefits: Builds isometric core strength; Develops hip-flexor and hamstring engagement; Foundational gymnastics and Pilates hold; Progresses toward L-sit and advanced calisthenics; No equipment needed; Improves balance and body control
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris); Quadriceps; Hamstrings (isometric stretch); Erector spinae

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Place your hands on your hips or extend them in front for balance. Step your right foot forward two to three feet into a lunge stance. Lower your back (left) knee toward the floor by bending both knees together. Descend until your back knee is just above the floor. Your front thigh should be parallel to the floor. Drive through your front (right) foot and step your back (left) foot forward past the right foot directly into the next lunge. Lower again with the left leg in front. Continue alternating, walking forward with each step. Keep your torso upright throughout. Do not lean forward or look down. Walk for the desired number of total steps. Progress by adding dumbbells or a barbell.
Benefits: Builds quads, glutes, and balance with no equipment; Trains coordination and proprioception; Excellent warm-up for lower-body training; Exposes and corrects left-right imbalances; Works anywhere — no equipment needed; Excellent stepping stone before adding load
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Calves (stabilizer); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart in a clear path. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Step forward with your right leg into a long lunge. Lower until the back knee nearly touches the floor. Drive through the front heel to stand up. As you stand up drive the trailing left knee high in front of you. Plant the left foot forward into the next lunge. Continue alternating lunge and high knee drive each step.
Benefits: Builds leg strength; Trains hip flexor power; Useful warm-up flow; No equipment required; Travel-friendly move; Strong dynamic warm up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hip flexors; Hamstrings

Description: Lie flat on your back. Extend both legs straight up toward the ceiling, perpendicular to the floor. Place your hands behind your head with fingers lightly touching, or extend them toward the ceiling. Brace your core. Keep your legs vertical and stable throughout. Crunch your upper body up by contracting your abs. Reach toward your feet. Lift your shoulder blades off the floor. Squeeze your abs hard at the top. Lower under control back to the starting position. Keep your legs straight and vertical the entire time. Do not let them lean forward. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Aim for 12 to 20 per set.
Benefits: Eliminates hip-flexor contribution for stricter ab work; Targets the rectus abdominis directly; Easier on the lower back than traditional sit-ups; No equipment needed; Builds visible ab strength; Excellent core finishing exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Transverse abdominis; Quadriceps (keeping legs vertical)

Description: Lie on your back with arms extended overhead and legs straight. Brace your core hard. Lift the legs and torso up at the same time into a V shape. Reach the hands toward the toes at the top. At the top crunch the body once more squeezing harder. Pause briefly with the abs fully contracted. Lower the legs and torso back down with control to the start. Keep tension in the core throughout.
Benefits: Strong abs builder; Doubles the contraction; Trains hip flexors; No equipment needed; Useful core finisher; Builds full core strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Start in a push-up position with your feet flat against a wall behind you. Place one foot on the wall, then the other. You should be in a high plank with feet on the wall. Begin walking your hands backward toward the wall while simultaneously walking your feet up the wall. Continue until your chest is near the wall and your body is roughly vertical (a handstand against the wall). Hold briefly at the top. Reverse the movement: walk your hands away from the wall while walking your feet down. Return to the starting push-up position. Repeat for the desired number of reps. This is challenging — start with 3 to 5 reps.
Benefits: Builds inversion confidence; Develops tremendous shoulder strength and stability; Trains the core in inverted positions; Foundation for handstand work; CrossFit benchmark movement; No equipment needed beyond a wall
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior and lateral deltoid (heavy); Triceps brachii; Trapezius; Serratus anterior; Core (entire trunk); Glutes and quads (controlling descent)

Description: Position two flat benches parallel to each other, roughly leg-length apart. Sit on the edge of one bench with your hands gripping the edge beside your hips. Place your heels on the opposite bench. Your legs should be extended or slightly bent. Have a partner place a weight plate on your lap, above your thighs near your hips. Slide your butt off the bench so your weight is supported by your hands and heels. Lower your body by bending at the elbows. Descend until your upper arms are parallel to the floor. Do not go deeper — excessive depth can strain the shoulders. Press back up by extending at the elbows. Squeeze your triceps at the top. Repeat for the desired reps.
Benefits: Allows progressive overload of the bench dip; Builds the triceps with heavier resistance than bodyweight; Easy to set up with two benches and a plate; Trains the chest and shoulders as secondary movers; Useful when parallel dip bars are unavailable; Easy to scale by adding or removing plates
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Pectoralis major (sternal head, secondary); Serratus anterior; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Stand with your back against a wall. Walk your feet out about 2 feet from the wall, hip-width apart. Slide down the wall until your thighs are parallel to the floor. Position your knees over your ankles, knees bent at 90 degrees. Brace your core and press your back firmly into the wall. From the parallel position, pulse down 1 to 2 inches. Pulse back up to the starting position. Maintain the wall sit and continue pulsing.
Benefits: Maximum quad time under tension; Burnout finishing exercise; No equipment required; Builds quad endurance; Easy to scale by adjusting depth; Useful for leg specialization
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Stand with feet much wider than shoulder-width, toes turned out slightly. Hold a kettlebell or dumbbell at your chest (goblet position). Shift your weight to the right by bending your right knee. Keep your left leg straight with the heel down. Lower your body to the right side. Drop as low as your flexibility allows. Your right foot may lift to the heel as you go deep — that’s fine. Left toes can point up. At the bottom, your right thigh is parallel or below, and left leg is fully extended. Drive through your right foot to stand back up. Keep the weight at your chest. Shift to the left and squat down on the left side. Continue alternating for the desired reps. Use moderate weight.
Benefits: Builds adductor strength and flexibility; Develops single-leg quad strength; Improves lateral hip mobility; Trains balance and coordination; Carries over to lateral athletic movements; Useful for combat sports conditioning
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (squat side); Adductors (extended leg, stretched and loaded); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Attach a weight plate to a dip belt and clip the belt around your waist. Alternatively, wear a weighted vest. Reach up and grip a sturdy pull-up bar with an underhand (supinated) grip, hands roughly shoulder-width apart. Hang with arms fully extended, feet off the floor. Cross your ankles behind you so the weight stays steady. Pull your shoulder blades down and back. Brace your core hard. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down toward your ribs. Lead with your chest. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats and biceps hard at the top. Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang with arms completely straight. Add weight in small increments (2.5 to 10 lbs). Aim for 3 to 8 reps per set with weight.
Benefits: Builds the lats and biceps with progressive overload; Stronger bicep position often allows more weight than pull-ups; Builds grip strength and shoulder stability under load; Strong predictor of relative upper-body strength; Direct carryover to all pulling strength; Develops core stability under loaded suspension
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii (heavy involvement); Brachialis and brachioradialis; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizers)

Description: Lie on your back with your head close to a wall. Reach up and press your palms hard into the wall. Bring your legs up to a 90-90 position with knees bent over hips. Brace your core and press your lower back into the floor. Maintain wall pressure throughout. Slowly lower one heel to tap the floor. Keep the knee bent at 90 degrees throughout. Return the leg to the start and alternate sides.
Benefits: Builds core stability; Trains anti-extension; Engages the lats; No equipment beyond a wall; Useful for spine health; Easy to learn dead bug variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Hip flexors; Latissimus dorsi

Description: Drape heavy chains over each end of a barbell. Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width and toes pointed slightly out. Grip the bar with hands inside your knees. Brace your core and keep your back flat. Drive through your heels and push the floor away. Stand tall with hips fully extended at the top. Feel the chain weight increase as you stand. Lower the bar back to the floor with control.
Benefits: Overloads the lockout phase; Accommodating chain resistance; Builds lockout strength; Strong glute and quad builder; Useful for plateau busting; Develops powerlifting strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Hamstrings; Spinal erectors

Description: Lie on your back. Hold a light dumbbell or weight plate straight up over your chest with both hands. Bend your knees to 90 degrees with shins parallel to the floor. Press your lower back firmly into the floor. Brace your core. Slowly extend your right arm overhead and your left leg straight out — both staying just above the floor. Keep your lower back pressed into the floor. If it lifts, reduce the range. Return to the starting position. Repeat with the opposite arm and leg. Continue alternating for the desired number of reps. Use light weight (5 to 15 lbs). Form is everything.
Benefits: Builds anti-extension core strength under load; Teaches core bracing for heavy compound lifts; Trains the deep ab muscles (transverse abdominis); Excellent rehab and prehab exercise; Easy to scale by changing weight; Develops mind-muscle connection to the core
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors (legs); Deltoids (arms holding weight)

Description: Set a decline bench to 30 to 45 degrees. Hook your feet under the foot pads. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell at your chest (easier) or behind your head (harder). Lie back on the decline bench. Sit up by flexing your spine. Drive your chest toward your knees. Squeeze your abs hard at the top. Lower under control back to the decline position. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per set. Do not use momentum — control every rep.
Benefits: Heavy ab loading from decline plus weight; Builds ab strength beyond bodyweight; Easy to load progressively; Greater range of motion than flat sit-ups; Excellent for ab hypertrophy; Simple setup
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Stand with the balls of your feet on a calf raise block (or step) facing a sturdy surface. Hinge forward at the hips, placing your forearms on the surface for support. Your back should be roughly parallel to the floor. Have a partner sit on your lower back or position a weight belt with a weight loaded on your hips. Brace your core. Stand firmly on the balls of your feet. Slowly rise up onto your toes by extending at the ankles. Squeeze your calves hard at the top. Lower under control, allowing your heels to drop below the block level for a deep stretch. Repeat for 15 to 25 reps per set.
Benefits: Heavy load directly on the calves; Bent-over position deeply stretches the calves; One of the most effective calf builders; Develops calf size and ankle strength; Used by classic bodybuilders for elite calf development; Builds toward unsupported standing variations
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gastrocnemius (heavy involvement); Soleus; Achilles tendon; Tibialis posterior

Description: Stand on one leg with a dumbbell held in both hands at chest level. Bend the non-working leg behind you with the foot off the floor. Brace your core and keep your chest up. Sit your hips back and bend your standing leg. Allow the back knee to lower toward the floor behind you. Extend the dumbbell out in front of you to counterbalance. Stop just before the back knee touches the ground. Drive up through the standing heel to return. Complete reps on one side before switching.
Benefits: Builds single-leg strength; Counterbalance allows deeper range; Sculpts quads and glutes; Improves balance and stability; Useful for athletic training; Fixes side-to-side imbalances
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core

Description: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent at roughly 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against your chest with both arms crossed over it. For more challenge, hold the weight extended overhead with arms fully extended. Brace your core and tuck your chin slightly. Press your lower back gently into the floor. Curl your upper body off the floor by contracting your abs. Lift your shoulder blades clear of the floor. Continue curling up until your shoulder blades are off the floor and your abs are fully contracted. Do not sit all the way up — this is a crunch, not a sit-up. Squeeze your abs hard for one second at the top. Lower your upper body under control back to the floor. Touch your shoulder blades briefly to the floor before the next rep. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Increase load progressively as you get stronger.
Benefits: Allows progressive overload of the abs for visible growth; Direct isolation of the rectus abdominis; Easy to scale by changing weight or weight position; Works at home with one dumbbell or weight plate; Builds strength and definition in the core; Easier on the lower back than full sit-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially the upper portion); Obliques (secondary); Hip flexors (minor)

Description: Stand with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell, plate, or kettlebell extended out in front of your chest with both hands. Keep your arms straight throughout the movement. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Squat down by bending your knees and pushing your hips back. Allow the held weight to act as a forward counterbalance. Continue down until your thighs are parallel to the floor or deeper. Drive up through your heels to stand back to the starting position.
Benefits: Counterweight allows more upright torso; Improves squat depth and form; Strong shoulder isometric work; Builds quad and glute strength; Useful for teaching squat form; Easy to scale by changing weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Anterior deltoid

Description: Wear a weighted vest or have a partner load your back. Place two boxes or stacks of plates a few inches off the floor, shoulder-width apart. Get into a push-up position with hands on the boxes. Brace your core and keep your body in a straight line. Drop your hands off the boxes onto the floor. Catch yourself in a push-up and absorb the impact. Press through the floor to push back up. Reset your hands on the boxes for the next rep.
Benefits: Builds explosive chest power; Eccentric overload from drop; Develops landing strength; Useful for athletes; Strong reactive power builder; Advanced push-up variation
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Front deltoid

Exercise Name: Weighted Floor Crunch Feet on Bench
Description: Lie on your back on the floor with legs resting on a bench. Knees should be bent at 90 degrees with calves parallel to the floor. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against the chest with both hands. Brace the core and exhale as you crunch up. Lift the shoulder blades off the floor while keeping the lower back down. Squeeze the abs hard at the top of the crunch. Lower the shoulders back to the floor with control. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hammers the upper abs with added load.; Bench position protects the lower back.; Easy to scale by changing the weight.; Builds visible ab strength and definition.; Strict tempo improves core control.; Carryover to compound lifts requiring strong abs.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Hip flexors

Description: Hold a light dumbbell in one hand at the side. Stand with the feet hip width apart. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Set the thumb pointing up like a thumbs up. Raise the dumbbell out and forward to shoulder height. Stop at shoulder height with the thumb up. Lower with control to the start. Finish all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds the rotator cuff; Strong shoulder health move; Trains the lateral delt; Useful warm-up; Builds shoulder stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Supraspinatus; Lateral deltoid; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a weight plate with both hands at your hips, gripping the sides of the plate. Brace your core. Pull your shoulders back and down. Lift the plate straight up in front of you with arms extended. Maintain a slight bend in your elbows throughout. Continue lifting until the plate reaches shoulder height. Pause briefly. Squeeze your front delts. Lower under control over two seconds back to your hips. Use moderate weight. Avoid swinging.
Benefits: Isolates the front deltoid; Two-handed grip allows heavier loading; Easy to set up at home; Builds front delt size and strength; No bench needed; Useful warm-up for pressing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid (primary); Lateral deltoid (slight); Upper trapezius; Pectoralis major (clavicular head, slight); Forearms (grip)

Description: Start in a forearm plank position with elbows directly under shoulders, body in a straight line. Have a partner place a weight plate on your upper back, between your shoulder blades. Brace your core hard. Engage your glutes. Maintain the straight body line — head, hips, and heels in alignment. Press your forearms into the floor. Push your shoulder blades apart slightly. Hold the position with the added weight for 20 to 60 seconds. Breathe steadily. Brace continuously. Have your partner remove the weight before you lower out of the plank.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to plank training; Builds elite anti-extension core strength; Useful when bodyweight planks become too easy; Develops shoulder stability under load; Easy to scale by adjusting plate weight; Time-efficient core exercise
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Erector spinae; Anterior deltoid; Gluteus maximus

Description: Sit on the floor with your upper back against a bench. Place a barbell, dumbbell, or weight plate across your hips. Use a barbell pad or folded towel to cushion the weight against your hip bones. Plant your feet flat on the floor, hip-width apart. Hold the weight with both hands to keep it steady. Brace your core. Tuck your chin slightly. Drive through your heels and squeeze your glutes to lift your hips and the weight. Continue until your body forms a straight line from knees to shoulders. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Do not hyperextend the lower back. Lower under control. Touch lightly, then drive up again.
Benefits: Allows progressive overload of the glutes; Most effective glute mass builder; Easy to scale by changing weight; Targets the glutes without spinal compression of squats; Easier on the lower back than heavy squats and deadlifts; Builds glute strength that carries over to all lower-body lifts
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Hamstrings; Adductor magnus; Quadriceps (secondary); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Place a dumbbell upright on the floor below a pull-up bar. Alternatively, wear ankle weights. Hang from the bar with an overhand grip. Lift your legs slightly to grip the dumbbell handle between your feet (squeeze hard). Pull your shoulders down and back. Brace your core. Keep your legs straight. Slowly lift your legs by contracting your lower abs and hip flexors. Continue lifting until your legs are at least parallel to the floor (90 degrees) or higher. Pause briefly at the top. Lower your legs under control over two to three seconds. Stop just before fully extended. Use light weight to start (5 to 15 lbs). The added load is deceptively challenging.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to lower-ab training; Builds elite core strength; Develops grip and hanging endurance; One of the most effective ab exercises available; Trains hip flexor strength; Direct progression from bodyweight hanging leg raises
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (especially lower); Hip flexors; Obliques; Forearms and grip; Latissimus dorsi (engagement)

Exercise Name: Weighted Floor Twisting Crunch Feet on Bench
Description: Lie on your back on the floor with legs resting on a bench. Knees bent at 90 degrees with calves parallel to the floor. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against the chest with both hands. Brace the core and exhale as you crunch up. As you lift, twist the torso so one shoulder points toward the opposite knee. Squeeze the obliques hard at the top of the twist. Lower back to the floor with control and untwist to neutral. Alternate sides on each repetition.
Benefits: Hits the obliques through controlled rotation under load.; Strengthens the upper abs in the crunch.; Bench position protects the lower back.; Easy to scale weight as needed.; Builds rotational core strength.; Improves twisting power for athletic carryover.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors

Description: Lie on your back. Bring the soles of your feet together and let your knees fall out to the sides (butterfly). Place a weight plate across your hip crease. Hold it with both hands. Press through the edges of your feet and squeeze your glutes to thrust your hips up. Squeeze your glutes hard at the top. Lower under control. The butterfly position minimizes hamstring involvement. Use moderate weight. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set. Focus on glute squeeze, not hip height.
Benefits: Isolates the glutes more than standard hip thrusts; Butterfly position minimizes hamstring involvement; Adds progressive loading with a weight plate; Excellent glute activation exercise; No bench needed; Easy to set up
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (primary); Gluteus medius (slight from abducted position); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Attach a weighted dip belt with a plate or wear a weighted vest. Stand under a chin-up bar. Reach up and grab the bar with an underhand grip. Hang from the bar with arms fully extended. Engage your lats and pull your shoulder blades down. Brace your core and keep your legs together. Hold the dead-hang position for as long as possible. Drop off when control is lost.
Benefits: Builds grip strength; Strengthens the shoulders; Useful for chin-up progression; Decompresses the spine; Builds lat endurance; Easy to scale loading
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearms; Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii

Description: Set up on a 45-degree hyperextension bench. Adjust the pad so it sits just below your hip bones, with your feet locked under the foot pads. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against your chest with both arms crossed over it. Brace your core hard and lock in your back angle. Start with your torso angled up so your body forms a roughly straight line from heels to head. Hinge forward at the hips by lowering your torso toward the floor. Keep your back flat — do not round. Lower until your torso is roughly perpendicular to the floor or until you feel a strong stretch in your hamstrings. Reverse the movement by squeezing your glutes and hamstrings to bring your torso back up to the straight-line position. Do not hyperextend (overarch) the lower back at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Increase load progressively over time.
Benefits: Allows progressive overload of the posterior chain; Builds the lower back, glutes, and hamstrings aggressively; Trains the hip-hinge pattern under load; Excellent accessory for deadlift and squat strength; Builds spinal erector endurance and capacity; Easy to scale up with progressively heavier loads
Muscles Worked (Raw): Erector spinae (lower back); Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductor magnus; Trapezius and rhomboids (isometric); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set an incline bench to about 45 degrees. Hold a weight plate between your palms in front of your chest. Lie back on the bench with feet flat on the floor. Squeeze your palms hard against the plate. Brace your core and keep your back against the bench. Press the plate straight up and forward away from your chest. Maintain the squeeze through your hands the entire rep. Lower the plate slowly back to your chest.
Benefits: Hits the upper inner chest; Strong chest contraction; Constant squeeze tension; Useful as a finisher; No bar required; Joint-friendly chest move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (upper); Pectoralis major (inner); Front deltoid

Description: Hold a dumbbell with both hands in front of your hips. Begin in a half kneeling position with one knee on the floor. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Drive through the front heel to stand up and step the back foot forward. As you rise, swing the dumbbell up to chest or shoulder height. Stand fully tall with the dumbbell at the top of the swing. Step the working leg back and lower into the kneeling start. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Builds single leg strength through the kneeling to standing transition.; Trains hip drive and glute activation under load.; Strengthens the core to control the dumbbell swing.; Improves get up coordination useful for daily life.; Combines lower body work with shoulder mobility.; Loads the legs unilaterally to expose strength imbalances.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus; Quadriceps; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Set a bar in a power rack at hip height. Lie underneath the bar. Place a weight plate flat on your chest, or wear a weighted vest. Grip the bar with hands slightly wider than shoulder-width, overhand grip. Hang from the bar with arms extended. Body straight from heels to head, supported on your heels. Pull your chest toward the bar by driving your elbows down and back. Row until your chest touches the bar (or as close as possible). Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Lower under control. Have a partner help you place and remove the weight plate safely.
Benefits: Adds load to bodyweight rows for progressive overload; Builds serious back strength; Easier on the lower back than barbell rows; Trains the back through full bodyweight pattern; Excellent at-home back exercise with minimal equipment; Bridge exercise to weighted pull-ups
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back on the floor with knees bent and feet off the floor. Hold a dumbbell on your chest with both hands. Brace your core and engage your abs. Crunch your shoulders off the floor while simultaneously extending your legs straight out. Reach the dumbbell forward as you crunch up. Continue until your shoulders are off the floor and your legs are extended. Squeeze your abs hard at the top. Slowly return to the starting position with control.
Benefits: Hits upper and lower abs together; Adds load to ab work; Time-efficient ab training; Builds total ab strength; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong functional movement pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques; Transverse abdominis

Description: Lie on your right side with legs stacked. Place a weight plate on your left outer thigh or wear an ankle weight. Support your head with your right hand. Left hand on the floor for stability. Keeping your left leg straight, lift it upward toward the ceiling. Lift to about 45 degrees. Squeeze your left glute medius. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps per side. Keep your hips stacked — do not let the top hip roll back.
Benefits: Isolates the gluteus medius with added load; Builds hip stability; Easy to set up; Lying position eliminates momentum; Useful for rehab and prehab; Easy to scale with weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus medius and minimus; Tensor fasciae latae; Gluteus maximus (slight)

Description: Lie face down on a bench with the head and shoulders off the edge. Hold a small weight plate on the back of the head with both hands. Brace your core and let the head hang down. Extend the neck up lifting the head against the plate. Continue lifting until the head is in line with the body. Squeeze the back of the neck at the top. Pause briefly at the contracted position. Lower the head back down with control.
Benefits: Strong neck builder; Builds rear neck size; Useful for athletes; Builds neck strength; Strong neck move; Useful for combat sports
Muscles Worked (Raw): Splenius; Trapezius; Sternocleidomastoid

Description: Lie face up on a flat bench with your head hanging off the end. Place a folded towel on your forehead. Place a light weight plate on the towel. Hold the plate with both hands to keep it secure. Start with your head tilted back (extended). Curl your chin toward your chest by flexing your neck forward. Squeeze the front of your neck at the top. Lower under control back to the starting position. Use very light weight. Aim for 15 to 20 reps. Protect your cervical spine.
Benefits: Builds front neck strength; Important for contact sport athletes; Develops the sternocleidomastoid; Helps prevent neck injuries; Simple setup with a plate and towel; Easy to load progressively with small increments
Muscles Worked (Raw): Sternocleidomastoid; Scalenes; Longus colli; Platysma

Description: Lie face up on a flat bench with the head off the end. Place a folded towel and a light weight plate on the forehead. Hold the weight in place with the hands. Brace the core and keep the shoulders pinned. Slowly rotate the head to one side under the weight. Pause briefly and rotate to the other side. Keep the motion smooth and controlled throughout. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Builds neck rotational strength.; Carryover to combat sports and contact sports.; Easy to scale by adjusting the weight.; Trains the neck through full rotation.; Reduces neck stiffness over time.; Develops total neck stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Sternocleidomastoid; Levator scapulae; Trapezius; Scalene

Exercise Name: Weighted Lying Neck Side to Side
Description: Lie on the back on a bench or floor. Hold a small weight plate flat on the forehead. Brace the core and keep the body relaxed. Set the chin in a neutral position. Rotate the head slowly to one side. Hold for a beat at the end range. Rotate slowly back through center to the other side. Continue alternating for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the neck rotators.; Reduces neck injury risk.; Useful for combat athletes.; Trains deep cervical muscles.; Improves neck stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Sternocleidomastoid; Trapezius; Levator scapulae

Description: Lie on your side on a flat bench with the head off the end. Place a folded towel and a light weight plate on the side of the head. Hold the weight in place with the top hand. Brace the core and keep the body steady. Lower the head toward the floor with control. Reverse the motion and lift the head up to the side. Stop when the neck is straight in line with the body. Repeat for all reps then switch sides.
Benefits: Builds lateral neck flexor strength.; Adds neck thickness for athletic durability.; Carryover to combat sports.; Easy to scale by adjusting the weight.; Trains the neck through full lateral range.; Develops total neck stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Sternocleidomastoid; Trapezius; Scalene; Levator scapulae

Description: Sit on a stability ball. Walk your feet forward and roll down until your upper back and shoulders rest on the ball. Bridge your hips up so your body is straight from knees to shoulders. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell with both hands, arms extended straight up above your chest. Rotate your torso to the right, rolling onto your right shoulder on the ball. Continue rotating until your arms point to the right side. Rotate back through center and to the left. Continue alternating for 10 to 15 reps per side. Maintain the bridge throughout. Use moderate weight.
Benefits: Loaded oblique rotation on an unstable surface; Bridge position engages the glutes and hamstrings; Develops rotational core strength; Ball surface adds instability; Excellent full-body core exercise; Easy to scale with weight
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Gluteus maximus (bridge hold); Hamstrings (bridge hold); Anterior deltoid (weight hold)

Description: Attach a weight plate to a dip belt and clip it around your waist. Approach a sturdy pull-up bar. Grip the bar with a false grip (wrists rolled over the bar) or standard overhand grip, hands shoulder-width apart. Hang with arms extended. Brace your core. Pull explosively as high as possible. Drive your chest toward the bar. As your chest reaches the bar, transition by rolling your wrists over and pressing your body up. Press up to a full straight-arm support position above the bar (lockout). Lower under control back to the dead hang. This is an advanced exercise. Master strict bodyweight muscle-ups before adding weight. Use 1 to 5 reps per set.
Benefits: Pinnacle of bodyweight pulling and pressing strength; Builds the lats, chest, triceps, and core; Develops explosive pulling power; Impressive calisthenics skill; Excellent measure of relative upper-body strength; Carries over to all pulling and pressing
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (heavy); Pectoralis major (transition); Triceps brachii (lockout); Biceps brachii (pull); Trapezius and rhomboids; Core (anti-extension throughout); Forearms and grip; Pull-Up; Weighted Pull-Up; Tricep Dip; Bodyweight Muscle-Up; Ring Muscle-Up; Strict Muscle-Up; Kipping Muscle-Up (CrossFit); Muscle Up; Kipping Muscle Up; Band Assisted Muscle Up

Description: Add weight to a dip belt or wear a weighted vest. Grip a pull up bar with one hand only. Hang from the bar with the arm fully extended. Brace your core and keep the body steady. Pull the chin up over the bar by bending the elbow. Squeeze the lat and bicep hard at the top. Lower back down with control to a full hang. Complete reps and switch hands.
Benefits: Elite back builder; Strong unilateral pull; Builds extreme lat strength; Trains the biceps; Useful for advanced trainees; Builds back size
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Forearm flexors; Rhomboids

Description: Sit on the floor with upper back against a bench. Place a weight plate or dumbbell on your right hip. Bend your right knee with foot flat. Extend your left leg straight forward or up. Drive through your right heel to thrust your hips up. At the top, your body forms a straight line from right knee to shoulders. Squeeze your right glute hard. Lower under control. Complete reps, then switch sides. Use moderate weight. Aim for 10 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Progressive glute loading per leg; Exposes left-right glute imbalances; Builds single-leg hip extension power; Easy to load progressively; Excellent for glute hypertrophy; Useful for athletic training
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (working leg); Hamstrings; Core (anti-rotation); Erector spinae

Description: Hold a weight plate with both hands by the edges. Stand with the feet hip width apart and knees soft. Hinge at the hips until the torso is at a forty five degree angle. Let the plate hang down toward the floor. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Pull the plate up to the lower ribs. Squeeze the lats and upper back at the top. Lower with control to the start.
Benefits: Builds the back; Trains the biceps; Strong row variation; Useful when only plates available; Builds upper back
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Rhomboids; Trapezius

Description: Hold a weight plate with both hands overhead. Stand with the feet hip width apart. Lock out the elbows overhead. Brace your core and keep the chest up. March in place by lifting one knee up high. Lower the leg and lift the other knee up. Keep the plate stable overhead throughout. Continue marching in place.
Benefits: Builds the shoulders; Trains the core; Strong combo move; Useful for athletes; Builds overhead stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Core; Hip Flexors

Description: Stand in front of a sturdy box with a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level. Set your feet at hip-width and brace your core. Place one foot flat on the box. Drive through the front heel to step up onto the box. As you reach the top, press the dumbbells straight overhead. Lock out the arms at the top. Lower the dumbbells back to shoulder level. Step back down with control. Alternate legs each rep.
Benefits: Trains legs and shoulders together; Combo move saves time; Builds full-body strength; Strong conditioning effect; Useful for athletes; Excellent functional move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii

Description: Attach a weight plate to a dip belt and clip the belt around your waist with the chain hanging in front. Alternatively, wear a weighted vest. Reach up and grip a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands slightly wider than shoulder-width. Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Hang with arms fully extended, feet off the floor. Cross your ankles behind you so the weight stays steady. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Brace your core hard. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down and out toward your hips. Lead with your chest, not your chin. Continue until your chin clears the bar or your chest touches the bar. Pause briefly at the top. Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang with arms completely straight. The weighted descent builds strength. Add weight in small increments (5 to 10 lbs) as you get stronger. Aim for 3 to 6 reps per set with weight.
Benefits: Allows continued progressive overload after bodyweight pull-ups become easy; Builds the lats, biceps, and grip with heavier resistance; Strong predictor of relative upper-body strength; Trains the entire back through full range of motion; Develops core stability under loaded suspension; Direct carryover to all pulling strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Biceps brachii and brachialis; Posterior deltoid; Forearms and grip; Core (stabilizers)

Description: Put on a weighted vest with the desired load. Begin in a high plank position with hands under the shoulders. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Lower the chest toward the floor by bending the elbows. Stop just before the chest touches the floor. Press back up to lockout. Squeeze the chest hard at the top.
Benefits: Strong chest builder; Adds load to push ups; Builds chest size; Useful push up progression; Strong vest move; Builds the triceps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Sit on the floor with knees bent at roughly 90 degrees and feet flat on the floor (or lifted off for more challenge). Hold a weight plate, dumbbell, or medicine ball with both hands at chest height. Lean back slightly so your torso is at roughly a 45-degree angle to the floor. Brace your core. Lift your feet off the floor a few inches for added difficulty (or keep them planted for an easier version). Rotate your torso to the right by twisting from the waist. Bring the weight to the right side of your body, just outside your hip. Briefly tap the weight to the floor on the right side (optional) or pause briefly without touching down. Reverse the motion and rotate to the left side, bringing the weight to your left hip. Continue alternating sides for the desired number of total reps. Rotate from the waist, not from the arms.
Benefits: Builds the obliques with progressive overload; Trains rotational core strength; Develops anti-rotation and rotation control; Carries over to throwing, swinging, and rotational sports; Easy to scale by changing weight or foot position; Works at home with one weight plate or dumbbell
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Hip flexors; Erector spinae (stabilizer)

Description: Stand tall with feet wider than hip width. Hold a dumbbell overhead in one hand with arm locked. Set the other hand on the hip. Brace your core hard. Bend the body sideways toward the side opposite the dumbbell. Reach the free hand down toward the floor as you bend. Keep the dumbbell stacked over the shoulder throughout. Drive back to standing through the obliques. Switch sides and repeat.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Builds shoulder stability; Trains the side bend pattern; Strong yoga inspired move; Useful core finisher; Builds rotational stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Anterior deltoid; Quadratus lumborum; Core

Description: Sit on a bench or chair. Place the balls of your feet on a step plate or block on the floor. Place a weight plate across your lower thighs, just above your knees. Hold it with your hands. Lower your heels as far as possible for a deep calf stretch. Press through the balls of your feet to raise your heels as high as possible. Squeeze your calves at the top. Hold briefly. Lower under control. Use moderate weight. Aim for 15 to 25 reps per set. Full range of motion on every rep.
Benefits: Targets the soleus specifically (seated position); Simple setup with a plate and step; Useful when no calf raise machine is available; Easy to load progressively; Builds lower calf thickness; Works at home or in any gym
Muscles Worked (Raw): Soleus (primary); Gastrocnemius (reduced in seated); Achilles tendon

Description: Stand tall holding a light dumbbell in each hand. Lift the arms out to the sides at shoulder height. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Begin circling the arms forward in small circles. Gradually grow the circles as you continue. After several circles, reverse direction and circle backward. Keep the arms at shoulder height the entire time. Continue circling for the duration.
Benefits: Strong shoulder endurance move; Builds shoulder stability; Useful warm-up; Trains all three deltoid heads; Builds shoulder stamina; Easy to do anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Anterior deltoid; Lateral deltoid; Posterior deltoid

Exercise Name: Weighted Seated One Arm Reverse Wrist Curl
Description: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor. Hold a dumbbell with one hand using a pronated grip. Rest the forearm on your thigh with the wrist hanging off the knee. Let the dumbbell hang down with the wrist fully flexed. Brace the core and stabilize the forearm with the free hand if needed. Curl the back of the hand up by extending the wrist. Squeeze the forearm extensors at the top. Lower the dumbbell slowly back to full wrist flexion and complete all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates the forearm extensors often missed in standard curls.; Builds wrist and forearm strength balance.; Improves grip and gripping endurance.; Single arm focus exposes imbalances.; Joint friendly with controlled tempo.; Carryover to compound lifts and grip sports.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Brachioradialis; Anconeus

Description: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with a neutral grip. Rest the forearms on the thighs. Let the wrists hang off the knees. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Set the dumbbells with palms facing each other. Curl the wrists up squeezing the forearms. Lift as high as the wrists allow. Lower the wrists back down with control.
Benefits: Strong forearm builder; Hammer grip targets brachioradialis; Builds grip strength; Easy to scale loading; Useful arm builder; Strong dumbbell move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors; Forearm extensors

Exercise Name: Weighted Seated Leg Raise on Floor
Description: Sit on the floor with the legs extended. Pinch a light dumbbell between the feet. Place the hands on the floor behind the hips for support. Lean back slightly with the chest up. Brace the core and lift both legs off the floor. Raise the legs up toward vertical. Squeeze the abs and hip flexors at the top. Lower with control and continue for the working set.
Benefits: Loads the lower abs hard.; Trains the hip flexors.; Bodyweight ab variation with load.; Useful core builder.; Builds the rectus abdominis.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Hip flexors; Rectus abdominis; Quadriceps

Exercise Name: Weighted Seated One Arm Wrist Curl
Description: Sit on a bench with feet flat on the floor. Hold a dumbbell with one hand using a supinated grip. Rest the forearm on your thigh with the wrist hanging off the knee. Allow the dumbbell to roll down to your fingertips at the bottom. Brace the core and stabilize the forearm with the free hand if needed. Curl the wrist up to flex the forearm flexors. Squeeze the forearm hard at the top. Lower the dumbbell slowly to full wrist extension and complete all reps then switch.
Benefits: Isolates the forearm flexors with strict form.; Builds grip and forearm size.; Single arm focus improves balance.; Sitting position braces the elbow for strict reps.; Joint friendly with controlled tempo.; Carryover to compound lifts and grip sports.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Brachioradialis; Biceps brachii

Description: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell in each hand with a pronated overhand grip. Rest the forearms on the thighs. Let the wrists hang off the knees. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Set the dumbbells with palms facing down. Curl the wrists up squeezing the top of the forearms. Lift as high as the wrists allow. Lower the wrists back down with control.
Benefits: Strong wrist extensor builder; Trains the top forearms; Builds grip strength; Easy to scale loading; Useful arm builder; Strong dumbbell move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm extensors; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors

Description: Sit on a bench holding a dumbbell vertically with both hands. Cup the hands under the top inside plate. Press the dumbbell overhead to lockout. Brace your core and keep the chest tall. Set the upper arms vertical pointing at the ceiling. Lower the dumbbell behind the head by bending the elbows. Stop when the elbows are fully bent. Press back up to lockout squeezing the triceps.
Benefits: Strong tricep builder; Trains the long head; Easy to scale loading; Builds tricep size; Useful arm builder; Strong dumbbell move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Anconeus; Forearm flexors

Description: Sit on a bench with the forearm braced flat on the thigh or bench. Hold a dumbbell by one end so it sits vertically. Let the wrist hang off the edge with palm facing down. Keep the forearm flat throughout. Rotate the wrist to turn the palm up toward the ceiling. Squeeze the forearm hard at the top. Rotate the wrist back to palm down with control. Complete reps and switch hands.
Benefits: Strong forearm builder; Trains wrist supination; Useful for grip strength; Builds the biceps brachialis; Strong arm wrestling carryover; Easy to scale
Muscles Worked (Raw): Forearm flexors; Biceps brachii; Brachioradialis

Exercise Name: Weighted Side Lying Side Neck Raise
Description: Lie on one side on a bench or floor. Place a small weight plate on the temple of the upper side of the head. Hold the plate in place with the top hand. Brace the core and keep the body relaxed. Lower the head toward the floor. Lift the head laterally toward the ceiling. Squeeze the side neck muscles at the top. Lower with control and continue for all reps then switch.
Benefits: Builds the lateral neck flexors.; Reduces neck injury risk.; Useful for combat athletes.; Trains the side of the neck.; Improves neck stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Sternocleidomastoid; Trapezius; Levator scapulae

Exercise Name: Weighted Seated Tuck Crunch on Floor
Description: Sit on the floor with the knees bent and the torso leaned back slightly. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell against the chest. Brace the core and lift the feet off the floor. Balance on your hips with the body in a v shape. Pull the knees in toward the chest while curling the torso forward. Squeeze the abs hard at the top. Extend the legs and lean back to open the v shape. Repeat the tuck and extend for all reps.
Benefits: Hammers the abs and hip flexors under load.; Builds core stability through balance.; Strengthens the deep abdominal wall.; Carryover to compound lifts and athletic core.; Easy to scale weight up or down.; Excellent ab finisher.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Obliques

Description: Choose your loading method: hold a dumbbell or kettlebell at your chest (goblet style), wear a weighted vest, or hold weight plates at your shoulders or sides. Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned out slightly. Brace your core. Lift your chest. Position the load against your body. Sit your hips back and down as if reaching for a chair. Bend your knees and lower until your hip crease drops below your knees. Keep your knees tracking over your toes. Drive through your full foot to stand. Squeeze your glutes at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to bodyweight squats; Bridge between bodyweight and barbell squats; Versatile — works with any loading method; Builds quad, glute, and hamstring strength; Easy to scale; Useful when no barbell is available
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Adductors; Core (stabilizer); Forearms (grip on dumbbells)

Description: Lie on the back on a flat bench or floor. Place a dumbbell between the feet and squeeze it tight. Brace your core and keep the lower back down. Place the hands at the sides palms down. Lift one leg straight up while keeping the other on the floor. Pause briefly at the top. Lower with control to the start. Alternate the working leg each rep.
Benefits: Loads the lower abs; Trains the hip flexors; Strong weighted variation; Builds the core; Useful ab builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip Flexors; Core

Description: Stand tall with feet shoulder-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at your sides with palms facing forward. Pin your elbows against your sides. Brace your core and pull your shoulders back. Curl both dumbbells up by bending only at the elbows. Continue until the dumbbells reach shoulder height. Squeeze the biceps hard at the top. Lower the dumbbells back down with control to full extension.
Benefits: Foundational bicep mass builder; Allows progressive heavy loading; Builds bicep size and strength; Strict bicep isolation; Useful for hypertrophy training; Strong forearm engagement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Brachioradialis

Description: Hold a weight in each hand at the sides. Stand with the feet hip width apart. Brace your core and keep the chest up. Squeeze the weights hard with the hands. Hold the squeeze briefly. Release and let the grip relax slightly. Squeeze hard again. Continue squeezing for the working set.
Benefits: Builds the forearms; Trains grip strength; Strong grip drill; Useful for grip endurance; Builds the hands
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors; Brachioradialis; Wrist extensors

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart on the balls of your feet (heels lifted). Hold a weight plate at your chest with both hands. Brace your core. Squeeze your glutes to lock your hips forward. Lean your torso backward as you bend your knees forward, lowering your hips toward your heels. Keep your hips locked forward — your body should form a straight line from knees to head. Lower as deep as you can while maintaining control. Drive through the balls of your feet to return to standing. Squeeze your quads. Use light weight to start. Hold a wall or chair with one hand if needed.
Benefits: Elite quad isolation; Builds quad strength and size; Strengthens the knees through full range; Easy to load progressively; No barbell needed; Builds knee stability when done with proper progression
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps (heavy isolation); Hip flexors; Calves; Core (anti-extension)

Description: Hook a dip belt with weight around the waist or wear a weighted vest. Grip a single straight bar with both hands at hip width. Press up to lockout with the bar in front of the body. Brace your core and lean slightly forward. Lower the body by bending the elbows. Allow the bar to slide up the body slightly as you descend. Lower until the upper arms are parallel to the floor. Press back up to lockout squeezing the triceps and chest.
Benefits: Strong tricep and chest builder; Adds weight to dips; Unique single bar angle; Builds upper body size; Useful tricep builder; Strong compound move
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major; Anterior deltoid

Description: Stand tall with the feet hip width apart. Hold a dumbbell with both hands at chest height. Brace your core and set the hips facing forward. Keep the dumbbell close to the chest. Rotate the torso to one side keeping the hips still. Squeeze the obliques hard at the end range. Rotate back through center and twist to the other side. Continue alternating side twists with control.
Benefits: Strong oblique builder; Trains rotational core; Easy standing setup; Useful core finisher; Builds rotational power; Strong functional pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Obliques; Rectus abdominis; Core

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold a dumbbell in each hand at shoulder level. Use a pronated grip with palms facing forward. Brace your core hard and keep your chest up. Press both dumbbells straight overhead. Lock out the arms with hands meeting above your head. Pause briefly at full extension. Lower the dumbbells slowly back to shoulder level.
Benefits: Builds shoulder strength; Trains core bracing; Strong shoulder builder; Standing setup improves stability; Builds front delt size; Useful for athletes
Muscles Worked (Raw): Front deltoid; Side deltoid; Triceps brachii; Traps

Description: Stand tall. Hold one or two weight plates between your palms at chest height. Press your palms together firmly. Maintain the inward squeeze throughout. Press the plates forward by extending your arms. Keep squeezing. Extend to full arm extension. Squeeze the inner chest hard. Slowly pull the plates back to your chest. Maintain the squeeze. Keep constant inward pressure throughout every rep. Use light to moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps. The squeeze is more important than the weight.
Benefits: Activates the inner chest fibers; Squeeze component targets pec adduction; No bench needed; Builds chest mind-muscle connection; Easy to set up with just a plate; Excellent chest finisher
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (inner fibers); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii; Serratus anterior

Description: Attach a weight plate to a dip belt and clip the belt around your waist. Alternatively, hold a dumbbell between your feet or wear a weighted vest. Mount the parallel dip bars with arms locked out, supporting your full weight plus the external load. Cross your ankles behind you (or below if holding a dumbbell). Brace your core. Keep your torso upright for tricep emphasis. Tuck your elbows close to your sides. Lower your body by bending at the elbows. Descend until your upper arms are roughly parallel to the floor. Press back up by extending at the elbows. Drive your hands into the bars. Lock out at the top. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Add weight in small increments (5 to 10 lbs) as you get stronger. Aim for 5 to 10 reps per set.
Benefits: Allows continued progressive overload after bodyweight dips become easy; Builds serious tricep, chest, and shoulder strength; Direct carryover to all pressing movements; Builds shoulder and core stability under load; Highly portable — needs only parallel bars and a dip belt; Excellent upper-body mass builder
Muscles Worked (Raw): Triceps brachii; Pectoralis major (sternal head); Anterior deltoid; Rhomboids and trapezius (stabilizers); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat. Hold a weight plate or dumbbell at your chest. Let both knees fall to the left so your lower body is rotated. Your upper body stays flat. Brace your core. Crunch straight up, lifting your shoulders off the floor. The rotated leg position emphasizes the right obliques. Squeeze your obliques at the top. Lower under control. Complete reps on this side, then switch legs to the opposite side. Use moderate weight. Aim for 12 to 15 reps per side.
Benefits: Adds progressive overload to side crunches; Builds oblique strength and size; Easy to scale by weight selection; Simple execution; No bench needed; Useful for core hypertrophy
Muscles Worked (Raw): Internal and external obliques; Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis

Description: Hang from a pull-up bar with an underhand grip wider than shoulder-width. Allow your arms to fully extend. Brace your core and pull your shoulders down. Pull your body up by bending at the elbows and driving them down. Continue until your chin clears the bar. Squeeze your lats and biceps at the top. Lower yourself back down with control to a full hang. Maintain the wide underhand grip throughout.
Benefits: Wide grip emphasizes outer lats; Underhand grip targets biceps; Different stimulus than standard chin ups; Builds back width and bicep size; Useful for breaking through pull plateaus; Functional pulling pattern
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Biceps brachii; Brachialis; Rhomboids

Exercise Name: Weighted Straight Leg Toe Touch Crunch
Description: Lie flat on your back with legs straight up toward the ceiling. Hold a dumbbell or weight plate with both hands above the chest. Brace the core and keep the legs straight up. Crunch the upper body up and reach the dumbbell toward the toes. Squeeze the upper abs at the top of the reach. Lower the shoulders back to the floor with control. Keep the legs straight and vertical throughout the set. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Hits the upper abs hard with added load.; Builds anterior core strength through the toe reach.; Improves shoulder mobility and stability.; Easy to scale weight up or down.; No equipment beyond a single weight needed.; Carryover to athletic core and compound lifts.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Hip flexors; Anterior deltoid; Obliques

Description: Stand with feet wider than shoulder-width. Toes turned out 30 to 45 degrees. Squat down by pushing knees out toward your toes. Descend to parallel or below. Drive through your full foot to stand. Keep torso upright. Push knees out — do not let them cave in. Aim for 15 to 20 reps. Useful warm-up before weighted sumo squats.
Benefits: Targets adductors and glutes with bodyweight; Develops wide-stance squat mobility; No equipment needed; Warm-up for weighted sumo squats; Builds hip mobility; Accessible for all levels
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Adductors; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Set up a low pull-up bar at about waist height. Sit on the floor under the bar with legs extended straight. Reach up and grab the bar with a wide overhand grip. Press your heels into the floor and brace your core. Pull your chest up toward the bar by driving your elbows down and back. Squeeze your shoulder blades together at the top. Continue until your chest is close to the bar. Lower yourself slowly back to the start.
Benefits: Builds the lats; Wide grip emphasizes back width; Useful as a pull-up progression; Reduces full bodyweight load; Builds back strength; Improves grip endurance
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Rhomboids; Biceps brachii; Rear deltoid

Description: Reach up and grip a sturdy pull-up bar with an overhand grip, hands roughly 1.5 times shoulder-width apart. Wrap your thumbs around the bar. Hang with arms fully extended, feet off the floor. Pull your shoulder blades down and back to set the start position. Brace your core. Pull your body up by driving your elbows down and out toward your hips. Lead with your chest. Aim to bring your upper chest to bar level. Squeeze your lats hard at the top. Lower yourself slowly under control to a full hang with arms completely straight. Avoid kipping or swinging. Strict reps are far more valuable than partial sloppy reps. Repeat for the desired number of reps. Add weight via a dip belt as you get stronger.
Benefits: Builds the upper lats and back width more than narrow-grip variations; Develops the V-taper look; Trains the lats with reduced bicep involvement; Builds grip strength and shoulder stability; Highly portable — needs only a pull-up bar; Excellent benchmark for upper-body strength
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (especially the upper fibers); Teres major; Trapezius (middle and lower); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii (less than standard pull-up); Forearms and grip

Description: Start in a wide push-up position. Perform one push-up. Walk your hands inward to a narrow (close-grip) position. Perform one push-up. Walk your hands back out to wide. Push-up. Continue alternating wide and narrow. Maintain body alignment throughout the transitions. Wide position emphasizes chest; narrow emphasizes triceps. Aim for 8 to 12 total reps (4-6 per width).
Benefits: Targets both chest and triceps in one set; Provides varied stimulus without rest; No equipment needed; Engaging push-up variation; Builds both pressing patterns; Time-efficient
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (wide); Triceps brachii (narrow); Anterior deltoid; Core (stabilizer)

Description: Kneel on the floor with an ab wheel in front of you. Grip the handles with both hands. Place a pad under your knees for comfort. Brace your core hard. Tuck your pelvis under (posterior tilt). Slowly roll the wheel forward, extending your arms and body away from your knees. Roll only as far as you can while maintaining a flat or slightly rounded back. Do NOT let your lower back arch or sag. At full extension, your body should form a straight line from knees to hands. Pull yourself back to the start by contracting your abs and pulling the wheel back. Start with 5 to 8 reps. Progress to standing rollouts only when kneeling is mastered.
Benefits: Elite anti-extension core builder; Builds rectus abdominis and obliques together; One of the hardest bodyweight core exercises; Develops shoulder stability under load; No bench needed — works at home; Carries over to all heavy lifting via core stability
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Transverse abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi (heavy involvement); Anterior deltoid; Hip flexors (slight)

Description: Kneel on the floor a few feet from a wall. Hold the ab wheel with both hands in front of you. Brace the core and squeeze the glutes. Roll the wheel forward keeping the arms straight. Continue rolling until the wheel reaches the wall. Hold the bottom position briefly with the body extended. Use the abs to pull the wheel back to the start. Repeat for the desired number of repetitions.
Benefits: Builds anterior core strength.; Wall stop limits range for safe progression.; Excellent foundation for full ab rollouts.; Trains anti extension through the core.; Carryover to plank and front lever progressions.; Develops total core stability.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis; Obliques; Latissimus dorsi; Hip flexors

Description: Set up a wrist roller — a short bar with a rope tied to the middle and a weight plate attached at the bottom of the rope. Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Hold the bar horizontally with both hands, arms extended in front of you at shoulder height. Begin rolling the bar away from you (overhand) by flexing one wrist down while extending the other up alternately. Continue rolling until the weight reaches the bar at the top. Reverse the motion: roll the bar toward you to lower the weight back down with control. Maintain extended arms throughout — the work is in the wrists and forearms. For variation: roll in the opposite direction (underhand). Use light weight to start — your forearms will burn intensely.
Benefits: Builds tremendous forearm endurance; Develops grip strength; Trains both wrist flexors and extensors; One of the best forearm exercises; Easy to load progressively; Useful for any grip-intensive activity
Muscles Worked (Raw): Wrist flexors and extensors; Brachioradialis; Forearm flexors and extensors (entire forearm); Anterior deltoid (isometric arm hold)

Description: Reach up and grip a pull-up bar with hands wider than shoulder-width — about 1.5 to 2 times shoulder width. Use an overhand grip. Hang from the bar with arms extended. Pull yourself up by driving your elbows down and slightly forward. Aim to bring the bar behind your head, lowering your head to clear the bar. Pull until the bar reaches the back of your neck or as close as your mobility allows. Lower under control to the full hang position. Keep your chest tall throughout. Engage your core. Stop immediately if you feel shoulder discomfort. Use lighter loads than front pull-ups.
Benefits: Heavily emphasizes the upper lats and traps; Builds back width; Different stimulus than front pull-ups; Useful variation for advanced lifters with good mobility; Trains shoulder mobility under load; No equipment needed beyond a pull-up bar
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi (especially upper fibers); Trapezius (middle and upper); Rhomboids; Posterior deltoid; Biceps brachii; Forearms

Description: Get into a push-up position with hands placed 1.5 to 2 times shoulder-width apart. Fingers point forward or slightly outward. Lower your chest to the floor. The wide hands create a deeper chest stretch. Press back up to lockout. Keep your body in a straight line. Elbows will flare more than standard push-ups. The wider position reduces range of motion but increases chest demand. Aim for 10 to 20 reps.
Benefits: Greater chest emphasis from wider hand position; Deeper chest stretch at the bottom; No equipment needed; Simple hand-width modification; Builds chest from a different angle; Reduces tricep involvement
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (increased); Anterior deltoid; Triceps brachii (reduced); Core (stabilizer)

Description: Begin in a high plank position. Set the body in a straight line from head to heels. Bend the elbows to lower the body to a low push up. Stop with the elbows at 90 degrees and upper arms parallel. Brace your core and keep the body steady. Lift one leg off the floor extending it straight back. Hold the three leg chaturanga position with steady breath. Lower the leg. Switch legs and repeat.
Benefits: Strong yoga upper body builder; Trains the chaturanga hold; Builds shoulder stability; No equipment needed; Strong core challenge; Builds the triceps
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major; Triceps brachii; Anterior deltoid; Core

Description: Begin in Downward-Facing Dog. Hips lifted, body in an inverted V, hands and feet planted. Shift your weight slightly forward into your hands. Lift your right leg straight up behind you. Keep your right hip square to the floor for the basic version. Reach the lifted leg high — aim for at least horizontal, ideally higher. Squeeze your right glute. Point your toes. Press evenly through both hands and your standing foot. Hold for 3 to 5 breaths, then return the right foot to the floor. Switch sides. For an open variation, allow the right hip to open up to the sky.
Benefits: Builds glute and hamstring strength in the lifted leg; Improves hip mobility and flexibility; Develops core stability and shoulder strength; Common vinyasa flow transition pose; Stretches the calves and hamstrings of the standing leg; No equipment needed
Muscles Worked (Raw): Gluteus maximus (lifted leg); Hamstrings (lifted leg, standing leg stretched); Anterior deltoid (weight bearing); Triceps brachii; Core (stabilizer); Calves (standing leg, stretched)

Description: For the seated butterfly version: sit on the floor with the soles of your feet pressed together. Let your knees fall open to the sides. Hold your ankles or feet with both hands. Sit up tall. Gently press your knees toward the floor with your elbows or hands. For a deeper stretch, hinge forward from the hips with a flat back. Feel the stretch through your inner thighs and groin. Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply. Release and shake out your legs. Alternative: Stand wide and shift weight side to side for a dynamic version.
Benefits: Stretches the adductors (inner thighs) and groin; Improves hip flexibility for sumo squats and wide-stance lifts; Helps prevent groin strains; No equipment needed; Multiple position options; Calming and restorative
Muscles Worked (Raw): Adductor magnus, longus, brevis; Gracilis; Pectineus; Hip flexors (slight)

Description: Lie face down on the floor with legs extended behind you. Place your hands on the floor under your shoulders, elbows bent and tucked close. Press your hips and thighs into the floor. Inhale and slowly press up, lifting your chest off the floor by partially or fully straightening your arms. Lift only as far as comfortable. Keep your hips on the floor. Feel the stretch through your abdominals and front of your body. Hold for 10 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply. Lower back down under control. Repeat two to three times.
Benefits: Stretches the rectus abdominis and front of the body; Counteracts forward-hunched posture; Improves spinal extension mobility; Opens the chest; No equipment needed; Gentle enough for daily use
Muscles Worked (Raw): Rectus abdominis (stretched); Hip flexors (stretched); Pectoralis major (stretched); Erector spinae (engaged)

Description: Stand tall. Reach both arms overhead and clasp your hands together with palms facing the ceiling. Pull your shoulders back and down. Lift your chest. Gently reach your hands up and slightly behind your head. Feel the stretch across your chest and front shoulders. Hold for 15 to 30 seconds. Breathe deeply into the stretch. For a deeper stretch, lean slightly backward while keeping your core braced. Release and shake out your arms. Repeat two to three times. This can also be done with hands clasped behind the back, pulling down and back. Avoid forcing the stretch — go only as far as your flexibility allows.
Benefits: Opens the chest and front shoulders; Counteracts forward-hunched posture; Stretches the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid; Improves shoulder flexibility; No equipment needed — works anywhere; Takes less than one minute
Muscles Worked (Raw): Pectoralis major (stretched); Anterior deltoid (stretched); Biceps brachii (stretched); Intercostal muscles

Description: Sit on the floor. Bend your right knee to 90 degrees in front of you with the outside of your right leg on the floor (external rotation). Bend your left knee to 90 degrees behind you with the inside of your left leg on the floor (internal rotation). Both shins should be roughly perpendicular to each other, forming a pinwheel shape. Sit up tall. Square your torso forward over your right shin. For a deeper stretch, lean forward over your right shin, keeping your back flat. Hold for 30 to 60 seconds. Breathe deeply. To switch sides, lift your knees and rotate both legs so the positions reverse. Perform 2 to 3 holds per side. Use a pillow under your hip if the position is uncomfortable.
Benefits: Stretches both hip internal and external rotation simultaneously; One of the most effective hip mobility drills; Improves squat depth and hip-hinge flexibility; Helps prevent hip and knee issues; No equipment needed; Used by physical therapists and mobility coaches
Muscles Worked (Raw): Piriformis and deep hip rotators (front leg, external rotation); Gluteus medius and minimus (front leg); Hip internal rotators (back leg); Tensor fasciae latae (back leg); Adductors (both legs)

Exercise Name: Alternate Shoulder Flexion Back to Wall
Description: Stand with the back, head, and hips against a wall. Plant the feet about a foot from the wall. Press the lower back gently into the wall. Brace the core and keep the ribs down. Slowly raise one arm up overhead toward the wall. Try to touch the back of the hand to the wall above the head. Lower the arm back to your side with control. Repeat with the other arm and continue alternating.
Benefits: Improves shoulder flexion mobility.; Wall feedback prevents excessive lower back arch.; No equipment needed.; Easy to perform anywhere.; Carryover to overhead lifts.; Reduces upper back stiffness.
Muscles Worked (Raw): Latissimus dorsi; Anterior deltoid; Trapezius; Pectoralis major

Description: Kneel on the floor with knees slightly apart and toes together. Sit your hips back onto your heels. Fold your torso forward over your thighs. Rest your forehead on the floor or on a folded block. Let your arms relax forward in front of you or back at your sides. Allow your shoulders to soften toward the floor. Breathe slowly and release tension across the back. Hold the pose for as long as feels good then come back up slowly.
Benefits: Releases lower back tension; Opens the hips; Stretches the hamstrings; Restorative active rest; Calms the nervous system; Useful between poses
Muscles Worked (Raw): Spinal erectors; Gluteus maximus; Hamstrings

Description: Start on all fours with hands under shoulders and knees under hips. Brace your core and keep the back flat. Lift one foot up toward the ceiling. Reach back with the same side hand and grab the lifted foot. Gently pull the heel toward the glute to stretch the quad. Hold the stretch with steady breath. Release the foot and lower it back down. Switch sides and repeat.
Benefits: Strong quad stretch; Stretches the hip flexors; Useful warm-up move; No equipment needed; Builds hip mobility; Easy to do anywhere
Muscles Worked (Raw): Quadriceps; Hip flexors; Rectus femoris

Description: Sit on a chair or stand with one foot lifted off the floor. Use a wall for balance if standing. Lift your right foot a few inches off the floor. Slowly rotate your right ankle in a large clockwise circle. Move only your foot — keep your shin still. Make the circle as large as possible. Each rotation should take 3 to 4 seconds. Complete 10 clockwise circles. Reverse direction and complete 10 counter-clockwise circles. Switch to the left ankle and repeat. Move slowly with control.
Benefits: Warms up the ankle joint; Improves ankle proprioception; Helps prevent ankle injuries; Quick and accessible; No equipment needed; Useful for runners and lifters
Muscles Worked (Raw): Tibialis anterior; Peroneals (fibularis longus and brevis); Tibialis posterior; Foot intrinsic muscles; Ankle joint mobility

Description: Stand tall with feet hip-width apart. Extend both arms out to the sides at shoulder height, palms facing forward. Swing both arms forward and across your body, crossing them in front of your chest. Right arm crosses over left on the first rep. Open your arms back out wide to the sides, opening your chest.
